ib-private-tutor.programmesIntro: An IB private tutor is not one job. The Diploma Programme, the Middle Years Programme, the Primary Years Programme and the Diploma core are assessed on different principles, and a tutor who is excellent at one is not automatically useful for another. The notes below say what each one assesses and what a tutor is therefore being paid to do.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, with final grades built from written papers sat in the May session and from internally assessed work marked in school and moderated by the board. The two-year structure concentrates risk: a weak first year leaves no room in the second, because the second year is already carrying coursework deadlines, the core and examination preparation at the same time. Tutoring in DP1 is cheaper in effect than the same spend in DP2, for that reason alone.
programmes.countryNote: Across the Kingdom almost every IB school sits the May session, which makes the planning calendar unusually uniform compared with the Cambridge and Edexcel routes. What is not uniform is school term dates, which international schools set themselves, so entry deadlines and internal coursework dates come from your own school's examinations officer and Diploma Programme coordinator rather than from any tutoring company.

programmes.name: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS
programmes.description: The core carries bonus points through a matrix pairing the Theory of Knowledge grade with the Extended Essay grade, and CAS must be completed for the Diploma to be awarded at all. Families underestimate it consistently, because it has no weekly homework and no obvious teacher. A student can hold every subject grade and still miss an offer on the core. The Theory of Knowledge exhibition and essay reward a specific kind of argument about knowledge itself, which is a taught skill rather than a natural one.
programmes.countryNote: The core is the most common reason a Saudi family comes looking for support in the middle of DP1. A school with a thin bench often allocates Extended Essay supervision broadly, so a student can end up supervised by someone outside the subject. A tutor can give feedback on the student's own drafts and teach the assessment criteria; the school supervisor stays the formal supervisor throughout.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against published criteria with their own strands and descriptors, rather than against a single terminal paper, finishing with the Personal Project. Criterion marking rewards planning, process and reflection, and students arriving from examination-led systems usually read the descriptors as vague until somebody walks them through the wording. That walk-through is the teaching job, and it pays off again in Diploma Internal Assessment work two years later.
programmes.countryNote: Middle Years Programme support in the Kingdom is often bought for the wrong reason. Parents ask for content coaching when the marks are being lost on criteria the student has never had explained. One or two sessions reading the descriptors against the student's own last piece of work frequently does more than a term of content revision.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry built around transdisciplinary themes rather than separate subjects, with no external examinations and an Exhibition at the end. Because nothing is externally assessed, weaknesses stay invisible until much later. The two that matter are arithmetic fluency and sustained writing in English. A child who leaves Year 6 without secure fractions and place value meets the consequence in Year 9 algebra, and then again in Diploma mathematics.
programmes.countryNote: Primary tuition is the one stage where a short, defined block is almost always the right purchase in the Kingdom: a term of number work, or writing stamina before an entrance assessment at another school. Receiving schools set their own assessments, so ask the destination school what it tests before paying for preparation aimed at it.

ib-private-tutor.subjectsIntro: The grid below is written round two questions a parent is actually asking: where does this subject lose marks, and how hard is the specialist to find? Those two things together explain almost every quote you will be given for an IB private tutor in the Kingdom.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The algebra-first route and the hardest specialist to source at Higher Level, which is why it sits at the top of every rate band. Marks are lost in unjustified steps rather than wrong answers, because the scheme pays for reasoning. Paper 3 at Higher Level is investigative and cannot be prepared for by memorising methods, so a tutor who only drills past questions adds little in the final term.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The usual bottleneck is algebraic confidence rather than physics. A student who cannot rearrange and substitute under time pressure drops marks on questions they fully understand, which is why a good tutor often spends the first fortnight on mathematics. The internally assessed investigation needs a measurable, controllable variable fixed early; a weak research question caps the mark whatever the write-up does.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Higher Level questions routinely combine two topics in one item, so a student who revised topic by topic stalls on them. Definitions are marked strictly and loose wording costs marks that knowledge cannot recover. This is the subject where a tutor who has read mark schemes repeatedly is worth measurably more than one who simply knows chemistry to degree level.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Chosen by students expecting a lighter course, and the statistics strands take most of them by surprise, because interpretation rather than calculation is what is assessed. The graphic display calculator is assumed throughout, and calculator fluency is a real source of marks. Higher Level adds matrices, graph theory and harder modelling, with Paper 3 paying for explaining what a model fails to capture.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The widest gap in the Diploma between what a student knows and what the scheme pays for. Outline, explain, distinguish and evaluate each demand a different answer shape, and a student who writes everything they know scores less than one who answers the command term. Data-based questions need practice against real schemes, and the statistical reasoning is assessed more directly than most candidates expect.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram discipline decides the grade. Unlabelled axes, curves without shift arrows, and evaluation that restates the argument instead of weighing it account for most lost marks. Higher Level adds quantitative questions and an additional paper. Each internally assessed commentary must use a genuinely recent article and a different section of the syllabus from the others, which students discover too late surprisingly often.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Assessed by applying tools and theories to real organisations, with pre-released case material for one paper. The common failure is description where application was asked for: a student explains what a company does instead of running a framework over it. The internally assessed project rests on the student's own research, and a weak choice of organisation limits the mark before any writing starts.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Frequently taught well and tutored badly, because the subject rewards argument rather than narrative. Source questions have their own mark logic, Paper 2 wants comparative structure, and the Higher Level regional option adds breadth that cannot be crammed. The internally assessed historical investigation needs a question narrow enough to argue in the word limit, which is where most of the avoidable marks go.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: A popular option that schools often staff with a non-specialist, which shows up in how students use studies. The scheme pays for using a study as evidence in an argument, not for recounting it, and ethical and methodological evaluation has to be specific to the study named. Higher Level extensions and the internally assessed experimental study both reward precise method description over interesting ideas.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Guided textual analysis, a comparative essay, the individual oral and, at Higher Level, an additional essay. Students from systems that rewarded summary must be retaught to argue from the text. The individual oral needs a global issue and two extracts chosen early in the course; postponed to the final term, it reliably becomes the weakest line on the transcript.

ib-private-tutor.regionsTitle: Where families across the Kingdom are booking from
ib-private-tutor.regionsIntro: An IB private tutor working online serves every one of these places equally, but the practical constraints differ: the school run in Riyadh, the three-city school market in the Eastern Province, and real distance everywhere outside the big three. The notes say what each setting does to a weekly lesson slot.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: Roughly an hour across north to south in traffic, which means two families attending the same school can have completely different school runs. Most households settle on a slot between half past five and seven, built around the slowest realistic journey rather than the fastest one.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: A long coastal spine running from the historic centre north to Obhur, so two schools described as being in Jeddah can be forty minutes apart. Families towards Obhur generally need a later start than those nearer the centre, and the gap widens in term time.

regions.name: Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran
regions.note: One labour and school market behaving as a single city. Families routinely live in one of the three and attend school in another, so the commute is a cross-city one and the workable slot usually sits later than parents first expect.

regions.name: Al Ahsa
regions.note: About an hour and a half inland from the Eastern Province cluster, which puts a daily commute to a city international school out of reach for most households. This is the clearest case in the Kingdom where online delivery is the only route to a Higher Level specialist.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: Around 25km apart at altitude in 'Asir, sharing a catchment between them. The combined market is small, so a particular Diploma subject may have no local teacher at all, and families here are usually looking for a named specialist rather than general support.

regions.name: Madinah and Taif
regions.note: Established cities with limited international-curriculum provision relative to their size, so families often compare a longer school commute against an online arrangement for one or two subjects. Fixed term-long slots work better here than week-by-week booking.

regions.name: Jubail and Yanbu
regions.note: Industrial cities where shift patterns rather than school runs shape the evening. A parent on shift is frequently unavailable at the hour the lesson runs, which makes the written note after each session the main channel between tutor and household.

regions.name: Tabuk, NEOM and AlUla
regions.note: The north-west, where distance is the binding constraint and school communities are newer. Mid-course arrivals are common, so the first session is usually an inventory of what transferred from the previous course rather than a normal lesson.

schoolClusters.note: The widest Diploma provision in the Kingdom, with Primary Years, Middle Years and Diploma routes all represented. Breadth at city level still does not guarantee a particular Higher Level combination at a particular school, so the question to ask any school is which Higher Level subjects actually ran with the last cohort.

schoolClusters.city: Jeddah and the Red Sea coast
schoolClusters.note: A mixed market of IB World Schools, Cambridge schools and long-established international schools spread along the coastal spine, with The KAUST School serving the university campus community at Thuwal to the north. Students we support attend schools of these kinds across the city.

The International Schools Group runs several campuses across the Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran cluster, and the Diploma is offered at some of them rather than all. British and Cambridge routes are well represented alongside. Confirm the programme and the specific subject before treating a transfer between campuses as straightforward.

ib-private-tutor.schoolDisclaimer: Schools appear here only to describe where IB and international provision sits in the Kingdom; IB Gram has no affiliation with any of them and claims none.
ib-private-tutor.modesIntro: Three arrangements cover nearly every IB enquiry, and the right one follows from how far the student is from a series rather than from how worried the family is. Buying the wrong shape is the most common way money gets wasted on tuition in this market.

modes.title: Weekly subject teaching, through the year
modes.description: The arrangement that produces the most grade movement per riyal, because it has time to fix causes rather than symptoms. Sixty or ninety minutes a week with one specialist, written work set and marked between sessions, and a slot recorded in Arabia Standard Time. Ninety minutes is the honest minimum for a Higher Level science, where a full past-paper question and the feedback on it will not both fit into an hour.

sections.heading: What moves the rate for an IB private tutor, in order of weight
paragraphs: Families comparing two quotes usually assume the difference is quality, and it is more often supply. The band an IB private tutor sits in is set mainly by how many people can do the job at all. A Mathematics Applications and Interpretation Standard Level tutor exists in every market; a Mathematics Analysis and Approaches Higher Level specialist who has marked for the board does not, and the price reflects the length of the queue rather than the length of the lesson. That is why the same tutor can be good value at SAR 220 for one subject and poor value at SAR 180 for another.

After scarcity comes marking experience, which is a real and specific thing rather than a credential. A tutor who has marked scripts against a published scheme knows which phrasings earn credit, where candidates lose method marks, and what a six-mark answer has to contain. It is most valuable in the final year on extended-response and data-based components, and least valuable for a Year 9 student who still needs content taught. Pay for it when technique is the bottleneck.

Level comes third. Higher Level sits above Standard Level, and both sit above Middle Years Programme work, because the teaching pool narrows as the content deepens. Travel is fourth and is the largest hidden line in any in-home quote in a Saudi city, since the tutor has to be paid for the journey as well as the hour. Package length is fifth and is the only one a family controls directly: a term booked as a term usually costs less per hour than the same lessons bought one at a time.

Two things that do not reliably move the rate deserve naming. A tutor's own university, however impressive, predicts very little about whether they can teach a specification. And a provider's marketing claims predict nothing at all: any success percentage, star rating or headcount is self-reported, unverifiable, and absent from this page for that reason.

sections.heading: Verifying a tutor actually knows the specification, not just the subject
paragraphs: Credentials are easy to assert and hard to check, so the useful test is a conversation rather than a document. Five questions do most of the work and all of them are specific. Which board and which version of this syllabus have you taught, and for how many cohorts? What does each paper contribute at this level? Where do candidates most often lose marks in the component my child is struggling with? What will you do with an Internal Assessment draft, and what will you refuse to do? And what will I receive after each lesson?

The answers separate people quickly. A specialist answers the paper question without pausing, because they have planned a two-year course against it. They answer the lost-marks question with something diagnosable: a command-term failure, an uncertainty treatment, a missing justification step, a case study with no named figures. A capable generalist answers in terms of confidence, foundations and motivation. Neither is dishonest. Only one of them is what a Higher Level candidate two terms from the May session needs.

Be sceptical of three specific claims. Any percentage, rating or headcount is self-reported and cannot be verified by you or by us. Any suggestion of approval, accreditation or partnership with the IB, Cambridge, Pearson or a Saudi regulator should be treated as a reason to stop: IB Gram holds no such status and nor does any tutoring company we have seen advertising one. And a promise about a final grade is not a stretch target, it is a sign that the person making it is not thinking about mark schemes at all.

Finally, ask what happens when the match is wrong, because sometimes it will be. The answer should be plain: say so after one or two lessons, the tutor changes, no argument and no penalty. A student who does not get along with a tutor will not do the written work between sessions, and the written work is where most of the progress happens. Fit is not a soft consideration here; it is the mechanism by which the teaching has any effect at all.

sections.heading: Where IB marks are actually lost, component by component
paragraphs: Parents usually describe the problem as a subject: physics is going badly. Tutors who are worth their rate restate it as a component: the student is fine on Paper 1 multiple choice and loses a third of the available marks on extended-response questions in Paper 2. Those are different problems with different fixes, and the second description is the one that produces a plan. The first session with any good IB private tutor should end with the problem restated in that form.

The failures repeat across cohorts and across countries, which is what makes them worth naming. In the sciences, the two biggest are algebraic weakness masquerading as conceptual confusion, and answers that describe when the command term asked for an explanation. In mathematics, it is working that jumps steps and therefore forfeits method marks. In the essay subjects, it is narrative instead of argument, and evaluation that restates a point rather than weighing it against another. In the internally assessed work across every subject, it is a research question chosen without thinking about whether it can be answered within the limits.

Diagnosing which one applies takes a marked script and about forty minutes, which is why we would rather run a trial lesson on a real question than discuss a plan in the abstract. A student's own last paper, marked properly against the published scheme, tells a specialist more than any report. The annotation matters more than the score: a student who sees only a mark learns nothing about why it was that mark.

One consequence of thinking in components is that the right amount of tutoring is often less than a family expected. If the problem is command terms in Biology, that is a handful of sessions plus a marking habit, not a year of weekly content revision. We would rather say that and lose the hours than sell a year of lessons for a problem that takes six weeks.

sections.heading: The Diploma year, counted backwards from the session
paragraphs: Everything above gets its value from where in the year it is bought, so here is the year read in reverse. Almost every IB school in the Kingdom sits the May session, which makes the sequence unusually consistent across cities, even though individual school term dates are not. We do not publish an examination or results date on this page, because those come from the IB and your school's Diploma Programme coordinator, and a date quoted by a tutoring company is a date nobody should act on.

Counting backwards is more useful than counting forwards because it tells a family what must already be true, rather than what might be nice. Eight weeks out, content teaching should be finished and every hour should be going into timed papers on the weakest component. A term out, Internal Assessments should be submitted and predicted grades should already reflect real assessed work rather than optimism. Two terms out, coursework should be drafted and the Extended Essay should exist as something more than a title. A full year out, the Higher Level subject choices should already be the right ones, because changing them later is the single most expensive correction in the Diploma.

Work further back than that and the picture changes character. In the first term of DP1 the job is diagnostic: find what the previous course left missing, which is almost always algebraic fluency in the sciences and command-term discipline in the essay subjects. That is also the cheapest point at which to buy help, in the sense that an hour then changes more than an hour later does.

The last thing on the backwards list is the part that happens after results, and it is the one families forget. A retake decision, a resit entry through the school's examinations officer, and the Ministry of Education equivalency paperwork all sit in a short window with little slack. Put them on the calendar during the final term rather than discovering them afterwards.

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week, Arabia Standard Time, and the slot that survives a term
paragraphs: The Kingdom's school week runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. Most tutoring material aimed at Saudi families was adapted from British or Indian copy that quietly assumes a Monday-to-Friday week, which is why arrangements made in week one fall apart in week six. A tutor based in India or the United Kingdom is working their own Monday-to-Friday timetable: your Sunday evening is their weekend, and your Thursday evening is their working night.

Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3, and the Kingdom does not observe daylight saving. The offset itself is manageable; the drift is what causes trouble. A slot agreed with a tutor in a country that changes its clocks will move by an hour twice a year unless it is recorded in Saudi local time at the outset. Pin it to the Kingdom's clock in writing and a family never has to think about it again.

The shape of the slot matters more than the number of hours in it. One ninety-minute session with marked written work in between beats three scattered half-hours, because the smallest useful unit in a Higher Level science is long enough to sit a full past-paper question and then take it apart. Two subjects belong on two separate evenings; two hours back to back reliably produces one useful hour. Friday and Saturday sessions are available and sometimes better, particularly where a parent works shifts or a student stays away during the week.

Whatever the pattern, agree it for a term and change it deliberately. Slots renegotiated weekly become slots that get filled by another family, and a tutor who has been cancelled on three times stops holding the hour. Flag the weeks you already know will be thin when the plan is written. Ramadan is the obvious one: school days shorten, the productive hour moves later, and it drifts across the academic year because it moves roughly eleven days earlier each year against the Gregorian calendar. We do not publish a date for it or for Eid, because both are confirmed by moon sighting and differ by a day between countries.

sections.heading: Academic honesty: what an IB private tutor may do, and what none may ever do
paragraphs: This section exists because the market a Saudi family is searching in contains companies that will offer to supply assessed work, and a family that accepts loses more than the money. Assessed work must be the student's own. A school that suspects malpractice is obliged to investigate, and the consequences reach the Diploma itself rather than a single piece of coursework. A tutor who will not hold that line is not a cheaper option; they are the most expensive mistake available in this market.

What a tutor legitimately does with coursework is substantial and worth paying for. They translate the assessment criteria into the subject's own language and show what each strand actually asks for. They test whether a research question can be answered inside the word limit, and say plainly when it cannot. They interrogate a method before data exists, which is the single highest-value hour in the whole process. They give written feedback on a draft the student has written themselves. And they teach the student to read the criteria independently, which is the habit that carries into every other component.

What no tutor does is write, redraft or dictate any part of it. We will not draft an Extended Essay, and we never produce a Theory of Knowledge essay, a Personal Project or any coursework on a student's behalf. We do not supply model answers to be adapted, and we do not rewrite paragraphs for a student to paste in. The school supervisor remains the formal supervisor of an Extended Essay throughout, and the number of drafts a school will formally review is set by the school, not by a tutor and not by us.

The boundary also protects the student if anything is ever questioned. Dated drafts, the student's own notes, and a record of feedback given rather than text supplied are what demonstrate authorship. Ask any prospective tutor the question directly, in those words: what will you do with a draft, and what will you refuse to do? The answer separates a teacher from an essay mill faster than any qualification check, and a hesitation is itself an answer.

sections.heading: When the match is wrong, or the specialist is not free
paragraphs: A page about buying tuition should say what happens when it does not work, because that is the part a family cannot find out by asking a salesperson. Two things go wrong often enough to plan for: the tutor is not right for the student, and the right tutor does not exist in your slot.

The first is common and cheap to fix if it is raised early. A mismatch usually shows within two or three sessions, and it rarely looks like a dispute: the student stops doing the written work, or answers in single words, or the parent notices the notes have become encouraging rather than informative. Say so. The tutor changes, no penalty and no argument, and the next tutor gets the previous one's notes so the student does not start from nothing. A family that waits a term to raise it has paid for a term of lessons the student was not using.

The second is the harder conversation and the more honest one. Scarce specialists are scarce: there are evenings in the week when nobody who can teach Mathematics Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is free, and periods before the May session when the people who can are fully booked. When that happens we will say so rather than offer a capable generalist for a Higher Level course and let you discover the difference in March. Sometimes the answer is a different evening. Sometimes it is a shorter arrangement with a specialist who has one slot. Sometimes it is waiting a term, which is a legitimate answer when the alternative is paying a specialist rate for non-specialist teaching.

Stopping is also a legitimate outcome and we will name it when the work is done. A tutor who cannot describe in one sentence what is left to fix is a tutor who should be finishing. The termly review exists to force that conversation while it still has consequences, rather than letting weekly lessons continue by inertia.

sections.heading: Outcomes: what the transcript says, and who reads which part of it
paragraphs: The point of all of this is a transcript that opens the doors the student wants open, and different audiences read it very differently. A Saudi university reads the certificate once it has been through the Ministry of Education equivalency process, mu'adalah, alongside the Qiyas results. An overseas university reads total points plus named Higher Level grades, and often ignores everything else. An employer, years later, usually reads only that the Diploma was awarded. Knowing which audience matters most changes what a family should protect.

For the Saudi route, two things sit outside the school's control and need their own place in the calendar. Equivalency is the Ministry of Education decision that lets a university treat an international certificate as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate, and it applies to the IB Diploma, A Levels and an American high school diploma alike. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, is run by the Education and Training Evaluation Commission through its National Center for Assessment and tests verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content; it can be sat in Arabic or English. Tahsili, the Achievement Test, covers mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English, and its content follows the Saudi national curriculum, which is exactly why Diploma students find it less familiar than their own papers.

Universities publish their own criteria combining school grades with the Qiyas results, with weightings that differ by institution and programme and competitive science, engineering and medicine programmes leaning hardest on Tahsili. No threshold or weighting formula appears here, because the numbers differ by institution and intake and third-party sites contradict each other. Take them from the university's own published criteria, and check whether it sets a maximum age for the secondary certificate it accepts.

For the overseas route, the thing to protect is the named Higher Level grade rather than the total. An offer expressed as points plus two Higher Level grades fails on the subject condition even when the total clears. That is why Higher Level subject choice a full year before the session is the highest-stakes decision in the Diploma, and why an honest tutor will sometimes advise dropping a subject to Standard Level rather than selling lessons to defend it.

process.title: Send the board, the level, the component and a marked script
process.description: The subject name is the least informative part of an enquiry. We need the level, the component in trouble, and ideally a photograph of the last marked paper. A specialist reads more from that in thirty seconds than from a twenty-minute conversation, and it is what lets us say honestly whether the right person is free for your slot.

process.title: A free trial lesson with the tutor who would teach
process.description: Not a consultation with a coordinator. Your child works with the actual specialist on a real question from their current topic, and you receive a short written note afterwards naming what the tutor found and what they would attack first. If the fit is wrong, say so and the tutor changes before anything is paid.

process.title: A quote with the drivers named
process.description: You are told the figure before any lesson is booked, along with what put it where it is: the subject, the level, the frequency, and whether marking experience is part of it. No registration fee, no assessment fee, and nothing charged before teaching happens. Compare it against the market bands set out on this page.

process.title: A plan written backwards from the session
process.description: The plan starts at the series and works back, naming what has to be true at each stage, in what order, and roughly how long each stage takes. Plans written in components can be checked against results. Plans written as promises of improvement cannot, which is why ours name papers and criteria instead.

process.title: Weekly teaching, marked work, and short notes
process.description: A fixed slot in Arabia Standard Time, written work set and marked against the real scheme before the next session, and a few factual lines to you afterwards: what was covered, what the student can now do, what is still weak. No scores, no projections, no encouragement dressed up as reporting.

process.title: A termly decision, including stopping
process.description: Each term we compare the plan's named targets against what actually moved, and the review ends in a decision: continue, change tutor, change frequency, or stop. Stopping when the work is finished is the outcome that costs a family least and the one most providers never raise.

whyPoints.title: The money is on the page
whyPoints.description: Market bands in SAR, attributed to the kind of source that advertises them, with the drivers that move a quote listed in order of weight. A family that can see the bands can judge any quote, including ours, which is the point of publishing them rather than hiding them behind a form.

whyPoints.title: One board, one subject, one level per tutor
whyPoints.description: Specialists work to a single specification rather than covering several approximately. That is what makes the paper-weighting question answerable on the spot, and it is the difference a Higher Level candidate feels in the final two terms of the Diploma.

whyPoints.title: Plans counted backwards from the session
whyPoints.description: Every plan starts at the series and works back to this week, naming what has to be true at each stage. It makes the plan checkable, and it stops a family buying late hours at a specialist rate for a problem that early hours would have fixed more cheaply.

whyPoints.title: A written line on academic honesty
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach criteria, interrogate methods and give feedback on the student's own drafts. They do not write, redraft or dictate assessed work, and the school supervisor stays the formal supervisor. This is stated because parts of this market do the opposite without saying so.

whyPoints.title: Honest answers about availability
whyPoints.description: When no specialist is free for your evening, we say that instead of offering a generalist for a Higher Level course. Sometimes the right answer is a different slot, a shorter arrangement, or waiting a term, and we would rather give it than take a booking that will disappoint you later.

whyPoints.title: Nothing claimed that cannot be checked
whyPoints.description: No success percentages, no star ratings, no tutor headcounts, no grade promises, and no claim of approval or partnership with any board or regulator. Everything stated here is either an attributed market rate or a verifiable fact about the system Saudi families work inside.

faqs.question: Which topics in Mathematics Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level most often need outside teaching?
faqs.answer: Proof, complex numbers and the harder calculus sit at the top of the list, together with the investigative demands of Paper 3. Proof fails because students have never been taught what counts as a complete argument rather than a convincing one. Complex numbers fail because the algebra underneath is shaky. Calculus fails selectively: differentiation is usually secure and integration techniques are not. Paper 3 is different again, since it rewards exploring an unfamiliar situation rather than recognising a known method, and it is the component least improved by past-paper drilling alone.

faqs.question: Why do strong Chemistry Higher Level students still lose marks on multi-topic questions?
faqs.answer: Because revision is organised by topic and the examination is not. A Higher Level item will routinely combine energetics with equilibrium, or organic structure with spectroscopy, and a student who has rehearsed each topic separately has never practised the join. The fix is specific: work through released questions sorted by how many topics they span rather than by chapter, and rehearse identifying which two areas a question is testing before attempting any calculation. Precision in definitions matters here too, since loose wording in an explanation loses marks that correct chemistry cannot recover.

faqs.question: Where does a Biology Higher Level candidate lose most marks, and is the cause content or command terms?
faqs.answer: Command terms, in most cases, which is why extra content revision so often fails to move the grade. Outline, explain, distinguish and evaluate each require a different answer shape, and a student who writes everything they know about a topic scores below one who answers the term precisely in half the words. The second largest loss is in data-based questions, where candidates describe a trend rather than interpret it against the biology. Both are trainable in a handful of sessions with real mark schemes, which makes Biology one of the cheaper subjects to improve.

faqs.question: What makes Physics Higher Level harder for a student who is comfortable in Standard Level mathematics?
faqs.answer: The physics assumes algebraic fluency that Standard Level mathematics does not demand at speed. Rearranging a relationship with three variables, substituting consistently and tracking units is routine in a Higher Level physics paper and occasional in a Standard Level mathematics one. Under examination pressure the gap widens, and the student loses marks on questions whose physics they understand completely. The practical response is to treat the algebra as its own target for two or three sessions, away from physics content, and then return to past papers once the manipulation is automatic.

faqs.question: Which Economics component do IB students most often underestimate?
faqs.answer: The internally assessed commentaries, because they look like short pieces of writing and are in fact tightly constrained. Each one must draw on a genuinely recent news article, apply a different section of the syllabus from the others, and work inside a word limit that punishes background description. Students lose marks by summarising the article instead of analysing it with a diagram and by reusing the same syllabus section twice. Choosing the articles early, with the syllabus sections mapped out in advance, prevents almost all of that and takes one planning session.

faqs.question: How should a student prepare for the individual oral in English A: Language and Literature?
faqs.answer: By choosing the global issue and the two extracts early in the course rather than in the final term, and then rehearsing the argument rather than the wording. The component assesses how the student connects a global issue to both texts through specific features of each extract, so a well-chosen pair of extracts does half the work. Students who leave the choice late end up with extracts that barely support the issue they picked, and no amount of rehearsal fixes that. Practice should be recorded and marked against the criteria, not simply timed.

faqs.question: What does the Theory of Knowledge exhibition ask for that an essay does not?
faqs.answer: It asks the student to connect abstract knowledge questions to specific real objects, which is a different skill from constructing a written argument. Students who write well often perform poorly here, because they treat the objects as illustrations of a point rather than as the thing being analysed. Each object has to be particular, personally connected and genuinely linked to the prompt. A tutor can teach that structure and question the reasoning in a student's own commentary; the selections and the writing remain the student's work throughout.

faqs.question: What qualification actually matters in an IB private tutor, and what matters less than families assume?
faqs.answer: What matters is documented experience teaching the specific board, subject and level, across enough cohorts to have seen moderation feedback and changing mark schemes. What matters less is the prestige of a tutor's own university, which predicts subject knowledge rather than the ability to teach a specification. A doctorate in physics does not imply knowing what a Higher Level examiner credits in a six-mark question. Ask about cohorts taught and about paper structure, and treat the degree as background rather than as the qualification itself.

faqs.question: What does examiner experience mean in practice, and how can a Saudi family verify the claim?
faqs.answer: It means the tutor has marked candidate scripts against a published scheme for a board, which builds a precise sense of what earns credit and where method marks disappear. Verification is partly a matter of specificity: ask which board, which subject, which component, and in which capacity. A genuine claim comes with those details immediately. A vague claim of being an examiner, without subject or component, should be treated as unverified. The value is also situational, at its highest in the final year on extended-response work and low for a student who still needs content taught.

faqs.question: Should a Higher Level student and a Standard Level sibling share the same tutor?
faqs.answer: Only if that tutor genuinely teaches both levels regularly, and never in the same session. The Higher Level extension changes how shared content is examined, not just how much there is, so a tutor whose experience is mostly Standard Level will teach the common material competently and the extension approximately. Where one tutor does cover both, separate sessions still matter: the two students have different immediate problems, and a shared hour becomes half an hour each plus the cost of switching between two courses.

faqs.question: Is a current classroom teacher a better choice than a full-time private tutor?
faqs.answer: Neither is reliably better, and the useful distinction is elsewhere. A current teacher brings familiarity with how schools sequence a course and with moderation feedback, but often limited availability and tired evenings. A full-time tutor brings more hours of one-to-one diagnosis and usually more past-paper range, but may be further from day-to-day classroom practice. The question that actually discriminates is the same for both: how many cohorts in this exact subject and level, and where do candidates lose marks in this component?

faqs.question: How do I check that a tutor knows the current syllabus rather than the one they studied?
faqs.answer: Ask them what changed in the most recent revision of the specification and how it altered their teaching. A tutor working from the current syllabus answers that concretely, naming a topic that moved, an assessment change or a shift in emphasis. Somebody teaching from memory of their own course will answer generally. A second useful question is which released papers they use and how recent those are: a tutor whose practice material is all from older sittings is teaching an examination that has since changed shape.

faqs.question: What happens if an IB private tutor becomes unavailable part-way through DP2?
faqs.answer: The handover matters more than the speed of replacement. A new tutor should receive the written plan, the record of what has been covered, the marked work and a note of the student's specific weaknesses, so the student is not re-diagnosed from scratch in the most time-pressured year of the course. Ask any provider in advance what they hold on file and what transfers. If the answer is that lessons are informal and nothing is recorded, a mid-course change will cost the student several weeks it does not have.

faqs.question: How many students should one IB tutor be carrying, and why does the number matter?
faqs.answer: There is no correct figure, but the question reveals something useful. A tutor carrying a very large number cannot be marking written work between sessions, and marked work is where much of the progress happens. A tutor carrying very few may be new to the specification. What you are really testing is whether written work gets marked before the next lesson and whether the tutor remembers the student's specific errors without being reminded. Ask about marking turnaround rather than headcount; it is the same question with a checkable answer.

faqs.question: What may a tutor do with an Internal Assessment draft, and what must they refuse outright?
faqs.answer: They may explain the assessment criteria in the subject's own language, test whether the research question can be answered inside the limits, interrogate the method before any data exists, and give written feedback on a draft the student has written. They must refuse to write, redraft, restructure or dictate any part of the text, to supply data or results, and to provide model answers for adaptation. The distinction is simple in practice: feedback points at the student's work, while a rewrite replaces it. Ask the question in those words before booking.

faqs.question: How many Extended Essay drafts can a tutor give feedback on?
faqs.answer: The limit on formal review belongs to the school, not to a tutor. Schools set how many drafts the assigned supervisor will comment on, and that supervisor remains formally responsible for the essay throughout. A tutor's feedback sits alongside that arrangement, and the sensible practice is to keep it to a small number of substantive rounds on work the student has written, with dated records of what was said. Continuous line-by-line commentary across many versions starts to look like co-authorship even where no text has been supplied, which is a risk worth avoiding.

faqs.question: What does legitimate tutor feedback on a mathematics exploration actually look like?
faqs.answer: It looks like questions rather than corrections. A tutor asks whether the chosen context genuinely needs the mathematics the student has reached for, whether the modelling can be taken further than a textbook treatment, and where the personal engagement criterion is currently unevidenced. They point at a paragraph that asserts rather than derives, and ask the student to justify it. What they do not do is supply the derivation, rewrite the commentary or choose the topic outright. The useful test is whether the student can explain, unprompted, why each step is there. If they cannot, the work has drifted away from them.

faqs.question: What happens if a school suspects malpractice on work a tutor was involved with?
faqs.answer: The school is obliged to investigate, and investigations examine the work's development as much as the finished text: drafts, notes, data files and the student's ability to discuss their own reasoning. Consequences can reach the award of the Diploma rather than one component, which is why the margin for carelessness is small. The protection is ordinary record keeping. Keep dated drafts, keep the student's own notes, and keep feedback that points at work rather than supplying text. A tutor who objects to that record being kept is telling you something.

ib-private-tutor.closingHeading: Send the component, and we will send the plan and the price
ib-private-tutor.closingBody: The quickest route to a useful answer is the board, the level, the component losing marks, and how far your child is from the session. From that a specialist can say what the first month would target, what has to be true at each stage between now and the series, and what it costs, before anything is booked. Lessons are one-to-one and online, over live video, recorded in Arabia Standard Time so the slot holds through the term. Ask for the trial lesson with the subject specialist rather than a call with a coordinator, and put the paper-structure question to them first. If nobody suitable is free for your evening, we will say so.

ib-pyp-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach inside the Primary Years Programme rather than around it. At this stage the useful credential is a primary teaching qualification and real experience of transdisciplinary units of inquiry, not a subject degree and not examiner work. The programme sets no external examinations, so there is nothing for anyone to have marked.

intro.heading: The money first, because the primary rate is where this market gives itself away
paragraphs: Advertised rates are the easiest thing to check in Saudi tutoring and the most revealing. A tutor-marketplace guide for Riyadh puts general private tuition for primary-age children at around SAR 50 an hour, and senior-school examination subjects at SAR 200 and above. Tutoring companies listing IB subject support in Riyadh advertise from about SAR 180. A general online tutoring platform advertises from roughly SAR 55 for a non-specialist hour. International providers quoting in dollars sit near $60. Every one of those is a figure a vendor published to attract enquiries. None is a market average, and none is what IB Gram charges.

Now read the primary number again. SAR 50 an hour is a homework-supervision price. It buys an adult who can keep a nine-year-old at the table, check spellings, hear reading aloud and sign the diary. That is a real service and some families need nothing more. What it does not buy is a teacher who can look at a unit of inquiry on water scarcity and work out that the child's difficulty is not the topic but place value, or who can separate a decoding problem from a vocabulary problem in a child who sounds fluent. The Primary Years Programme asks a tutor to teach through a transdisciplinary unit rather than through a textbook chapter, and the number of people in the Kingdom who have actually planned and taught one is small.

So the honest answer to what an IB PYP home tutor costs is that the primary band and the specialist band have very little to do with each other. A trained primary teacher who has run units of inquiry, taught early reading systematically and worked with children learning in a second language is priced by scarcity, not by the age of the student. Parents who arrive expecting primary to be cheap because the child is young have the causation backwards: the pool is smaller at this age, not larger, because almost every tutor who can charge an examination-year rate does so.

Two things pull the weekly figure back down. A primary session is usually 30 to 45 minutes rather than an hour, because that is the honest limit of a seven-year-old's useful attention on screen after a full school day. And a primary problem is often finite. A child who cannot subitise, or who has never been taught a written method for subtraction with exchange, needs a sequence of lessons with an end to it, not an open-ended term. Both of those matter more to what a family actually spends than the headline rate does.

The rest of this page is organised the way the decision is made. Rates and bands first. Then who the tutor has to be when there is no examination to have marked, and the four claims most worth testing. Then the trial lesson, the alternatives to one-to-one, what a parent sees each week, and how to change tutor without unsettling a child. Delivery is the one fixed point: every lesson is one-to-one over live video, on Arabia Standard Time. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Saudi address, and home visits are a service we offer only in India.

ib-pyp-home-tutor.programmesIntro: A primary child in the Kingdom is usually inside one of four structures, and the one they are in decides what support should look like. The Primary Years Programme is the page's subject; the others matter because they are what the child is heading into, or the route the family may switch to when a school place changes.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: An inquiry framework rather than a syllabus. Learning is organised into transdisciplinary units built on a central idea, with lines of inquiry running through subject content instead of alongside it. Children are assessed continuously against learning outcomes and a portfolio, and the final year culminates in the exhibition, an extended piece of collaborative inquiry the student presents. There is no external examination and no published grade, which is precisely why parents find progress hard to read.
programmes.countryNote: In the Kingdom the programme appears in a small set of international schools, concentrated in Riyadh, Jeddah and the Eastern Province cluster. Several schools run the Primary Years Programme without running the Diploma above it, so a family's primary choice does not settle the secondary one. Outside the three main population centres the nearest inquiry primary school may be in another city, which is the honest reason online support exists at this age.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups taught with explicit assessment criteria, each scored out of eight against four strands. The shift out of the Primary Years Programme is sharper than most parents expect: the same inquiry habits remain, but marks now attach to named criteria, deadlines harden, and a student is expected to write at length in a specified form. The Personal Project in the final year carries the same independence burden the exhibition introduced.
programmes.countryNote: Some Saudi schools run the Middle Years Programme and then move students to Cambridge or Pearson qualifications at sixteen rather than to the Diploma. A family leaving a Primary Years Programme school in Year 6 should ask the receiving school which route it actually runs, because the answer changes which habits are worth building in the last primary year.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher or Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Papers are externally examined in the May session for almost every Saudi school, with internally assessed components moderated by the board. It is mentioned here only because it sets the market price a primary family is quoted against, and because the writing and research demands a Year 6 exhibition starts to build end here.
programmes.countryNote: The Diploma is where Saudi tutoring money concentrates, which is the structural reason a primary specialist is harder to book than a Higher Level one. A tutor who can teach Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level has no financial reason to take a Year 3 reading case, so the families who find good primary teaching are usually the ones who went looking for a primary teacher rather than a cheaper tutor.

programmes.name: Cambridge Primary and Lower Secondary
programmes.description: A sequenced curriculum framework with published learning objectives per stage and optional checkpoint testing. Content is organised by subject rather than by central idea, so progress is easier for a parent to read and harder for a child to see as connected. Many British-curriculum schools in the Kingdom use it, and it is the most common destination when a family moves off the inquiry route mid-primary.
programmes.countryNote: Mid-primary moves between an inquiry school and a Cambridge school happen often in Saudi Arabia, usually because of a posting, a compound allocation or a waiting list clearing. The transfer is rarely a disaster, but it exposes exactly one thing: whether the child has secure written methods and secure sentence-level writing underneath the inquiry. That is the gap primary tutoring in this market most often fixes.

ib-pyp-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: The Primary Years Programme does not timetable subjects the way a secondary school does, so support is scoped by strand rather than by subject name. These are the strands a Saudi primary family most often asks for, with the year groups where the work usually sits.

subjects.name: Early reading and phonics
subjects.description: Systematic decoding, blending and the irregular high-frequency words English refuses to make phonetic. Children who were taught to read by whole-word recognition in one country and by phonics in the next often arrive with gaps that look like carelessness. The assessment is diagnostic: which graphemes are secure, which are guessed.

subjects.name: Reading comprehension and inference
subjects.description: The move from retrieving a stated fact to inferring an unstated one is where fluent readers stall. A child can read every word of a passage aloud and still not answer why a character behaved as they did. Work here is on question type, evidence selection and the habit of returning to the text.

subjects.name: Writing and composition
subjects.description: Sentence-level control first, then paragraph structure, then form. Inquiry units ask children to write explanations, reports and reflections long before anyone has taught them how those forms differ. Much primary writing support is simply teaching the shape of a paragraph and the difference between describing and explaining.

subjects.name: Mathematics: number and place value
subjects.description: Counting, subitising, place value, and written methods for the four operations including exchange. This is the single most common hidden cause of later difficulty: a child who does not hold place value securely can still pass a mental maths test and will then fail every long-division question for three years.

subjects.name: Mathematics: fractions, measurement and data
subjects.description: Equivalence, comparison and operations with fractions, plus units of measure, perimeter, area and the reading of graphs that inquiry units lean on heavily. Children who learnt fractions as a picture rather than as a number struggle the moment two denominators differ, and the fix is a sequence rather than a worksheet.

subjects.name: Science within units of inquiry
subjects.description: Observation, fair testing, recording and explanation, taught inside whatever central idea the school's unit is built on. The tutoring job is rarely the science content. It is usually teaching a child to record what they did in a form somebody else could repeat, which is the scientific skill the programme actually assesses.

subjects.name: Social studies and research skills
subjects.description: Finding sources a ten-year-old can read, deciding what a question is really asking, and noting where information came from. Research skills are assumed by inquiry units and taught systematically in very few primary classrooms, so this is frequently the fastest improvement available to a Year 5 or Year 6 student.

subjects.name: English as an additional language
subjects.description: Academic vocabulary, the language of instruction, and the grammar a child needs to explain rather than name. Many primary children in Saudi international schools are learning in their second or third language, and a subject gap and a language gap look identical on a piece of work until someone separates them.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Script, sound and the gap between classroom Arabic and the Arabic a child hears outside. Children who join a Saudi school mid-primary from a country with no Arabic provision land in a class that began two or three years earlier, and catching up needs a sequence rather than extra homework.

subjects.name: Handwriting, presentation and work habits
subjects.description: Letter formation, spacing, and the physical stamina to write for ten minutes without the hand failing. This looks trivial and is not: a child whose handwriting costs them effort writes shorter answers, and shorter answers are read as weaker understanding by every teacher who marks them.

subjects.name: The Year 6 exhibition
subjects.description: An extended collaborative inquiry with a presentation at the end. A tutor's role is teaching research method, questioning, structure and rehearsal, and giving feedback on what the student has produced. A tutor who offers to take the research or the writing off the child's hands is offering something no honest teacher would.

ib-pyp-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a family lives in the Kingdom changes the price they are quoted and the pool they are quoting from, more at primary level than at any other stage. These are the clusters Saudi primary enquiries come from, and what the local market actually looks like in each.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: The deepest pool in the Kingdom and the only city where in-home primary tuition is routinely available at the advertised SAR 50 band. The city is roughly an hour across in traffic, so an in-home tutor's reach is a handful of districts, and a family in Al Olaya and a family in Al Malqa are not choosing from the same list.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: A long coastal spine from the historic centre north to Obhur, which means travel time rather than distance decides who will take a primary booking. Several international schools sit at the northern end while much of the residential market sits south of them, and an in-home tutor loses an hour to that journey each way.

regions.name: The Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran cluster
regions.note: One labour and school market behaving as three cities. Families live in one and attend school in another, which makes school-gate recommendations unusually useful here and in-home scheduling unusually messy. Compound residence adds a gate-pass problem to every in-home arrangement that online lessons simply do not have.

regions.name: Jubail and Yanbu
regions.note: Industrial cities with international school provision tied to the plants and the companies around them. Primary cohorts are small, specialist primary teachers scarcer still, and a family looking for systematic early-reading teaching is usually looking outside the city whether they planned to or not.

regions.name: Thuwal and the KAUST community
regions.note: A campus community north of Jeddah where The KAUST School serves residents. The academic household density is high and parental expectations are specific, which tends to produce enquiries about enrichment and depth rather than remediation. Distance from the Jeddah tutoring market is the practical constraint.

regions.name: Al Ahsa
regions.note: Roughly an hour and a half inland from the Eastern Province cluster, which is far enough to put a weekday in-home primary slot out of reach for most tutors based in Al Khobar. Families here are among the most consistent users of online primary support in the Kingdom, for straightforward geographic reasons.

regions.name: Makkah and Madinah
regions.note: Large cities with limited inquiry-primary provision, and calendars that bend around Hajj and Umrah seasons in ways a visiting tutor cannot plan around. A fixed online slot survives those weeks better than an arrangement that depends on somebody crossing the city at a particular hour.

regions.name: Tabuk, NEOM and AlUla
regions.note: The north-west, where project-driven relocation brings primary-age children into places with thin or new school provision. Mid-year arrivals are common and the usual presenting problem is a child a year out of step with a different curriculum, which is a diagnosis-and-sequence job rather than a general tutoring one.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: Two 'Asir cities about 25km apart at high altitude, sharing a catchment and a shallow tutoring market. Primary-specialist availability locally is close to nil, so families either accept a generalist or look online. Saying so plainly is more useful to a parent here than pretending a local option exists.

ib-pyp-home-tutor.regionsTitle: Where you are, and what it does to the primary market you are buying in

schoolClusters.note: The capital holds the widest range of primary provision in the Kingdom, including schools running the Primary Years Programme and schools running Cambridge Primary alongside a national stream. Students we support attend schools including these. A family comparing them should ask each school directly which primary framework it runs and what happens at the end of Year 6.

Jeddah's international schools run a mix of IB, Cambridge and national-system curricula, with primary sections of very different sizes. The KAUST School at Thuwal serves the university campus community to the north. Students we support attend schools across this group, and their primary routes diverge well before Year 6.

The International Schools Group operates several Eastern Province campuses, and not every campus runs every programme. British and Cambridge-curriculum schools sit alongside them in the same cluster. Students we support attend schools including these, and many commute between the three cities daily.

ib-pyp-home-tutor.modesIntro: Four shapes cover almost every primary booking. The choice is driven by the child's stamina and the nature of the gap rather than by the family's budget, although the budget follows from it. All four run as one-to-one lessons over live video.

modes.title: One short weekly session
modes.description: Thirty to forty-five minutes, same slot each week, aimed at one named strand. This is the right shape when the gap is specific and the child is otherwise coping: a written method that was never taught, a comprehension question type that keeps costing marks, a fraction concept that never landed. It is also the cheapest honest arrangement, because the session length is short and the end point is visible from the start.
bullets: Best for one diagnosed gap rather than general catch-up
Charged on the time used, so a 30-minute lesson is not an hour

modes.title: Two short sessions a week
modes.description: The shape early reading actually needs. Decoding is built by frequency, not by duration, and twenty-five minutes twice a week beats fifty minutes once for any child under about nine. The same logic applies to times tables, spelling patterns and anything else that depends on recall rather than reasoning. Parents are given a two-minute daily task between sessions, because that is where most of the gain comes from.

Short daily parent task between lessons, written out after each session
Fits either side of the Sunday-to-Thursday school run without a late night

modes.title: A holiday block
modes.description: A concentrated run of sessions across a school break, used when a child has a specific thing to build before a term starts or has just moved country and needs the gap measured before September. Blocks suit mid-primary transfers particularly well: a diagnostic in the first session, a sequence across the break, and a short written handover the family can give the new class teacher.

Useful before a move between an inquiry school and a Cambridge one

modes.title: Reading with a parent in the room
modes.description: A deliberately different arrangement for the youngest children, where part of the point is teaching the adult. The tutor runs the session with the child, then spends the last few minutes showing the parent exactly how to hear reading, what to correct and what to leave alone. Families who want the support to end rather than continue indefinitely usually get there fastest this way.

sections.heading: What a primary hour is advertised at in the Kingdom, and what each band buys
paragraphs: Start with the published numbers, because they are checkable and because the spread between them is the most informative fact in this market. The bands below come from vendor marketing: tutor-marketplace guides, tutoring-company listings and platform pages. They are advertised rates, which means they are the lowest number each vendor was willing to print to attract an enquiry. Treating any of them as a market average would be wrong, and none of them is IB Gram's price.

The pattern across the table is the thing to notice. The primary band and the examination-year band differ by a factor of four for the same sixty minutes of an adult's time. That difference is not about the difficulty of the content, since nothing in Year 4 maths is harder than Higher Level calculus. It is about who the market pays. Tutors with a credential that works in examination years take examination-year work, so the people left advertising at the primary rate are, on average, people without that credential.

This is why a family can pay the advertised primary rate for a year and see very little change. The hour was bought honestly and delivered honestly; it simply was not a teaching hour. Supervision keeps a child working, and a child who works more usually improves slightly. Teaching changes what the child can do. The two are priced differently because they are different things, and the only reliable way to tell which you are buying is to ask what the tutor will have diagnosed by the end of the first session.

A secondary point about currency. International providers quoting in dollars publish a number near $60 an hour, which arrives on a Saudi card with an exchange spread and sometimes a cross-border fee on top. Comparing that honestly with a riyal rate means comparing what leaves the account, not what appears on the website. Families who book in a foreign currency should ask what the charge looks like on the statement before the second lesson, not after the tenth.

sections.heading: Who the tutor has to be when there is no examination to have marked
paragraphs: Every other page in this market leans on examiner experience as the proof of quality, and at primary level that proof does not exist. The Primary Years Programme sets no external examinations. Nobody has marked a Year 3 paper for a board, because there is no board paper to mark. A tutor who offers marking experience as their headline credential for a primary child is either talking about a different stage of their career or has not noticed the question they were asked.

What replaces it is narrower and easier to check. The first thing is a primary teaching qualification, which always names an age phase on the certificate: early years, lower primary, primary, or a span. A secondary-trained teacher can be excellent with an eleven-year-old and still have never been taught how a child learns to decode. The second is experience inside the programme itself, which means having planned and taught transdisciplinary units, not having read the framework. Those two together account for most of the difference a family can feel.

The third thing is specific training in whatever the child's actual problem is. Systematic phonics is a taught method with named programmes behind it, and a tutor either has that training or is guessing from experience. The same applies to teaching children who are learning in an additional language, which is the majority of primary students in Saudi international schools. Separating a language gap from a subject gap is a skill, and a tutor without it will spend a term teaching maths to a child whose problem was the word 'altogether'.

The table below is written to be used as a checklist in a message. Every row has a question a family can send before paying for anything, and every question has an answer a competent primary teacher gives without hesitating. Vague answers at this stage are not shyness; they are the information you were asking for.

sections.heading: Four claims a primary tutor makes, and the question that tests each one
paragraphs: Credentials are the floor. Above the floor, a family is buying judgement, and judgement is only visible in answers to specific questions. The useful questions are not about philosophy. A tutor asked what they believe about learning will give a pleasant answer that cannot be wrong. A tutor asked how they check whether a child's place-value understanding is secure either has a method or does not, and the difference is audible in the first sentence.

The questions in the table are deliberately small. Each one is answerable in two or three sentences by someone who has done the work, and each one is unanswerable by someone who has not. Send them before the trial lesson, not during it. A tutor who writes back with a real method has told you more than an hour of pleasant conversation will.

Pay particular attention to how a tutor answers about the Year 6 exhibition, because that is where the honesty line sits at primary level. The exhibition is the student's own extended inquiry. A tutor may teach research method, help a child sharpen a question, show them how to structure a presentation, rehearse it with them and give feedback on what the child has produced. A tutor may not write it, research it on the child's behalf or produce the final piece. If a tutor's answer to 'how would you help with the exhibition' is an offer to take work off the child, the answer has disqualified them.

One more claim deserves scepticism: a results claim at primary level. There is no external grade in this programme, so any number offered as proof of outcomes has been constructed by the person quoting it. A statistic without a sample, a date and a method behind it is marketing. The honest version of that claim is a description of what will be measurable after six weeks, in terms a parent can check themselves.

sections.heading: Why a primary specialist is scarcer and dearer in the Kingdom than a Diploma one
paragraphs: The shape of the Saudi tutoring market is set by where families feel pressure, and families feel pressure in examination years. That pressure funds a deep bench of Higher Level subject tutors and leaves primary almost unserved by comparison. Any teacher who can hold a Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches Higher Level case will take that work at the advertised senior band rather than take a Year 4 number case at the advertised primary band. The result is that the easiest tutor to find in Riyadh is a Diploma specialist and one of the hardest is a trained primary teacher with inquiry experience.

Geography compounds it. In-home primary tuition only works where a tutor can reach a child, stay for a short session and get home, which in practice means a few districts of Riyadh, a stretch of Jeddah, and the Dammam to Dhahran corridor. A thirty-minute lesson does not justify a forty-minute drive at either end for anyone, which is why in-home primary slots in this market are either expensive, badly timed, or quietly stretched to an hour the child cannot use.

Outside those corridors the local pool is not thin but absent. In Al Ahsa, in 'Asir, in Tabuk and across the north-west, a family looking for a primary teacher trained in systematic phonics is looking for someone who may not live within two hours. Pretending otherwise is the standard move in this SERP and it wastes a parent's time. The honest statement is that distance is the binding constraint at primary level outside three clusters, and that online delivery is what removes it.

That is also the argument for online on its merits rather than as a compromise. A family in Khamis Mushait choosing from everyone who can teach early reading, rather than from whoever is within a twenty-minute drive, is choosing from a different order of pool. The lessons are one-to-one over live video, pinned to Arabia Standard Time so the slot does not drift when another country changes its clocks. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Saudi address; home visits are a service we offer only in India.

sections.heading: The trial lesson, run as an interview with a child in the room
paragraphs: A trial lesson at primary level is doing two jobs at once, and most families only notice the first. The obvious job is seeing whether the child will work with this adult. The less obvious one is finding out whether the adult can diagnose. Those are different tests and the second is the one that predicts whether the next term is worth paying for.

Watch for sequence. A primary teacher who knows what they are doing does not open with the topic the parent named. They open a layer below it, because the topic the parent named is usually a symptom. A child presented as weak at fractions is checked on place value and division first. A child presented as a reluctant writer is asked to read something aloud, because reluctance to write is very often an undisclosed reading problem. If the trial lesson goes straight to the stated topic and stays there, the tutor is working from the parent's diagnosis rather than their own.

Watch the talking ratio too. In a good primary session the child does most of the talking and most of the doing, and the adult asks short questions and waits. A tutor who explains fluently for twenty minutes is performing competence rather than teaching. With a seven-year-old on a screen, a long explanation is simply lost, and a parent who can hear the lesson from the next room can judge this without understanding any of the content.

Then ask for the diagnosis in writing. Not a report, just a few lines: what the tutor found, what they think the cause is, what the first six sessions will do about it and what will be visibly different at the end. A tutor who can write that paragraph has a plan. A tutor who sends a warm note about how lovely your child is has not said anything you can hold them to. The trial lesson itself is free, and nothing about it obliges a family to continue.

sections.heading: One-to-one against the other three things families buy at this age
paragraphs: One-to-one teaching is not automatically the right purchase for a primary child, and a page that pretends otherwise is selling rather than advising. There are four things a Saudi family routinely buys for a struggling primary student, they cost very different amounts, and each one reaches a different kind of problem. Picking wrongly is the most common waste of money at this stage, more common than paying too much per hour.

The decisive question is what kind of gap the child has. A gap in fluency, where the child understands the method but is slow and unreliable with recall, responds well to repetition and therefore to an app or a group. A gap in understanding, where the child has never held the concept, does not respond to repetition at all: more practice on a method they do not understand simply builds a faster wrong answer. That gap needs teaching, in sequence, by somebody watching the child's face. And a gap in habit or organisation often needs supervision rather than either.

There is also the school's own provision, which families underuse. International schools in the Kingdom run intervention groups, and the school has assessment data a private tutor starts without. Asking the class teacher what they have already identified, and what the school is doing about it, is free and frequently changes the brief. It can also reveal the honest limit: a school that has not noticed a gap cannot be intervening on it, and a school that cannot staff a strand will say so if asked directly.

Where one-to-one earns its price is a diagnosed understanding gap, taught in the right order, with the parent told each week what changed. That is a narrow claim, and it is the right one. It also means the arrangement should have a visible end: a sequence completed, a method secure, a review that recommends stopping. Open-ended primary tutoring with no end point in view is usually supervision being billed as teaching.
