sections.heading: What a parent actually sees: the platform, the whiteboard and the weekly note
paragraphs: Online primary teaching stands or falls on whether a young child can operate it without an adult, and the honest answer is that the youngest cannot, and should not be expected to. A Year 1 or Year 2 child needs someone to open the link and sit within earshot. By Year 4 most children join on their own. Planning around that saves a great deal of friction, and it is worth deciding before the first lesson which adult in the house owns the three minutes before the session starts.

The lesson itself runs in a browser with a shared whiteboard, so there is nothing to install on a family laptop or a school-issued device. The whiteboard matters more at primary level than at any other stage, because a young child's thinking is visible in their working and not in their explanation. A tutor needs to see the child form a number line, partition a quantity or lay out a column subtraction. A stylus and a tablet alongside a laptop makes that natural; a finger on a touchscreen works; typing does not.

A phone does not work for a primary lesson and it is better to say so than to let a family discover it in week three. The screen is too small to hold a whiteboard and a face at once, and a child who cannot see the adult's reaction loses the feedback that keeps them going. A laptop or a tablet is the floor. A wired or stable connection matters less than most people expect, because a primary session is mostly voice and ink rather than high-definition video.

After each session the parent gets a short written note: what was covered, what the child could do by the end, what they could not, and the two-minute task for the days in between. That note is the thing to read, not the lesson recording. Recordings exist and a parent can request one, but almost nobody watches forty minutes of a Year 3 maths lesson. The note is where the information is, and a tutor who cannot write a useful one after a session did not have a clear plan going into it.

sections.heading: Changing a primary tutor without unsettling the child
paragraphs: Primary matches fail differently from secondary ones. A teenager who dislikes a tutor says so, loudly, and the problem announces itself. A seven-year-old who is bored or lost usually says the lesson was fine, because the adult was kind and the child wants to please. So a parent cannot rely on the child's report, and has to read the evidence instead: is anything the child could not do six weeks ago now something they can do unprompted?

The commoner failure is the opposite of the one parents expect. It is not a tutor the child dislikes; it is a tutor the child likes very much and who is teaching almost nothing. Warm, patient, encouraging sessions in which the adult does most of the work produce a happy child and a flat trajectory. This is the hardest case to act on, and the reason the weekly note and the six-week review exist. If the notes read identically in week two and week eight, the arrangement is not working however pleasant it is.

Changing tutor is straightforward and does not have to cost the term's work. The new tutor gets the diagnosis, the sequence and the notes from the previous sessions, so the first lesson starts where the last one finished rather than back at the beginning. For a young child the handover matters more than the paperwork: one short joint session, or a clear explanation from the parent that the new teacher already knows what they have been working on, removes most of the unsettlement.

The honest caveat is availability. A primary specialist in a particular strand at a particular time on a Sunday-to-Thursday evening is a narrow intersection, and sometimes the right replacement is not free at the usual slot. When that happens a family is told so directly, with the options being a different time, a short wait, or a different teacher whose strengths are described accurately rather than oversold.

sections.heading: What the money is actually building: the move out of the Primary Years Programme
paragraphs: Primary tutoring is easier to justify when a family can see what it is for, and in the Kingdom it is usually for one of three transitions. The first is into the Middle Years Programme, where marks suddenly attach to named criteria and a student has to write at length in a specified form. The inquiry habits transfer. What exposes a child is sentence-level writing control and the ability to structure a paragraph, which is why written composition is the most valuable thing to secure in Years 5 and 6.

The second transition is into a Cambridge or Pearson route at eleven, which happens often here because school places, compounds and postings move families between systems. That route asks immediately for secure written methods in mathematics and for accurate, conventional writing. A child who has spent six years explaining their thinking and very little time practising a formal algorithm can look weaker than they are in the first term, and the fix is a sequence of specific methods rather than a general confidence problem.

The third is a change of country, which Saudi expatriate families face more often than most. What travels is not content; curricula differ. What travels is reading fluency, written stamina, number facts and the habit of working independently for twenty minutes. Those four things make a child employable in any classroom, and they are exactly what short, frequent primary sessions build. A family planning a move within a year should spend the tutoring budget there rather than on the current school's topic list.

None of this is a promise about an outcome, and nobody can honestly offer one at primary level. There is no external examination, no published grade and no mechanism by which anyone could guarantee a result. What a family can reasonably expect is a diagnosis they can read, a sequence with an end point, a weekly note that says what changed, and a recommendation to stop when stopping is right. That is a smaller claim than this market usually makes and it is the one that survives contact with a real child.

process.title: Tell us the strand, the year group and the evening
process.description: The three facts that decide whether a match exists: which strand the child needs, which year group they are in, and which evenings work after the school run. A line about what the school has already said is worth more than a long description of the child, because it tells us what has been assessed and what has not.

process.title: A free trial lesson, with a diagnosis at the end
process.description: Forty minutes with the tutor, the parent welcome in the room, and a written diagnosis afterwards: what the tutor found, what they think the cause is, what the first six sessions will do and what will be visibly different. No obligation follows from the trial, and a tutor who cannot write that paragraph has told you something.

process.title: Fix a slot in Arabia Standard Time
process.description: The slot is pinned to Saudi local time, not to the tutor's, so it does not move when another country changes its clocks. Most primary families settle on two short sessions a week rather than one long one, placed either side of the Sunday-to-Thursday school run rather than late in the evening.

process.title: A short note after every session
process.description: What was covered, what the child could do by the end, what they could not, and the two-minute task for the days between. The note is deliberately short enough to read on a phone. Over six weeks the sequence of notes is the only honest record of whether anything is changing.

process.title: Review at six sessions, including the option to stop
process.description: A diagnosed primary gap should have an end point, and the review names it. The three outcomes are continue on the same sequence, change the sequence, or stop because the thing is secure. A recommendation to stop is a normal result here, not a failure of the arrangement.

whyPoints.title: Primary-trained, not secondary-trained
whyPoints.description: The age phase on a teaching certificate decides whether somebody was taught how children learn to decode, and that is not a detail at primary level. We match on the phase and the strand, which is why the answer to an enquiry is sometimes that the right person is not free this week rather than a yes.

whyPoints.title: A diagnosis you can read
whyPoints.description: Every trial lesson ends in a few written lines naming what was found, the suspected cause and what the first six sessions will do about it. A family can hold that against the weekly notes later. It is also the fastest way to tell a teacher with a method from a pleasant adult with good intentions.

whyPoints.title: Sessions sized for the child, not the invoice
whyPoints.description: Thirty to forty-five minutes, often twice a week, because that is what a primary child can use after a full school day. Decoding, spelling and number facts are built by frequency rather than duration, and stretching a session to fill an hour serves the billing rather than the learning.

whyPoints.title: Delivered online, said plainly
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video, pinned to Arabia Standard Time. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Saudi address; home visits are a service we offer only in India. The gain is the pool: a family outside Riyadh, Jeddah or the Eastern Province chooses from everyone who can teach the strand, not from whoever is nearby.

whyPoints.title: The honesty line is stated, not implied
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches research method, structure and rehearsal for the Year 6 exhibition and gives feedback on the student's own work. A tutor does not research it, write it or produce the final piece. We say that in advance because the alternative is widely sold in this market and it puts a child's own work at risk.

whyPoints.title: An end point rather than a subscription
whyPoints.description: A specific primary gap can be closed, and when it closes the right advice is to stop. The six-session review includes that option explicitly. Families who come back later for a different strand are a better outcome than families paying indefinitely for supervision labelled as teaching.

faqs.question: What does a Primary Years Programme lesson look like on screen when the child cannot type yet?
faqs.answer: It runs on a shared whiteboard rather than in a document. The child writes, draws, partitions quantities and lays out column methods with a finger or a stylus, and the tutor can see the working form in real time, which is where a young child's thinking actually shows. Reading is done aloud from a book or a shared page. Typing is avoided entirely below about Year 4, because the mechanics of the keyboard would become the lesson. Nothing needs installing: the session opens in a browser on a family laptop or tablet.

faqs.question: Does a parent need to sit beside a Year 2 child for the whole online lesson?
faqs.answer: Not for the whole lesson, but somebody has to own the three minutes before it starts. Children in Years 1 to 3 usually need an adult to open the link, check the sound and settle them, then can work alone with a parent within earshot. By Year 4 most children join independently. Parents are welcome to stay for every session and many do for the first two, which also lets them judge the talking ratio: in a good primary lesson the child does most of the talking and the doing.

faqs.question: Is a primary session recorded, and what would a parent realistically use a recording for?
faqs.answer: A recording can be requested, but it is rarely the useful artefact. Almost nobody watches forty minutes of a Year 3 maths lesson. The thing to read is the written note that follows each session: what was covered, what the child could do by the end, what they could not, and the short task for the days in between. Recordings earn their place in two cases, both narrow: showing a class teacher exactly what method is being taught, and letting a parent who was travelling see how their child responds to this particular adult.

faqs.question: Is a household tablet enough for these lessons, or does a young child need their own laptop?
faqs.answer: A tablet is enough, and with a stylus it is often better than a laptop, because handwriting and drawing are how a primary child shows what they know. A laptop works too. A phone does not: the screen cannot hold a whiteboard and a face at once, and a child who cannot see the adult's reaction loses the feedback that keeps them going. Connection quality matters less than families expect, since a primary session is mostly voice and ink rather than high-definition video.

faqs.question: What happens if the connection drops while a seven-year-old is working alone in the room?
faqs.answer: The tutor rejoins first and calls the parent's number if the child does not reappear within a minute or two, which is why that number is taken before the first lesson. Work on the shared whiteboard survives the drop, so the session resumes at the same point rather than starting again. Time lost beyond a few minutes is added to the next session or returned, and with children this young the tutor ends the lesson on a settled note rather than mid-task if the connection has been unstable throughout.

faqs.question: Why is a Primary Years Programme hour priced closer to a Diploma hour than to a general primary one?
faqs.answer: Because the pool is small, not because the content is hard. Advertised Riyadh rates put general primary tuition near SAR 50 an hour and senior examination subjects at SAR 200 and above, so every teacher who can work in examination years has a financial reason to do so. What is left advertising at the primary band is largely supervision. A trained primary teacher with inquiry experience and systematic early-reading training is priced by scarcity. Those are advertised vendor figures rather than a market average, and none of them is IB Gram's price.

faqs.question: Riyadh primary tuition is advertised near SAR 50 an hour - what is a family getting at that price?
faqs.answer: Usually supervision, honestly delivered. An adult who keeps a child at the table, checks spellings, hears reading and signs the diary. For a child whose problem is organisation or completion, that may be exactly right and nothing more expensive is needed. What it does not reliably include is somebody who can diagnose: who can tell that a fractions difficulty is really place value, or that a reluctant writer is an undisclosed reading problem. The test is simple. Ask what the tutor will have diagnosed by the end of the first session.

faqs.question: Is a 30-minute primary session charged as half an hour, and is it worth less than a full one?
faqs.answer: It is charged on the time used, so a thirty-minute lesson costs less than a sixty-minute one. It is not worth less in learning terms for a child under about nine. Decoding, spelling patterns and number facts are built by frequency rather than duration, so twenty-five minutes twice a week beats fifty minutes once. Stretching a primary session to fill an hour serves the invoice and not the child, who stops using the last fifteen minutes anyway after a full school day.

faqs.question: Is a small group ever better value than one-to-one for early reading?
faqs.answer: For fluency work, sometimes. If several children need the same practice at the same level, a group gives repetition at a lower price per child and the social element helps. For decoding it rarely works, because a decoding gap is specific to which graphemes a particular child has and has not secured, and no two children in a group have the same set. The practical rule: groups suit gaps in fluency, one-to-one suits gaps in understanding, and more practice on a method a child does not understand only builds a faster wrong answer.

faqs.question: What does the free trial lesson involve when the student is eight years old?
faqs.answer: About forty minutes, with the parent welcome in the room. The tutor usually starts a layer below the topic the parent named, because the named topic is often a symptom: a child presented as weak at fractions gets checked on place value and division first. Afterwards the parent gets a few written lines naming what was found, the suspected cause, what the first six sessions will do and what will be visibly different at the end. Nothing is owed if the family does not continue, and no card details are needed to book it.

faqs.question: Can we pay for a short block across one school holiday rather than committing to a term?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for mid-primary transfers a holiday block is often the better purchase. The shape is a diagnostic in the first session, a fixed sequence across the break, and a short written handover the family can give the new class teacher. Blocks also suit a child who has just moved country and needs the gap measured before the next school year begins. The point of a block is that it ends: a stated number of sessions, a named target, and no rolling commitment afterwards.

faqs.question: Examiner experience means nothing in a programme with no examinations, so what should a family look for instead?
faqs.answer: Three things, in order. A primary teaching qualification, checked by asking which age phase is printed on the certificate rather than accepting the initials. Experience inside the programme itself, checked by asking which transdisciplinary units they taught, in which year group, and what the central idea was. And specific training in the child's actual problem, which for early reading means a named systematic phonics programme and a method for assessing decoding. A tutor offering marking experience as the headline credential for a Year 3 child has not read the question.

faqs.question: How do we check that a tutor has really taught a transdisciplinary unit rather than read about one?
faqs.answer: Ask three concrete questions in a message before paying for anything. Which unit was the last one you taught, under which theme, and what was the central idea? What did the children actually produce at the end of it? And what did you teach explicitly inside the unit that was not the topic? A teacher who has planned units answers all three in a few sentences, with the grubby detail that only comes from having done it. A tutor who has read the framework produces vocabulary and no specifics.

faqs.question: Should a primary tutor be a trained primary teacher or a strong subject graduate?
faqs.answer: A trained primary teacher, for a child in Years 1 to 4 especially. A mathematics graduate knows far more mathematics than any primary child needs and may never have been taught the sequence in which a child builds place value, or what to do when a written method breaks down. The content ceiling is irrelevant at this stage; the method is everything. From about Year 5 a strong graduate with real primary classroom experience can work well, but the classroom experience is the part that matters, not the degree.

faqs.question: Does it help if the tutor has worked in an international school in the Kingdom before?
faqs.answer: It helps with fit rather than with teaching. A tutor who has taught here knows the Sunday-to-Thursday week, knows that a 4pm slot collides with a long school run in Riyadh or Jeddah, and expects a class where most children are learning in an additional language. They also tend to understand that term dates differ school by school in the same city. None of that substitutes for primary training, and a well-trained teacher who has never worked in Saudi Arabia will usually outperform a local generalist.

faqs.question: Our child likes the tutor but very little seems to be changing - how do we handle that?
faqs.answer: This is the commonest primary failure and the hardest to act on. A warm, patient adult who does most of the work produces a happy child and a flat trajectory, and a seven-year-old will report that the lesson was fine because the adult was kind. Read the written notes instead of asking the child. If week two and week eight say the same things, raise it at the six-session review. A change of tutor carries the diagnosis, the sequence and the notes across, so the next lesson starts where the last one finished.

faqs.question: How many primary students does one tutor carry, and why does that matter more at this age?
faqs.answer: Ask the number and ask how many are primary. The reason it matters more here is the between-lesson work: a primary arrangement depends on a short written note after every session and a two-minute task for the parent, and that discipline is the first thing to slip when a timetable is full. A tutor carrying a heavy Diploma load alongside a few young children will usually protect the examination cases. It is a fair question to put directly, and the answer is more informative than any claim about results.

ib-pyp-home-tutor.closingHeading: Start with the diagnosis, not the hour
ib-pyp-home-tutor.closingBody: The useful first step for a primary child is not booking a term. It is finding out what the actual gap is, in writing, from somebody trained to look. Tell us the strand, the year group and which evenings survive the school run, and we will arrange a free trial lesson with a primary-trained tutor who has taught inside the programme. You get a written diagnosis afterwards, whether or not you continue. Lessons run one-to-one over live video, pinned to Arabia Standard Time, in sessions of thirty to forty-five minutes. If the right specialist is not free at your slot, we will say so rather than offer a substitute.

ib-pyp-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below are primary teachers rather than subject specialists, which is the right qualification at this age. Each has taught inside an inquiry-based primary programme, and each is available inside the Saudi late-afternoon window rather than only at the evening hours that suit older students.

intro.heading: Start with what you can actually measure, because there is no grade to point at
paragraphs: The Primary Years Programme has no external examination, no grade boundaries and no paper to mark. Progress is reported through units of inquiry, teacher judgement, a portfolio and, in the final year, the exhibition. All of that is sound educational practice and none of it answers the question a parent asks at the end of a term of paid tutoring, which is whether anything changed. Without something checkable, the honest answer is that nobody knows, and the dishonest answer is a cheerful report about growing confidence.

So we agree the measures first, before any plan is written. Six of them work well at this age and a parent can watch all six at the kitchen table. How long a child takes to produce a number fact, counted in seconds rather than marked right or wrong. How many words they read aloud without hesitating, and whether they can answer three questions about the passage without being prompted. Whether a plan exists before they start writing, before anybody worries about whether it is a good plan. Whether they can say why a method works rather than only perform it. How many minutes pass before the first request for help on a task they can do. And whether a method survives being wrapped in an unfamiliar question.

Those six are not a substitute for the school's reporting. They are the things that move in four to six weeks when teaching is working, and they are specific enough that a tutor cannot claim credit for them without evidence. Every plan we write for a primary child names two or three of them as the target, says what the current reading is, and says what should be different by the review. A parent who knows the number before and the number after does not have to take anybody's word for anything.

The second half of this page is about something less obvious and more limiting: time. A primary-age child in the Kingdom has a usable window of roughly two hours. School finishes in the early afternoon, the child needs to eat and stop being a passenger, and by seven in the evening a seven-year-old is not learning anything from a screen. That leaves about 4pm to 6pm Saudi time, Sunday to Thursday. An IB PYP tutor therefore has to be somebody whose own working day still has teaching in it at that hour, which is a far harder constraint than the one a Diploma student imposes, and it quietly removes most of the world's tutors.

Run the arithmetic and the shape of the available pool becomes clear. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 with no daylight saving. A 4:30pm Saudi lesson is seven in the evening in India, half past five in the Gulf, half past one in the afternoon in Britain during their winter, and half past eight in the morning on the eastern seaboard of North America. The British and European hours fall inside a working day, which rules out any tutor who is currently standing in a classroom, however good they are. The table further down sets this out country by country, because it is the single fact that decides whether a weekly primary slot is sustainable.

Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video. Nobody is sent to a Saudi address; in-home visiting is a service we run only in India. For a young child that model needs defending rather than asserting, so there is a section on exactly how an online session works with a six-year-old, what the adult in the house has to do, and the ages at which we say no. We would rather turn down a four-year-old than take the fee.

ib-pyp-tutor.programmesIntro: The Primary Years Programme covers nine years of a child's life and almost nothing about it is constant across them. Below is what each stage is doing and what a tutor at that stage should actually be for.

programmes.name: Early Years
programmes.description: Play-based inquiry, oral language, listening stamina and the beginnings of number sense. This is not a tutoring age, and we say so to several families a month. A child of four who is behind is almost always behind in spoken language or in attention span, and neither is addressed by a screen. The useful intervention at this age is more talk, more being read to, and a conversation with the class teacher.
programmes.countryNote: Families arriving into the Kingdom with a three or four-year-old frequently worry about the English-medium transition into a Primary Years Programme setting. That worry is usually misplaced: at this age a child acquires the language of the playground within a term or two. What we will do is a single free conversation about whether anything is needed, which more often than not ends with nothing being bought.

programmes.name: Lower Primary
programmes.description: Decoding and early reading, number bonds, written methods and the first sustained writing. This is where a measurable gap can first be identified and closed quickly, because the skills are discrete. A child who cannot decode fluently cannot access anything else, and fluency responds to short, frequent, well-structured practice far better than to a long weekly session.
programmes.countryNote: Lower Primary is where the effects of moving education systems show up most in the Kingdom's international schools. A child taught one written method for subtraction in a previous country and a different one here will often stop trusting either, and the hesitation reads as weak arithmetic rather than as a method conflict. Finding out which method came first is the whole diagnosis.

programmes.name: Upper Primary
programmes.description: Fractions and proportional reasoning, extended writing, research skills, note-taking and independence. The content gets harder and the real change is in what the school expects a child to manage alone. A tutor at this stage works as much on self-management as on content, because a child who cannot start a task without being told what to do first will stall in the Middle Years Programme regardless of what they know.
programmes.countryNote: Upper Primary is the stage at which Saudi families most often ask for support, and the request is usually framed as maths. On inspection the problem is frequently reading: a child who reads slowly cannot extract a word problem's structure, and the maths looks weak. Diagnosing which of the two is the cause changes what should be bought, sometimes from maths to reading entirely.

programmes.name: The final year and the exhibition
programmes.description: The exhibition is the culminating piece of the programme: a sustained, student-led inquiry, presented. It is assessed on the child's own thinking and the process behind it, not on the polish of the output, which is why a tutor's role here is tightly bounded. We teach questioning, planning, note-taking and how to present and handle questions. We do not choose the line of inquiry and we do not shape the content.
programmes.countryNote: The transition out of the Primary Years Programme in the Kingdom goes two ways: into the Middle Years Programme at the same or another school, or into Cambridge Year 7 at a British-curriculum school. The two destinations ask for different things, and the summer between is the most efficient time to build whichever is missing. Ask the receiving school what it assumes a Year 7 arrival can already do.

ib-pyp-tutor.subjectsIntro: The Primary Years Programme is transdisciplinary, so these are strands rather than subjects. Each entry says what is actually being built and the specific thing that tends to be missing when a family makes contact.

subjects.name: Number and calculation
subjects.description: Number bonds, times tables, written methods and mental strategies. The commonest gap in the Kingdom's international primary classrooms is recall speed rather than understanding: a child who computes seven eights correctly but slowly cannot hold a multi-step problem in working memory. Recall time is measurable in seconds and improves with short daily practice, which makes it the single best first target.

subjects.name: Pattern, function and early algebra
subjects.description: Sequences, relationships, the beginnings of generalisation. This strand is where mathematical thinking either starts or does not, and it is the one most often skipped at home because it does not look like arithmetic. A child who can describe a rule in words is ready for algebra years later; one who can only continue a pattern is not.

subjects.name: Fractions and proportional reasoning
subjects.description: The hardest content in the whole programme and the most common reason an Upper Primary family makes contact. Fractions fail when a child has learned procedures without a model of what a fraction is, and the repair involves going back to representations that feel too young. Parents often resist that; it is the fastest route through.

subjects.name: Measurement, shape and space
subjects.description: Units, conversion, area and perimeter, angle, position. Mostly straightforward and mostly taught well, with one recurring exception: children who have moved between education systems frequently carry a mixture of unit conventions and get caught by conversion questions that assume a single system throughout.

subjects.name: Data handling and early probability
subjects.description: Collecting, representing and interpreting data, and the language of chance. The strand matters more than it appears because it is where mathematics meets the units of inquiry, and a child who can read a graph properly has an advantage in science and social studies work for the rest of their schooling.

subjects.name: Reading and comprehension
subjects.description: Decoding first, then fluency, then comprehension and inference. Fluency is the hinge: a child reading slowly spends all their working memory on the words and has none left for meaning. It is measurable, it responds to practice, and it is the most common hidden cause of apparent weakness in every other strand.

subjects.name: Writing and composition
subjects.description: Sentence construction, paragraph structure, planning, and writing for different purposes. The intervention that moves this most is making the plan compulsory and visible before the writing starts. Children resist planning because it delays the part that feels like work, and almost every structural weakness in primary writing traces back to its absence.

subjects.name: Oral and visual language
subjects.description: Speaking, listening, presenting and interpreting visual texts. Underrated by families and heavily used by the programme, especially in the exhibition year. A child who can explain their thinking aloud writes better and is also easier to teach, because a tutor can hear the misconception rather than inferring it from a wrong answer.

subjects.name: Science within the units of inquiry
subjects.description: Living things, materials, forces, earth and space, approached through inquiry rather than as a syllabus. What a tutor can usefully build is the method underneath: asking an answerable question, recording what happened, and saying what the evidence shows. Those three transfer directly into Middle Years science and later into Diploma practical work.

subjects.name: Social studies and research skills
subjects.description: People, places, systems and change, plus the research skills the programme builds alongside them. Finding a source, judging whether it is any good and taking notes from it in your own words are teachable skills and are rarely taught explicitly. They are also exactly what the exhibition assesses, which makes them the highest-value thing to build in Year 5.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Most international schools in the Kingdom teach Arabic, with classes grouped by whether a child is a first-language or additional-language speaker. Additional-language learners can fall behind quietly because the subject sits outside the home routine. Short, frequent support works far better here than a long weekly session, and the gains show up in confidence first.

ib-pyp-tutor.regionsTitle: Primary provision across the Kingdom, and what the late-afternoon window looks like locally
ib-pyp-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a family lives changes two things for a primary child: which inquiry-based primary schools exist nearby, and how much of the 4pm to 6pm window survives the journey home. These are the places we are asked about most, with both in mind.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: The widest choice of inquiry-based primary provision in the Kingdom, and the city where the afternoon window is most often eaten by the drive. The city is about an hour across in traffic, so two families at the same school can have thirty minutes' difference in when a child is genuinely available.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: Primary provision runs along the coastal spine, skewing British and American with a smaller set of full-continuum schools. Families in the far north of the city lose most of the window to the return journey, which pushes a primary slot to the very end of it at around half past five.

regions.name: Dhahran and Al Khobar
regions.note: Dense international primary provision for the size of the population, including company-community schooling. Journeys inside the conurbation are short, so the window here is wide and a 4pm start is genuinely available, which matters more at this age than at any other.

regions.name: Dammam and Qatif
regions.note: The provincial capital has the broadest school choice on the east coast and the heaviest end-of-day traffic. Families commonly attend school in one town and live in another, so the practical start time is set by the direction of the run rather than by the distance.

regions.name: Jubail
regions.note: Industrial city provision including international primary schooling, north of the main cluster and against the commuting flow. The window is comfortable, and the common request here is Arabic as an additional language rather than mathematics or reading.

regions.name: Thuwal and the KAUST community
regions.note: A university campus community north of Jeddah with a school serving it and an unusually mobile population. Children arrive mid-year from every education system imaginable, so the first task is almost always an audit of what a child has and has not met rather than teaching.

regions.name: Yanbu
regions.note: A Red Sea industrial city with limited international primary provision and a long road to the nearest alternative. Families here are the clearest case for online teaching at primary level, because the local pool of inquiry-trained primary teachers available after school is effectively nil.

regions.name: Tabuk and NEOM
regions.note: The north-west, where communities are forming faster than school provision. Primary-age arrivals are frequent and often come in part-way through a school year, which is the hardest time for a young child to move. Short, frequent sessions settle a child faster than long ones.

regions.name: AlUla
regions.note: A small and growing community with the longest distances to alternatives of anywhere on this list. The window is wide because journeys are short, and the constraint is entirely about who is available to teach rather than about when.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: About twenty-five kilometres apart in 'Asir at altitude, sharing a catchment. Primary provision is limited relative to the population, and families routinely ask whether a specialist exists at all before asking what one costs. The honest local answer is usually no, and the online answer is yes.

schoolClusters.note: Riyadh holds the Kingdom's largest set of schools running the Primary Years Programme, some as part of the full continuum through to the Diploma and some alongside other curricula. Which year groups and which programmes run varies by campus, so confirm directly with each school. Students we support attend schools including the following.

schoolClusters.city: Jeddah, Thuwal and the Red Sea coast
schoolClusters.note: Primary provision on the western coast is mostly British and American in character, with a smaller number of schools appearing in IB listings and the KAUST campus community school at Thuwal to the north. A primary child's school here is often chosen for the commute as much as for the curriculum.

The International Schools Group runs several campuses in the province and the company communities operate their own schooling, which together give the east coast dense primary provision for its population. Not every campus runs the same programme, and provision changes with cohort size.

ib-pyp-tutor.modesIntro: Three shapes, and the right one follows from the child's age rather than from a price list. The shortest is usually the most effective at primary level, which is the opposite of how tutoring is normally sold.

modes.title: Two short sessions a week, inside the window
modes.description: Twenty-five to thirty minutes, twice a week, at the earliest end of the 4pm to 6pm window. This is the default for Lower Primary and for any fluency work at any age, because decoding speed and number-fact recall respond to frequency rather than to duration. A single long weekly session is a worse purchase at the same price, and we will say so.
bullets: Two short slots rather than one long one, for anything fluency-based
Scheduled at 4pm or 4:30pm Saudi time, before a young child tires
The same tutor both times, with the same five-minute opening routine
A one-line note to the parent after each session

modes.title: One weekly session with tasks between
modes.description: Forty to forty-five minutes once a week for Upper Primary, with two or three short tasks for the days in between. At this age the point of the session shifts from drilling a skill to building independence, so some of the work has to happen without the tutor in the room. The tasks are specific and small enough to be finished in ten minutes.
bullets: Forty to forty-five minutes, which is the attention limit at this age
Two or three ten-minute tasks between sessions, named explicitly
Self-management worked on alongside content, not after it
A review against the agreed measures every four to six weeks

modes.title: Exhibition and transition coaching
modes.description: For Year 5 and Year 6: research skills, note-taking in the child's own words, planning an inquiry, and rehearsing a presentation with questions at the end. The boundary is strict and stated up front. We teach the skills and rehearse the delivery. We do not choose the line of inquiry, write any part of the presentation, or touch the content the school is assessing.

sections.heading: Six things you can measure in a primary child when there is no grade
paragraphs: A Primary Years Programme report tells you about dispositions, inquiry and the learner profile, and it is written honestly by people who know your child. What it cannot do is tell you whether a term of paid tutoring was worth the money, because it is not designed to isolate that. So the first thing we do with a primary family is agree what we are going to count. Six measures cover almost every case, and all six can be read at home by a parent with a timer and a book.

Take recall time. A child who answers seven eights correctly in nine seconds and a child who answers it in two seconds are in completely different positions, even though a mark scheme would score them identically. The slow child spends their working memory on retrieval and has none left for the structure of a multi-step problem, which is why their word problems collapse while their arithmetic looks fine. Recall time is countable, it moves in weeks, and it is the single most useful number to track at Lower Primary.

Reading fluency behaves the same way. Give a child an unseen page at their level, listen for hesitations and finger-tracking, then ask three questions they have to answer without prompts. A child who stumbles four times a line is not a weak reader of ideas, they are a slow decoder, and the two need completely different teaching. Families routinely arrive asking for maths help when the measurement says the problem is on this row of the table instead.

The last three measures are about independence rather than skill: whether a plan exists before writing starts, whether the child can say why a method works, and how many minutes pass before the first request for help. Those predict Middle Years success better than any content measure, and they are the ones a school report is least able to quantify. The table lists all six with what to watch, how we check it in a session, and what four to six weeks of work should actually move.

sections.heading: Working backwards from the measure to the plan
paragraphs: Once the measures are agreed, the plan writes itself, and it is usually smaller than a family expects. Pick two of the six, not all of them. Take a reading at the start, in front of the parent so there is no dispute about it later. State what should be different in four to six weeks. Then choose the shortest format that can plausibly move those two numbers, which at primary level is very often two short sessions a week rather than one long one.

The format matters more here than at any other stage. Decoding fluency and number-fact recall are retrieval skills, and retrieval improves with frequency and spacing rather than with duration. Two twenty-five-minute sessions beat one fifty-minute session at the same price, and a parent paying for fifty minutes once a week is buying the less effective arrangement. We will not sell the longer version for a fluency target, and if that is the only slot available we will say the arrangement is compromised rather than pretending it is equivalent.

The review is where the whole structure earns its keep. At four to six weeks we put the new readings next to the old ones. If the numbers moved, we either continue on the next two measures or stop, and stopping is a perfectly normal outcome at primary level because fluency gaps close and stay closed. If the numbers did not move, that is information about the plan rather than about the child, and we change the approach rather than extending the booking to see what happens.

What this structure refuses to do is produce a grade. There isn't one, and inventing a proxy for one would be worse than useless at this age, because it would push the teaching towards whatever the proxy rewarded. Nor do we predict future attainment. A tutor who tells you that a seven-year-old is on track for a seven in the Diploma is selling you something. The measures above are deliberately short-horizon, because short horizons are the only ones anybody can be honest about at this stage.
bullets: Two measures per plan, not six, with a reading taken in front of the parent
Fluency targets get two short sessions a week, never one long one

sections.heading: The two-hour window, and why a primary tutor is harder to staff than a Diploma one
paragraphs: A Diploma candidate can take a lesson at half past seven in the evening and get something out of it. A seven-year-old cannot. School in the Kingdom finishes in the early afternoon, and once a primary child has travelled home, eaten and stopped being a passenger, the part of the day in which they can concentrate on a screen runs from roughly four o'clock to six. After that the returns fall away quickly, and by seven a tired child is absorbing nothing while a parent is paying full price for the hour.

That two-hour window, Sunday to Thursday, is the real constraint on this entire service, and it is a constraint on the tutor rather than on the family. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not change its clocks. Work out what 4:30pm in Riyadh is elsewhere and the shape of the available pool appears immediately. It is seven in the evening in India, half past five in the Gulf, the same time in Turkey, half past one in the afternoon in Britain during their winter and half past two in their summer, and half past eight in the morning on the eastern seaboard of North America.

The British and European numbers are the important ones, because that is where a great many well-qualified primary teachers are. Half past one on a weekday afternoon is the middle of a school day. A serving classroom teacher in London or Madrid simply cannot hold that slot, no matter how suitable they are, which means the European part of the pool narrows to full-time tutors who are not in a classroom. Tutors in the Gulf, Turkey, East Africa and South Asia can hold it comfortably. Tutors in East Asia and Australia cannot hold it at all.

This is why we ask for your available hour before we ask about the subject, and it is why the match sometimes takes longer at primary level than for an older sibling. A good match at 4:30pm Saudi time is a narrower intersection than a good match at 7pm. When nobody suitable is free in the window, we say so and offer a different day, a different hour at the edge of the window, or a waiting position, rather than placing a child with someone who is available but wrong.

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week, and what it does to a young child's stamina
paragraphs: The school week here runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. For a primary child that produces a predictable stamina curve across the week, and ignoring it wastes money. Sunday is a recovery day after two days off and is rarely the best teaching slot. Monday and Tuesday are the strongest. By Wednesday and Thursday a six or seven-year-old is tired, and a session that would have gone well earlier in the week produces half as much. Where a family has a choice of two slots, we ask for the earlier ones.

Imported tutoring arrangements get this wrong twice over. A tutor whose own working week runs Monday to Friday has their quietest day on your weekend and their busiest on your Sunday, and an arrangement built without noticing it collapses in the third week rather than the first. We build the week outward from the Saudi school calendar and ask tutors to fit it, which is also why the available pool is narrower than a platform's total tutor list would suggest.

Friday and Saturday sessions do work for some primary families, and the trade-off is worth stating. A weekend morning with a rested child is a better teaching hour than a Thursday evening with a tired one. The cost is distance from the school week: homework set on a Friday has to survive until the following Friday, which at this age means the task has to be smaller and more specific than it would be mid-week. Some families run one weekday and one weekend slot for exactly that reason.

Ramadan reshapes the pattern completely for a primary child, and because the Islamic calendar moves against the Gregorian one by roughly eleven days each year, it drifts across the academic year rather than sitting in one term. School days shorten, routines move later and a young child's available concentration moves with them. We shift slots and shorten sessions for that period rather than cancelling, and families who prefer to pause keep the slot at no charge. We publish no dates for it: the start is confirmed by moon sighting and differs by a day between countries.

sections.heading: Year group by year group: what to build underneath the inquiry
paragraphs: The Primary Years Programme teaches through units of inquiry, and the inquiry rests on a set of unglamorous skills that the units themselves do not have time to drill. That is not a criticism of the model; a classroom of twenty-four children cannot deliver the frequency that fluency requires. It does mean the most useful thing a tutor can do at primary level is build the layer underneath, which is different at each stage and gets misjudged in both directions by anxious families.

In the Early Years the honest answer is almost always that nothing is needed. A four-year-old who seems behind is usually behind in spoken language or in attention, and the remedy is conversation and being read to, not a screen. We turn these enquiries down regularly and offer a free conversation instead. In Lower Primary the targets are narrow and the gains are fast: decoding fluency and number bonds, drilled in short frequent sessions, measured in seconds.

In Upper Primary the content gets genuinely harder — fractions and proportional reasoning are the hardest mathematics in the programme — and the expectation of independence rises sharply at the same time. A tutor working only on content here misses half the job. The child who stalls in Year 7 is usually not the one who knew less, it is the one who could never start a task without being told what to do first, and that is trainable with deliberate silence inside a session.

The final year adds the exhibition and the transition out. Whether the next step is the Middle Years Programme or Cambridge Year 7, both assume a child can plan, take notes in their own words, manage a deadline and write to a given structure. The summer before is the most efficient time in the whole nine years to build those, because nothing else is competing for the hours. The table sets out each stage with the session shape that actually works at that age.

sections.heading: What a primary school in the Kingdom staffs, and what it leaves to the family
paragraphs: Primary provision in the Kingdom is generally good and in the larger cities it is plentiful, so the gap families run into is rarely about teaching quality. It is about frequency and about the specialisms a primary school is not built to carry. A class teacher with twenty-four children cannot hear each of them read daily, and daily is roughly what a struggling decoder needs. That is arithmetic rather than a failing, and it is the single most common reason a Lower Primary family makes contact.

The specialisms are the second gap. Many international primary schools in the Kingdom carry an English-as-an-additional-language teacher and an Arabic department, and far fewer carry a specialist for a child who is well ahead or who has a specific learning difference. Schools are also licensed by the Ministry of Education and evaluated through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, which is about the institution rather than about the individual provision a particular child needs; a strong evaluation report tells a parent nothing about whether this school can stretch their Year 5 mathematician.

The third gap is geographic and it is absolute rather than relative. In Yanbu, AlUla, Tabuk or Abha the question is not which of the local inquiry-trained primary teachers is best available at half past four in the afternoon; it is whether any exists. Families in those places arrive at online teaching by elimination rather than by preference, and the honest argument for it is simply that the alternative is nothing at all.

What to ask a school, in order. How often will my child read aloud to an adult? What happens if they are significantly ahead of the class in mathematics? Who supports an additional-language learner in Arabic, and how often? What do you expect us to do at home, specifically? Schools answer questions in that form directly, and the answers tell a family exactly where the boundary between school provision and home responsibility sits for their child.
bullets: Ask how often a child reads aloud to an adult, and compare it with what they need

sections.heading: Honesty at primary level: the exhibition, the portfolio and whose work it is
paragraphs: Academic honesty is discussed as a Diploma problem and starts much earlier. In the Primary Years Programme the assessed artefacts are the portfolio, the work inside the units of inquiry and, in the final year, the exhibition. All of them are assessed on what the child can do and think, which means an adult who improves the artefact has damaged the assessment. A tutor is an adult with unusual leverage over exactly that, so the boundary has to be explicit rather than assumed.

What a tutor may do is teach the skill on different material. If the unit of inquiry needs a child to find and judge a source, the tutor teaches that on a topic unrelated to the child's own inquiry, then steps back. If the exhibition needs a presentation, the tutor rehearses delivery, timing and handling unexpected questions, without touching the content. If a portfolio piece needs a paragraph with a topic sentence, the tutor teaches paragraph structure on a different paragraph entirely. The principle is simple: teach beside the assessed work, never on it.

What a tutor must not do is choose the line of inquiry, find the sources, supply the notes, write any part of a presentation or improve a piece that is going into the portfolio. We decline those requests, including the gentle version of them that arrives as a parent asking whether the tutor could just tidy it up before it goes in. Tidying it up removes the only thing the piece was collected to show. The table sets each task against what is permitted and what the school is actually assessing.

There is a parental version of the same boundary and it is harder, because a parent sits with the work every evening. The useful test is whether you could honestly say the child did this. Helping a child reread a question, asking what they think the answer is, and sending them back to try again are all fine. Writing a sentence for them to copy is not, even when it is faster and the child is tired. At this age the habit being built is the one that matters in the Diploma eight years later.

sections.heading: Switching into or out of the Primary Years Programme
paragraphs: Primary-age children move between education systems in the Kingdom constantly, usually on a parent's posting and often part-way through a year. The reassuring part is that primary content is broadly similar everywhere: numbers, reading and writing do not change across borders. The part that catches families out is sequencing and method, because the same content arrives in a different order and is taught with different procedures, and a child who meets a familiar topic taught unfamiliarly will often conclude that they have got worse.

Moving into the programme from a British or American primary school, the content transfers almost entirely and the shift is in how learning is organised. Inquiry asks a child to ask and investigate rather than to complete, and children used to finishing worksheets can look lost for a term while they work out what is wanted. That is an adjustment and not a gap, and treating it as a gap by buying content tutoring wastes a term. What helps is explicit teaching of the research and note-taking skills the inquiry assumes.

Moving out of the programme is the direction that needs more attention, in both destinations. A child entering Cambridge Year 7 meets a timetable of separate subjects, more written work and regular assessment, having come from an integrated model. A child entering the Middle Years Programme keeps the inquiry structure and meets criterion-based marking, which is a genuinely new thing to learn. Either way the receiving school has a view about what a Year 7 arrival can already do, and asking them is more useful than guessing.

The practical method for any switch is an audit before any teaching. Take the new school's expectations, go through them, and sort each item into covered properly, covered differently, and never met. The middle pile is the dangerous one, because a child believes they know that topic and will not flag it. For a primary child the audit takes one session and saves most of a term, which makes it the cheapest thing a transferring family can buy.

sections.heading: How an online lesson actually works with a child of seven
paragraphs: This model needs defending at primary level rather than asserted, so here is what a session looks like. The child sits at a laptop with a shared whiteboard on screen and the tutor in a corner of it. The tutor writes with a stylus, the child writes on the same board or on paper held up to the camera, and almost all the writing is the child's. The structure is deliberately repetitive: the same five-minute opening retrieval routine every session, then one new thing, then a short game-shaped application. Young children work better inside a predictable frame.

An adult needs to be nearby for the first few sessions, not in the lesson. The job is logistical: the device charged and in a quiet spot, headphones on, paper and a pencil to hand, and the child sitting down a minute before the start rather than arriving at a run. After two or three sessions most children do not need anybody in the room, and for many that independence is part of the point. A parent who wants visibility should read the note afterwards rather than hovering, because a six-year-old performs for an audience.

A tablet is workable for Lower Primary and awkward by Year 5, when a child needs to see a page and write on it at the same time. Headphones make a measurable difference in a busy household. Nothing needs installing beyond a browser. If the connection drops, the tutor reconnects and lost minutes are added on; if it is unstable rather than dropped, the session continues on audio with the whiteboard still running, which uses far less bandwidth and keeps a young child's momentum.

The limits are real and we state them. We will not take a child under five. We will not run sessions longer than about forty-five minutes at primary level, whatever a family is willing to pay for, because the last fifteen minutes of a sixty-minute session with a nine-year-old produce nothing. And we will say when a child's difficulty looks like something that needs assessment by a specialist rather than teaching, which is not a diagnosis on our part but is information a family should have early rather than late.
bullets: A fixed opening retrieval routine every session, because young children work inside frames
An adult nearby for the first few sessions, for logistics rather than for teaching
A laptop beats a tablet from Year 5 onwards; headphones help in any household
No sessions for under-fives, and nothing longer than about forty-five minutes

sections.heading: Starting, and the point at which we tell you to stop
paragraphs: The first session is free and is used to take the opening readings rather than to teach a sample lesson. Bring a book at the child's level, a recent piece of written work and the last school report. The tutor listens to the child read, times a set of number facts, watches how they approach a short task, and talks to them. At the end you get two or three measures with a starting number against each, and a recommendation that sometimes amounts to buying nothing at all.

If it proceeds, the plan names the measures, the format and the review date. Notes go to the parent after every session and are one or two lines long, because a long note about a twenty-five-minute session with a seven-year-old is padding. The note says what was practised, what the child found hard, and the one small thing to do before next time. At four to six weeks we take the readings again and put them beside the originals.

Then there is a decision, and it genuinely can be to stop. Fluency gaps close and stay closed; a child whose recall time has come down to two seconds does not need a standing weekly appointment to keep it there. We would rather make that recommendation and be the people a family comes back to in Year 5 than hold a slot out of habit. Where the gap has closed but a different one is now the priority, we say that too and the plan changes rather than continuing.

If nothing has moved, we change something. Usually one of three things is wrong: the measure was the wrong target, the format was too infrequent for a retrieval skill, or the tutor is not the right fit for this particular child, which matters more at seven than at seventeen. Reassignment is free and the new tutor gets the notes and the readings. And if the pattern suggests something that teaching is not the right answer to, we say so plainly, even though it ends the arrangement.

process.title: Tell us the year group and your available hour
process.description: The year group, the school, and which part of the 4pm to 6pm window actually works once your child is home and fed. The hour filters the tutor list before anything else does at this age, so giving it first avoids proposing someone who cannot hold the slot in the first place.

process.title: Free first session to take the readings
process.description: Bring a book at the child's level, a recent piece of writing and the last report. The tutor listens to the child read, times a set of number facts and watches how they start a task. You leave with two or three measures and a number against each, which is the baseline everything afterwards is judged against.

process.title: A plan with two measures and a review date
process.description: Two targets, not six. The format that suits them, which for anything fluency-based means two short sessions a week rather than one long one. A review date four to six weeks out. No predicted attainment, because nobody can honestly forecast a seven-year-old's Diploma grade.

process.title: Short sessions, early in the window
process.description: Twenty-five to thirty minutes twice a week for Lower Primary, forty to forty-five once a week with tasks between for Upper Primary. Scheduled at the start of the window rather than the end, and earlier in the Sunday-to-Thursday week rather than later, because stamina falls across both.

process.title: One or two lines to the parent after every session
process.description: What was practised, what was hard, and the single small task before next time. Short deliberately. These notes also carry the readings forward, so the review is a comparison of numbers rather than an exchange of impressions about how things seem to be going.

process.title: Review the readings, then continue, switch target or stop
process.description: The new readings go beside the old ones. If the gap closed, we stop or move to the next target. If nothing moved, we change the target, the format or the tutor, at no cost. If the pattern points at something teaching is not the answer to, we say that even though it ends the booking.

whyPoints.title: Measures before money
whyPoints.description: The Primary Years Programme produces no grade, so we agree what will be counted before anything is bought and take the opening readings in the free session. A parent who holds the number from week one and the number from week six does not have to trust a report about growing confidence.

whyPoints.title: Built around the hour a child can actually learn in
whyPoints.description: Sessions sit inside the 4pm to 6pm Saudi window and earlier in the Sunday-to-Thursday week, because stamina falls across both the day and the week at this age. Slots are pinned to Arabia Standard Time so a tutor's own clock change cannot push a young child's lesson into the evening.

whyPoints.title: Primary teachers, not subject specialists
whyPoints.description: The right qualification at this age is primary teaching experience inside an inquiry-based programme, not a degree in the subject. A physics graduate is the wrong person for a nine-year-old whose problem is place value, and we match on that basis even though the other version is easier to sell.

whyPoints.title: The short format when the short format is better
whyPoints.description: Retrieval skills improve with frequency rather than duration, so fluency targets get two short sessions a week instead of one long one. That is the cheaper arrangement and the more effective one, and we recommend it rather than selling the hour a family expected to buy.

whyPoints.title: A stated boundary on assessed primary work
whyPoints.description: We teach the skill beside the assessed work and never on it. We decline to choose a line of inquiry, supply notes, write a presentation or tidy up a portfolio piece, including when the request is gentle. Tidying it up removes the only thing the piece was collected to show.

whyPoints.title: We say no, including to paying families
whyPoints.description: No children under five. Nothing longer than about forty-five minutes at primary level. No tutoring for a four-year-old whose issue is spoken language, where the answer is conversation and being read to. And no claim about a future Diploma grade, which nobody can honestly make about a seven-year-old.

faqs.question: Which year groups do Saudi PYP schools actually run, and what happens after Year 6?
faqs.answer: It varies by campus and changes with cohort size, so the school itself is the only reliable source. Some run the full continuum from the Primary Years Programme through to the Diploma on one site; others run the primary years and feed into a different school for the middle years. Company-community schools in the Eastern Province have historically concentrated on the younger years, with senior schooling meaning a move or a commute. Ask in writing which year groups will be running when your child reaches them, not only which run now.

faqs.question: Why is a Primary Years Programme specialist harder to find in the Kingdom than a Diploma one?
faqs.answer: Because of the hour rather than the subject. A Diploma student can take a lesson at half past seven in the evening, which suits tutors across most of the world. A primary child's window closes around six, which in Arabia Standard Time is the middle of the working day in Britain and Europe and mid-morning in North America. Any serving classroom teacher in those places is unavailable at that hour, so the pool narrows to the Gulf, Turkey, East Africa, South Asia and full-time tutors elsewhere.

faqs.question: What does a PYP school expect a family to arrange at home?
faqs.answer: More than most parents realise, and schools will tell you if asked directly. Reading aloud to an adult daily is the main one, because a class teacher with twenty-four children cannot hear each child read every day and a struggling decoder needs roughly that frequency. Number-fact practice is the second. Beyond those, schools expect the inquiry to be talked about rather than worked on: asking a child what they are investigating and what they have found is useful, and completing their task for them is not.

faqs.question: Our school teaches Arabic as an additional language and our child is behind. What should we do?
faqs.answer: Treat it as a frequency problem rather than a difficulty problem. Additional-language Arabic sits outside most expatriate families' home routine, so the only exposure is the school timetable, and that is rarely enough to build confidence. Short, frequent sessions work far better than one long weekly lesson here: fifteen or twenty minutes several times a week moves a child faster than an hour once. Ask the school which strand is weakest — spoken, reading or script — because the three need different work and families usually assume it is all three.

faqs.question: How does class size in a Saudi primary school affect how much individual attention a child gets?
faqs.answer: Directly and predictably. In a class of twenty-four, a teacher hearing each child read individually for three minutes spends over an hour doing nothing else, which is why individual reading happens weekly rather than daily in most settings. The same arithmetic applies to checking written methods. A child who is close to the middle of the class generally does fine on that; a child who needs daily correction of a specific habit is the one who falls through, and that is the gap outside support actually fills.

faqs.question: What are the options if our city has no inquiry-based primary school at all?
faqs.answer: Three, realistically. A national-curriculum or other private school locally with additional support at home for the things it does not cover. A move or a long commute to a city that has one, which some families do and most find unsustainable at primary age. Or local schooling plus one-to-one online teaching for the specific strands you want built. The last is the only one that does not require relocating a family, and in Yanbu, AlUla, Tabuk or Abha it is frequently the only realistic option.

faqs.question: What may a tutor do with a Year 6 exhibition, and what must they never do?
faqs.answer: A tutor may teach how to turn a topic into an answerable question, how to plan an inquiry, how to take notes in the child's own words, and how to present and handle questions afterwards. All of that can be taught on material unrelated to the child's own inquiry. A tutor must never choose the line of inquiry, find the sources, supply notes or shape the content of the presentation. The exhibition is assessed on the child's own thinking and the process behind it, so an adult who improves the output has removed what was being assessed.

faqs.question: How much help with a unit-of-inquiry research task is too much?
faqs.answer: The test is whether you could honestly say the child did this. Asking what they are trying to find out, where they might look and whether a source seems reliable is teaching. Opening the page, choosing the facts and dictating the sentence is not, even when it is faster and everyone is tired. A tutor working properly teaches the research method on a different topic and then steps back entirely, so that the child's own task is genuinely their own attempt, mistakes included.

faqs.question: Can a tutor work on a piece that is going into my child's PYP portfolio?
faqs.answer: Not on the piece itself. The portfolio exists to show what the child can do unaided over time, and an improved piece has lost its only function. What a tutor can do is teach the same skill on a different piece of work entirely: if the portfolio needs a paragraph with a topic sentence, teach paragraph structure on another paragraph and let the child write the portfolio one alone. We decline requests to tidy up a portfolio piece, including when they are framed as light proofreading.

faqs.question: How do I know a piece of my child's work is genuinely their own at this age?
faqs.answer: Ask them to explain it back to you a day later. A child who wrote something themselves can say what they meant and why they chose it; a child who copied an adult's sentence cannot, and the gap is obvious within a minute. The habit is worth building deliberately at primary level, because it is the same habit the Diploma relies on eight years later when a supervisor asks a student to talk about their own Extended Essay.

faqs.question: What should a tutor do when a child's homework is clearly beyond them?
faqs.answer: Tell the parent and the school, and not finish it. Homework that a child cannot access is information: either the classwork behind it did not land, or the task was misjudged, and both are things the class teacher needs to know. A tutor who completes it hides the signal and the child falls further behind next week. The right move in the session is to find the step the child is actually stuck on, teach that, and let the unfinished homework go back unfinished with a note.

faqs.question: What transfers when a child moves from a British primary school into the PYP in Year 4?
faqs.answer: Almost all the content, and very little of the working style. Numbers, reading and writing are broadly the same at this age across systems, so a child rarely arrives with a genuine knowledge gap. What changes is that the inquiry asks a child to ask and investigate rather than to complete a worksheet, and children used to finishing tasks can look lost for a term while they work out what is wanted. Teaching the research and note-taking skills explicitly shortens that term considerably.

faqs.question: Our child is moving from the PYP into Cambridge Year 7. What will they be missing?
faqs.answer: Not content, generally. What they will meet for the first time is a timetable of separate subjects with separate teachers, regular formal assessment, and more written output produced to a given structure. Children who come through the Primary Years Programme usually arrive strong on research, questioning and oral explanation, and less practised at writing a required format against a deadline. The summer before is the efficient time to build that, because nothing else is competing for the hours.

faqs.question: What happens to a child who has changed country twice before Year 5?
faqs.answer: Usually they are fine on content and carry a tangle of methods. Written subtraction taught one way, then another, then a third leaves a child who does not fully trust any of them, and the hesitation reads as weak arithmetic rather than as a method conflict. The repair is to pick one method, name it as the one we use, and drill it to fluency. That takes weeks rather than a term, and it is the most common single piece of work we do with a mobile primary child in the Kingdom.

faqs.question: Is it worth switching a child into the PYP for the last two primary years?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on where they go afterwards. Moving in for Years 5 and 6 and then continuing into the Middle Years Programme is coherent: the inquiry structure, the criterion-based thinking and the exhibition all feed forward. Moving in for two years and then switching to a British-curriculum Year 7 means two adjustments in three years for a ten-year-old, which is a lot of change for limited benefit. Decide the Year 7 destination first and let that decide the primary question, rather than the other way round.

faqs.question: Why can't our primary lesson be at half past seven like our older child's?
faqs.answer: Because the hour does not work at this age, not because the slot is unavailable. A seven-year-old at half past seven in the evening is tired, and the session produces a fraction of what the same session produces at half past four while a parent pays the same price. We schedule primary lessons at the start of the 4pm to 6pm window and senior lessons later, which is why two children in one household usually have slots two or three hours apart rather than back to back.

faqs.question: Can a tutor based in the United Kingdom hold a 4:30pm Saudi slot for a primary child?
faqs.answer: Only if they are a full-time tutor rather than a serving classroom teacher. Half past four in the Kingdom is half past one in the afternoon in Britain during their winter and half past two in their summer, which is the middle of a school day. A teacher currently in a classroom cannot hold it, however suitable they are. We pin the slot to Arabia Standard Time so that the tutor absorbs the twice-yearly clock change rather than your child's lesson drifting into the evening.

ib-pyp-tutor.closingHeading: Agree what will be counted, then book the hour
ib-pyp-tutor.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB PYP tutor in Saudi Arabia, start by deciding what would count as progress, because the Primary Years Programme will not hand you a grade to point at. Tell us the year group, the school and which part of the 4pm to 6pm window genuinely works once your child is home. The first session is free and is used to take the opening readings rather than to teach a sample lesson, and you keep those readings whether you continue or not. Lessons are one-to-one and delivered live online, Sunday to Thursday on Arabia Standard Time.
