ib-summer-tuition.tutorsIntro: These are the Diploma specialists families ask for when a block has to be booked early: subject teachers who can hold three mornings a week through a long break, and who mark a script between sessions.

intro.heading: A summer block is only worth buying if you can say what it moved
paragraphs: Start with the measurement, not the hours. A summer block of IB work has no examination at the end of it, which means the only honest way to judge it is to fix the evidence before it starts. That means a marked script going in — a past paper sat under time, marked against the published mark scheme, recorded question by question rather than as a total — and a second script of the same kind coming out at the end. A total of forty-two tells a family nothing. Four marks lost on every explain question, and eleven lost on the last two questions of the paper, tells a tutor what to teach.

The second thing to settle is what a summer can realistically move. Technique responds quickly: command terms, the shape of a six-mark answer, how working is set out so a marker can award method, what to do with the last fifteen minutes of a paper. Content breadth responds slowly, because it is volume and volume takes term time. A block pointed at technique on material the student has already been taught usually produces a visible change on the second marked script. A block trying to teach a whole Higher Level option from nothing in six weeks produces notes, and the family finds that out in the autumn term.

Then comes the week, which is the part most providers writing about the Kingdom get wrong. During term, schools run Sunday to Thursday and a lesson has to survive a late school run and the homework the school still expects to receive. Over the long summer break that constraint disappears for the family, and a mid-morning slot becomes the strongest one available: a teenager works better at ten in the morning than at eight at night, and the whole block can be timetabled on consecutive days so that one session builds on the last. The constraint does not vanish, though. It simply moves to the other side of the screen, where a tutor who was free on a Monday evening in the autumn term may be unreachable for six weeks in a row.

That is why availability, rather than price, decides most summer blocks in Saudi Arabia. Subject specialists spend parts of the break marking for boards, teaching their own schools' summer programmes, or taking the leave they have earned. The pool able to hold three fixed mornings a week for six consecutive weeks is much smaller than the pool able to take one evening lesson in the autumn term. Lessons are delivered live online, one to one, which is what makes a specialist in another country reachable at all — and it is also why the slot is written down in Arabia Standard Time rather than in anybody's local hour.

ib-summer-tuition.programmesIntro: Summer intensity is worth more at some stages than others. These are the three IB programmes a Saudi family buys holiday hours against.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led primary learning assessed by teachers against learning outcomes, with no external papers. There is no examination technique here for a block to compress.
programmes.countryNote: Riyadh and Jeddah families ask about holiday hours here after a move. Two short reading and number sessions a week do more than a block.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups marked against published criteria, plus the Personal Project in the final year. Criterion marking is learnable, so a block can target one criterion.
programmes.countryNote: The break before the last MYP year is the useful one. A student can learn to read a criterion descriptor before the Personal Project starts consuming the week.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher or Standard Level, Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and an internally assessed component in every subject. Written papers are sat in the May session.
programmes.countryNote: This is where summer blocks earn their money. The gap between the two Diploma years is long enough for timed rehearsal and marked homework without a school timetable competing.

ib-summer-tuition.subjectsIntro: A block needs a nameable target. These are the Diploma subjects Saudi families most often buy summer hours in, and what a holiday run rehearses in each.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Proof, calculus depth and the Paper 3 investigation at Higher Level. A block buys fluency with the formula booklet and working a marker can follow.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics carry the grade. Hours pay off on turning calculator output into a sentence a mark scheme accepts.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Marks leave in explanation chains and in uncertainty treatment, not in the algebra. A break is the time to rebuild the explanation habit.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Energetics and organic mechanisms are the usual repair jobs. The data booklet has to become fluent rather than merely allowed.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Volume disguises the real issue, which is command terms. Separating state, outline, explain and evaluate recovers known marks.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams must be labelled to a standard and evaluation earned rather than asserted. The commentaries remain the student's own work.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Unseen analysis under time pressure is the one thing a holiday run can rehearse repeatedly without the school's scheme of work.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: The source paper rewards provenance and the essay rewards argument rather than narrative. Both are practised on retired papers.

ib-summer-tuition.regionsIntro: Where a family spends the break changes a block more than where they live in term. These are the patterns that come up when a Kingdom-wide timetable is set.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: An hour across in traffic during term, which stops mattering in the break. Mid-morning slots are the easiest to hold here.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: A long coastal spine running north to Obhur. Heat pushes families indoors before noon, which suits a mid-morning session.

regions.name: Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran
regions.note: One school market across three cities. Many families leave for part of the break, so a block is planned in two halves.

regions.name: Makkah and Taif
regions.note: Makkah sits roughly 80km east of Jeddah, and Taif takes much of the region for the hottest weeks. A block has to survive the move.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: About 25km apart at altitude, sharing one catchment and a cooler summer. Families often stay, which makes a six-week run easy to hold.

regions.name: AlUla, Tabuk and NEOM
regions.note: Newer communities where a local Diploma specialist may not exist. Online delivery is the whole of the answer here, in the break and in term.

schoolClusters.note: Students we support over a long break attend schools including these. Each sets its own holiday dates, so read the family's own school calendar first.
Holiday dates differ between a British-curriculum school and an IB school in one city, so two siblings can be on different breaks. Plan around the later return.

modes.description: A two-week run at the end of the break, aimed at restarting work habits rather than repairing a grade. The cheapest block, and the likeliest to be free late.

sections.heading: What a summer block can be measured against
paragraphs: A summer block has no examination at the end of it, so the evidence has to be built in at the start. Sit a full past paper under timed conditions in the first session, mark it against the published mark scheme, and record the result question by question rather than as a total. The total is the least useful number on the page. Four marks lost on every explain question, and eleven lost on the final two questions, is a diagnosis a tutor can actually teach against.

At the end of the block, sit another paper from the same family under the same conditions and compare the two breakdowns. That comparison is the product. It shows whether the explain questions came back, whether the end of the paper is still being rushed, and which topics are still unreliable. It also gives the school something concrete in the autumn term, which matters when predicted grades are being discussed from classwork and mock performance rather than from a summer invoice.

The other half of the measurement is honesty about reach. Technique moves quickly because it is a small number of learnable habits. Content breadth moves slowly because it is volume, and volume needs term time. A block aimed at a whole Higher Level option that was never taught properly will produce a set of notes and very little else. A block aimed at the way answers are written will usually show up in the second marked script, and a family can see it for themselves.

sections.heading: The week the long break gives back
paragraphs: During term, a Saudi family has five usable evenings. Schools run Sunday to Thursday, Friday and Saturday are the weekend, and a weekday session has to sit after a school run and before the homework the school still expects to receive. That is why term-time slots cluster between seven and nine in the evening, and why a family trying to buy four sessions a week during term usually ends up cancelling one of them and paying for it anyway.

The long break removes that constraint, and the best use of it is a mid-morning slot. A teenager at ten in the morning is a different student from the same teenager at eight at night: attention holds for a full hour, timed work under exam conditions is possible, and homework set at eleven can be marked the same day rather than at midnight. Consecutive days also become available, which is what makes a short block cumulative rather than a series of unconnected lessons.

Public schools run by the Ministry of Education follow a two-semester year that ends in late June, while international and British-curriculum schools set their own calendars and most run three terms. Two children in the same Riyadh household can therefore be on different breaks, and the family's own school calendar is the only reliable source for either of them. Plan the block around the later return date, and read the published calendar rather than a regional summary of it.

sections.heading: Arabia Standard Time when the family travels and the tutor does not
paragraphs: Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not change its clocks. That single fact makes Saudi slots easier to hold than most, provided the slot is written down in Saudi local time rather than in the tutor's. A tutor in a country that moves its clocks twice a year absorbs the shift automatically if the agreement says ten in the morning Saudi time. If it says eight in the morning their time, the student quietly loses an hour twice a year.

A long break complicates this from the family's side rather than the tutor's. Families travel for part of it — to Taif, to Europe, to India, to a family home somewhere else entirely — and a slot pinned to Saudi time becomes an awkward hour in the place the student is actually sitting. The fix is to agree the travel weeks in advance and move the slot deliberately for those weeks only, rather than cancelling and hoping it is still there in the autumn term.

The table below reads the same ten o'clock Saudi start from the tutor's side, because that is the number deciding whether a specialist will commit to six weeks of mornings. Ten in the Kingdom is a civilised half past twelve in India and an early eight o'clock in the United Kingdom during their summer. It is three in the morning on the United States east coast, which is why that pool is not available for a morning block at all.

sections.heading: Why a specialist's break is harder to book than their term-time evening
paragraphs: Price is not what limits a summer block. Advertised rates published by tutoring companies in Riyadh start from around SAR 180 an hour for IB subject tutoring, with premium Higher Level tracks advertised at roughly SAR 200 to 220. Tutor-marketplace guides put general senior-school private tuition in the city above SAR 200, and budget online platforms advertise from around SAR 55 for non-specialist general tutoring. Those are other providers' advertised numbers, not a market average and not what any single family pays.

What moves the number is scarcity, and scarcity is what moves availability too. A Higher Level Physics or Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches specialist is scarce in every market at every time of year. In the break that pool shrinks further: some are marking for boards, some are teaching their own schools' holiday programmes, and some are taking the leave they are owed. A specialist who can hold three fixed mornings a week for six consecutive weeks is a narrow subset of an already narrow group.

The practical consequence is that a block is booked early or not at all. Families who settle the subject, the hours and the session times before the term ends get the specialist they asked for. Families who start looking in the second week of the break choose from whoever is left, which usually means a generalist. If nobody in the subject is genuinely free, the honest answer is to plan an autumn-term start rather than sell hours from a tutor who does not know the paper.

sections.heading: Reading the mock script before you buy any hours
paragraphs: The most useful document a Saudi family owns at the end of the school year is the last marked mock script, and most families have never read it properly. Ask the school for the script itself rather than the grade, and if question-level marks are available, ask for those too. Then look for the pattern instead of the total. Marks lost evenly across a paper point at a content problem. Marks lost on one command term in every question point at technique, and technique is the cheaper problem.

Three patterns come up repeatedly in Diploma scripts. The first is the unfinished paper: strong marks early, blanks at the end, which is a timing problem and nothing else. The second is the correct-but-unrewarded answer, where the student knows the material and has answered a different question from the one printed. The third is a collapse on one topic that reappears in every paper, and that is the only one of the three genuinely needing new teaching rather than new habits.

A tutor who reads the script first will tell a family which of the three they are buying and roughly how long it takes. Timing and command terms respond inside a six-week run. A missing topic takes as long as the topic takes. A weak foundation from two years earlier is a term-time project, not a holiday one, and any provider who agrees to repair it over a break is selling optimism rather than teaching.

sections.heading: Internal assessment work over a long break, and the line a tutor does not cross
paragraphs: Most Diploma students carry internally assessed work into the break: a scientific investigation, a mathematical exploration, an economics commentary, a draft of the Extended Essay. The break is when that work actually gets done, because term time is crowded and the school's own deadlines usually sit early in the following term. It is also when the temptation to buy a finished document is strongest, and the search results a parent lands on are full of providers who will quietly sell one. Knowing where the line sits is part of buying summer hours safely.

The line is simple and worth stating plainly. A tutor may teach the skills the task assesses, explain the criteria and what each descriptor asks for, discuss whether a research question is answerable, point at a flaw in a method, and give written feedback on a draft the student produced themselves. No tutor should ever supply text, data, analysis or a conclusion that then appears in assessed work. The work is the student's own, and the school will ask them to confirm exactly that.

There is a second reason beyond the rules. An internally assessed component is marked on the student's own thinking, and a document produced by somebody else reads like one. Supervisors see the gap between a polished submission and a student who cannot explain it, and a malpractice finding follows the candidate rather than the provider. Over a break, the honest version is slower, produces a weaker first draft, and ends in a better mark.

sections.heading: Handing the summer block over to the autumn term
paragraphs: A block that ends without a decision about the autumn term wastes most of what it built. The habits a six-week run installs — timed practice, marked homework, reading the question before answering it — decay within a month of a full school timetable returning. The handover is therefore part of the block, and it is agreed in the last two sessions rather than once the term has started and the specialist's evenings have already gone.

The handover has three parts. The second timed paper and the written comparison, so the school has evidence when predicted grades are discussed with the subject teacher. A decision on the term-time slot: whether the same subject continues weekly, whether a second subject takes its place, or whether the student carries on alone with a monthly review. And the slot itself, booked into a Sunday-to-Thursday evening before term-time demand arrives and the usable hours are taken by somebody else.

Families who stop entirely after a block are not making a mistake, provided they stop deliberately. A student whose timing problem was repaired may not need weekly teaching at all, and paying for one anyway teaches the student that somebody else owns the subject. What goes wrong is drifting: no second paper, no report, no decision, and a vague intention to restart if the first school assessment goes badly. By then the term is underway, the evenings are full, and the whole block is remembered as something that did not work.

process.title: Send the marked evidence
process.description: Share the most recent marked script and the school report before anything is booked. A mock paper with question-level marks tells a tutor more in ten minutes than a conversation does in an hour.

process.title: Free trial lesson
process.description: One session, no charge, with the specialist who would teach the block. The student does a short piece of timed work and the tutor explains where the marks went and why.

process.title: Agree the block in writing
process.description: Hours, weeks, subject, session times in Arabia Standard Time, and the two timed papers that will bracket the run. Settled before the first paid session rather than after it.

process.title: Close the block and hand over
process.description: A second timed paper, a written comparison question by question, and a decision about the autumn-term slot while subject specialists are still free to take one.

whyPoints.title: Specialists, not whoever is nearby
whyPoints.description: A block delivered online means the search runs across subject specialists rather than whoever lives within a reasonable drive of the family's district.

whyPoints.title: Morning slots while the school week is gone
whyPoints.description: The break frees hours a term-time slot can never have. A ten o'clock session is a different lesson from an eight o'clock one, and the homework shows it.

whyPoints.title: Slots pinned to Arabia Standard Time
whyPoints.description: The Kingdom does not change its clocks. Writing the slot in Saudi local time means a tutor whose country does change theirs absorbs the shift.

whyPoints.description: Availability over a long break is finite. If no specialist in the subject can hold the run, the better answer is to plan an autumn-term start.

faqs.question: How do we judge what an IB summer block achieved when there is no examination at the end of it?
faqs.answer: Bracket it with two timed papers from the same family, marked against the published mark scheme and recorded question by question. The first one, sat in the opening session, is the diagnosis. The second, sat in the closing session, is the evidence. Compare the breakdowns rather than the totals: command-term marks recovered, the end of the paper finished, topics still unreliable. That comparison is something a school can read in the autumn term.

faqs.question: Can a summer block change the predicted grade a Saudi school sets once the autumn term starts?
faqs.answer: Not directly. A predicted grade is the school's professional judgement, based on its own classwork, assessments and mock performance, and no outside tutor sets or negotiates it. What a block can do is change the evidence the school is judging. A student who comes back finishing papers and answering the question set produces better classwork, and that is what moves a prediction. Ask the subject teacher what evidence they weigh most.

faqs.question: Do command terms need teaching separately from content inside a six-week summer block?
faqs.answer: Yes, and separating them is usually the fastest win available. Students lose marks writing a correct answer to a different instruction: outlining when asked to explain, describing when asked to evaluate. An hour spent on what each term requires, followed by the same question answered twice, recovers marks the student already knows. Content teaching alone does not fix it, because the gap is between knowing something and being paid for it.

faqs.question: How does a tutor mark a summer past paper when the school keeps its own mark schemes?
faqs.answer: Retired papers and their published mark schemes are what a tutor works from, and they are enough. The school's internal assessments are its own, but the board's published schemes show the same command terms, the same mark allocations and the same accepted wording. A tutor who has marked for a board reads them differently from someone who has only taught the course, which is the difference families are usually paying for.

faqs.question: What does a summer diagnostic session cover that an end-of-year school report does not?
faqs.answer: A report gives a grade and a sentence of comment. A diagnostic gives a question-level account of where the marks went: which command terms cost marks, whether the paper was finished, which topics collapse under time, and whether the working would earn method marks if the final answer were wrong. It takes one timed paper and one hour of marking. The report tells you there is a problem; the diagnostic tells you which one.

faqs.question: How far into a summer block should a family expect the first written report?
faqs.answer: After the diagnostic session, not after a month. The first written note should name the subject, the paper, the marks lost by question type, the two or three things the block will target, and the homework pattern between sessions. Over a six-week run, waiting four weeks for a first report leaves no time to change anything. Expect a short written update each week after that, and a full comparison at the end.

faqs.question: What should a family do if a summer block is plainly not working by the third session?
faqs.answer: Say so immediately rather than at the end. Three sessions is enough to tell whether the student is engaging and whether the tutor has diagnosed the right problem. Ask for the marked homework and compare it with the diagnostic. If the tutor cannot name what has changed, change the tutor while weeks remain. A block is short; six weeks of a poor match leaves nothing to show the school in the autumn term.

faqs.question: Is the summer between the final MYP year and the first Diploma year worth buying hours in?
faqs.answer: It is, but for a narrower purpose than most families expect. Pre-teaching Diploma content rarely sticks before the course gives it a context. What does help is the step in writing demanded by Higher Level subjects: structured argument, handling a data set, setting out mathematical working so it can be followed. Two subjects, a handful of sessions each, aimed at writing rather than content, is the version that pays off.

faqs.question: What should a first-year Diploma student finish over the summer before the second year begins?
faqs.answer: Three things, in order. The internally assessed component that has already been set, taken as far as the school's deadline allows and written by the student. A clear plan for the Extended Essay, with a research question the supervisor has already questioned. And one weak subject rebuilt to the point where a timed paper is survivable. That ordering matters: internal assessment work left until the second year competes with revision and loses.

faqs.question: Does a Year 10 student gain anything from summer work before IGCSE teaching starts?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the test is whether the foundation is secure. Algebraic fluency, scientific notation, reading a question, writing a paragraph with evidence in it: weakness in any of these compounds across two IGCSE years. If the last school report flags one of them, a short run before the course starts is good value. If the report is solid, the hours are better saved for the term when real coursework begins.

faqs.question: Why is a specialist's summer availability harder to secure than a term-time evening slot?
faqs.answer: Because a block asks for far more of the week than a weekly lesson does, at the exact point in the year when subject specialists are least available. Some are marking for boards, some are teaching their own schools' holiday programmes, and some are on leave. Holding three fixed mornings a week for six consecutive weeks is a real commitment, and the pool able to make it is small. Book before the term ends.

faqs.question: Does a mid-morning session genuinely work better than an evening one while school is out?
faqs.answer: For most teenagers, yes, and the marked homework shows it. A full hour of timed work at ten in the morning holds attention in a way the same hour at eight at night does not, and homework set in the late morning can be completed the same day rather than after midnight. The gain disappears the moment the Sunday-to-Thursday timetable returns, which is exactly why the break is worth using.

faqs.question: How does a November-series candidate use the long break differently from a May-session one?
faqs.answer: The break sits much closer to the papers, so it is revision rather than rebuilding. A May-session candidate uses it to repair a weak topic with months of term time still ahead. A November-series candidate has weeks, so the block is timed papers, mark schemes and the two components carrying the most marks. Content left untaught at that point is usually better triaged than attempted. Confirm the entry window with the school's examinations officer.

faqs.question: Is six weeks of summer teaching long enough to rebuild a Higher Level topic taught badly?
faqs.answer: One topic, yes, if it is genuinely one topic and the student has the prerequisites. Thermodynamics, or a single calculus technique, or one organic mechanism family can be taught properly and rehearsed in that time. A whole Higher Level option taught badly across a year cannot, and a provider promising otherwise is selling hours. Name the topic, test it before and after, and keep the rest for term time.

ib-summer-tuition.closingHeading: Settle the summer block before the specialists are gone
ib-summer-tuition.closingBody: Send the last marked script and the school's holiday dates, and say which subject and how many weeks the family is in one place. A subject specialist takes a free trial lesson, reads the script, and says which of the three patterns it shows and whether a block can move it. Everything runs live online, one to one, at a time written in Arabia Standard Time. If no specialist in that subject can hold the run, you will be told rather than sold a generalist.

ib-tuition.tutorsIntro: Each tutor below is listed against the programme, subject and level they have actually taught, with the components they have marked or prepared students for. A family can interrogate every one of those claims using the questions in the table further down this page, and we would rather you did.

intro.heading: A dropped IB grade is usually a teaching mismatch, not a student problem
paragraphs: A student who was comfortable in the Middle Years Programme and is sliding in the Diploma has almost never stopped being capable. Something specific has gone wrong, and in our experience of enquiries from across the Kingdom it is one of four things. A Higher Level extension topic was taught thinly because the option group was small. A component is being prepared as though it were a different component, which is what happens to Paper 3 and to practical papers. An Internal Assessment was scoped in week one and capped from that moment. Or the student is answering a question the command term did not ask, and losing marks they are certain they earned.

Every one of those four is fixable, and every one of them needs a particular kind of person to fix it. That is the part families cannot easily see from the outside, and it is why this page is built around the tutor rather than around a price list. A graduate in chemistry is not the same as someone who has taught Higher Level Chemistry on the current syllabus. Someone who has taught the course is not the same as someone who has marked it against a published scheme. Both of those gaps are invisible in a profile photograph and obvious in ten minutes of specific questioning.

The Saudi market makes this harder than it needs to be. Rates are advertised with no explanation of what sits behind them, from about SAR 35 an hour on budget platforms to SAR 200 to 220 on listings that specify Higher Level work, and the number tells a parent almost nothing about whether the person can teach their child's paper. Several providers visible in search results for IB tuition in Saudi Arabia will also offer, with varying degrees of euphemism, to write coursework on a student's behalf. A family with no way to interrogate a claim is left choosing on price and on tone of voice.

So this page publishes the test rather than the sales pitch. There is a table of what each credential actually proves and what it does not. There is a table of six questions to ask before the first lesson, with what a strong answer and a weak answer sound like for each. There is a table showing why Higher Level and Standard Level are different teaching jobs subject by subject. Use all three on us, and use them on anybody else you are considering. A provider who cannot survive that conversation is telling you something useful at no cost.

The delivery model follows from the same logic. IB tuition for families in the Kingdom is delivered one-to-one over live video, on Arabia Standard Time, Sunday to Thursday. Nobody is sent to a Saudi address; in-home visiting is a service we run only in India. That is not a limitation dressed up as a feature. The set of people who can teach a scarce Higher Level course well is small in any country, and insisting they live within driving distance of Riyadh, Abha or Tabuk removes almost all of them. Teaching over video is what makes the match in this page's title possible at all.

One more thing, stated before you read any further. No tutor can promise a grade. Grade boundaries move between series, a predicted grade is a school's professional judgement rather than a forecast, and anyone offering a guaranteed seven is describing their marketing rather than your child. What a matched specialist can honestly do is tell you where the marks are going and teach the student to stop losing them, and show you the marked work that proves it.

ib-tuition.programmesIntro: The IB runs as a continuum, and the kind of tutor who suits each stage is different. Below is what each stage is assessed on and the specific thing to look for in whoever teaches it.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Assessed internally through units of inquiry, teacher judgement and the Year 6 exhibition, with no external papers anywhere in it. What to look for in a tutor is primary teaching experience rather than subject expertise. A physics graduate is the wrong person for a nine-year-old whose problem is place value and reading stamina, however patient they are, because the skill in question is diagnosing a procedural habit rather than explaining a concept.
programmes.countryNote: Primary Years Programme schools across the Kingdom draw children who have moved through two or three education systems before Year 5, often following a parent's posting between Riyadh, the Eastern Province and overseas. Ask a prospective tutor how they would find out which written method a child was first taught, because that question is the whole of the diagnosis at this age.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight, converted to a one-to-seven grade, with the Personal Project in the final year. What to look for is a tutor who can quote the criteria for your child's subject and say what each one rewards. Criterion-based marking is the thing students and parents most often misread, and a tutor who talks about it only in general terms has not taught it.
programmes.countryNote: Students arriving into the Middle Years Programme from a British or American school in the Kingdom meet criterion marking for the first time and are frequently baffled by a lower grade on work they consider stronger than last year's. Ask a tutor to explain why that happens. If the answer is about effort rather than about how the criteria are applied, keep looking.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three Higher and three Standard Level, graded one to seven, with Internal Assessment carrying roughly a fifth to a third of most subject grades. What to look for is specific: the subject, the level, the syllabus version and the component. A tutor who answers "I teach IB Maths" has not answered the question, because Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level and Applications and Interpretation at Standard Level share a name and little else.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma cohorts in most Saudi cities are small, and Higher Level option groups smaller still, so a student may be one of two or three people in the Kingdom sitting a particular combination. That is the common reason a family needs an outside specialist. Ask your school's Diploma Programme coordinator which Higher Level groups are smallest before subject choices lock.

programmes.name: The Diploma core: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS
programmes.description: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay together contribute up to three points through a published matrix, and Creativity, Activity, Service is a completion requirement rather than a graded one. What to look for is a tutor who teaches the assessment criteria and interrogates a student's own drafts, and who says clearly that they will not draft the work. The core is where the essay mills concentrate, so this is the sharpest test of a provider.
programmes.countryNote: The Extended Essay is supervised at school, and the supervisor certifies the work as the student's own. A tutor's honest role sits alongside that: teaching how a research question is narrowed, what the reflection requirement is for, and how to read a criterion. Any provider offering to produce the essay is proposing something that puts the whole Diploma at risk, not just one grade.

ib-tuition.subjectsIntro: Subject by subject, here is what the tutor actually needs to have taught. The pattern is consistent: the scarce thing is never the subject, it is the level, the option and the component.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The tutor must have taught Paper 3 at Higher Level, not merely covered the syllabus. Paper 3 is two unscaffolded extended questions worth a fifth of the grade, and the skill it tests is problem setup rather than technique. Ask a candidate to talk through the first ninety seconds of a Paper 3 question. Someone who has taught it will describe choosing and stating a model; someone who has not will start calculating.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Calculator-permitted throughout, built on modelling, statistics and interpretation in context. The tutor needs to have taught the interpretation habit, because that is where the marks are: a bare numerical answer with no statement of what it means in context scores a fraction of the available credit. The Higher Level course adds matrices and graph theory, which a Standard Level specialist may never have taught.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Ask which extension topics they have taught as content rather than as revision, and how far a derivation is expected to go in an extended-response answer. Those two questions separate a physics graduate from a Higher Level Physics teacher almost immediately. The data booklet is a working tool in this course, and a tutor who treats it as a reference sheet will leave a student slower in the examination than they need to be.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The tutor needs both the Higher Level content extension and the Internal Assessment criteria, because this is the subject where a strong candidate most often underscores on internally assessed work. Ask what makes an uncertainty treatment defensible at this level, and what they would say to a student whose research question cannot be answered with the apparatus available. Vague answers to either are disqualifying.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Examined on precision of language, which makes the tutor's own habits matter. Someone who speaks loosely about things moving into cells will teach a student to write answers that a mark scheme cannot credit. Ask how they teach a six-mark question, and listen for whether the answer involves counting creditable points against the marks available.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy decides more Economics marks than content does, and the Internal Assessment is three commentaries on published news articles with word limits. Ask the tutor what caps a commentary mark. If the answer is not about the link between the diagram, the article and the analysis, they have taught economics rather than this course.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Higher Level adds an extra approach, deeper research methods and a third paper. Ask which approaches they have taught and how they prepare the research-methods component, since that is what the Higher Level paper assumes. A tutor from a clinical or counselling background may know psychology thoroughly and have never taught the assessment structure this course is built on.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: The in-depth regional study at Higher Level is chosen school by school, so a tutor who has taught a different option has not taught your child's course. This is the clearest example on the whole page of why the question must be specific. Ask which prescribed subject and which regional option, then ask what a top-band source evaluation looks like in it.

subjects.name: French B and Spanish B
subjects.description: Language acquisition courses are assessed on task type and register, not on general fluency. A native speaker who has never taught the course will correct grammar and leave the marks on the table. Ask how they prepare the individual oral and what distinguishes a Higher Level written task from a Standard Level one; the difference is structural, not just longer.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Three assessed components, two of them internally assessed and heavily weighted, with strict requirements on how work is presented and documented. Ask the tutor how they would support the process portfolio without touching the student's own work, because the honest answer is narrow: teaching documentation, critical vocabulary and curation decisions, and nothing else.

ib-tuition.regionsTitle: Where in the Kingdom this matters most, and why the answer differs by city
ib-tuition.regionsIntro: The question behind an IB tuition search changes with the city. In Riyadh it is usually about finding the right specialist among several options; in a smaller centre it is about whether a specialist exists locally at all. Both have the same answer over video, for different reasons.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: The largest Diploma market in the Kingdom and the one with genuine local choice, which makes verification the whole task rather than availability. The city is roughly an hour across in traffic, so a family in the north and a family in the south have different evenings even with the same school.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: The second international-school market, skewing British and American, with smaller Diploma cohorts than Riyadh. A student taking an uncommon Higher Level subject here is often the only one in their year group doing it, which removes the study group as well as the specialist teaching.

regions.name: Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran
regions.note: One labour and school market behaving as a single conurbation, with families routinely living in one of the three and attending school in another. Diploma provision is concentrated in a few campuses, so option-group sizes rather than distance decide what a student can take.

regions.name: Jubail
regions.note: An industrial city with international provision including a Diploma campus, north along the coast from the Dammam cluster. Families here weigh a northward school commute against a southward one, and the Higher Level staffing question is the same as everywhere else on this coast.

regions.name: Al Ahsa
regions.note: Roughly an hour and a half inland from the Eastern Province cluster, which puts a Dhahran specialist out of reach for a weekday evening in person. For Higher Level subjects the local pool is thin enough that online teaching is not a preference but the only route to a specialist.

regions.name: Makkah and Madinah
regions.note: Both have international schooling, and both run academic years that bend around Hajj and Umrah seasons in a way other cities do not. Makkah sits roughly eighty kilometres east of Jeddah, so a Jeddah campus is a plausible commute and a Jeddah tutor is not a local one in any useful sense.

regions.name: Taif
regions.note: Up in the mountains above Makkah with a cooler climate and a smaller international cohort. Families here are used to travelling for specialist services of every kind, and the academic version of that problem is identical: the subject specialist is not in the city and will not be.

regions.name: Tabuk, NEOM and AlUla
regions.note: The north-west, where new communities are forming faster than school provision is. Mid-course arrivals are common, and a student may move into the Diploma part-way through from a completely different system. Online teaching reaches these addresses on the same terms as it reaches Riyadh.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: About twenty-five kilometres apart in 'Asir at altitude, sharing a catchment. Distance from the main international-school markets is the defining constraint, and families here ask the availability question rather than the verification question when they first make contact.

regions.name: Thuwal and the KAUST community
regions.note: North of Jeddah on the coast, serving a university campus community with unusually high academic expectations and a highly mobile population. Students arrive mid-course from everywhere, and the common request is a specialist who can audit what transferred from a previous system.

schoolClusters.note: Riyadh holds the Kingdom's widest set of IB provision, with schools running the Primary Years, Middle Years and Diploma programmes, some across the full continuum. Which Higher Level options actually run varies year to year with cohort size. Students we support attend schools including the following.

Jeddah's international schools lean British and American, with a smaller set offering the full IB continuum and a German-curriculum school running to Grade 12. The KAUST community north of the city at Thuwal has its own school serving the university campus.

The International Schools Group operates several campuses across the province, and the Diploma runs at some of them and not others. The British-curriculum schools here follow Cambridge. Confirm current programme provision with each school directly, because it changes with cohort size.

Sessions run sixty minutes for Middle Years work and seventy-five to ninety for Diploma candidates attempting whole papers. The tutor is named and their teaching history is specific enough to interrogate, which is the point of the whole arrangement rather than a detail of it.

We do not write, redraft or produce any part of an Extended Essay or a Theory of Knowledge essay, and we say no to that request in writing.
bullets: Criteria taught explicitly, with examples on topics the student is not assessed on
The research question narrowed before any writing begins
The student's own draft interrogated, never rewritten
Supervision at school remains the formal relationship

sections.heading: The four ways an IB grade slips, and the kind of tutor each one needs
paragraphs: The useful question is never "is my child weak at chemistry". It is which component the marks are leaving through, because the answer determines what kind of person you need. Lay out the last two marked papers, add up the marks lost per component, and the shape appears in twenty minutes. In almost every case it points at one of four patterns, and each of the four is a different hire.

The first pattern is a thinly taught Higher Level extension. A small option group gets the department's second specialist, or shares lessons with the Standard Level class, and the extension topics are covered at speed. This needs someone who has taught those specific topics as content, not as revision, and who knows how far a derivation or an evaluation is expected to go. A good general subject teacher cannot supply that, because the boundary of what is examinable is learned by teaching the course repeatedly.

The second is a component prepared as the wrong kind of component. Paper 3 is treated as more of Paper 2. A practical paper is revised as theory. A commentary is written as an essay. This needs a tutor who has prepared that component specifically and has its own past papers to hand, and the fix is usually short — four or five sessions, not a term, because the student already has the content.

The third is the Internal Assessment capped by its research question, which needs someone fluent in the criteria and willing to spend the first hour on the question before any data exists. The fourth is command-term failure, where a capable student answers a slightly different question from the one asked, and it needs a tutor who marks against published schemes rather than against their own sense of a good answer. Three of those four are technique rather than content, which is why diagnosis has to come before any purchase.
bullets: A thinly taught Higher Level extension needs taught content, not revision
A mis-prepared component usually needs four to six targeted sessions, not a term
A capped Internal Assessment needs the research question narrowed first
Command-term failure needs someone who marks against the published scheme

sections.heading: What a credential actually proves about an IB tutor, and what it does not
paragraphs: Every credential a tutor can show you proves something real and narrower than it appears. A subject degree proves command of the discipline well above Diploma level, which matters, and says nothing about whether the person knows what a mark scheme pays for. A teaching qualification proves trained classroom practice and general assessment literacy, and says nothing about this programme in particular. Years of IB teaching prove repeated exposure to how students fail, which is the single most valuable asset a tutor has — provided the years were recent and at the level in question.

Marking experience is the credential families understand least and should weigh most. A tutor who has applied a published mark scheme to real scripts under moderation has internalised the ordering of marks in an answer, and the teaching consequence is immediate: they interrupt a student mid-sentence to ask what the examiner will pay for next, rather than checking whether the final answer is right. Boards do not publish examiner lists, so there is no register to consult. What you can do is test it, and the table below says how.

At the other end, a platform profile with a photograph and a star rating proves very little on its own. It does not establish identity, subject match, syllabus currency, or that the rating was left by students taking the same course at the same level. Ask any platform, including this one, how a profile was verified and what the rating is calculated from. A provider who will not explain their verification process has told you what it is worth.

The practical conclusion is to stop treating credentials as a ranking and start treating them as claims to be tested. Each row of the table pairs a credential with the specific question that tests it. None of those questions is hostile, and a tutor who has done the job enjoys answering them, because they are the questions that distinguish them from a cheaper profile that looks similar from the outside.

sections.heading: Six questions to ask before the first lesson, and what the answers sound like
paragraphs: A trial lesson is usually wasted as an audition. The tutor arrives, teaches a topic they are comfortable with, and the student nods. Nothing has been established. Spend the first ten minutes on these six questions instead, and you will know more about whether this match works than an hour of demonstration teaching could tell you. They are published here deliberately so that you can use them on us.

Notice what the six have in common. Each one is answerable in a sentence by someone who has taught the course and cannot be answered convincingly by someone who has not. That is the whole design. A confident generalist will produce plausible, general answers: exam technique, past papers, building confidence. A course teacher will produce specifics with numbers and names in them: the weighting of a component, the topic students misread, the ordering of marks in a six-mark answer.

The sixth question is the one most providers will not answer at all, and it is the most informative. Asking a tutor what would make them tell you to stop forces them to state a condition under which they lose revenue. Someone who has a real answer — the component is fixed, the student has stopped doing the work between sessions, the problem turned out not to be academic — is describing a professional relationship. Someone who says they would continue as long as you wanted is describing a subscription.

Use the answers comparatively rather than as a pass mark. Two tutors can both answer well and suit different students: one is better with a confident candidate chasing a seven, another with a student who has lost belief in the subject. The questions filter out the mismatch; the trial session then tells you about the fit, which is the thing a conversation genuinely cannot establish.

sections.heading: Examiner experience: what it means, what it cannot mean, and how to test it
paragraphs: Examiner experience means a tutor has marked candidate scripts for an awarding body against its published mark scheme, usually as an assistant examiner working under a team leader with their marking sampled and moderated. The value is not inside knowledge of future papers, which nobody has and anybody claiming it is lying. The value is calibration. Someone who has marked two hundred scripts on the same question knows precisely which phrasings get credit and which near-misses do not, and that knowledge transfers directly into how they teach an answer.

There are things it cannot mean. It does not mean the tutor can predict what will appear on a paper. It does not confer authority over another subject or another level, and marking Standard Level scripts in one subject says nothing about Higher Level teaching in a different one. It does not mean the tutor is a better teacher than a non-examiner; marking and teaching are related skills, not the same one. And it is not an accreditation. No board publishes examiner lists, and no tutoring provider, including this one, holds any approval from the IB, Cambridge or Pearson.

Because there is no register, the claim has to be tested rather than verified. The test is simple and takes fifteen minutes. Give the tutor a piece of your child's marked work with the school's marks removed and ask them to mark it against the published scheme, then justify each decision. Someone who has done the job will award and withhold marks in a specific order and explain why a particular sentence did not qualify. Someone who has not will give an overall impression and a grade.

A second test is to ask what the most common avoidable loss is on a particular component. Examiners develop strong views about this because they see the same error hundreds of times in a single marking session, and those views are concrete: candidates omit the units, candidates evaluate without a criterion, candidates answer the first half of a two-part question. A vague answer here, from someone claiming marking experience, is the clearest signal available.

sections.heading: Higher Level and Standard Level are different teaching jobs, subject by subject
paragraphs: Families reasonably assume that Higher Level is Standard Level with more of it, and that a tutor who can teach one can teach the other. For most subjects that is wrong in a way that costs marks. The extension is not extra volume; it is different content, assessed in a different format, often in an additional paper, with a different expectation about depth. A tutor who has taught only the Standard Level course has never had to decide how far a Higher Level answer should go, and that judgement is exactly what the extension papers test.

Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches is the sharpest case. Higher Level adds Paper 3, proof, and a substantially larger syllabus, and the examination skill it demands — setting up an unscaffolded problem under time pressure — simply is not present at Standard Level. Physics and Chemistry add extension topics with no Standard Level equivalent at all. History adds a third paper on a regional in-depth study that is chosen school by school, so a tutor who taught a different option has not taught your child's course in any meaningful sense.

This has a practical consequence for how a family buys tuition. If a student needs support in two subjects, one at each level, it is usually two tutors rather than one, and that is not an upsell. The specialist who is excellent on Higher Level extension content is often not the best choice for a Standard Level student whose problem is confidence and pace, where a lighter touch and a wider view matter more than depth. Matching to the level is the single highest-value decision in the whole process.

The table below sets out, for the subjects we are asked about most, what the Higher Level extension adds, what the tutor must demonstrably have taught, and what a Standard Level specialist will miss. Use it as a checklist in the conversation. Every row is a question you can ask in under ten seconds and that a mismatched tutor cannot answer well.
