ib-tutor.programmesIntro: Four IB routes turn up in Saudi enquiries, and they fail in different ways. What follows is what each one asks a student to produce and what typically goes wrong with it inside the Kingdom.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: No examinations and no external marking. Units of inquiry run across subjects, and the final year closes with an exhibition where students research and present a question of their own. A parent judges progress by the quality of a child's reasoning and extended writing, because there is no paper mark to read.
programmes.countryNote: PYP enquiries in the Kingdom are rarely about grades. They are about an English reading level that is holding a child back in every other subject, or about written explanation that stops at one sentence. Both are worth fixing here rather than in Grade 9, where the same weakness reappears as an inability to develop a point.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each marked against four published criteria out of eight, reported as achievement levels rather than percentages. The Personal Project in the final year is assessed against its own criteria and moderated. The programme's real purpose, for a family thinking two years ahead, is teaching a student to write to a descriptor.
programmes.countryNote: The commonest Saudi MYP problem is a student scoring in the middle band everywhere with no identifiable weakness. That pattern almost always means criterion wording rather than content: the work is good and it is not answering the strand. It is the cheapest thing in the IB to fix and the one most often left until the Diploma makes it expensive.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects graded one to seven, usually three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. The core contributes up to three points through a published matrix. The award depends on a minimum total alongside published conditions covering low grades and the Higher and Standard Level halves of the programme.
programmes.countryNote: This is where nearly every Saudi enquiry sits, and the pattern repeats: a strong student, one subject below expectation, and an internally assessed component nobody in the building has marked before. The constraint is rarely teaching quality. It is that a school with one Diploma cohort cannot staff every Higher Level option it offers on paper.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme course candidates
programmes.description: Students registered for individual Diploma courses rather than the full Diploma, receiving certificates for the subjects they complete. The subject assessment is identical, papers and internally assessed component alike; what differs is that the core and the full six-subject structure do not apply.
programmes.countryNote: A useful route inside the Kingdom when a school cannot timetable a full Diploma, or when a student has arrived too late in the cycle to carry the core. It is also the route families understand least, so confirm with the school exactly what the student is registered for before planning support around it.

ib-tutor.subjectsIntro: These are the Diploma subjects most often requested from outside a Saudi school, described by the mark that goes missing rather than by the topic list. A tutor is being hired to close a specific gap, and naming it is the first half of the work.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Marks live in the working, not the answer. A correct result with an unshown derivative, an unjustified line or a missing condition collects a fraction of the credit on offer. The Higher Level content is a genuine extension rather than more of the same, which is why revising Standard Level harder never reaches it.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The calculator is part of the course, and the loss is interpretation. Students produce a regression line or a test statistic and stop before saying what it means in the context the question set. Statistical tests are quoted without their conditions, which is a predictable and teachable loss.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Definitions and uncertainty are marked strictly. A derivation that quietly assumes something, or a graph with no treatment of error, loses credit a confident student assumes is safe. The internally assessed investigation needs a question narrow enough to control with the equipment that actually exists.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Three habits decide the grade: calculation laid out in steps, mechanism reasoning written as a sequence, and precise language for energetics and equilibrium. Students who can state Le Chatelier's principle still lose marks by describing a shift without naming the change that caused it.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The highest-value skill is writing to the command term. Outline, explain and evaluate are three different jobs on the same content, and the same paragraph scores very differently against each. Data questions reward reading the axes and the units before reasoning about the trend.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: The evaluation half of every extended answer is where this subject is won and lost. A correct diagram with unlabelled axes and no stated shift scores poorly, and a well-argued answer with no judgement sits mid-band. Higher Level adds quantitative work that punishes loose definitions.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study discipline is the whole game. Students answer from theory and never return to the organisation in the stimulus, losing application marks they had effectively earned. The internally assessed work needs a real organisation and a question the available evidence can actually answer.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The paper asks how a text works on a reader, not what it says. Confident writers in English-medium schools often describe technique accurately and never connect it to effect, audience or purpose, which is exactly the move the mark scheme pays for.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: A language acquisition course with text types that have conventions of their own. A blog, a formal letter and a speech are partly marked on whether they look like themselves. Fluent speakers lose marks on register and format rather than on vocabulary.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: The choice between the A and the B course is one of the most consequential subject decisions in the Diploma and it is made early, often on fluency in conversation rather than on written evidence. A students analyse literature in Arabic; B students write in controlled registers.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Examined on paper, which surprises students who code comfortably. Pseudocode conventions, trace tables and written explanation of an algorithm carry the marks. The internally assessed solution needs a real client and success criteria agreed before any code exists.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS
subjects.description: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay contribute up to three points through the published matrix, and a failing grade in either is a condition that can cost the Diploma. CAS carries no points and is still required. The core is the single most postponed part of the programme.

ib-tutor.regionsTitle: Where Diploma families are in the Kingdom, and what each market can staff
ib-tutor.regionsIntro: Saudi Arabia is not one tutoring market. What a family can find locally differs sharply between a city with several Diploma cohorts and a town with none, and that difference is the practical reason outside support exists. Distance, not quality, is the constraint.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: The deepest international-school market in the Kingdom and roughly an hour across in traffic, which makes an in-home arrangement expensive in time before it is expensive in money. Even here the scarce Higher Level sciences and the Analysis and Approaches route are the subjects families end up sourcing from outside their school.

regions.name: Jeddah and the Red Sea coast
regions.note: A long coastal spine from the historic centre north to Obhur, with several established international schools and The KAUST School further north at Thuwal. The Jeddah difficulty is less about availability and more about a school run that crosses the whole city before a lesson can start.

regions.name: Dhahran, Dammam and Al Khobar
regions.note: One conurbation behaving as a single school and labour market, with families routinely living in one city and schooling in another. Compound and camp schooling shapes the week here, and not every campus running international curricula runs the Diploma.

regions.name: Jubail and Yanbu
regions.note: Industrial cities with international provision built around the plants and their workforce. Subject choice narrows quickly at Higher Level because cohorts are small, which makes the course-candidate route and outside subject support more common than they are in Riyadh.

regions.name: Makkah and Taif
regions.note: Makkah sits roughly 80km east of Jeddah and Taif climbs into the hills beyond it. Families here often look to Jeddah for international schooling, and the commute is the reason a weekly online slot holds better across a year than any travelling arrangement.

regions.name: Madinah
regions.note: A growing private sector with very little international provision at Diploma level, so families work around a school that teaches the national curriculum plus a handful of international subjects. Jeddah is about two hours away on the Haramain line, which is a real but heavy option.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: Two 'Asir cities about 25km apart at altitude, sharing a catchment and a thin specialist pool. This is where the honest argument for online teaching is strongest: the nearest Higher Level Physics specialist may be several hundred kilometres away in any direction.

regions.name: Tabuk, NEOM and AlUla
regions.note: The north-west is where mid-course arrivals cluster, as families relocate for new projects and heritage development. Students arrive part-way through a Diploma with subjects already started elsewhere, which makes an audit of what transfers the first piece of work.

regions.name: Al Ahsa and Qatif
regions.note: Al Ahsa sits about ninety minutes inland from the Eastern Province cluster, with Qatif on the coast between Dammam and Ras Tanura. Both are close enough to the cluster for a school commute and far enough that an evening in-home tutor arrangement rarely survives a full year.

regions.name: Buraidah, Ha'il, Jazan and Najran
regions.note: Provincial cities where international-curriculum provision is limited and a Diploma cohort may not exist at all. Enquiries from here are frequently about covering a whole subject rather than topping one up, which needs a different frequency and a syllabus checklist from the start.

schoolClusters.note: The Kingdom's largest concentration of IB World Schools, listed in directories as running the Primary Years, Middle Years and Diploma Programmes across different campuses. Students we support attend schools including these. Named here as context for a family comparing options, with no affiliation implied or held.

schoolClusters.city: Jeddah, Thuwal and the western region
schoolClusters.note: Jeddah carries both Cambridge and IB provision, with long-established international schools serving expatriate communities and The KAUST School north of the city at Thuwal. A family in Makkah, Taif or Madinah comparing schools is usually comparing options on this list.

The International Schools Group runs several campuses in the province and the Diploma is offered at some but not all of them, which is a distinction worth confirming before enrolling. British and Cambridge curricula are also well established around Dhahran.

sections.heading: The six places Diploma points actually go missing
paragraphs: Before buying anything, find the leak. Diploma marks are lost in a small number of recurring ways, and each has a different fix, a different cost and a different urgency. Treating them as one problem called 'needs a tutor' is how families spend a term on content teaching and watch the same mark come back.

The first and largest is the command term. Both the IB and its mark schemes are explicit about what each instruction demands, and an answer written to the wrong one is a good answer to a question nobody asked. The second is internally assessed work that describes rather than evaluates, which is the single most common criterion failure across every subject group. The third is paper timing, where a student who could have answered the last question never properly reaches it. The fourth is the core, postponed into the second year and then colliding with paper practice. The fifth is a Higher Level choice that was wrong at the point it was made. The sixth is a foundation gap from the year before the Diploma, usually algebraic, which surfaces as an apparent weakness in a topic that is really arithmetic in disguise.

Each of these is diagnosable from the student's own work, usually in a single session, and the diagnosis matters more than the hours bought afterwards. A student losing command-term marks needs four of their own answers taken apart against four instructions. A student with an algebra gap needs that gap closed, not more practice in the topic where it showed up. A student whose core is late needs a schedule, not a lesson. The table below pairs each failure with what it costs and what actually fixes it.

The reason to start here rather than with a price list is that the fixes differ by an order of magnitude in effort. Two of the six are short blocks of a few sessions. Two are a term of weekly work. One is a decision rather than teaching, and one may mean reconsidering a subject at Higher Level. Buying a year of weekly lessons without knowing which of the six you are dealing with is the most expensive mistake available in this market.

sections.heading: Fix one: command terms, the cheapest marks in the Diploma
paragraphs: The IB publishes its command terms and its mark schemes are built on them. State, outline, describe, explain, analyse, evaluate, justify, discuss, compare and contrast, deduce and show that are not interchangeable. Each one tells the examiner what to look for and tells the student how many distinct moves the answer needs. A student who answers an evaluate question with a thorough explanation has produced good work that the mark scheme cannot pay for, because the judgement it required is absent.

The pattern is easy to recognise once a parent knows to look for it. Marks cluster in the middle band across subjects. Teachers write that the student knows the material. Short-answer questions go well and extended responses do not. That combination is almost never a content problem, and it is almost always worth a grade band in a Diploma where the same instructions appear in every subject's papers.

The repair is short and it is specific. Take four of the student's own answers written to four different instructions, put the published mark scheme beside each, and have the student rewrite one. Most students see the pattern in the first session and need two or three more to make the new habit survive under timed conditions. This is the highest return available on a tutoring hour in the Diploma, and it transfers across every subject they take, which is why it is the first thing a good tutor does rather than the last.

It is also the thing a general tutor most often misses. Somebody teaching the subject from a textbook will correct the physics and leave the structure of the answer untouched, because the structure looks adequate. Somebody who has marked papers reads the same answer and sees four separate marks that the student has already earned and will not be given. That is the difference families are buying when they pay for marking experience, and it is worth asking about directly.
bullets: Describe asks for features; explain asks for a mechanism; evaluate asks for a supported judgement
Mark schemes pay for development, not for the same point restated in new words
Middle-band marks with strong content is the signature of a command-term problem
Four of the student's own answers diagnose it faster than any placement test
The habit transfers to every subject, which is what makes it the cheapest fix available

sections.heading: Fix two: internally assessed work, done so that it counts and stays honest
paragraphs: Every Diploma subject carries internally assessed work that the teacher marks against published criteria and the IB moderates. It is the part of the grade a student has the most control over, and it is where points are lost most quietly, because nothing about it happens in an examination hall. The commonest failure is the same in every subject group: the work describes a process accurately and never evaluates it. The second commonest is a question too broad for the evidence available, which guarantees a weak conclusion no matter how good the work that follows.

The right support is early and it is narrow. The research question or the investigation focus has to be interrogated before any data is collected, because an unanswerable question cannot be rescued later by effort. Then each criterion gets read as written: not as a general standard of quality, but as a description of what distinguishes one band from the next. A student who can say which criterion a given paragraph is serving is writing to the task. A student who cannot is writing an essay and hoping.

The limits here are not ours and they are not negotiable. A tutor may teach the skills the task needs, question a research question, explain a criterion, point out that a conclusion evaluates nothing, and give feedback on a draft the student has written themselves. A tutor may not write any part of an assessed piece, may not rewrite a paragraph into better English, and may not supply a structure the student fills in without understanding. Work produced by somebody else is academic misconduct, the school is required to act on it, and the consequence lands on the student rather than on whoever typed it.

Several pages competing for this search offer the opposite in plain language. It is worth being clear about what that trade actually is: a family buys a better-looking draft and takes on a risk that sits entirely with their child, in a system where the penalty can reach the award of the Diploma. The honest version is slower and it is the only one that leaves the student able to do the same work alone, which is what the papers will ask of them a few months later.

sections.heading: Fix three: paper timing, and the questions nobody reaches
paragraphs: A surprising share of lost marks belong to questions the student could have answered. They ran out of time, or they spent eleven minutes on a four-mark question because it was interesting, or they wrote a full introduction to an extended response that the mark scheme awards nothing for. Timing is a learnable skill and it is almost never taught directly, because it looks like something that sorts itself out with practice. It does not. Students practise the way they already work, and repeat the same distribution of time in the real paper.

The method is mechanical. Work out a time budget per mark for each component, practise under it, and stop the student at the budget rather than when they finish. Then read what the interruption cost: whether the answer was nearly complete or barely started tells you whether the problem is speed, planning or knowledge. Most students discover the problem is planning, and that an extended response written from a thirty-second plan beats one written from a two-minute introduction.

Paper order matters too, and it is a personal decision rather than a rule. Some students should start with the question type they are strongest at to bank marks and settle their nerves. Others should take the heaviest extended response first while they are fresh, because it carries the most marks and suffers most from fatigue. Either strategy beats working through the paper in the order it was printed without having decided anything, which is what most students default to.

This is also the fix with the shortest timescale, which makes it the sensible choice for a family starting support late. A student eight weeks from a series cannot build a Higher Level foundation, but they can change how they spend three hours in a hall, and that routinely moves marks. It is the one intervention whose value increases as the series gets closer rather than decreasing.

sections.heading: Fix four: the core, counted backwards from the school's deadlines
paragraphs: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay contribute up to three points through a published matrix, and a failing grade in either is a condition on the award of the Diploma. CAS carries no points and is still required for the award. Those three sentences explain why the core is the most dangerous part of the programme: it is the part with the least weekly homework pressure and the highest tail risk, which is exactly the combination that gets postponed.

The practical failure is scheduling rather than ability. A student who settles an Extended Essay question in the first year, drafts through the quieter weeks and submits on the school's internal deadlines carries nothing into their final term. A student who leaves the question open into the second year is drafting an essay in the same weeks they should be doing timed papers, and both pieces of work suffer. The decisive variable is when the question was settled, not how clever the essay is.

Theory of Knowledge fails differently. Students treat the essay as an opinion piece and lose marks for an argument with no counter-position, or they write about knowledge in general terms without anchoring the discussion in specific examples. The exhibition rewards precision about objects and prompts that students often skip past. Neither problem is about intelligence, and both respond to a few focused sessions with somebody who has read the assessment instruments.

Build the schedule by working backwards from the school's own internal deadlines rather than from the external ones, because the internal dates are the ones a student is actually judged against day to day, and they are earlier. Ask the Diploma coordinator for them in writing at the start of the year. A family who has those dates on a wall has already removed most of the risk in the core without buying a single lesson.

Ask the coordinator for internal deadlines in writing and work backwards from them

CAS carries no points and can still block the award, so it needs a calendar of its own

sections.heading: Fix five: the Higher Level choice that was wrong, and the mathematics route behind it
paragraphs: Some underperformance is not a teaching problem at all. It is a subject at Higher Level that should have been Standard Level, or the wrong mathematics route chosen for the degree the student is aiming at. These decisions are made early, often on a conversation rather than on evidence, and they are expensive because they shape two years of work and the offers a student can reach at the end of it.

The mathematics decision is the one worth the most attention. Analysis and Approaches is the algebraic route, built on proof, calculus and function work. Applications and Interpretation is the modelling and statistics route, with technology integrated into the course rather than tolerated. Both exist at Higher and Standard Level, and both are respectable. They are not interchangeable for university purposes: engineering, physics, mathematics and many economics courses are more likely to expect Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level, while courses in the social sciences, business and design frequently accept either. The only reliable source for a given course is that university's own stated requirements.

The review itself is simple and uncomfortable. Look at the first year's marks subject by subject, separate the subjects where technique is the problem from the subjects where the content is genuinely out of reach, and ask whether a change is still administratively possible. Schools can often move a student between levels or routes early in the programme and rarely late. A student carrying one Higher Level subject they cannot reach is also losing marks in the other five, because of where their time goes.

Where a change is no longer possible, the honest conversation is about damage limitation and the published conditions on the award, not about a miracle. A tutor who tells a family in the second year that a wrong Higher Level choice can be fully recovered is selling something that does not exist. What can be done is to secure the points the student can reach, protect the subjects that are working, and make sure the core is not also at risk.

sections.heading: What fixing each of these costs in this market
paragraphs: Now the money. Every figure in this section is a rate somebody else advertises, named with the kind of source that publishes it. None of them is a market average, because no regulated average exists, and none is what IB Gram charges. They are useful for one purpose: working out whether a quote you have been given is high for a reason.

The spread is wide. General online tutoring with no subject specialism is advertised from around SAR 55 an hour, and budget platforms quote IGCSE one-to-one from as little as SAR 35. Tutor-marketplace guides put general private tuition for a primary child at about SAR 50 and senior-school examination subjects at 200 and above. Tutoring companies list IB subject tutoring from around SAR 180, with Higher Level and premium tracks at roughly SAR 200 to 220. International providers quoting in dollars sit around sixty dollars an hour, which is a different budgeting problem because the figure moves with the exchange rate rather than with the teaching.

What moves a number inside that range, in order of weight: subject scarcity, marking or examining experience, level, travel and package length. Scarcity dominates everything else. A Higher Level Physics or Analysis and Approaches specialist is priced above a Standard Level generalist in every market in the region because the number of people who can genuinely do the work is small. Travel is the one loading online teaching removes entirely, which is why published in-home rates in the larger Saudi cities carry a premium that buys nobody any extra teaching.

Two questions turn a price list into a decision. Ask what this particular rate is high for, and expect a specific answer: scarcity, examining experience, or a commute built into the hour. Then ask what the hour includes, because marking written work between lessons, reading a draft against published criteria and writing a note to the parent either sit inside the rate or they do not, and across a term that difference is larger than the difference between two hourly numbers.

sections.heading: What a Saudi school can staff, and what it usually cannot
paragraphs: Private and international schools in the Kingdom are licensed by the Ministry of Education, and school evaluation and accreditation run through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission. ETEC operates services for national school accreditation and for the approval of international accreditation bodies. What that system tells a parent is whether a school is permitted to operate and how it has been evaluated as an institution. What it cannot tell a parent is whether one subject at Higher Level has a specialist teacher this year, which is the question that actually determines a grade.

The gap between those two things is the whole reason outside support exists here. A school with one Diploma cohort may list eight Higher Level options and timetable five, depending on which subjects got enough candidates. A teacher may be genuinely strong at Standard Level and have never taught the Higher Level extension. A school entering candidates through an examination centre may be well organised on the written papers and have limited laboratory access for the internally assessed investigation. None of that is a scandal and all of it is survivable, provided the family knows before the entry window rather than after it.

Ask specifically. Which Higher Level subjects are running this year, and who teaches each one. Who supervises the Extended Essay, and how many essays are they supervising. Where does the internally assessed investigation get done, and with what equipment. What are the internal deadlines for each component. Schools answer specific questions honestly; general ones produce reassurance. Get the answers in writing, because a Higher Level option withdrawn in the autumn term after numbers fall changes a student's position materially and early action is the only cheap response.

Compound and camp schools add a second variable. A school serving a company community has a cohort shaped by its workforce, which can make a subject group unusually strong one year and absent the next. Families in those communities often have the best informal information in the Kingdom about which subjects are genuinely taught well, and it is worth asking other parents before asking the school.

sections.heading: Switching into the Diploma from another curriculum
paragraphs: Relocation inside and into the Kingdom is constant, and a large share of Diploma enquiries come from students who did not start the programme where they are finishing it. The switches that matter are four: national curriculum into an international programme, British into IB, American into IB, and IB into IB across countries. Each loses something different, and knowing which one you are dealing with saves a term.

A student from a British school usually arrives with strong subject depth in three or four areas and no experience of breadth, the core, or criterion-marked internal assessment. The content shock is small and the structural shock is large: six subjects, a Theory of Knowledge course, an Extended Essay, and a mark scheme that pays for evaluation rather than coverage. A student from an American school arrives with the opposite profile: comfortable with breadth, continuous assessment and coursework, and often short of the depth a Higher Level science or mathematics course assumes from its first week. A student from the national curriculum arrives with real mathematical fluency and an unfamiliar assessment language, and the first job is translation rather than teaching.

Timing decides what is recoverable. A switch before the Diploma begins is a planning exercise. A switch early in the first year is manageable with an audit and some catch-up teaching. A switch in the second year is difficult, because internally assessed work begun elsewhere may not transfer cleanly, the Extended Essay may need rescuing, and the student is learning a new assessment language while sitting mock papers in it. That is when the course-candidate route becomes worth discussing with the school rather than dismissing.

The first piece of work is always an audit, not a lesson: what has been covered against the published syllabus, what assessed work exists and in what state, which command terms and criteria the student has never seen, and what the new school can actually timetable. Everything else follows from that document. Families who skip it end up paying for teaching in the subjects that feel urgent rather than the ones that are.

sections.heading: What to ask a prospective IB tutor, and what a good answer sounds like
paragraphs: Families in this market are usually choosing between providers whose claims cannot be checked. Percentages of students improving, star ratings, counts of tutors and success rates are all self-reported, and none of them carries a sample size, a date or a method. The only reliable filter available to a parent is the quality of a tutor's answers to specific questions, and those questions are easy to ask.

Ask which level and which route the tutor has taught, not which subject. Ask whether they have marked for a board, and what that taught them about where candidates lose marks; somebody who has marked will answer with a specific, slightly unflattering observation about typical candidates, because that is what marking is like. Ask them to name the components of the course from memory. Ask what they would do in the first month, in order. Ask, on internally assessed work, exactly what they will and will not do. Then ask the one that separates teachers from salespeople: having seen my child's two marked papers, where are the marks going?

A good answer is specific and slightly deflating. It names a component, a pattern in the work, and a sequence to address it, and it says what will not be possible in the time available. A poor answer talks about confidence, potential and personalised plans without naming a single part of the course. Both answers can come from a well-presented company, which is why the question has to be about this student's work rather than about the provider.

Finally, ask what happens if the match is wrong. A tutor and a student can simply not work together, and the honest arrangement allows for a change after a lesson or two without a penalty. Any provider who treats that as an unusual request is telling you something about how often it comes up.

process.title: Name the leak, not the subject
process.description: Tell us the subject, the level, and what the marks look like: short answers fine and extended responses weak, a late exploration, a mistimed paper, a whole subject untaught. The diagnosis determines the shape of the support, and getting it right at this stage saves a term of general lessons.

process.title: Send two pieces of marked work
process.description: A marked paper and a piece of internally assessed work in progress tell a tutor more in ten minutes than any conversation. They show whether the loss is content, structure or the command term, and those three problems have three entirely different fixes and three different timescales.

process.title: Meet a matched specialist in a free trial lesson
process.description: The trial is a working session. The tutor should name the components of the course, say where this student is losing marks, and set out what the first month covers in order. If the conversation stays on motivation and potential without naming a component, ask for a different tutor.

process.title: Pin the slot to Arabia Standard Time
process.description: Agree the weekly time in Saudi local terms, in writing, so a clock change in the tutor's own country cannot move it. Four weekday evenings are genuinely available against a Sunday-to-Thursday school week, and a fixed slot survives a term far better than a flexible one.

process.title: Review against components, then decide
process.description: After a month, measure progress against parts of the course: a paper type, a criterion, a topic, a timing budget. Components are visible and confidence is not. If the agreed thing has not moved, change the approach or the tutor rather than buying more of the same.

whyPoints.title: Diagnosis before purchase
whyPoints.description: The first session works from the student's own marked papers to establish which of the recurring failure points is actually in play. Families regularly discover the problem is three sessions of command-term work rather than a year of content teaching, and that is a cheaper answer than the one they came for.

whyPoints.title: Matched on level and route, not subject name
whyPoints.description: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, Applications and Interpretation at Standard Level and a course candidate in the same subject need three different teachers. We match on the registration the school has actually made, which is why the first question is the level and the route.

whyPoints.title: Rates named with their sources
whyPoints.description: Every SAR figure on this page is a rate another company advertises, attributed to the kind of source that publishes it, so a family can see the spread and interrogate a quote. We do not publish a market average, because none exists, and we do not present anybody else's rate as ours.

whyPoints.title: The core treated as a deadline problem
whyPoints.description: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay are scheduled backwards from the school's internal dates rather than left until the second year. That removes most of the tail risk in the Diploma, including the conditions on the award that have nothing to do with subject grades.

whyPoints.title: Assessed work stays the student's own
whyPoints.description: A tutor questions a research question, explains a criterion, points out an unevaluated conclusion and gives feedback on drafts the student has written. No part of an assessed piece is produced for them. The limit is stated to the family in the first session and recorded in the session notes.

whyPoints.title: No claims that cannot be checked
whyPoints.description: No grade guarantees, no success percentages, no ratings, no tutor headcounts, and no suggestion that any board or Saudi authority endorses us. IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform with no affiliation to the IB, Cambridge, Pearson, the Ministry of Education or ETEC.

faqs.question: Why can a Saudi school offer the Diploma and still not run the Higher Level subject my child needs?
faqs.answer: Because a timetabled class needs enough candidates to justify a teacher, and a school with one Diploma cohort rarely has that in every option it lists. The subjects that lose their class are the ones with the fewest students, which tend to be the minority Higher Level sciences, the less-chosen languages and sometimes a mathematics route. It is a staffing arithmetic problem rather than a comment on the school. Ask in the year before the Diploma starts which Higher Level options are actually running and who teaches each, and get the answer in writing so a later withdrawal is visible early.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a school's ETEC evaluation and the subject qualification of a tutor?
faqs.answer: They answer different questions. The Education and Training Evaluation Commission evaluates and accredits institutions, and operates services covering national school accreditation and the approval of international accreditation bodies. That tells a parent how a school has been assessed as an organisation. A tutor's subject qualification, teaching level and marking experience tell a parent whether one person can teach one syllabus at one level. A well-evaluated school can still be unable to staff a particular Higher Level option this year, and no institutional evaluation speaks to that. Both pieces of information are useful and neither substitutes for the other.

faqs.question: How does the Ministry of Education license private and international schools, and what does that tell us as parents?
faqs.answer: Private and international schools in the Kingdom operate under licence from the Ministry of Education, with evaluation and accreditation running through ETEC. The licence establishes that a school is permitted to operate and under what terms, which is genuinely important when comparing schools. What it does not establish is this year's subject-level staffing: who teaches the Higher Level extension of a science, how many Extended Essays one supervisor is carrying, or whether the laboratory access needed for an internally assessed investigation exists. Ask to see the licence, then ask the subject-level questions separately, because the second set is what determines a grade.

faqs.question: Our school runs the Middle Years Programme but stops before the Diploma. What do families in that position usually do?
faqs.answer: Three routes, in rough order of frequency. Some move to a school that runs the Diploma, which often means another city and is the largest intervention. Some stay and switch to a Cambridge or Pearson route for the final two years, which needs fewer specialist staff and can be examined through an examination centre. Some stay and register as course candidates for individual Diploma subjects where the school can support them. The decision turns on what the student is aiming at afterwards, so work backwards from the universities under consideration and check their stated requirements before choosing.

faqs.question: How do schools on a company compound or camp differ from city schools for a Diploma student?
faqs.answer: The cohort is shaped by the workforce rather than by the city, which cuts both ways. Community stability is high, the informal information parents hold about which subjects are taught well is usually excellent, and the school run is short. Subject breadth is the weak point: a subject group can be strong one year and absent the next, depending on who is posted in and out. For a Diploma student the practical step is to ask other parents in the community which Higher Level options have run consistently, then confirm with the school before subject choices are locked.

faqs.question: What should we ask a school about Higher Level subject availability before enrolling a Diploma student?
faqs.answer: Five questions, in writing. Which Higher Level subjects ran in each of the last two cycles. Which are confirmed for the coming one, and at what minimum candidate number a class is withdrawn. Who teaches each Higher Level option and what level they have taught before. Who supervises Extended Essays and how many each supervisor carries. Where internally assessed investigations are carried out and with what equipment. A school that answers all five specifically is a school that has thought about it; vague answers to specific questions are themselves information.

faqs.question: What exactly may an IB tutor do with a draft of my child's internal assessment?
faqs.answer: A tutor may read it, question the research question, explain what a criterion is asking for, point out that a conclusion describes rather than evaluates, identify a method problem, and give feedback the student then acts on themselves. A tutor may not write any part of it, may not rewrite a paragraph into better English, and may not hand over a structure to be filled in. The test a family can apply is simple: if the student cannot explain out loud why a paragraph changed, the help went too far. Keeping the drafts and the session notes makes that easy to demonstrate.

faqs.question: How many drafts of an Extended Essay can a student reasonably have reviewed?
faqs.answer: The school's own policy governs this and it is the one that counts, so ask the coordinator rather than a tutor. The IB's framework centres on the student's own work with formal supervision at defined points, and schools differ in how much additional feedback they treat as acceptable. What matters more than a number is the nature of the feedback: comments that name a kind of problem teach the student something, and comments that fix each instance do the work for them. Agree the position with the school in writing early, then keep every draft so the progression is visible.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help choose an internal assessment topic without crossing into misconduct?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is one of the most valuable things a tutor does. Discussing possible areas, explaining what makes a question answerable with the evidence available, and warning that a topic is too broad are all teaching. Handing a student a ready-made question and a plan is not, because the choice and the reasoning behind it are themselves assessed in most subjects. The useful version of this conversation is a tutor rejecting three of the student's four ideas and explaining why, leaving the student to sharpen the fourth into something they can defend as their own.

faqs.question: What happens if a school suspects an internal assessment is not the student's own work?
faqs.answer: The school is required to act, and the process runs through the school to the IB rather than through the tutor. Outcomes can include the piece not being accepted, a mark of zero in that component, or a wider malpractice finding, and consequences can extend to the award of the Diploma. The person who wrote the work faces nothing. This asymmetry is the reason to be precise about boundaries from the first session: keep drafts, keep session notes, and make sure the student can explain every part of their own argument without help.

faqs.question: Can an IB tutor proofread assessed work before my child submits it?
faqs.answer: This sits in a genuine grey area and the school's policy decides it, so settle it with the coordinator rather than assuming. The defensible version names the kind of problem rather than fixing the instance: telling a student that three consecutive paragraphs open with the same construction teaches them to vary it, while rewriting those paragraphs does the work and teaches nothing. Correcting language line by line on a piece that assesses written communication is where the risk lies. Ask the school what language support it considers acceptable, in writing, and keep to that.

faqs.question: How do we keep a record showing the Extended Essay is genuinely our child's own work?
faqs.answer: Keep the trail. Dated drafts, the reflection work the school requires, notes from supervision meetings and a short record of what each tutoring session covered together form a convincing history of a piece of work developing. Research notes and discarded avenues help as much as the drafts, because a real research process leaves dead ends behind it. The simplest test remains the strongest: a student who can talk through why the argument changed between drafts owns the essay, and that conversation is one a parent can have at the kitchen table.

faqs.question: Where does the school's supervision end and tutoring begin on the Personal Project?
faqs.answer: The school supervises: it assigns a supervisor, holds the formal meetings, and marks the project against its criteria before moderation. A tutor sits outside that and works on the skills the project needs, which are mostly about narrowing a goal, planning realistically and writing a process journal that evidences the criteria rather than narrating the week. The project is assessed on the student's own process, so a tutor who shapes the product rather than the skills is actively harmful. Tell the supervisor that outside support is in place; schools generally prefer to know.

faqs.question: We are moving from a British school into the Diploma. What is the hardest part of that switch?
faqs.answer: Not the content. The structural change is what costs marks: six subjects instead of three or four, a Theory of Knowledge course with its own way of arguing, an Extended Essay, and internal assessment marked against published criteria rather than against a general sense of quality. Students accustomed to demonstrating coverage write thorough answers that sit mid-band because the mark scheme pays for evaluation. The first term should be spent on command terms, criterion wording and the core schedule, which is cheaper and more effective than content teaching the student probably does not need.

faqs.question: What does an American-curriculum student have to build to cope with Higher Level sciences?
faqs.answer: Depth and examination endurance. Students arriving from a continuous-assessment system are usually comfortable with coursework, breadth and regular submission, and short of the mathematical and conceptual depth a Higher Level science assumes from its first weeks. Two things need front-loading: the algebra and graph work the subject leans on constantly, and practice at writing long answers under time pressure to a command term. Both are teachable in a term if the work starts at the beginning of the Diploma rather than when the first mock paper arrives.

faqs.question: Can a student join the Diploma a term late, and what gets lost?
faqs.answer: It happens regularly with relocations and it is workable early in the programme. What gets lost is rarely content, which can be covered, and usually progress on internally assessed work plus the Extended Essay question, which carry deadlines that do not move for a late arrival. The first task is an audit: what the previous school covered against the published syllabus, what assessed work exists and in what state, and what the new school can timetable. Join late in the second year and the conversation shifts to the course-candidate route, which the coordinator can explain.

faqs.question: What happens to coursework a student completed at a school in another country?
faqs.answer: It depends on the component and on how far it had progressed, and the Diploma coordinator at the receiving school is the only person who can answer definitively. Work that was already complete and moderated is in a different position from a half-finished exploration using data from a laboratory the student no longer has access to. Ask the question in the first week rather than the first term: if a component has to be restarted, the student needs that time. Carry copies of everything, including notes and raw data, because recreating evidence later is far harder than moving a file.

faqs.question: How long does it take a student to adjust to IB command terms after switching curriculum?
faqs.answer: Most students recognise the pattern within a session or two and need around a term for the new habit to survive timed conditions. Recognition is fast because the problem is obvious once a mark scheme sits beside their own answer; the habit is slower because old writing patterns return under pressure. Deliberate practice closes it: a handful of their own answers rewritten against the published instructions, then timed questions where the first move is to identify what the instruction is asking for. Done early in the first year, this is the cheapest marks a switching student will ever gain.

ib-tutor.closingHeading: Find the leak before buying the hours
ib-tutor.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB tutor in Saudi Arabia, the most useful hour is the first one, and it should start with your child's own marked work rather than with a syllabus. Send a marked paper and whatever internally assessed work exists, say which subject and which level, and a matched specialist will tell you in a trial lesson whether the marks are going on content, on structure, on the command term or on the clock. Those four problems have four different fixes, four different timescales and four different costs. Lessons run one-to-one over live video, pinned to Arabia Standard Time and built around the Sunday-to-Thursday week.

ib-tutor-fees.heroSubtitle: IB tutor fees in Saudi Arabia are quoted as a single number and almost never explained. The number is really a description of who is on the other end of the call: how scarce their subject and level are, whether they have marked for the board, and which version of the subject guide they have actually taught. This page puts the advertised SAR bands in a table with their sources, sets out the five things that move them, and gives you the questions that tell you what a quote is buying. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video.

ib-tutor-fees.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach named IB courses at a named level. Fees in this market track scarcity more than anything else, so the honest way to read a quote is to ask how many people could have taught that exact course, and then to ask the tutor the questions further down this page.

intro.heading: The fee is a description of the tutor, not of the subject
paragraphs: Published rates first, since that is why most people arrive here. Advertised rates for IB subject tuition in the Kingdom start at about SAR 180 an hour on tutoring-company listings. Higher Level and Advanced Placement routes are advertised nearer SAR 200 to 220. Tutor marketplaces quote general senior-school private tuition in Riyadh at SAR 200 and above, and primary-stage tuition at around SAR 50. Non-specialist general online tutoring is advertised from about SAR 55, and budget online platforms advertise IGCSE support from as little as SAR 35. Some international providers quote in dollars, around USD 60 an hour.

Every one of those numbers is an advertised rate published by the provider or the marketplace itself. None of them is a market average, none of them has been audited by anybody, and none of them is what IB Gram charges. We publish them because a parent cannot judge a quote without a reference range and nobody in this market will supply one. Read them as a shop window, not as a transaction, and read the spread rather than any single line.

A spread from SAR 35 to SAR 220 for what looks like the same hour is not a quality ladder. It is almost entirely a statement about who is available to teach the thing. A great many people can take a willing student through a Standard Level statistics topic. Very few can take a Higher Level Physics candidate through an extended-response question and explain, in mark-scheme language, why a physically correct answer scored two marks out of five. The second person is rare, and the fee is what rarity costs.

That is why this page is organised around the tutor rather than around the price list. The useful question is never 'is SAR 200 a lot?' It is 'what does the person charging SAR 200 know that the person charging SAR 90 does not, and how do I find out before I pay for a term?' Those questions have concrete answers: which board and which version of the subject guide they have taught, which components they have marked and in what capacity, how many students they currently carry in that exact course, and what they say when asked where candidates lose marks in a specific paper.

Two structural facts about the IB make the scarcity real rather than rhetorical. A Higher Level course is built on roughly 240 recommended teaching hours against about 150 at Standard Level, and Higher Level carries components Standard Level does not sit, including a third paper in both mathematics routes. A tutor who has only taught Standard Level has not taught a third of the Higher Level course, however well they know the subject. Fees that do not distinguish between the two levels are usually priced for the easier one.

Delivery is online, one-to-one, over live video, with the tutor's screen shared so papers, mark schemes and working are visible on both sides. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in Saudi Arabia; home visits are a service we offer only in India. That is not a limitation dressed up as a feature. Travel is a real line in an in-home quote, a cancelled visit still costs somebody the journey, and the pool of people who can teach a scarce Higher Level course inside a twenty-minute drive of your district is usually empty.

ib-tutor-fees.programmesIntro: Fees differ by programme because the teaching differs, not because one stage is more valuable than another. These four are where the hours go, and the note under each explains what a family in the Kingdom is actually buying at that stage rather than what the programme is for.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus the core. This is where almost all paid tutoring in the Kingdom goes, and where the fee spread is widest. The gap between a Standard Level humanities hour and a Higher Level science hour is the clearest illustration of scarcity pricing anywhere in the market: same student, same week, very different pool of people able to deliver it.
programmes.countryNote: In the Kingdom the Diploma years also carry the equivalency and Qiyas work in the background, which families frequently fail to budget for because it is not a subject. Preparation for Tahsili is a separate strand from subject tuition and it is priced separately wherever it is offered at all. Plan the two as different lines in the same budget rather than discovering the second one in the final year.

programmes.name: The Diploma core: Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge, CAS
programmes.description: The core carries Diploma points through the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay matrix, and both written components are marked against published criteria. Support here is billed by session rather than by term, because the work comes in bursts around drafting deadlines. It is also the part of the market with the most dishonest offers in it, since an essay is easier to sell than a term of teaching.
programmes.countryNote: What a family should pay for here is criterion teaching and feedback on the student's own drafts: stress-testing a research question, explaining which band a draft currently sits in, and setting the next revision for the student to make. We do not write, redraft or supply text for an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay or any assessed work, and the student is told that directly. Any provider quoting a price per essay in this market is quoting for something else.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Assessed against published criteria rather than a terminal paper, finishing with the Personal Project. Hours here are cheaper per unit and better value per mark eventually gained, because the work is foundational: algebraic fluency, writing to a command term, reading a question properly. None of that is glamorous and all of it is cheaper to fix at thirteen than at seventeen.
programmes.countryNote: Families in the Kingdom often arrive at these years mid-course after a relocation between Riyadh, Jeddah and the Eastern Province, and the first thing worth paying for after a move is a baseline rather than lessons. Two campuses running the same programme can be a term apart in coverage, and paying for general support without knowing which topics are missing wastes most of the money.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led primary teaching with no external examination, ending in the exhibition. Advertised primary tuition rates in Riyadh sit around SAR 50 an hour on marketplace guides, well below the IB subject bands, because the teaching requires a good primary practitioner rather than a subject specialist. That is a genuine difference in the labour market and not a discount.
programmes.countryNote: The primary enquiries we take from the Kingdom are mostly about an upcoming transition rather than a current problem: a move into an international-curriculum school, or a relocation to a city with a different provision. Written English and number fluency are the two things worth buying at this stage, and one or two sessions a week across a term does more than any intensive block.

ib-tutor-fees.subjectsIntro: Fees track the size of the pool able to teach a course, so this list is ordered roughly by how scarce the specialist is rather than by how popular the subject is. The note under each one is about who can teach it, which is what a quote is actually describing.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The scarcest common request in this market, and consistently the dearest. The Higher Level extensions have no Standard Level counterpart, and the teaching demand is as much in the written answers as in the problem-solving. A tutor who can explain why a physically correct extended response scored two out of five is doing something a physics graduate cannot necessarily do, and that is the premium in the quote.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The algebraic route, and the one most engineering and physics courses expect. Higher Level carries a third paper that Standard Level does not, and it is a distinct skill rather than more of the same, so it needs its own teaching time. A tutor who has taught only the Standard Level course has not taught Paper 3, and the fee should reflect which of the two they have actually delivered.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and equilibrium are where outside teaching earns its fee, and the internally assessed investigation is where families most often buy time they could have had free from the school. Definitions are marked strictly, so part of what a good tutor sells is vocabulary discipline rather than chemistry, which parents rarely expect and which moves marks quickly.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The modelling and statistics route with technology permitted throughout. The pool of tutors is wider than for the analysis route, which shows up in the quotes, but Higher Level here is not a soft option and the written justification carries real weight. Ask specifically which route a tutor has taught; the two share a name and very little else.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: A broad pool of tutors and therefore the more modest end of the IB fee range, which misleads families into buying content revision. The marks are usually lost on long-answer technique and on data questions about unfamiliar experiments, so the hour that changes a grade is a technique hour, and a cheaper tutor who only teaches content is poor value at any price.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Written papers plus an internally assessed portfolio of commentaries built from published news articles. Evaluation is the Higher Level dividing line and it is the part most candidates practise least. A tutor billing for content teaching in Economics is usually billing for the easy half; ask what proportion of sessions will be spent on marked evaluation writing.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Application to the organisation in front of the candidate decides the band, not recall of the tools. That makes the subject unusually responsive to a small number of well-marked sessions, which is worth knowing before agreeing a long block. Fees here sit in the middle of the IB range because the teaching pool is reasonably deep.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Guided textual analysis, a comparative essay and oral work, with an additional written task at Higher Level. Analysis of how a text works, rather than what it says, is the trainable skill and the one that separates the bands. Beware a quote from someone who teaches English generally rather than this course: the assessment model is specific and the oral components are easy to under-prepare.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Popular, content-heavy and frequently taught in schools by a non-specialist, which pushes it into the outside market more often than its difficulty warrants. The marks are in the use of studies as evidence for an argument, not in how many studies a candidate can name. A tutor who tests that distinction in a trial lesson is worth the fee.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: A narrow pool of tutors who can teach both the programming and the written paper, which keeps quotes at the upper end. Students who code confidently often write poorly about what they have coded, and the paper marks the explanation. Pseudocode discipline and trace tables are the quickest available gains, and neither requires an expensive specialist to deliver.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: A smaller cohort subject, which cuts both ways on fees: there are fewer tutors, and the ones who exist are often teaching it alongside Biology or Geography. Ask whether they have taught this course specifically, because the systems approach and the way the paper rewards it are not shared with either of its neighbours.

ib-tutor-fees.regionsIntro: Advertised rates in this market are mostly Riyadh rates, because that is where the in-home trade is largest and where the marketplaces collect their figures. The notes below are about what each city does to a quote, which is useful even where lessons are delivered online, because the in-home alternative is what a family is comparing against.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: The reference market for every published figure on this page. Senior-school examination subjects are quoted here at SAR 200 and above by marketplace guides, and the city is roughly an hour across in traffic, so an in-home quote is pricing a journey as well as an hour of teaching.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: A long coastal spine from the historic centre north towards Obhur, which makes travel loading on a visiting arrangement unpredictable rather than merely expensive. Families here commonly compare an in-home quote against an online one and find the gap is mostly the drive.

regions.name: Dhahran
regions.note: Compound and camp living adds access time to any visit, so a visiting tutor prices in a gatehouse as well as a journey. The International Schools Group operates several campuses in the region, and families often want a specialist for a subject their campus covers thinly.

regions.name: Al Khobar
regions.note: The King Fahd Causeway links the city to Bahrain, and families here genuinely do compare provision and prices across the water. An online arrangement priced in SAR and pinned to Arabia Standard Time removes both the crossing and the currency question from the decision.

regions.name: Jubail
regions.note: An industrial city where parental rotation rosters, not traffic, decide what a schedule can hold. A fixed visit is the first thing to break against a roster, and a cancelled visit is the line in an in-home fee structure that families understand least until it happens.

regions.name: Al Ahsa
regions.note: Roughly ninety minutes inland from the Eastern Province cluster, which is far enough that an in-home quote either includes a substantial travel charge or does not exist for the subject in question. This is where the fee comparison stops being about money and becomes about availability.

regions.name: Thuwal
regions.note: The KAUST School serves the university campus community north of Jeddah. A visiting tutor needs campus access, and the cohort is highly mobile, so families here buy targeted catch-up work on named topics far more often than they buy a year of general support.

regions.name: Tabuk, NEOM and AlUla
regions.note: The thinnest provision in the Kingdom and effectively no local in-home market to quote against. Families relocating here part-way through a Diploma have one practical option for a scarce Higher Level subject, and the fee conversation is about hours needed rather than rate compared.

regions.name: Makkah
regions.note: Roughly 80 km east of Jeddah, with a school calendar that bends around the Hajj and Umrah seasons in ways a published term list does not fully show. Blocks agreed for the quieter weeks of a term hold better than blocks booked week by week.

schoolClusters.note: Riyadh holds the broadest IB provision in the Kingdom, which is also why the published fee figures come from here. Students we support attend schools in this cluster. The useful thing to ask a school is which Higher Level subjects it will actually staff with a specialist next year, because that is what decides whether you need an outside tutor at all.

The KAUST School serves the university campus community at Thuwal. In the Eastern Province the IB Diploma is offered at the American School of Dhahran and at ISG Jubail rather than across every campus, while British School Dhahran and Multinational School Dhahran follow British and Cambridge curricula. Provision shapes demand, and demand shapes the local fee.

The British International School of Jeddah is both an IB World School and a Cambridge school, which makes it one of the clearer places to see the two routes priced side by side in the same city. Several other long-established international schools sit along the coastal spine, and the commute between them affects what a visiting tutor charges.

ib-tutor-fees.modesIntro: Four arrangements cover nearly every IB enquiry, and they are priced differently because the work is different. All four run one-to-one over live video, with slots written in Arabia Standard Time so a tutor abroad changing their own clocks does not move your lesson.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one, billed by block
modes.description: The default and the best value per mark gained. A fixed weekly slot across a term, with a block of hours agreed up front and a review at the end of it. Blocks exist so the tutor can plan beyond the next session and so progress can be measured against a baseline, which a lesson-by-lesson arrangement never allows.

modes.title: A single diagnostic session
modes.description: One session whose only output is a written baseline: what is secure, what is missing, and which of the lost marks are technique rather than content. Families who buy this first spend less overall, because the two diagnoses lead to completely different plans and budgets and nobody can tell them apart from a conversation.

modes.title: Internal Assessment and core review sessions
modes.description: Short sessions on the student's own draft, billed individually because the work arrives in bursts around deadlines. The tutor teaches the criteria, explains which band the draft sits in and why, and sets the next revision for the student. No text is written, supplied or redrafted on the student's behalf, and the student is told so at the start.

modes.title: A pre-series intensive
modes.description: A compressed block before the May session, built on past papers and mark schemes rather than new content. Rates advertised close to a series reflect demand rather than quality, so the calendar matters more than the quote: a block booked in the autumn term gives you a choice of tutor, and the same block booked late gives you whoever is free.

sections.heading: What IB tutor fees actually look like in the Kingdom
paragraphs: The table below is every advertised SAR rate we could attribute to a source type, ordered from the cheapest claim to the dearest. It exists because the alternative on offer in this market is 'contact us for pricing', which is not information. Each figure is published by the provider or the marketplace that collected it, which means it is marketing. It is still the only reference range a parent has, and a reference range is what makes a quote interrogable.

Three things stand out in the spread. The low end, from about SAR 35 to SAR 55, belongs to platforms selling general or budget tutoring rather than named-syllabus teaching; the figure describes a business model, not a level of expertise. The middle, around SAR 180 to SAR 200, is where IB subject tuition and senior-school examination work actually sit. The top, about SAR 200 to 220, is Higher Level and Advanced Placement work, where the pool of people able to deliver it is genuinely small.

The right-hand column matters more than the price column. What a quote excludes is where families get surprised: marking between lessons, Internal Assessment feedback, written reports to the family, whether Higher Level is billed differently from Standard Level, and what happens to the fee when a session cannot run. A provider who can answer all five is quoting for a service. A provider who answers none is quoting a number that will move.

One note on the dollar line. International providers quoting around USD 60 an hour are quoting a figure that moves with the exchange rate and often arrives with a card charge on your statement. That is not dishonest, but it makes a year of weekly lessons harder to budget than the same arrangement priced in SAR. Ask to be quoted in riyals if the arrangement is going to run for a term or more.

sections.heading: What moves the fee, and how a family checks each claim
paragraphs: Five things move an IB tutoring fee in any market, and they do not carry equal weight. Scarcity of the subject and level does most of the work. Marking or examining experience comes next, and it is the one premium genuinely worth paying for. Whether the tutor travels comes third and is entirely avoidable. Package length and the proximity of a series come fourth. Qualification in the subject comes last, not because it is unimportant but because it is a floor rather than a differentiator.

Each of those is checkable, which is the point of the table. The questions in the right-hand column are deliberately narrow, because a narrow question is hard to answer impressively without the underlying experience. 'Do you have examiner experience?' invites a yes. 'Which board, which component, and in what capacity?' invites either a precise answer or a retreat, and both outcomes are useful inside a trial lesson.

The question that reveals most is the one about current students. A tutor carrying several candidates in the same course this term is inside the current guide, knows what schools are doing with it, and has recent marked work in their head. A tutor who taught the course two guides ago can still be excellent, but their past-paper library is partly obsolete and their sense of what examiners currently reward is secondhand. Fees rarely distinguish between the two, so the family has to.

What should never move a fee is a claim about the outcome. No tutor, however well they know a mark scheme, can guarantee a grade, and a quote that leans on an improvement rather than on the work is selling something it cannot deliver. The same applies to percentages, star ratings and headcounts offered without a sample size, a date or a method. Treat all of them as marketing and price the teaching instead.
