sections.heading: Examiner experience: the one premium worth paying, and how to test it
paragraphs: Of all the things that raise a quote, marking experience is the one that reliably buys something a family cannot get elsewhere. A tutor who has marked a component has read several hundred answers to the same question and knows what the scheme credits, what it tolerates and what it quietly ignores. That knowledge is not in the textbook, it is not in the subject guide, and a student cannot infer it from a published mark scheme, because a mark scheme describes the target and not the common near-misses.

It is also the claim most often asserted and least often evidenced in this market, which is why the price attached to it needs testing. The useful questions are narrow. Which board. Which component, by paper number. In what capacity, and how recently. A precise answer is checkable in the sense that it is internally consistent and specific enough to be awkward to invent; a vague answer about extensive examining experience is a sentence rather than a credential.

Then test it functionally, inside the trial lesson, with one question: where do candidates lose marks in this paper? Somebody who has marked it answers with patterns. They will say that candidates describe when the command term says explain, that the second half of a six-mark question is routinely left blank because of time rather than knowledge, that units go missing under pressure, that a correct method with a transcription error loses more than students expect. Those are marking observations. They cannot be improvised.

A final caution on how to value it. Marking experience raises the ceiling of what a tutor can teach; it does not substitute for having taught the current course. The best combination for a Diploma candidate is somebody who has both delivered the present guide and marked a component of it, and that combination is what sits at the top of the advertised range. Where you can only have one, ask which matters more for the problem you actually have: a student who cannot do the content needs a teacher, and a student losing marks on work they know needs a marker.

sections.heading: A degree in the subject, and what it does not tell you
paragraphs: Every provider in this market leads with qualifications, and a degree in the subject is worth having. It is also the weakest predictor of a good IB tutor among the things a family can check, because it answers a question nobody is asking. The student does not need someone who knows more physics. They need someone who knows the examined physics, in the form it is examined, and who can see from a written answer which of a dozen specific habits is costing marks.

The gap shows up fastest in the core components and the internal assessment. A chemistry graduate without teaching experience will often give excellent scientific advice on an investigation that scores poorly, because the criteria reward things the research itself does not: the framing of the question, the treatment of uncertainty, the evaluation. The same is true of an Extended Essay supervised by somebody who knows the field and not the criteria. The work gets better and the grade does not.

Three questions separate subject knowledge from course knowledge quickly. Which version of the subject guide have you taught, and what changed in the one before it? Which internally assessed components have you given feedback on, and against which criteria? And what are the three places this syllabus differs from the way the subject is taught at university? A tutor with course knowledge enjoys all three questions. A tutor with only subject knowledge changes the subject.

None of this argues for hiring somebody unqualified. It argues for reading the qualification as a floor and then paying for what sits on top of it: delivery of the current guide, experience with the internal assessment, and marking exposure. That stack is what the upper end of the advertised range is for, and it is why two tutors with identical degrees can reasonably quote fees eighty riyals apart.

sections.heading: Higher Level against Standard Level, and why the fee gap is real
paragraphs: Families often assume the Higher Level premium is a markup on the same work. It is not. A Higher Level course is built on roughly 240 recommended teaching hours against about 150 at Standard Level, so there is substantially more course to cover inside the same two years. Higher Level also carries components Standard Level does not sit, and in both mathematics routes that includes a third written paper which examines problem-solving as a distinct skill rather than as more of the same content.

The extension material is the part that gets rushed. Because it sits at the end of most schemes of work, a school running slightly behind delivers the Higher Level extension in the final term, which is also when mocks and internal assessment deadlines land. That timing, not the difficulty, is why Higher Level extension topics dominate requests for outside teaching in the second Diploma year, and why they are the most expensive thing to buy late.

There is also a supply-side reason the gap is real. The pool of tutors who have delivered the Higher Level course, as opposed to knowing the subject at that level, is markedly narrower. A tutor who has taught Standard Level for years has genuinely not taught a third of the Higher Level syllabus or any of its additional components. When a quote does not distinguish between the two levels, the safest assumption is that it is priced for the Standard Level work.

Before using the fee gap as a reason to drop a subject to Standard Level, check what the level is for. Where a university course requires a subject, it usually requires it at Higher Level, and some competitive programmes are explicit about it. Dropping a level to save on tuition can close a course two years later, which is a far larger cost than the one it avoided. Read the university's own published prerequisites, and read them before the decision rather than after.

sections.heading: What the fee should buy between the lessons
paragraphs: An hourly rate invites a family to think they are buying hours, and the hours are the smaller half. What changes a mark is the work done between sessions: written work set, collected, marked against the published scheme, annotated, and then used as the agenda for the next lesson. A tutor who arrives, teaches well for sixty minutes, and leaves with nothing to mark is selling a tutorial. Useful, but not what moves a grade over a term.

Ask explicitly what is included, because this is where identical-looking quotes diverge most. Marking of written work between lessons. Feedback on Internal Assessment drafts, and how many. A written report to the family, and how often. Past papers and mark schemes supplied, or expected from the school. Access to ask a question between sessions, or not. A provider at SAR 200 including all five may be better value than one at SAR 140 including none, and you cannot see that from the rate.

Reports are worth a separate paragraph because they are where a family's money becomes visible. A useful report names topics and marks: this question type went from two out of six to five out of six, these two topics are still unsecured, this is the plan for the next four weeks. A report that describes effort, engagement and a positive attitude is a customer-service document. It tells you the sessions are pleasant and nothing about whether they are working.

The same logic applies to the diagnostic at the start. A baseline built from marked questions, separating missing content from lost technique, is the thing everything afterwards is measured against. It usually costs one session and it reliably saves more than that, because the two diagnoses lead to different plans at different prices. Families who skip it tend to buy a term of general support for a problem that was six weeks of technique work.

sections.heading: The trial lesson as a fee decision, not a sales call
paragraphs: A free trial lesson is standard across this market and it is usually wasted, because families treat it as a chemistry test between tutor and student. Rapport matters, but it is not the expensive thing. The trial is the one hour in which you can establish, at no cost, whether the fee being quoted corresponds to the knowledge being claimed. Use it as an interview with a demonstration attached.

Insist the trial runs with the tutor who would actually teach, not with a coordinator or a stand-in, and insist the student works on something real rather than on a prepared showcase. A recent piece of marked schoolwork is ideal, because it gives the tutor something to diagnose and gives you something to compare their diagnosis against. If the school has already identified the problem, you can see whether the tutor finds the same one.

Then ask the four questions that price the hour. Which version of the subject guide have you taught? Which components have you marked, for which board, in what capacity? How many students are you carrying in this exact course this term? And where do candidates lose marks in the paper my child is weakest at? The last question is the single best predictor of the next six months, and it costs nothing to ask.

Listen for specificity rather than fluency. The answer you want names topics, question types and command terms. The answer that should worry you, however warmly delivered, is about confidence, motivation and building a strong foundation. Both tutors will be pleasant. Only one of them has read a few hundred scripts and can tell you what the examiner was looking at. Decide on that, and the fee becomes a straightforward judgement rather than a guess.

sections.heading: When a cheaper non-specialist is the right call
paragraphs: Not every problem needs the top of the range, and a page about fees that only argues upwards is not being honest. There are several situations in which the cheaper option is the correct one, and recognising them saves real money. The test is always the same: is the thing that needs fixing specific to this course, or is it underneath the course?

The clearest case is a foundation gap. A Diploma physics candidate who cannot rearrange an equation under time pressure has a mathematics problem, and a competent mathematics tutor at the lower end of the range will fix it faster and cheaper than a Higher Level physics specialist charging to do the same drilling. The same applies to writing fluency underneath an essay subject, and to basic study organisation underneath everything.

The second case is volume work. Where a student needs to sit and complete past papers with someone present to keep them honest and to mark objectively against a scheme, that is supervision rather than specialist teaching. It is a legitimate purchase, it is worth considerably less per hour than diagnosis, and a family paying specialist rates for it is overpaying for a function that does not require the expertise.

The third is the Standard Level subject that is merely untended. A student who has fallen two topics behind in a Standard Level humanities course, with no technique problem, needs catching up rather than coaching. Where specialist money should go is narrower than most families assume: Higher Level sciences and mathematics, internal assessment and core components, and any paper where a student knows the content and is still losing marks. Spend there, and economise elsewhere deliberately rather than by accident.

sections.heading: What no fee buys: grades, guarantees and other people's coursework
paragraphs: Some things are not for sale at any price, and the providers who imply otherwise are the reason this section exists. No fee guarantees a grade. Grade boundaries are set after the papers are marked and move between series with the difficulty of the papers and the performance of the cohort, which means nobody can promise a number in advance. A tutor can make a specific improvement more likely and can tell you honestly what is realistic. That is the whole of what is on offer.

No fee buys a predicted grade either. Predicted grades are made by the school, on the school's evidence, by the teacher who holds the course. An outside tutor can supply marked work that informs the school's view, and that is a legitimate and sometimes decisive contribution. A tutor who offers to change a prediction, or implies influence over the school's judgement, is describing something they do not control.

And no fee buys assessed work. We do not write, redraft, translate or supply text for an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay or a Personal Project, and the student is told that in the first session rather than discovering it later. What a tutor may legitimately do is teach the criteria, question the argument, read what the student has written and explain which band it currently sits in, and set the next revision for the student to carry out themselves.

This is worth paying attention to as a buyer, not only as a principle. A malpractice finding sits outside a family's control, arrives slowly, and can cost a grade or an entry in a way that no amount of subsequent work repairs. A weak grade can be resat. The arithmetic is not close. Any provider in this market quoting a price per essay has told you what they are selling, and the right response is to stop reading rather than to negotiate.

process.title: Tell us the course, the level and the problem
process.description: Subject, level, year group, and what the marked work actually shows: missing content, lost technique, or an internal assessment deadline. A quote means nothing without that, and the difference between the three is the difference between six weeks and two terms of hours. Online IB tuition in the Kingdom is matched from this, not from a subject name.

process.title: A free trial lesson with the tutor who would teach
process.description: An hour with the actual proposed tutor, working on a recent piece of marked schoolwork. Use it as an interview: which guide have you taught, which components have you marked, how many students in this course this term, and where do candidates lose marks in this paper. Four questions, no cost.

process.title: A written baseline before any block is agreed
process.description: Marked questions produce a short written baseline separating content gaps from technique losses. This is the document the fee is justified against later, and it is the reason a family can tell in November whether the money spent since the autumn term moved any marks. Nothing is billed as a block before it exists.

process.title: Agree the block, the inclusions and the review date
process.description: Hours, slot, what is marked between lessons, how often a written report comes, and when the block is reviewed. Slots are written in Arabia Standard Time so a tutor abroad changing their clocks does not move the lesson. Everything that is included is written down, which is how a fee stops being a surprise.

process.title: Review on marked work, then continue, change or stop
process.description: At the end of each block, a review against the baseline using annotated work: what moved, what did not, whether the plan or the tutor should change. If a match is wrong we re-match early rather than extend it, and if the work is finished we say so instead of selling another block.

You can take the table to any provider and ask which line their quote sits on. Vagueness about money in this market is usually evasion rather than discretion.

whyPoints.title: The fee is explained as a description of the tutor
whyPoints.description: Scarcity, level, marking experience, travel and timing are what move a quote, in that order. Each one has a narrow question attached to it that a family can ask in a trial lesson. That is more useful than any rate card, because it tells you what you are comparing.

whyPoints.title: Higher Level is treated as a different job
whyPoints.description: About 240 recommended teaching hours against 150 at Standard Level, plus components Standard Level does not sit. A quote that does not distinguish the two levels is priced for the easier one, and we say which level a tutor has actually delivered rather than which they could.

whyPoints.title: What is included is written down
whyPoints.description: Marking between lessons, Internal Assessment feedback, written reports and what happens to a cancelled session are agreed before a block starts. Identical-looking rates diverge most on exactly these points, and that is where families are surprised later rather than at the headline figure.

whyPoints.title: No outcome claims, at any price
whyPoints.description: No fee guarantees a grade, because boundaries are set after the papers are marked. No success percentages, no star ratings, no counts we cannot evidence. Nothing here claims approval or partnership from the IB, Cambridge, Pearson, the Ministry of Education or the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, because we hold none.

whyPoints.title: Assessed work stays the student's own
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches criteria and gives feedback on the student's own drafts. We do not write, redraft or supply text for an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay or a Personal Project. Providers quoting a price per essay are selling something else entirely.

faqs.question: Why does Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches Higher Level carry a third paper, and does it change the fee?
faqs.answer: Higher Level in both mathematics routes carries a third written paper that examines extended problem-solving rather than additional content, and it is a separate skill from the first two papers. It needs teaching time of its own, which is one reason Higher Level quotes sit above Standard Level ones. The practical consequence for a family is narrower than the fee question: a tutor who has only delivered the Standard Level course has never taught that paper. Ask which Higher Level components they have taught by name before agreeing a rate for Higher Level work.

faqs.question: What are command terms, and why does a tutor spend paid time on them?
faqs.answer: Command terms are the verbs that open an IB question: state, outline, describe, explain, analyse, evaluate. Each one specifies the kind of answer the mark scheme will credit, and each carries an expected depth. A candidate who explains when the question said describe wastes time and gains nothing; one who describes when it said explain loses marks for content they knew. Teaching them directly is among the cheapest interventions available, because it needs marked answers and a few sessions rather than a term of content, and it transfers across every subject a student is sitting.

faqs.question: How do IB grade boundaries move, and what does that mean for a target grade?
faqs.answer: Boundaries are set after papers are marked, taking account of the difficulty of that series and the performance of the cohort, so the mark needed for a given grade is not fixed in advance. This is why no fee can guarantee a grade and why any quote that leans on one is misleading. What it means practically is that a target should be set in marks on specific question types rather than in grades: moving a six-mark extended response from two to five is measurable and controllable, where a promised grade is neither.

faqs.question: What is a predicted grade, and can a paid tutor change it?
faqs.answer: A predicted grade is the school's judgement of what a student is likely to achieve, made by the teachers who hold the course and used by universities before results exist. An outside tutor cannot change it and should not claim to. What a tutor can legitimately do is produce marked work that gives the school better evidence than it had, which sometimes shifts a view. The honest framing is that the tutor supplies evidence and the school makes the judgement. Any provider implying influence over a prediction is describing something outside their control.

faqs.question: How much of a Diploma subject grade is settled before the May session begins?
faqs.answer: A meaningful share, because most subjects carry an internally assessed component completed and marked well before the written papers. The exact weighting varies by subject and is set out in the subject guide your school works from, so ask the teacher rather than relying on a general figure. The planning consequence is the point: internal assessment deadlines sit in a term that already contains mocks, and work banked there cannot be recovered later. Families who protect those deadlines ahead of everything else spend less on emergency teaching in the final term.

faqs.question: What does the first diagnostic session cover, and is it charged separately?
faqs.answer: It covers marked questions rather than conversation. The student works through material the tutor can diagnose from, and the output is a short written baseline: which topics are secure, which are missing, and which lost marks are technique rather than content. Those two diagnoses lead to completely different plans at different costs, which is why the session is worth buying before a block rather than after. Where a trial lesson already produces enough evidence, the baseline comes out of it and there is nothing extra to bill.

faqs.question: What should a first written report from an IB tutor actually contain?
faqs.answer: Topics and marks. A useful report says that a particular question type moved from two out of six to five out of six, that two named topics remain unsecured, and what the next four weeks will address. It should be readable in two minutes and comparable against the baseline. A report describing effort, engagement and a positive attitude is a customer-service document: it tells you the sessions are pleasant and nothing about whether they are working. Ask to see an anonymised example before agreeing a block, since this is where the money becomes visible.

faqs.question: How soon after starting should a parent expect to see movement in marked work?
faqs.answer: Where the problem is technique, within three to five sessions, because the gains come from habits rather than knowledge: answering the command term, showing the method line, labelling a diagram, allocating time by mark tariff. Where the problem is missing content, movement takes a term, because the content has to be taught and then practised. This is the single best reason to buy a diagnostic first. Expecting technique-speed results from a content problem is how families conclude that tutoring does not work when what failed was the forecast.

faqs.question: What happens to the fee if the first tutor turns out to be the wrong fit?
faqs.answer: The match changes, early rather than late. Blocks are reviewed against the written baseline, and a mismatch is usually visible by the second or third session: the diagnosis does not land, the work set does not fit, or the student stops bringing anything to mark. Our position is that re-matching in week three is cheaper for everybody than defending a pairing into a second term. Agree before the block starts what happens to unused hours in that situation, and get the answer in writing, whoever you buy from.

faqs.question: What should a parent do between paid lessons to make them worth more?
faqs.answer: Three things, none of which requires subject knowledge. Make sure the work set is done before the next session, because an unmarked week turns a diagnosis into a guess. Keep the slot: a rescheduled lesson loses the rhythm that makes marked work useful. And read the reports against the baseline rather than skimming them, because that is where you find out whether to continue. What does not help is supervising the content, which tends to introduce a second method and leave the student arbitrating between two adults.

faqs.question: How many hours a week does a first-year Diploma student need, and what does a term of that cost?
faqs.answer: One subject, one hour a week is the normal starting point in the first Diploma year, with written work marked in between. Two subjects go on separate evenings rather than back to back. At the advertised bands on this page, a single weekly hour across a term is a meaningful but predictable commitment, and the figure is a provider-published rate rather than ours. What inflates it is starting late with three weak subjects at once, which produces three partial efforts. One subject taken properly outperforms three taken thinly at any budget.

faqs.question: Is it worth paying for support in the final weeks before the May session?
faqs.answer: Yes, but only for the right work. In the last six to eight weeks the syllabus is either covered or it is not, and the available marks sit in technique: command terms, time allocation against the mark tariff, knowing when to abandon a question, and writing the method line rather than the answer. Paying for new content in the final fortnight has the worst return of anything available, because it displaces paper practice. Rates quoted close to a series also reflect demand rather than quality, so the calendar matters as much as the budget.

faqs.question: When should a family start paying for Internal Assessment support rather than content teaching?
faqs.answer: At the point the task is set and before the first draft is written, because the expensive mistakes are made in the framing. A research question that cannot be assessed against the criteria produces good work and a poor mark, and no amount of later feedback repairs it. Sessions here are billed individually rather than folded into a term block, since the work arrives in bursts around deadlines. What is being bought is criterion teaching and feedback on the student's own drafts, never text, and the student should be told that explicitly.

faqs.question: What does a Middle Years Programme student need before the Diploma, and is it cheaper?
faqs.answer: Cheaper per hour and better value per mark eventually gained, because the work is foundational rather than remedial. Algebraic fluency, writing to a command term, and reading a question properly are the three things that decide how hard the Diploma feels, and all three cost less to build at thirteen than to repair at seventeen. The criteria-based assessment in these years also teaches a student to read a band descriptor, which is the habit the Diploma core depends on. Maintenance teaching across these years consistently outperforms intensive buying later.

faqs.question: Does a November-session candidate pay a different rate from a May-session one?
faqs.answer: The rate follows scarcity and timing rather than the series, but the timing pressure differs. November-session candidates are often resitting, which means the diagnosis already exists in a marked script and the work can be narrower and shorter than a full year of teaching. That usually makes it cheaper in total even where the hourly figure is the same. The practical advice is to decide on a resit as soon as results arrive rather than a term later, because the tutors who know the paper fill their schedules in the weeks immediately afterwards.

faqs.question: Is it worth paying for a second subject in the same term?
faqs.answer: Only if the two go on separate evenings and both have a baseline. Two subjects taken back to back after a Sunday-to-Thursday school day produce one good hour and one wasted one, and paying for the second is paying for attendance. The deeper question is whether the second subject needs specialist teaching or only supervision while past papers get done. If it is the latter, buy the cheaper thing deliberately. Spreading specialist money thinly across three weak subjects is the most common way a term's budget produces nothing measurable.

ib-tutor-fees.closingHeading: How to turn a quoted fee into a decision
ib-tutor-fees.closingBody: Send the subject, the level, the year group and what the marked work shows. We will propose a named tutor who has delivered that course at that level, set up a free trial lesson with that person, and produce a written baseline from marked questions before any block of hours is agreed. What is included between lessons is written down first: marking, Internal Assessment feedback, reports and the review date. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Arabia Standard Time. Every SAR figure on this page is an advertised market rate with its source named, and none of it is presented as our own price list.

intro.heading: Evidence first, then the system the Diploma sits inside
paragraphs: Parents who search for an IB tutor for girls in Saudi Arabia are rarely asking for anything unusual. They have a daughter in the Diploma or the Middle Years Programme, a subject that is not going well, and a preference about who sits with her for an hour at a time over the next two years. The preference is easy to meet. The harder part, and the part this page is mostly about, is the system the Diploma sits inside here: who licenses the school, who evaluates it, and what has to happen to a Diploma before a Saudi university can act on it.

That second half is the one almost nobody writes about. A family can run two years of good teaching, land the points, and then discover in the final months that an international certificate needs an equivalency decision from the Ministry of Education before a local university treats it as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate, and that two separate tests run through ETEC sit alongside it. None of that is difficult. All of it takes time, and time is what a final-year family has least of.

So this page is built on evidence rather than reassurance. It opens with what measurable progress actually looks like in the Diploma, using documents you already hold: marked past papers, criterion marks on a practice Internal Assessment, a predicted grade, a topic checklist. From there it works backwards to a plan that fits a Sunday-to-Thursday week. Then it covers licensing, evaluation, equivalency, Qudurat and Tahsili, and the line a tutor may not cross on assessed work. Each of those is a question with a checkable answer, and a page that gives you the answer is more use than one that tells you how much it cares.

Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video, on a slot pinned to Arabia Standard Time. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Saudi address, and home visits are a service offered only in India. The upside is the one that matters for a scarce Higher Level subject: your daughter is matched to a specialist in Chemistry HL or Mathematics AA HL rather than to whoever teaches science within driving distance of your district.

Where a family asks for a woman to teach their daughter, that is recorded alongside the subject, the level and the evening slot, and the match is made against all of it. It is a preference, not a negotiation, and no reason has to be given for it. What the request cannot do is invent a specialist who does not exist, so the honest sequence is subject specialism first and gender inside that pool. In the common subject groups that costs nothing at all; in a scarce Higher Level subject it can mean a short wait, and you will be told which it is before lessons are booked rather than after.

sections.heading: What progress looks like, in numbers a parent can check
paragraphs: Start with evidence, because the Diploma produces a great deal of it and most families never see it used. A marked past paper is not a score out of sixty; it is a list of the question types where a method failed. Criterion marks on a practice Internal Assessment say whether your daughter understands what the analysis criterion actually rewards. A topic checklist, honestly marked, says where the next six lessons should go. All three exist before any tutor is hired.

What that evidence should do is move in a direction you can see. Not in a straight line every fortnight, because content gets harder as the course runs, but visibly: the same question type stops costing marks, the checklist shifts from unsafe towards secure, and practice criterion marks climb a band. If after a full term nothing in the written record has changed, the plan is wrong, and that conclusion is available to you without needing anybody's opinion.

The predicted grade sits above all of it and is often misread. It is the school's statement of what it expects on current evidence, and it travels with a university application. It is not a target and it is not a promise; no tutor and no school can guarantee what the May session produces. Reading it as a reading of the evidence, rather than a verdict on your daughter, is the difference between a useful conversation with the school and a defensive one.

sections.heading: Working back from the evidence to a plan that fits the week
paragraphs: Once the record is in front of you, the plan builds itself in reverse. Name the component losing the most marks. Name the topics it rests on. Put those topics in the order the papers test them rather than the order a textbook prints them. Then count the weeks left before the May session and divide. A plan that cannot survive that arithmetic is a wish, and it is far better to find that out in the autumn term than in the final fortnight.

The week is the constraint that decides what is possible at all. Schools here run Sunday to Thursday, Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3, and the Kingdom never changes its clocks, so a tutor abroad has to convert into your evening and keep converting when their own country shifts. Two subjects in one evening is usually a mistake for a student carrying six subjects and the core. One well-prepared hour, repeated weekly, beats three hours assembled in a panic.

Write the plan down and keep it to a single page: components, topics, weeks, and what evidence will show it worked. Review it at the end of each term against the same marked papers and checklists you started from. If the evidence has moved and the schedule holds, carry on. If it has not, change the plan or change the tutor, because those are the only two useful responses, and both are easier when the plan was written in a form that can be checked.

sections.heading: The system your daughter's school sits inside
paragraphs: Private and international schools in the Kingdom hold a licence from the Ministry of Education. School evaluation and accreditation runs through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, ETEC, which operates e-services for national school accreditation and for the approval of international accreditation bodies. Separately, a school has been through the authorisation process the IB runs before a programme may be taught under its name. Three bodies, three different jobs, and none of them is a statement about one teacher.

What that structure does decide is real. It decides whether a school may operate, how it is evaluated, and whether it may call its sixth form a Diploma Programme at all. What it leaves entirely to the school is the timetable: which subjects appear in the option blocks, which run at Higher Level, how many students a group needs before it is viable, and who teaches it. A fully licensed, well-evaluated school can still tell you that Physics HL is not running.

So read an evaluation report for what it is. It will tell you about leadership, safeguarding, provision and outcomes at the level of the institution. It will not tell you that the Mathematics AA HL group has four students and a teacher who last taught the course somewhere else. For that you ask the school directly, in the term before option forms go in, and you ask about the subjects your daughter actually intends to take. The answer is usually given freely when the question is that specific.

sections.heading: Equivalency: the step that makes a Diploma usable at a Saudi university
paragraphs: A certificate earned on an international curriculum is not automatically treated as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. An equivalency decision, mu'adalah, from the Ministry of Education is the step that makes it usable, and it applies to the IB Diploma, to A Levels and to an American high school diploma alike. Families routinely meet this in the final school year, which is the worst time, because the paperwork sits between the certificate arriving and an application being considered.

The useful thing is the order. The school and the awarding body issue the final certificate. The Ministry issues the equivalency decision on that certificate. ETEC, through its National Center for Assessment, Qiyas, runs the two tests universities ask about. Each university then publishes its own admission criteria by programme, and those published criteria are the only place the actual requirement lives. Nobody else's summary of them is worth planning around, including this one.

What a tutor contributes here is modest and worth naming honestly. We process no paperwork and hold no standing with the Ministry or with ETEC. What a subject tutor can do is make sure the grades on the certificate are the ones the family wanted, and make sure nobody is surprised in the final year by a step they had not left time for. Ask your school's Diploma Programme coordinator who has done this most recently; that person has the current version, and a current version is the only kind worth having.

sections.heading: Qudurat and Tahsili, and why Tahsili is the harder one here
paragraphs: Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, measures verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, and it is sat in Arabic or in English. A Diploma student is usually reasonably placed for it, because the reasoning is trainable and the mathematics sits below Higher Level. Practice matters mostly for pace and for the shape of the questions, which are unlike anything in an IB paper. That is technique work, and a few focused weeks is the honest prescription.

Tahsili is the one that catches families out. It covers the science-stream subjects, mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English, and its content follows the Saudi national curriculum. An IB student has studied the same science, but framed differently, sequenced differently and examined differently. The overlap is real and the framing is not, which is why a student holding strong Higher Level grades can still find the paper unfamiliar. It is a translation problem rather than a knowledge problem.

We publish no score thresholds and no university's weighting, because they differ by university, by programme and over time, and third-party sites disagree with one another. Competitive engineering, medicine and science programmes lean hardest on Tahsili, which is the one generalisation worth making. For everything else, go to the university's own published criteria, which are revised and are the only version that binds anyone. If a provider quotes you a number to beat, ask where it came from before you plan a year around it, because a figure copied from a forum post has cost families a sitting.

sections.heading: Asking for a woman to teach your daughter, and what the request changes
paragraphs: A family searching for an IB tutor for girls in Saudi Arabia is usually making one specific request: the person teaching their daughter one-to-one, several evenings a month, across a two-year course, should be a woman. It is a preference you state and it is recorded with the board, the subjects and the levels. Gender-segregated schooling exists in parts of the system here, so for many students this is the arrangement they already know from school.

What the request changes is the length of the list, not the price. Online, a tutor's location is irrelevant, so the pool is the whole set of specialists rather than the ones living within a drive of your district. In the Diploma the real scarcity runs by subject and level: Mathematics AA HL, Physics HL and Chemistry HL have fewer experienced teachers than their Standard Level equivalents everywhere in the world, and that is what moves availability.

What the request does not change is the order of the decision. A woman who has not taught Mathematics AA HL is still the wrong tutor for Mathematics AA HL. Subject specialism comes first, gender inside that pool second, the evening slot third. Where both are available, which is the usual case across the six subject groups, you get both. Where only one specialist is free for a scarce Higher Level subject, you will be told plainly, and the choice stays yours rather than being made quietly on your behalf.

sections.heading: The Internal Assessment and the Extended Essay: where a tutor stops
paragraphs: Every Diploma subject carries internally assessed work, and the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge sit on top of it. All of it has to be the student's own. A tutor may teach the skill a task needs, read what the student has written and say which criterion is underserved. A tutor may not supply content, rewrite a paragraph or settle the argument. The school supervisor runs the formal process, holds the reflection sessions and signs the honesty record.

In the Extended Essay the line is easiest to see in the research question. A tutor may teach what makes a question answerable in four thousand words, show two worked examples from other subjects, and ask whether the sources exist to answer it at all. Handing over a question is a different act, and a supervisor who has sat through hundreds of these can usually tell. The same holds for an Internal Assessment variable: teach the reasoning and let her choose it.

Tell the school that an outside tutor is involved. Supervisors would rather know, and a component with dated drafts, written feedback and a clear record of what each session covered is straightforward to defend if anybody ever asks. That record is also the only real protection your daughter has, which is why a tutor who prefers to leave no written trail of their own comments is telling you something useful about how they work. Ask for the feedback in writing from the first session.

faqs.question: Can we specify a woman to teach our daughter every one of her six Diploma subjects?
faqs.answer: You can ask, and it is recorded subject by subject. Most families need one or two subjects rather than six, and across the common groups a female specialist is usually available. The honest exception is a scarce Higher Level subject: Mathematics AA HL and Physics HL have a smaller experienced pool everywhere, so insisting on both specialism and gender can mean waiting. You will be told which subject is the constraint.

faqs.question: Does a single-sex school in the Kingdom change what a Diploma student needs from an outside tutor?
faqs.answer: Not academically. The syllabus, the components and the May session are identical whatever the intake looks like. What it changes is the habit a student arrives with: somebody taught in a single-sex class for years may work more easily with a woman. The substantive differences between schools are size and staffing, because a small cohort means fewer Higher Level groups.

faqs.question: Which Diploma subjects does a small school in the Kingdom drop first when it cannot staff them?
faqs.answer: The pattern is consistent: the Higher Level sciences beyond Biology, Mathematics AA at Higher Level, and smaller options such as Economics at Higher Level. These are the groups that attract four or five students, and a group that small is hard to justify against a timetable. Schools rarely announce it as a staffing decision; the subject simply does not appear in the option block.

faqs.question: If a school is licensed and evaluated, why can it still not run Physics HL for our daughter?
faqs.answer: Because licensing and evaluation operate on the institution, not the timetable. The Ministry of Education licenses private and international schools, and ETEC handles school evaluation and accreditation. Neither one guarantees that any particular Higher Level group will run in any particular year. That depends on how many students choose it, whether a specialist is on the staff, and whether the timetable can carry another small group. A strong evaluation report and an unavailable Physics HL class are entirely compatible.

faqs.question: How do we tell whether a school here runs the full Diploma or stops at the Middle Years Programme?
faqs.answer: Ask which programmes the school is authorised to run and which it is actually teaching this year, because they are not always the same list. Then ask for the subjects offered in the final two years, at which level, and how many candidates sat the last May session. A school running the Middle Years Programme and then switching students to IGCSE is a perfectly normal arrangement, but it changes what your daughter leaves Year 11 with, so it is worth knowing early.

faqs.question: Does a tutor reviewing our daughter's Biology Internal Assessment need to tell the school?
faqs.answer: The family tells the school, and it is worth doing. Supervisors are responsible for confirming the work is the student's own, and they would rather know that a second adult is reading drafts than find out later. Nothing about outside teaching is prohibited; what is prohibited is somebody other than the student producing the work. Say who is involved, keep the dated drafts and the written feedback, and the supervisor has everything needed to sign off with confidence.

faqs.question: Who signs the academic honesty declaration on an Internal Assessment, and what is a tutor's part in it?
faqs.answer: The student and the school supervisor are the signatories; a tutor is not party to it. The declaration says the submitted work is the student's own and that sources are acknowledged. A tutor's part is to behave in a way that keeps the declaration true: teaching the technique, reading what has been written, naming the criterion that is weak, and never supplying text or conclusions. If a tutor's involvement would make that declaration awkward to sign, the involvement has gone too far.

faqs.question: Our daughter's Personal Project supervisor has left the school — what happens to the project?
faqs.answer: The school reassigns a supervisor, and the process journal becomes the important document, because it is the record of what was done and when. Ask the new supervisor to confirm the goal and the remaining meeting dates in writing, and make sure the journal is up to date before the handover rather than after. An outside tutor can help by keeping the student's own record orderly and by teaching the research and reflection skills the criteria ask for, without touching the project itself.

faqs.question: Is it acceptable for a paid tutor to suggest our daughter's Extended Essay research question?
faqs.answer: Suggesting the question outright is the wrong side of the line. What is legitimate, and genuinely useful, is teaching what separates an answerable question from an unanswerable one: a defined scope, sources that actually exist, and a method that fits four thousand words. Work through examples from other subjects, then let her draft three candidates and test them against those criteria herself. The supervisor approves the final question, and a question the student built is also one she can sustain for a year.

faqs.question: Our daughter is moving from a girls' national-curriculum school into the Diploma — what actually transfers?
faqs.answer: Subject knowledge transfers more than families expect, particularly in mathematics and the sciences. What does not transfer is the assessment culture: command terms, mark schemes that reward a specific move, internally assessed components, and the expectation that a student evaluates rather than recounts. Written academic English is usually the real workload. Plan the first term around assessment literacy, because a misread command term costs marks invisibly for two years.

faqs.question: Is the Middle Years Programme a better bridge into the Diploma than IGCSE for a student arriving at fifteen?
faqs.answer: Each prepares something different. The Middle Years Programme teaches criterion-based assessment and a long independent project, which maps directly onto Diploma internal assessment. IGCSE teaches terminal written papers under timed conditions, which maps onto the Diploma examinations. A student arriving at fifteen usually has no real choice, since it depends on what the school offers. Where there is a choice, pick the one the school staffs properly, because a well-taught course beats a theoretically better fit every time.

faqs.question: If our daughter sits the May session, when should the equivalency step start relative to university applications?
faqs.answer: Start gathering information in the first year of the Diploma, not after results. The equivalency decision is issued on the final certificate, so it cannot be completed early, but what a family can do early is confirm what the Ministry asks for, what the chosen universities require, and whether any document needs attesting. That way the only thing left when the certificate arrives is submission. Your school's Diploma Programme coordinator will know who has been through it most recently.

faqs.question: Does Tahsili cover anything our daughter will not have met in Diploma Biology and Chemistry?
faqs.answer: Mostly it covers the same science from a different direction. Tahsili follows the Saudi national curriculum, so topics are sequenced differently, named differently in places, and examined in a style no IB paper uses. A Higher Level chemist will know the chemistry; what is unfamiliar is the pace, the question format and the breadth expected in a single sitting. It is a reframing exercise, which is why preparation for it is a separate piece of work rather than more subject teaching.

faqs.question: Can our daughter prepare for Qudurat with the same tutor who teaches her Mathematics AI?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth asking directly. Qudurat tests verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, so a mathematics tutor can cover the quantitative half comfortably if they know the question formats. The verbal section, and the choice of sitting it in Arabic or English, is a different skill set. Many families run a short separate block for it rather than losing subject time, and that keeps the Diploma plan and the test preparation from competing for the same evening.

ib-tutor-for-girls.closingHeading: Start from the evidence you already have
ib-tutor-for-girls.closingBody: Send three things: the subjects and levels, the most recent marked work or school report, and the evenings that work in Arabia Standard Time. Say if you want a woman to teach your daughter and it is recorded with the rest. You will get a free trial lesson that marks a real past-paper question, a one-page plan naming the components and the weeks left, and a fee for that subject and level before anything is booked. Lessons run online, one-to-one, over live video, anywhere in the Kingdom.

ib-tutor-near-me.tutorsIntro: Each tutor profile below names the Diploma subjects they teach, the levels, and which components they prepare students for: the written papers, the internally assessed task, or coursework at the planning stage. Read the component line rather than the biography, because that is what decides whether a tutor can help with the problem you actually have.

intro.heading: Start with how the Diploma is assessed, and the rest of the decision follows
paragraphs: A near-me search makes sense for a plumber and very little sense for a Diploma tutor. The Diploma is not one course; it is six subjects at two levels, each broken into components with published weightings, plus a core of three elements assessed in entirely different ways. A grade moves when the component that is leaking marks is fixed. Whether the person fixing it lives twenty minutes away or in another country has no bearing on whether they know that component, and in the Kingdom the honest answer is usually that the nearest specialist is not nearby at all.

Here is the structure in one paragraph, because everything else on this page is derived from it. Six subjects are graded 1 to 7, which accounts for forty-two points. Three are taken at Higher Level, carrying more taught hours, extra content and in several subjects an additional paper. Most subjects include an internally assessed component, marked by the school against published criteria and then moderated, typically worth a fifth to a third of the subject grade. Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay are graded A to E and read together on a matrix worth up to three further points, taking the maximum to forty-five. Creativity, activity, service carries no points but is required.

Once that is on the table, a parent can diagnose rather than guess. Strong classwork with weak examination marks is a written-paper technique problem and needs somebody who has taught or marked that paper. Coursework that never reaches a finished draft is a criteria problem and needs somebody fluent in the descriptors for that subject. An Extended Essay with an unanswerable research question needs a subject graduate working alongside the school supervisor at the planning stage. These are three different purchases, and families routinely buy the first when they needed the second.

Geography still matters, just not in the way the search phrase implies. IB provision in the Kingdom is concentrated: Riyadh holds the widest choice of Diploma Programme places, Jeddah has a substantial cluster along its coastal spine, the Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran conurbation behaves as one school market, and The KAUST School serves the campus community at Thuwal. Outside those, distance is the constraint, and schools in smaller markets cannot always staff every Higher Level course they list. That is the real reason a near-me search returns advertising rather than a specialist.

Lessons for families in the Kingdom are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Saudi address; home visits are a service we run only in India. Slots are written in Arabia Standard Time, which does not change with the seasons, and the week is built around Sunday to Thursday. The practical effect is that the filter becomes the syllabus and the component rather than the postcode, which is the right filter for a qualification examined the way this one is.

ib-tutor-near-me.programmesIntro: The IB runs four programmes and a Saudi family may meet any of them, though not with equal frequency. Each is assessed differently, which changes what tutoring can usefully do: there is no external examination before the Diploma, so support in the earlier programmes is about criteria and habits rather than papers.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Transdisciplinary units of inquiry instead of separate subjects, with no external examinations and a final-year exhibition that the student plans, researches and presents. Assessment is formative and descriptive, so a parent sees commentary rather than marks. What carries into later programmes is reading stamina, number fluency and the habit of writing down reasoning rather than answers alone.
programmes.countryNote: PYP requests across the Kingdom are mostly from families who have just arrived into an inquiry-led classroom from a more traditional one, or who are preparing a child for a move between international schools. The gap is almost never arithmetic; it is writing an explanation in English at the length the exhibition will demand.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Five years across eight subject groups, with each subject marked against four criteria out of eight. The Personal Project closes the programme and is assessed on planning, applying skills and reflecting. Some schools enter candidates for MYP eAssessment, pairing on-screen examinations with ePortfolios for the MYP Certificate. Criterion descriptors, not content coverage, decide the grade.
programmes.countryNote: The commonest MYP request in the Kingdom concerns Criterion D, the evaluating and reflecting strand, where strong students who know the content score in the middle band because nobody has shown them what the top band asks for. It is also the stage where a family first meets published criteria, which is useful preparation for the Diploma's internal assessments.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across the groups, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Subjects are graded 1 to 7 and the core adds up to three points from the matrix. The Diploma has pass conditions beyond the total, including requirements on the core and limits on how many low grades are permitted.
programmes.countryNote: This is the programme nearly every near-me search is about. Saudi schools enter candidates for the May session, and a family should take the exact internal deadlines from their own Diploma Programme coordinator rather than from any published summary, because school deadlines for coursework arrive well before the board's.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: A smaller framework combining at least two Diploma courses with a career-related study, a core of personal and professional skills, service learning, a reflective project and language development. It is designed for students heading towards applied or vocational pathways rather than the full six-subject Diploma, and it is assessed through a mixture of Diploma components and the career-related study's own requirements.
programmes.countryNote: The Career-related Programme is rare in the Kingdom and a family is unlikely to meet it unless a specific school offers it. Where it does appear, tutoring usually concerns the Diploma courses taken inside it, which are examined exactly as they are for a full Diploma candidate, and the reflective project's criteria.

ib-tutor-near-me.subjectsIntro: These are the Diploma subjects that generate the most requests from the Kingdom, described by component rather than by topic list. The component is what a family needs to identify before choosing a tutor, because the skill that earns marks in a non-calculator paper is not the skill that earns them in a source-based one.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Higher Level runs Paper 1 and Paper 2 at thirty per cent each, Paper 3 at twenty and the exploration at twenty. Paper 1 is sat without technology, so weak manipulation is exposed immediately rather than hidden behind a calculator. Paper 3 is two extended problems where marks accumulate along a chain of reasoning and stop the moment the chain breaks.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Technology is permitted throughout and the statistical and modelling content is heavier. Standard Level is Papers 1 and 2 at forty per cent each with the exploration at twenty. The component that costs marks is interpretation: a correct calculation presented without a contextual conclusion, or a model used without its limitations stated.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics, fields, waves, electricity and nuclear physics, with the Higher Level extension adding whole topics rather than extra detail. The written papers carry eighty per cent between them and the scientific investigation twenty. Definitions are marked strictly and graph questions reward values read from the line of best fit rather than from individual points.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Quantitative chemistry, energetics, kinetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms, with the investigation at twenty per cent. Multi-step calculations lose marks to dropped units and prematurely rounded intermediates; mechanisms lose them to missing curly arrows, which the mark scheme expects to see drawn rather than described.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Concept-led content from molecular biology to ecology, with data-based questions on experiments the candidate has never seen and an investigation worth twenty per cent. The recurring loss is length rather than knowledge: a page of accurate recall where the question is paying for three developed, distinct points.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Paper 1 is source-based on a prescribed subject, Paper 2 covers world history topics by essay, and Higher Level adds Paper 3 on a regional option, which is the largest single component at that level. The historical investigation is internally assessed and capped at two thousand two hundred words. Source evaluation and the use of specific evidence carry the marks.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Biological, cognitive and sociocultural approaches, research methods, and options studied in more depth at Higher Level, which also adds a further paper. The internally assessed component is a simple experimental study written up as a report. Students lose marks by describing studies rather than using them as evidence for a stated argument.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Microeconomics, macroeconomics and the global economy. Higher Level runs Paper 1 at twenty per cent, Paper 2 at thirty, the quantitative Paper 3 at thirty and the commentary portfolio at twenty; at Standard Level the portfolio carries thirty. Accurate, labelled diagrams and application to a named real example decide most extended-response marks.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is a guided analysis of an unseen text at thirty-five per cent for both levels; Paper 2 is a comparative essay; Higher Level adds the HL essay at twenty per cent and the individual oral is internally assessed. The examined skill is close reading at speed, which improves only through weekly timed unseen practice with detailed marking.

subjects.name: Language B and ab initio
subjects.description: Receptive, productive and interactive skills across prescribed themes, with text types that must be produced in the right register: a blog post is not a formal letter. Many students in the Kingdom speak a second or third language confidently and still lose marks in writing, where structure and the accuracy of less common tenses are assessed.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Assessed through a comparative study, a process portfolio and a curated exhibition with written rationale, rather than by examination. Tutoring here is almost entirely about the written components and the criteria behind them, which are where strong practical students most often under-score because the writing is treated as an afterthought.

ib-tutor-near-me.regionsTitle: Where a near-me search actually lands, across the Kingdom
ib-tutor-near-me.regionsIntro: IB provision is not spread evenly, and knowing where it concentrates explains why the search phrase disappoints. These are the markets requests reach us from, with what each one means for finding a specialist in a particular subject at a particular level.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: The widest choice of Diploma places in the Kingdom and therefore the widest range of Higher Level combinations. The city is roughly an hour across in traffic, so even here a family in one district and a tutor in another have a commute that makes a weekday evening session difficult.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: A long coastal spine from the historic centre north to Obhur, with a substantial international and IB cluster along it. Subject availability is good; the constraint is travel along the spine at the exact hour an after-school lesson would have to run.

regions.name: Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran
regions.note: One labour and school market in practice, with families living in one city and attending school in another. The International Schools Group runs several campuses here and the Diploma is offered at the American School of Dhahran, while the British-curriculum schools carry a large IGCSE cohort.

regions.name: Jubail and Yanbu
regions.note: Industrial cities with small international-school sets serving their complexes. Courses run when cohorts fill, so a student with an unusual Higher Level combination may be studying with very little specialist contact time even though the school lists the subject.

regions.name: Thuwal and the KAUST campus
regions.note: The KAUST School serves the university campus community north of Jeddah on the coast. The academic environment is unusually strong, and the requests that come from here tend to be for depth in a Higher Level science or mathematics rather than for remediation.

regions.name: Makkah and Madinah
regions.note: Makkah sits roughly eighty kilometres east of Jeddah, so some families use the Jeddah school market directly. Household calendars here bend around the Hajj and Umrah seasons, which is a scheduling fact worth putting into a lesson plan rather than discovering mid-term.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: About twenty-five kilometres apart in 'Asir at high altitude, sharing one catchment. International provision is limited relative to the population, so families here are often choosing between relocation, boarding and online teaching for a specific subject.

regions.name: Tabuk, AlUla and NEOM
regions.note: The north-west is changing quickly, and mid-course arrivals are common as families relocate for new projects. A student joining a Diploma cohort part-way through needs a different plan from one who has been in it since the start, and the difference is mostly about sequencing.

regions.name: Al Ahsa, Qatif and Ras Tanura
regions.note: Al Ahsa is roughly an hour and a half inland from the Eastern Province cluster, while Qatif and Ras Tanura sit on the coast between it and Jubail. Families here commonly commute into the cluster's schools, which pushes any evening lesson late.

regions.name: Buraidah, Ha'il, Najran and Jazan
regions.note: Provincial centres where international-curriculum provision is thin. The practical options are a national-curriculum school with outside support for an international qualification, relocation, or boarding, and online teaching is what makes the first of those viable at all.

schoolClusters.note: IB World Schools in the capital are named in the IB's own directory and span the Primary Years, Middle Years and Diploma Programmes, so a family can usually find the level they need somewhere in the city. Whether a specific Higher Level course runs in a given intake still depends on how many students chose it, which is the question to ask at an admissions meeting.

schoolClusters.city: Jeddah and the Red Sea coast
schoolClusters.note: The British International School of Jeddah is both an IB World School and a Cambridge school, Deutsche Internationale Schule Jeddah runs through to Grade 12, and several other schools appear in IB listings. The American International School of Jeddah and the International Indian School Jeddah are long-established international schools serving different communities along the same spine.

The International Schools Group operates several campuses in the Dhahran area and beyond, and the Diploma is offered at the American School of Dhahran and at ISG Jubail, though not at every campus. British School Dhahran and Multinational School Dhahran follow British and Cambridge curricula. The KAUST School serves the campus community at Thuwal.

ib-tutor-near-me.schoolDisclaimer: Schools are named here as context for where IB provision sits in the Kingdom; no affiliation, partnership or endorsement is implied, and current programme availability should be confirmed with each school and against the IB's own school directory.
ib-tutor-near-me.modesIntro: Three arrangements cover the requests that arrive from a near-me search, and which one fits depends entirely on the component at fault. A content gap needs weekly teaching, a technique problem close to the session needs timed papers, and coursework needs criterion feedback on the student's own draft.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one on a single subject
modes.description: One subject, one component focus at a time, one fixed slot in the week. Work is set after each lesson and marked before the next, so each hour starts from evidence rather than from a recap. This is the arrangement that shifts a technique problem, because technique shifts through repeated feedback on the same question type rather than through explanation.
bullets: A fixed slot written in Arabia Standard Time, Sunday to Thursday
Marked work returned before the next lesson
A short note naming the component worked on and what changed
Switch component focus mid-term when the evidence says to

modes.title: Component rehearsal before the session
modes.description: A short, intense block aimed at one or two components, built from whole timed papers rather than topic revision. The syllabus should already be covered; what is bought here is pacing, question selection and command-term discipline. Families usually take two or three sessions a week for a fixed number of weeks and then stop.
bullets: Whole papers sat under the clock, then marked to the published scheme
A minute-by-minute timing plan per paper, rehearsed not just written
A short list of topics to leave alone when time runs out
Only useful once the course has been covered at least once

modes.title: Coursework supervision support
modes.description: Sessions arranged around an internally assessed component, the Extended Essay or a Personal Project, in which the tutor reads what the student has written and teaches against the published criteria. The school supervisor remains the person who authenticates the work and holds the reflection sessions. The student writes every word of it.
bullets: Research questions stress-tested for scope before writing begins
Feedback mapped to criterion descriptors rather than line edits
Method, sampling and data-handling review for science and psychology
A written record of each session, visible to the school if asked

sections.heading: What a near-me search is really asking
paragraphs: Most families typing IB tutor near me are not measuring distance. They are asking whether anybody within reach genuinely knows the course their child is sitting, and whether that person is free at a time when a teenager can still concentrate. Those are availability and fit questions wearing a geography costume. Outside Riyadh, Jeddah and the Eastern Province cluster, the honest answer to the geographic version is usually no, and a page that pretends otherwise is wasting a parent's evening.

The reason sits in the structure of the qualification rather than in the size of any city. A Diploma cohort splits across six subject groups and two levels, which means a school of five hundred students may have four candidates taking a particular Higher Level subject. The number of adults in any given district who have taught that course recently, let alone marked its papers, is correspondingly small. Proximity selects from a pool of a handful; syllabus experience selects from everyone who teaches the course.

There is one case where local does matter, and it is worth saying plainly. A young student who cannot yet work independently on screen for an hour benefits from somebody in the room, and for them a school clinic or an in-home arrangement may be the better purchase this term. For a Diploma candidate with a specific component problem, the trade is the other way round: the gain from a genuine specialist is larger than anything proximity provides, and that is the trade this page is built on.
bullets: Near-me usually means available and competent, not close
A single Higher Level cohort in one school is often tiny
Proximity selects from a handful; syllabus experience selects from everyone
Younger students who need somebody in the room are the real exception

sections.heading: The Diploma, component by component
paragraphs: Everything a family decides should follow from this table rather than from a general impression of the qualification. Six subjects are graded 1 to 7, giving forty-two points; three are taken at Higher Level with more taught hours and extra content; the core adds up to three points through a matrix that reads Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay together; and CAS is required but unscored. The pass conditions matter too, because a Diploma can be missed on a failing core grade or on too many low subject grades even when the total looks adequate.

The internally assessed components are the part families underestimate most consistently. They are completed over weeks, against criteria published in the subject guide, and they commonly account for a fifth to a third of a subject grade. That makes them the most controllable marks in the whole qualification: no timing pressure, no unseen material, and a mark scheme the student is allowed to read. A candidate who treats them as an administrative chore is handing back the one component where effort reliably converts into grade.

Higher Level is the other structural fact worth understanding early. It does not earn more points than Standard Level; a 7 is a 7 at either level. What Higher Level buys is eligibility, because university prerequisites are written in terms of Higher Level subjects. Choosing levels is therefore a decision about degree options rather than about point maximisation, and it is close to irreversible once the first year is under way.

sections.heading: From the symptom to the kind of tutor it needs
paragraphs: Once the components are visible, matching becomes a diagnostic exercise instead of a shopping one. The symptom a parent can see is rarely the problem: a student described as weak at chemistry is usually losing marks in one identifiable place, and the place determines who can help. A tutor who is excellent at teaching content will not fix a pacing problem, and somebody brilliant on examination technique is the wrong person for an investigation that has no workable method.

The table below maps what a family can observe onto the component most likely responsible, the kind of tutor that addresses it, and the question to ask that tutor before booking anything. That last column is the useful part. A specialist answers it immediately and specifically, naming papers, mark schemes and common losses; a generalist answers it in adjectives. The difference takes about ninety seconds to detect and saves a term.

Use the trial lesson to test the match against the diagnosis rather than against warmth. A good trial opens the student's most recent marked script, finds the pattern, and states it plainly enough that you could repeat it to the school. If the hour ends with encouragement and no diagnosis, the tutor has not done the only thing that distinguishes a specialist from a well-meaning graduate, and there is no reason to buy a second hour.

One further point about matching, since it decides how long an arrangement lasts. A single tutor rarely covers every column of this table equally well, and the honest ones say which column is theirs. A teacher who is excellent on written-paper technique may not be the right supervisor-side support for an investigation, and the right answer is sometimes two short arrangements in sequence rather than one long one with the wrong focus. Expect the component focus to change at least once across a year, and expect to be told when it should.

sections.heading: The two years, counted backwards from the session
paragraphs: The Diploma is a two-year arc with one fixed point at the end, and almost every avoidable crisis in it comes from treating an early deadline as distant. The school's internal dates arrive before the board's, the Extended Essay is scoped long before anyone feels urgent about it, and entries are made months ahead of the papers. Counting backwards from the examination session puts each of those in the right order, which is the only thing that stops three pieces of work landing in the same fortnight of the final year.

Saudi schools enter candidates for the May session, and the exact dates belong to your school rather than to any page on the internet: the Diploma Programme coordinator holds the internal deadlines and the examinations officer holds the entry and examination dates. Ask for both at the start of the final year and put them on one calendar with the coursework deadlines from all six subjects, because a clash between two subjects' internal assessments is the single most common self-inflicted problem in the second year.

The stage families most often skip is the long break between the two years. It is the last period in the Diploma when a student has time without a deadline, which makes it the right moment to repair a foundation or to get an investigation's method settled. Work done there costs nothing in term-time attention and removes a problem that would otherwise consume the autumn term of the second year, when every subject is demanding something at once.

sections.heading: Why the local school cannot always cover the course it lists
paragraphs: Private and international schools in the Kingdom are licensed by the Ministry of Education, and school evaluation and accreditation run through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, which operates e-services for national school accreditation and for the approval of international accreditation bodies. Those processes say something about the school as an institution. They say nothing about whether a particular Higher Level option will be staffed by a specialist in a particular intake, which is the thing a Diploma family actually needs to know.

Subject availability is decided by cohort arithmetic. A school timetables a course when enough students choose it; where numbers are marginal, the course runs as a combined Higher and Standard Level class, or is taught by a teacher whose specialism is the neighbouring subject, or is withdrawn after choices are collected. This happens in strong schools as well as struggling ones, and it is the most common reason a family in the Kingdom ends up looking outside the school for teaching. The IB publishes its own directory of World Schools, which is where to check whether a school currently offers the programme at all.

Compound and camp schools add their own pattern. Families living on a company or university campus often have short commutes, facilities on site and a tightly bounded social week, which makes a weekday evening slot easier to protect than it is in a city. The trade is a smaller cohort, so the same subject-availability arithmetic bites harder: a campus school may offer the Diploma while running only the Higher Level courses its own community happened to choose that year.
bullets: Licensing and evaluation describe the school, not the staffing of one option
