sections.heading: Academic honesty: supervision, tutoring and the line between them
paragraphs: The Extended Essay shows the distinction most clearly, so it is worth working through. The school appoints a supervisor, who holds three recorded reflection sessions with the candidate, including a final discussion, and records comments on the reflections form submitted with the essay. The supervisor also authenticates the work as the candidate's own. A tutor sits outside that relationship entirely: useful, legitimate, and with no role in authentication or in the recorded reflections.

What a tutor may legitimately do is teach. They can explain what a criterion descriptor means in practice, test whether a research question can be answered within the word limit, suggest reading, teach a statistical technique or a referencing convention the student has not met, review a method for an experimental study, and read a draft the student wrote and say which criterion it is failing and why. That is subject teaching applied to assessed work, and it is the most valuable hour a coursework candidate can buy.

What a tutor may not do is produce any part of the work. No Internal Assessment, Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge essay or Personal Project is drafted, rewritten or supplied by a tutor, and handing over text to be adapted is the same breach as writing it. Similarity-detection software is part of how schools check this, and it is worth understanding its limits: it finds matched strings against sources it can see, so it catches copied passages and misses a competent ghostwritten essay entirely. That is precisely why schools also rely on supervision, reflection records and a teacher's knowledge of how a student writes. A school that suspects malpractice must investigate it, and the consequence lands on the candidate's diploma, not on the tutor's reputation.
bullets: The school supervisor holds the reflection sessions and authenticates the work
A tutor teaches criteria, method, technique and reading, and reviews the student's draft
Nothing assessed is ever written, rewritten or supplied by a tutor
Similarity software catches copying, not ghostwriting; supervision exists for the rest

sections.heading: Switching into the Diploma, including mid-course
paragraphs: Relocation into the Kingdom part-way through a course is common, and the curriculum a student is leaving changes what catching up involves. From a British school with IGCSE or AS Levels, the subject knowledge usually maps well and the gap is in the IB's own architecture: command terms, criteria-based internal assessment, Theory of Knowledge, and the expectation that a student writes a reasoned explanation rather than a worked answer. From an American high school, the breadth is familiar but Higher Level depth is not, particularly in the sciences, where the extension topics assume a level of detail that an unstreamed course does not reach.

From a national-curriculum or Indian-curriculum school, the position is often reversed. Mathematical technique and factual recall are frequently ahead of the IB cohort, while open-ended writing, source evaluation and the habit of justifying a method are behind. The first month should therefore be spent on question style rather than content: what analyse and evaluate demand, how marks are allocated to a six-mark answer, and how a criteria-marked piece of coursework differs from a test with right answers.

Timing decides what is realistic. A student joining at the start of the first Diploma year has time to absorb any of these gaps. A student joining mid-way through the first year can usually recover, with the internal assessments scoped quickly so they do not collide with the second year's teaching. A student arriving during the second year faces a harder arithmetic, because coursework in six subjects has deadlines that do not move for a new arrival, and the honest conversation is about which subjects to prioritise rather than about catching up everywhere. Coursework completed at a previous school may or may not be transferable; that is a question for the receiving school's coordinator and it should be asked before the move, not after.
bullets: From a British school: content maps well, IB architecture is the gap
From an American school: breadth is familiar, Higher Level depth is not
From a national curriculum: technique is often ahead, open writing behind
Mid-second-year arrivals need prioritisation, not a plan to catch up everywhere

sections.heading: Scheduling against the Sunday-to-Thursday week
paragraphs: The school week in the Kingdom runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend, and the Kingdom stays on Arabia Standard Time, UTC+3, all year with no daylight saving. Both facts have to be written into an arrangement rather than assumed. Tutoring copy produced for other markets takes a Monday to Friday week for granted and quietly offers Saturday morning sessions, which for a Saudi family lands on the wrong side of the weekend.

The time zone is the detail that goes wrong most often. A tutor in India is two and a half hours ahead; one in Pakistan two hours ahead; one in the United Kingdom three hours behind in their winter and two in their summer. Fix the slot in Saudi local time at the start and the tutor absorbs their own clock change. Leave it in the tutor's time zone and the lesson silently moves by an hour twice a year, which is usually discovered by a student sitting in front of an empty screen.

Local rhythms then do the rest of the work. School runs in Riyadh and along the Jeddah spine push a realistic start past seven in the evening; campus and compound households can often manage earlier. School days shorten during Ramadan and study moves into the evening, so lessons usually shift later for that period and shift back afterwards. The long summer break is the only time of year a student can work in the morning, which is why it is the right window for rebuilding anything substantial.
bullets: Friday and Saturday are the weekend; Sunday is a school day
UTC+3 all year, so a tutor's clock change must not move the lesson
Write the slot in Saudi local time, not in the tutor's
Shorter school days during Ramadan usually mean later, shorter sessions

sections.heading: What this costs in the Kingdom, and what the figure reflects
paragraphs: Published rates in this market are mostly advertised figures from providers rather than any measured average, and they should be read that way. Tutoring-platform listings advertise general non-specialist online tutoring from around SAR 55 an hour, and budget platforms advertise IGCSE one-to-one from around SAR 35. Tutor-marketplace guides put general private tuition for primary-age students at around SAR 50 and senior-school examination subjects at SAR 200 and upwards. Tutoring companies list IB subject tutoring from about SAR 180, with Higher Level and premium tracks advertised at roughly SAR 200 to 220. Some international providers quote in dollars, at around USD 60 an hour.

What moves a quote inside those bands is predictable. Subject scarcity does most of the work, because fewer people can teach Mathematics AA at Higher Level than Mathematics AI at Standard Level. Examiner or marking experience comes next and is worth paying for when the problem is technique rather than content. Then level, with Higher Level above Standard Level and both above Middle Years Programme work. Whether a tutor travels is absorbed into in-home rates whether or not it is itemised, and package length is the only variable that usually pushes a number down.

None of those figures is an IB Gram price, and a page quoting a single number for a qualification assessed this variably is not telling a parent anything useful. Our quote follows the trial lesson, because it depends on the subject, the level, the component and the frequency. The more useful question to ask any provider is what the hour includes: marking between lessons, past papers and mark schemes, a written note after each session, and whether a change of tutor is possible without starting again.
bullets: Every figure in this market is an advertised rate, not a market average
Scarcity, marking experience and level move a quote more than anything else
In-home rates absorb travel time whether or not it is shown
Ask what the hour includes before comparing two numbers

process.title: Name the component, not just the subject
process.description: Tell us the subject, the level, the session the student is entered for and which component is going wrong: a written paper, the internal assessment, the Extended Essay or pace across the whole paper. If that is not yet clear, send the most recent marked script and we will say what it looks like before any lesson happens.

process.title: A free trial lesson that ends in a diagnosis
process.description: The tutor works through the marked script and a question or two from a past paper, then states plainly what is costing marks and what it would take to change it. Nothing is paid before that. You should be able to repeat the diagnosis to the school in one sentence.

process.title: A plan positioned against the session
process.description: Teaching order, components to rehearse, coursework deadlines and a review date, all placed relative to the examination session and the school's own internal dates. The coordinator's deadlines go in first, since they almost always arrive before the board's do.

process.title: Weekly teaching with marking in between
process.description: A fixed slot written in Arabia Standard Time, Sunday to Thursday, with work set after each lesson and marked before the next. Each note names the component worked on and whether the identified loss pattern has moved, so a term of notes reads as a record rather than as reassurance.

process.title: A review, and an honest answer
process.description: At the review we compare current evidence against the opening diagnosis and say one of three things: continue, change something specific, or stop. If no specialist is free for a scarce subject at the time you need, we say so rather than offering a generalist and hoping.

whyPoints.title: Matched on the component, not the map
whyPoints.description: The tutor is chosen because they teach that subject at that level and know that component, which is the only variable that moves a grade. In a Kingdom where Diploma places concentrate in three markets, filtering by distance throws away almost everyone who could actually help.

whyPoints.title: The calendar, in the right order
whyPoints.description: The plan is built backwards from the examination session, with the school's internal coursework deadlines entered first because they arrive earlier. That ordering is what prevents two internal assessments and a mock landing in the same fortnight of the second year.

whyPoints.title: A diagnosis you can check
whyPoints.description: The trial lesson ends with a stated loss pattern taken from the student's own marked work, not with an impression. That gives a family something to measure against four weeks later, and something to take to the school if the school's view differs.

whyPoints.title: Straight about assessed work
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach criteria and give feedback on drafts the student wrote. No Internal Assessment, Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge essay or Personal Project is produced for a candidate, and the school supervisor keeps the reflection sessions and the authentication. The record of what was taught stays visible.

whyPoints.title: Built for the Saudi week
whyPoints.description: Slots are written in Arabia Standard Time and held there through a tutor's own clock changes, on a Sunday to Thursday pattern, with later starts in Ramadan and mornings available in the long break. The arrangement follows the household's week rather than a template from another market.

faqs.question: Why does a search for an IB tutor near me in the Kingdom rarely return a subject specialist?
faqs.answer: Because the pool near any given address is tiny. A Diploma cohort divides across six subject groups and two levels, so even a large school may have only a handful of candidates in a particular Higher Level subject, and correspondingly few local adults who have taught it recently. What the search does return is advertising, because providers optimise for the phrase. Filtering by subject, level and component instead returns everyone who teaches the course, which is a far larger and more relevant pool than everyone who lives within a short drive.

faqs.question: What does it mean that a school is licensed by the Ministry of Education, and what does ETEC evaluate?
faqs.answer: Private and international schools in the Kingdom operate under licence from the Ministry of Education, which is the permission to run as a school. Evaluation and accreditation run through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, which operates services for national school accreditation and for approving international accreditation bodies. Both describe the institution. Neither tells a parent whether a specific Higher Level course will be taught by a specialist in a given intake, which is a staffing question that only the school can answer, intake by intake.

faqs.question: What happens when a Saudi school cannot run a Higher Level subject a student has chosen?
faqs.answer: Several things, depending on numbers. The course may be timetabled as a combined Higher and Standard Level class, taught by a teacher whose specialism is a neighbouring subject, offered online through a third-party provider the school contracts, or withdrawn once choices are collected, which forces a student to re-choose. Ask at the admissions stage which Higher Level courses actually ran in the last two intakes rather than which ones appear in the prospectus. The two lists are often different, and the difference is the one that affects your child.

faqs.question: Where in the Kingdom are IB Diploma places actually concentrated?
faqs.answer: Riyadh holds the widest range of Diploma provision and therefore the broadest choice of Higher Level combinations. Jeddah has a substantial cluster along its coastal spine, and the Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran conurbation functions as one school market with the Diploma offered at some campuses and not others. The KAUST School serves the campus community at Thuwal. Outside those, provision thins quickly. The IB maintains a searchable directory of its World Schools, and that is the authoritative place to check what a particular city currently offers.

faqs.question: How do compound and camp schools differ from city schools for a Diploma student?
faqs.answer: Favourably on time and unfavourably on choice. A campus or company compound usually means a short commute, facilities within walking distance and a predictable week, which makes protecting a weekday evening slot much easier than it is for a family crossing a large city. The trade-off is cohort size: a small community produces small option groups, so the Higher Level courses available in any year reflect what that year's students happened to choose. Outside teaching for one scarce subject is a common pattern in exactly these schools.

faqs.question: What may a tutor do with an Extended Essay draft, and where does the school supervisor's role begin?
faqs.answer: A tutor may test whether the research question is answerable in four thousand words, suggest reading, teach a method or referencing convention, and read a draft the student wrote to say which assessment criterion it is failing and why. The supervisor's role is separate and cannot be shared: the school appoints them, they hold the recorded reflection sessions including the final discussion, they comment on the reflections form submitted with the essay, and they authenticate the work as the candidate's own. A tutor has no part in authentication.

faqs.question: What does similarity-detection software catch in an Internal Assessment, and what does it miss?
faqs.answer: It catches matched text: passages copied from web sources, published papers, or another candidate's submitted work where the system can see it. It also flags poorly disguised paraphrase. What it cannot see is original writing produced by somebody other than the candidate, which is why schools do not rely on it alone. Supervision records, drafting history, reflection sessions and a teacher's familiarity with how a student writes all form part of the check. A clean similarity report is not a finding of authenticity.

faqs.question: How many Extended Essay reflection sessions are there, and what is recorded in them?
faqs.answer: Three formal sessions with the school supervisor: an initial one about the topic and approach, an interim one once research is under way, and a final discussion after the essay is complete. The candidate writes reflections on planning and progress, and the supervisor adds comments on the form that is submitted alongside the essay. The reflections are assessed, so they are not an administrative formality. A tutor can help a student think clearly before a session, but neither the sessions nor the form involve anybody outside the school.

faqs.question: Can a tutor proofread a Theory of Knowledge essay before it is submitted?
faqs.answer: Not in the sense most families mean. A tutor can teach what the prescribed title is actually asking, discuss whether the essay's claims are supported, and point out that a paragraph asserts rather than argues. What they cannot do is correct the text, rewrite sentences or edit the essay into shape, because the submitted work has to be the candidate's own writing. The distinction is practical: teach the student to see the problem and they fix it themselves, which is both legitimate and more useful for the next piece of work.

faqs.question: How is the Personal Project assessed in the Middle Years Programme, and what may a tutor contribute?
faqs.answer: It is assessed against three criteria covering planning, applying skills and reflecting, with a report or product plus the student's own process documentation. A school supervisor oversees it. A tutor can teach what each criterion's top band expects, help a student test whether a goal is specific enough to be achievable, and review the student's own draft report against the descriptors. The project itself, including the product and every word of the report, has to be the student's work, and the documentation is part of what is marked.

faqs.question: What happens if a school suspects malpractice in a piece of coursework?
faqs.answer: The school is required to investigate rather than to let it pass. In practice that means comparing the submitted work with the candidate's drafting history and classroom writing, discussing it with the student, and reporting the case to the board where the suspicion stands up. Outcomes range from the component being refused a mark to the diploma being withheld. The consequence falls entirely on the candidate, which is the practical reason to keep a written record of what outside help was given and when.

faqs.question: What transfers when a student moves from a British school into the IB Diploma in the Kingdom?
faqs.answer: Subject content usually transfers well, particularly in mathematics and the sciences, where an IGCSE or AS background covers much of the early Diploma material. What does not transfer is the architecture: command terms, criterion-marked internal assessment, Theory of Knowledge and the expectation that answers justify a method rather than reach an answer. Breadth is the other adjustment, because a student used to three or four subjects now carries six plus a core. The first term should therefore be spent on question style and workload management.

faqs.question: What does an American-curriculum student have to catch up for Higher Level sciences?
faqs.answer: Depth, mostly, and the quantitative treatment that comes with it. The breadth of an American high school course maps reasonably onto the Diploma's coverage, but Higher Level extension topics assume a level of detail and mathematical handling that an unstreamed course rarely reaches, and the internally assessed investigation demands an experimental design the student may never have been asked to produce alone. A term spent on the extension topics and on investigation design is usually more valuable than general revision of material already met.

faqs.question: Can a student join the Diploma a term late, and what is realistic to recover?
faqs.answer: A term into the first year is recoverable for most students, provided the internal assessments are scoped early so they do not collide with the second year. Joining during the second year is much harder, because coursework in six subjects has deadlines that do not move for a new arrival, and the realistic conversation is about which subjects to prioritise. Whether coursework already completed elsewhere can be carried over is a question for the receiving school's Diploma coordinator, and it should be asked before the move rather than after it.

faqs.question: How does a student from a national-curriculum school adapt to IB command terms?
faqs.answer: Faster than most families expect, because it is a style problem rather than a knowledge problem. Such students often arrive with stronger manipulation and recall than the cohort and lose marks only on the form of the answer: describing when asked to evaluate, or giving a correct result with no reasoning shown. The fix is mechanical. Identify the command term, plan the shape of answer it demands, write to the mark allocation, and practise on marked past papers until the shape is automatic. Four to six weeks is typical.

ib-tutor-near-me.closingHeading: Tell us the component, and we will tell you who teaches it
ib-tutor-near-me.closingBody: Send the subject, the level, the examination session and the component that is costing marks, or just a photograph of the most recent marked script if that is not clear yet. A tutor who teaches that course will take a free trial lesson and end it with a stated diagnosis you can repeat to the school. If no specialist is free for a scarce subject in the slot you need, we will say so rather than offer a generalist. Teaching for families in the Kingdom is online, one-to-one, over live video, written into Arabia Standard Time and fitted around the Sunday to Thursday week.

ib-tutors.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach IB subjects to families across the Kingdom over live video. Each holds a weekly slot agreed in Arabia Standard Time rather than their own, which is the part that decides whether a term of lessons actually happens. Subject and level are matched first; the slot is then built around the school run.

intro.heading: The slot comes first, because a slot that fails ends the tuition
paragraphs: Almost every page about IB tutors in Saudi Arabia starts with the teaching and treats scheduling as an afterthought. That is the wrong way round, and anyone who has watched a promising arrangement collapse in week six knows it. The teaching only matters if the lesson happens. A term is roughly a dozen sessions, and a slot that is awkward loses two to a school event, one to a late school run, one to a tutor's public holiday, and one to simple attrition. Four lost sessions out of twelve is not a scheduling inconvenience, it is a third of the teaching.

The Kingdom makes this harder than most places, for two reasons that compound. The school week runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. That means Sunday morning behaves like a Monday, Thursday evening behaves like a Friday night, and a student is at their freshest on the two days most tutors abroad are least available. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not change its clocks at all, so any agreement with a tutor in a country that does will silently move by an hour twice a year unless the slot is pinned to Saudi local time rather than to theirs.

Layer on the tutor's own working week and the problem becomes concrete rather than abstract. A tutor in India is two and a half hours ahead, so a seven o'clock lesson in Riyadh lands at half past nine at night for them. A tutor in the United Kingdom is two or three hours behind depending on the season, so the same lesson falls in their late afternoon, which works well if they are a teacher finishing the school day and badly if they are collecting their own children. A tutor in Singapore is five hours ahead and simply cannot teach a Saudi school-night evening at all.

None of this is a reason to hire locally. It is a reason to ask about it. Lessons here are delivered one-to-one over live video, which is the only arrangement that lets a family in Jubail or AlUla reach a Higher Level specialist at all, and it is also the arrangement where a timetable mistake is invisible until it has cost you a month. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Saudi address; home visits are a service we offer only in India. What a Saudi family gets instead is a choice of specialist unconstrained by driving distance, on a slot that has to be engineered properly.

So the order of this page is the order of the decision. The clock first: what seven in the evening in Riyadh looks like from nine different tutor time zones, and which of those can hold a weekly school-night slot. Then the week itself, day by day, including why Sunday evening is often the easiest slot to fill and Thursday the hardest to protect. Then what breaks a slot and how to fix it. Then Ramadan, the autumn break and the long summer. Only after all of that does the page turn to whether the tutor is any good, how the first month is supposed to go, and what the hour is actually spent on.

ib-tutors.programmesIntro: The IB runs four programmes, and the scheduling problem is different in each. A ten-year-old can hold a late-afternoon slot that a Diploma student cannot, and a Diploma student can work at an hour that would be useless for a younger child. Here is what each programme asks for in practice.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The Primary Years Programme is inquiry-led and has no external examinations, so tuition here is never about papers. It is about the two things that make everything afterwards cheaper: number fluency and the ability to read a question for what it actually asks. Sessions are short, because attention rather than content is the limiting factor, and the gains show up three or four years later rather than at the end of term.
programmes.countryNote: This is the one programme where the Saudi school day helps rather than hinders. Primary finishing times leave a genuine late-afternoon window, so a slot can sit before the evening meal rather than after it, and a tutor in a time zone behind Arabia Standard Time finds that hour easy to hold. Short, frequent and early beats long and late at this age, every time.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The Middle Years Programme marks against four published criteria per subject rather than against a percentage, which is why a parent can read a report and still not know what went wrong. A student may know the content and still sit in the middle band because the criterion asked for something the answer never did. Years 4 and 5 also carry the Personal Project, assessed on process as much as product.
programmes.countryNote: Middle-years students in the Kingdom are usually the easiest to schedule and the most likely to be scheduled badly, because nothing is urgent yet. A fixed weekly slot that holds for a year is worth more here than a block of intensive work later, and this is the stage where a slot can be placed on a Monday or a Tuesday rather than competing for the crowded end of the week.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and the creativity, activity and service requirement. The Diploma total runs to 45 points: up to 7 in each of six subjects, with up to 3 further points from the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay matrix. Internal assessment carries a substantial share of most subject grades and is submitted long before the written papers.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students are the hardest scheduling problem in the Kingdom. They finish school late, they have evening commitments attached to the creativity, activity and service requirement, and they need two or three subjects supported rather than one. The workable pattern is almost always one protected evening carrying two subjects back to back, plus one more session at the weekend, which here means Friday or Saturday.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme combines Diploma Programme courses with a career-related study, a reflective project and a core that includes personal and professional skills and language development. It is offered at far fewer schools than the Diploma, so a student on it frequently has no local cohort and no local tutor who has seen the structure before.
programmes.countryNote: Because the programme is rare in the Kingdom, the scheduling advantage of teaching over video stops being about convenience and becomes the only route to anyone familiar with the structure. Families on this programme should ask specifically whether a tutor has taught the Diploma courses inside it, rather than whether they have taught the Diploma, since those are not the same claim.

ib-tutors.subjectsIntro: Subject by subject, the weekly slot has to be long enough for the work the subject actually requires. A mathematics hour and a history hour are not interchangeable: one needs working space and a shared screen, the other needs reading done before the session or the hour is wasted. These are the IB subjects families across the Kingdom ask for most.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The subject that most rewards a short, frequent slot over a long, occasional one, because fluency decays between sessions. Higher Level carries a third paper of extended problems with no Standard Level equivalent, and method marks are lost by students who write answers without working. The internal exploration is marked on mathematical communication as well as on the mathematics.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Heavier on modelling, statistics and calculator technique than students expect, so a session needs the student's own graphical display calculator in their hand rather than described over video. Conclusions that are not tied back to the data lose marks routinely. Higher Level adds matrices, graph theory and more demanding statistical testing.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Explanation chains are where the marks sit, and students compress them into a single sentence. The Higher Level additional content layers onto the shared core, so a weak core topic is examined twice over. The scientific investigation needs a research question narrow enough to be answered with the apparatus the school actually has, which is a conversation worth having early.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Three recurring losses: mole calculations with no visible working, organic mechanisms drawn without charges or curly arrows, and energetics answers that state a sign without justifying it. The data booklet is permitted and under-used. A session on mechanisms needs a shared writing surface, so this subject is one where the tooling in the lesson genuinely matters.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Examined far more strictly than it looks. Definitions are marked to the word, data questions want manipulation rather than description, and extended responses are credited against a list of specific points, so a fluent essay missing four of them scores badly. Higher Level adds real depth in genetics, plant biology and physiology.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The one subject where homework set before the session matters more than the session, because an hour spent reading aloud is an hour wasted. Guided analysis of an unseen passage rewards close work on technique and structure and punishes context-dumping. Higher Level adds a formal essay on a studied work, marked separately from both papers.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: A diagram subject with an essay attached: an answer without a correctly labelled and correctly shifted diagram cannot reach the top band however well written. Higher Level adds a quantitative policy paper with no Standard Level counterpart. The internal assessment is three commentaries on recent news articles, each marked on the application of a named key concept.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Tool-driven and stimulus-driven. The examination wants named frameworks applied to the material in front of the student rather than described in the abstract, and Higher Level adds a third paper built on a pre-released case study that rewards preparation months out. Students often pick an organisation that will not supply what the commentary needs.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Pseudocode precision and trace tables carry the written papers, and the Higher Level extension into abstract data structures and resource management is where candidates separate. The developed product needs documented design and testing: students who build first and write up afterwards lose criterion marks unrelated to how good the program is.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Not a subject with content to revise, which is exactly why it is mistaught. The essay answers a prescribed title and the exhibition works from objects and a prompt, and both are assessed on the quality of the argument about knowledge rather than on examples collected. A tutor's job here is to interrogate the argument, never to supply it.

ib-tutors.regionsTitle: Where IB families are, and what the week looks like from each
ib-tutors.regionsIntro: The Kingdom is not one commute or one school calendar. International and British-curriculum schools set their own term dates, so two families in the same city can be on different years, while the Sunday-to-Thursday week is the one thing they share. These are the places IB families write to us from, and what shapes the slot in each.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: Roughly an hour across north to south in traffic, which means two families at the same school can need slots ninety minutes apart. The largest set of Diploma schools in the Kingdom sits here, and so does the deepest local tutor pool, which makes Riyadh the one city where families compare a local option against an online one on something other than availability.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: A long coastal spine running from the historic centre north to Obhur, so a northern household and a central one have very different school runs to the same school. Evening slots here tend to sit later than in Riyadh, which suits a tutor in a time zone behind Arabia Standard Time and squeezes one in India.

regions.name: Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran
regions.note: One labour and school market rather than three cities: families routinely live in one and attend school in another. The Diploma runs at some campuses in the cluster and not others, so a student's Higher Level combination may be available at only one or two schools in the whole conurbation.

regions.name: Jubail and the industrial cities
regions.note: Shift and rotation work shapes the household week here more than the school run does, and a parent on a rotation cannot supervise a fixed Tuesday slot every week. Families in this position do better with a slot the student owns independently and a written note after each session than with one that depends on a parent being home.

regions.name: Makkah and Madinah
regions.note: Both cities have seasons that bend the week around pilgrimage traffic in a way no school calendar records. Families here benefit from agreeing in advance which weeks will be missed and which will be moved, rather than cancelling week by week, because a pattern of cancellations is what loses a scarce specialist's slot.

regions.name: Thuwal and the KAUST campus
regions.note: A campus community north of Jeddah on the coast, with a strongly international population and a school serving it. Students here are often several years into one curriculum and then relocate, so continuity of tutor across a move is worth more to these families than anything a local arrangement can offer.

regions.name: Abha and Khamis Mushait
regions.note: About twenty-five kilometres apart in 'Asir, at altitude, sharing a catchment. The international-curriculum cohort is small, which means subject specialists are scarce locally in a way that is structural rather than temporary. Distance, not preference, is the honest reason families here teach over video.

regions.name: Tabuk, AlUla and NEOM
regions.note: The northwest is where mid-course arrivals are most common, as families relocate into new developments part-way through a Diploma year. Catching up mid-course is a specific job with a specific sequence, and it starts with finding out what the previous school had and had not covered.

regions.name: Al Ahsa, Qatif and Yanbu
regions.note: Smaller centres where the nearest international-curriculum school may be an hour or more away, so the school run already eats the early evening before any lesson is considered. A later fixed slot, agreed once and left alone for the term, outlasts an earlier one that has to be renegotiated monthly.

schoolClusters.note: The largest concentration of Diploma and Cambridge provision in the Kingdom, and the only market where a family has a real choice of schools running the same Higher Level combination. Students we support attend schools including these.

The second major cluster, mixing IB World Schools with Cambridge schools and long-established international schools serving particular communities. Term dates differ school by school here, so two students in the same tutor's week can be in different terms.

Campus and compound schooling shapes the week here, and the Diploma is offered at some campuses and not at others. Families often commute between Dammam, Al Khobar, Dhahran and Jubail for a school that runs the subjects they need.

ib-tutors.modesIntro: Four shapes a week of IB tuition can take, chosen by what the student's timetable will actually bear rather than by what sounds thorough. All of them are one-to-one over live video, and all are agreed in Arabia Standard Time so the slot does not move when a tutor's own country changes its clocks.

modes.title: One protected school-night evening
modes.description: A single evening held for the whole term, carrying one subject or two shorter back-to-back sessions. This is the pattern that survives, because one evening can be defended against school events and family commitments in a way that three scattered half-hours cannot. Sunday and Monday evenings hold better than Wednesday and Thursday ones.

Pinned to Saudi local time, not the tutor's

modes.title: A Friday or Saturday weekend session
modes.description: The Saudi weekend is the tutor's working week in most countries, which makes Friday and Saturday the easiest slots to staff and the best place for the longer piece of work: a full timed paper, a coursework review, a topic taught from the beginning. It is also the slot a student is least tired in.

modes.title: Two subjects, two tutors, one evening
modes.description: A Diploma student rarely has one problem. Two shorter sessions on different subjects with different specialists, back to back on the same protected evening, costs the family one evening instead of two. It works when the subjects use different parts of the brain, and fails when both are numerate, because the second hour always gets the tired student.

A real break between the sessions, not a handover
Shorter sessions, because concentration is the binding constraint
Both tutors briefed on the same diagnostic

modes.title: A pre-series block, then stop
modes.description: A compressed run of sessions in the weeks before a session, built on timed papers marked to the published mark scheme rather than on new content. The block has an end date written into it from the start, which is the part families forget: tuition that does not know when it stops tends not to.

Scheduled around the school's own mock and revision weeks
Booked early, since scarce specialists fill their blocks first

sections.heading: Seven in the evening in Riyadh, read from the tutor's clock
paragraphs: A Saudi family picks a lesson time by looking at their own evening. The tutor is looking at a different number on a different clock, and whether the arrangement survives depends on what that number is. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3. A tutor in India is two and a half hours ahead of you; one in Pakistan is two ahead; one in the United Arab Emirates one ahead. Going the other way, a tutor in Egypt or South Africa is an hour behind, one in the United Kingdom two or three behind depending on the season, and one in eastern Canada or the eastern United States seven or eight hours behind.

Those offsets decide which evenings exist. Seven o'clock on a Tuesday in Riyadh is half past nine at night in India, which is a real lesson but not an indefinite habit for a tutor who also teaches at seven the next morning. The same hour is half past four in the afternoon in the United Kingdom in their winter, which is comfortable for a teacher who has just finished a school day. In Singapore it is midnight, which is why a Singapore-based tutor can teach Saudi weekends and not Saudi school nights. None of this is anybody's fault, and all of it is knowable before the first lesson.

The second column of the table is the one families never ask about: the tutor's own working week. A tutor in India or the United Kingdom rests on Saturday and Sunday, so Saudi Sunday, a school night here, is their day off and one of the easiest slots in the week to fill. Thursday evening in the Kingdom is the start of your weekend and the middle of theirs, which is why Thursday is both the slot families most want and the slot that quietly gets cancelled most often.

sections.heading: Arabia Standard Time does not move. Most tutors' clocks do.
paragraphs: This is the single most common way a working arrangement quietly breaks, and it is entirely preventable. The Kingdom sits at UTC+3 all year and does not observe daylight saving. A great many of the countries tutors live in do. Twice a year, those countries move their clocks by an hour, and if the weekly slot was ever agreed as a time in the tutor's own city rather than a time in yours, it moves with them. Nobody announces it. The tutor arrives at what they still think is five o'clock and the student has been waiting for an hour, or has gone out.

The fix costs one sentence at the start. Write the slot down as a Saudi local time, name the city, and state explicitly that it does not change when the tutor's clocks do. Tuesday, seven in the evening, Arabia Standard Time, all term. If the tutor needs to shift it when their own clocks change, that is a conversation to have in advance and a change to confirm in writing, not a drift to discover. Calendar invitations are worth checking too: an invitation created in the wrong time zone will display correctly to one of you and incorrectly to the other.

There is a related trap in the half-hour offsets. India is two and a half hours ahead of the Kingdom, not two or three, and families converting in their head routinely land thirty minutes out. Nepal and parts of Australia sit on similar fractional offsets. The practical rule is simple: never convert mentally, always write both times down once, and have the tutor confirm the Saudi time back to you in their own words before the first lesson. A term saved by one sentence is a good return on the sentence.
bullets: Write the slot as a Saudi local time and say so explicitly
Confirm the tutor has read it back as a Saudi time, not theirs
Expect a conversation when their clocks change, not a surprise
Treat half-hour offsets as the likeliest arithmetic error

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week, day by day
paragraphs: Treating the Saudi week as a Monday-to-Friday week with different labels is the mistake most tutoring copy makes, because it was written for another market and had the city names changed. The days here do not behave like their western counterparts. Sunday is the first school day and carries first-day energy, so it is a poor slot for difficult new content and a good one for review. Monday and Tuesday are the strongest teaching days of the week in the Kingdom, for the same reason Tuesday and Wednesday are elsewhere: far enough into the week for the student to be in rhythm, far enough from the weekend to still be trying.

Wednesday is where school fatigue starts to show in Diploma students who have also been carrying evening commitments. Thursday is effectively a Friday night. A Thursday evening lesson is agreed with great enthusiasm in the first week of term and is the first casualty of every social arrangement thereafter, which is why we try to talk families out of it unless it is the only option. The weekend, Friday and Saturday, is where the long work belongs: a full timed paper, a coursework review session, a topic taught properly from the start.

There is a useful asymmetry to exploit. Because most tutors live in countries that rest on Saturday and Sunday, Saudi Sunday evening is simultaneously a school night for your child and a day off for them. That makes it the single easiest slot in the week to fill with a scarce specialist, and the one most likely to still be available when you ask. Families who want a Higher Level physics or analysis-and-approaches tutor and are flexible about the day should ask for Sunday first.

sections.heading: What breaks a weekly slot, and what fixes it
paragraphs: Arrangements fail in a small number of recognisable ways, and every one of them has a cheap fix applied at the start and an expensive fix applied in week eight. The most common is a start time set from an optimistic week rather than a normal one. A slot that begins fifteen minutes late every week loses the quarter hour at the end, which is where the practice was, so the family pays for an hour and receives forty-five minutes of the less valuable part of it. Setting the slot after the latest normal arrival home, not the earliest, costs nothing and saves the term.

The second is the parent-dependency problem. A slot that only works when a particular adult is home does not survive a rotation, a business trip or a late meeting. The repair is to make the student the owner of the session: they join, they have the materials, and the parent receives a written note afterwards rather than supervising during. The third is unmanaged absence. A family that cancels week by week will eventually lose a scarce specialist's slot, because that hour is the tutor's livelihood and somebody else wants it. Agreeing the term's known absences in advance keeps the slot.

The fourth is subject overload disguised as diligence. Three subjects with three tutors across three evenings looks thorough on paper and produces a student with no free evenings, who then resents all three. Two subjects on one protected evening and one weekend session is almost always the better shape. The fifth is the drift problem already described: a slot defined in the tutor's own time, which moves when their clocks do.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the autumn break and the long summer
paragraphs: Three predictable disruptions, and families handle all three better by deciding in advance than by reacting. During Ramadan the school day shortens and household rhythms shift towards the evening and the night. For tuition the useful conversation is not whether to continue but when: a slot that worked in the afternoon may be better placed much later, and a reduced number of sessions held reliably beats a full timetable abandoned in the second week. Ramadan also moves roughly eleven days earlier against the Gregorian calendar each year, so it drifts across the academic year rather than sitting in one term.

Public-sector schools in the Kingdom run a two-semester year starting in late August and ending in late June, with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break. International and British-curriculum schools set their own calendars and most run three terms, so two families in the same city can be in different terms on the same day. Nobody should take a term date from a web page, including this one: your own school's published calendar is the only authority, and tuition should be planned against it rather than against a national pattern.

The long summer is where plans are won and lost. For a student sitting papers in the next series, the summer is not downtime, it is the last block of uninterrupted time they will get, and three or four weeks of steady work in it is worth more than twice as much squeezed into the term. For a November-entry candidate the summer is the main revision period outright. The practical question to settle in advance is whether the slot is paused or held: a held slot costs something and survives, a paused one is often gone when you come back for it.
bullets: Decide the Ramadan pattern before it starts, not during
Take term dates from your own school, never from a national calendar
Treat the summer as the last uninterrupted block before a series
Agree whether the slot is paused or held before the holiday starts

sections.heading: A slot that works is not the same as a tutor who is right
paragraphs: Once the clock problem is solved, the harder question returns. The claim families cannot easily check is subject-level expertise, because every tutor in this market says they teach the IB. What distinguishes the ones who do is specificity. Ask which subject guide version they have taught to, which components they have marked or moderated, and which paper they would look at first given the student's current marks. Someone who has taught Chemistry at Higher Level answers in one sentence and names a component. Someone who has not talks about building confidence.

Examiner and marking experience is worth asking about and worth understanding properly. A tutor who has marked for a board knows what the mark scheme credits and, more usefully, what it refuses to credit, which is the knowledge that turns a competent answer into a scoring one. It is not a magic qualification and it does not make someone a good teacher of a struggling fifteen-year-old. A current classroom teacher brings scheme-of-work awareness and knows what schools actually do; a full-time tutor brings volume across many schools and boards. Both are legitimate, and they are different products.

Then check the things that are checkable. Ask for a trial lesson that is taught rather than sold, using a question the student has already got wrong, and watch what the tutor does with the wrong answer. Ask what they will do if a coursework draft arrives in poor shape two days before a school deadline; the honest answer involves the student and sometimes the school, never a quiet offer to tidy it up. Ask who you contact if the tutor is ill. Treat any unverifiable success statistic as marketing, because that is what it is.
bullets: Ask which components they have taught, marked or moderated
Ask which paper they would attack first, and why that one
Insist the trial lesson is taught, not pitched
Treat any unsourced success rate as a sales claim, not evidence

sections.heading: The diagnostic, the first month, and what gets reported
paragraphs: A first session should produce a diagnosis, not an impression. That means working from evidence the student has already generated: a marked paper, a past-paper question they got wrong, a coursework draft, a mock script. The output is a statement a parent can hold onto, naming the component and the topics where the marks are going missing and the order in which they will be addressed. If after the first session nobody can tell you which paper the problem is on, the session was a conversation rather than a diagnostic.

The first month then has four jobs. Confirm or correct the diagnosis against more evidence. Establish that work happens between sessions, because the hour is where the teaching is and the week is where the learning is. Produce at least one piece of work marked against the real mark scheme, so you can see the standard rather than take it on trust. And settle the logistics: the slot, the materials, the way homework arrives and comes back. A month is also long enough to tell whether the student will talk honestly to this particular adult about not understanding something, which matters more than most qualifications.

Reporting should be short and specific. A note after each session covering what was taught, what was set and what the work showed takes a tutor a few minutes and gives you something checkable. A longer review at the end of each term is where honest judgement belongs: whether the component is improving, whether a different subject is now the bigger problem, whether to continue at all. Be wary of reporting that only ever contains good news. A tutor who has never told you something you did not want to hear is not reporting, they are reassuring.
bullets: A diagnostic names the component and the topic, not the ability
Expect one piece of work marked to the real mark scheme in month one
A short written note after each session beats a long monthly essay
A report with no bad news in it is not a report

sections.heading: What the hour is actually spent on
paragraphs: Parents paying by the hour are entitled to know what the hour buys, and the honest answer changes with the stage of the course. Early on it is content and foundations: the algebra that will otherwise resurface in three subjects, the writing structure that every essay subject assumes, the laboratory and data skills the internal assessment will need. Mid-course it shifts to technique applied to content, which means past-paper questions taken apart, mark schemes read against the student's own answer, and command terms treated as examinable vocabulary rather than as instructions in the margin.

Late in the course it is almost entirely execution. The marks a student loses in the final weeks are lost to timing, to misreading what a command term is asking for, and to two or three recurring topic weaknesses that nobody has named out loud. The method is unglamorous: a paper sat under timed conditions, marked against the published mark scheme, and the pattern in the lost marks named and drilled before the next paper. New content in the last stretch is almost always displacement activity, and a tutor proposing it has misread where the marks are.

Across all of it, one category of work stays off limits in every session. Internal assessments, the Extended Essay, the Theory of Knowledge essay and the reflective project must be the student's own work. A tutor reads the draft, maps it against the published criteria, asks the questions a reader will ask and sends the student away to redraft it themselves. They do not write a sentence of it. That boundary protects the student from a malpractice finding that can cost an entire Diploma, which is a far larger risk than any grade it might buy.

process.title: Send the subject, the level and the school

process.description: The city, the realistic arrival home across a normal Sunday-to-Thursday week, the evenings already committed, and whether a parent needs to be present. We would rather set a later slot that survives the term than an earlier one that slips every week until it stops happening.

process.title: We propose a tutor and a slot in Saudi time
process.description: You get a named tutor with a stated subject background and a proposed slot written as an Arabia Standard Time appointment, with their own rest days declared. If the only workable option is a weekend session rather than a school night, we will say that instead of pretending otherwise.

process.title: A free trial lesson, taught not pitched
process.description: The tutor teaches something real, usually a question the student has already got wrong. You are watching for whether they identify the component, explain it in a way your child follows, and name what they would change first. Ask them directly which paper the marks are on.

process.title: Diagnostic, plan, then weekly work
process.description: The first working session establishes the starting point against the actual mark scheme. Out of it comes a short plan naming components in priority order. Then the pattern that produces the gains: work set after each session, marked before the next, with a short written note to you.

process.title: Review at the end of the term
process.description: Whether the component that was costing marks has stopped costing them, whether the plan should change, and whether a different subject is now the bigger problem. If the match is wrong we change the tutor rather than asking you to persist, and we will tell you when tuition should stop.

whyPoints.title: The slot is engineered, not assumed
whyPoints.description: Every arrangement is written as an Arabia Standard Time appointment, with the tutor's own rest days and clock changes known in advance. That one discipline prevents the most common failure in online tutoring across time zones, which is an hour of silent drift twice a year that nobody attributes to the calendar.

whyPoints.title: Matched to a syllabus, not to a postcode
whyPoints.description: Distance is irrelevant to a video lesson, which means a family in Jubail, Tabuk or AlUla is choosing from the same pool as a family in central Riyadh. For scarce specialisms, Higher Level physics and the analysis-and-approaches mathematics course in particular, that is the difference between a specialist and a generalist.

whyPoints.title: The Saudi week treated as the real week
whyPoints.description: Sunday is a school night and Thursday evening is the weekend. Our scheduling starts from that rather than from a Monday-to-Friday template inherited from another market, which is why we will argue a family out of a Thursday slot and towards a Sunday one.

whyPoints.title: One student in the room
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video, so the hour is spent on this student's errors rather than on a group's average. The work set between sessions is marked before the next one, because the marking is where the diagnosis lives and a session without it is a conversation.

whyPoints.title: Assessed work stays the student's work
whyPoints.description: On an internal assessment, an Extended Essay or a Theory of Knowledge essay the tutor reads, questions and maps against the published criteria, then the student redrafts. Nothing is written for them. The written feedback trail is deliberate, because it also evidences that the work is genuinely their own.

whyPoints.title: We say when we cannot help
whyPoints.description: If no specialist in your subject and level has a slot that fits your week, we will tell you rather than offer a generalist with an opening. Examination and results dates come from your school. University and Qiyas requirements come from the institution's own published criteria, not from us.

faqs.question: Our tutor is in the United Kingdom - what happens to our slot when their clocks change?
faqs.answer: Nothing, if the slot was written as a Saudi time. The Kingdom stays on UTC+3 all year and does not change its clocks, so a Tuesday seven o'clock Arabia Standard Time appointment stays at seven for you whatever the United Kingdom does. What moves is the tutor's end: the same lesson falls at four in their afternoon in one half of the year and five in the other. That is their adjustment to make, and it should be confirmed in writing before it happens rather than discovered on the day somebody waits.

faqs.question: What does the two-and-a-half-hour difference to India mean for an evening lesson in the Kingdom?
faqs.answer: It means a seven o'clock Riyadh lesson is half past nine at night for the tutor, and a six o'clock one is half past eight. Both are workable; neither is comfortable as a permanent arrangement for someone teaching early the next morning. The half-hour is also where families go wrong, converting mentally and landing thirty minutes out. Write both times down once, have the tutor confirm the Saudi time back to you in their own words, and prefer an earlier Saudi evening if the student's school run allows it.

faqs.question: Can an IB lesson run on a Friday or a Saturday in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the Saudi weekend is often the easiest part of the week to staff. Friday and Saturday fall inside the working week in most of the countries tutors live in, so a specialist who cannot hold a Saudi school night can usually hold a weekend morning or afternoon. Those sessions are also the right place for long-form work: a full paper under timed conditions, a coursework review, or a topic taught from the beginning. Protect one weekend day for it rather than both.

faqs.question: Why is Sunday evening often the easiest slot to fill with a tutor based abroad?
faqs.answer: Because of a mismatch that works in your favour. Sunday is the first school day of the week in the Kingdom, so your child is at home in the evening and ready to work. In most of the countries tutors live in, Sunday is a rest day, so their evening is free. That combination makes Saudi Sunday one of the few hours where a scarce specialist is genuinely available. If you want a Higher Level physics or analysis-and-approaches tutor and you can be flexible about the day, ask for Sunday first.

faqs.question: How late can a Diploma lesson start on a school night and still be worth having?
faqs.answer: Later than most parents think, and earlier than most teenagers claim. The limit is not the clock, it is whether the student can still produce written work at that hour, because a session where they only watch is a session with no diagnosis in it. A lesson that starts after the evening meal and runs to an hour works for most Diploma students. Two hours late at night does not. If the only workable school-night slot is genuinely too late, move the subject to a Friday or Saturday instead of accepting a bad hour.

faqs.question: What happens to a weekly slot during Ramadan, when school hours shorten?
faqs.answer: The slot usually moves rather than stops. School days shorten and household rhythm shifts later, so an afternoon slot often works better much later in the evening, and some families prefer fewer sessions held reliably to a full timetable abandoned in the second week. Decide the pattern in advance with the tutor and write it down, including which weeks are paused. Because the month moves around eleven days earlier against the Gregorian calendar each year, it does not sit in the same part of the school year twice.

faqs.question: Do we lose our tutor's slot over the long summer break?
faqs.answer: Only if you leave it undecided. A slot that is explicitly held by agreement survives the break; one that is simply abandoned in the final week of term is frequently gone when you come back for it, because that hour is the tutor's income and somebody else is asking for it. Decide before the holiday whether you are pausing or holding, and say which. For a candidate sitting papers in the next series, the summer is usually the last long uninterrupted block of work available, so pausing it entirely is rarely the right call.

faqs.question: How much notice is needed to move a regular weekly slot to a different evening?
faqs.answer: A fortnight is a fair expectation for a permanent change, because the tutor has to find another home for the hour they are giving up and may be holding slots for other families on the same evenings. A one-off move, for a school trip or an examination clash, usually needs only a few days and should be rescheduled rather than cancelled. A single lesson cancelled with less than a day's notice is reasonably charged for; that is the convention in this market and it is not unreasonable.

faqs.question: Can a Diploma student take two subjects in the same evening?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and for a student carrying two weak subjects it is usually the better shape, because it costs one protected evening rather than two. It works when the subjects are genuinely different in kind, so an essay subject followed by a numerate one rather than two sciences back to back. Keep both sessions shorter than a single session would be, put a real break between them, and accept that the second hour always gets the more tired student. Brief both tutors on the same diagnostic.

faqs.question: How many hours a week does a Diploma student carrying two weak subjects actually need?
faqs.answer: Less contact time than families expect and more independent work than students want. One hour a week per subject, with work set after each session and marked before the next, moves a grade over a term if the student does the work. Doubling the contact time without changing the work between sessions rarely does. The exception is a student who has fallen genuinely behind on content rather than technique, where a short intensive run to close a specific gap, with an end date written into it, is the right instrument.

faqs.question: How is a starting point diagnosed when a student has no recent marked work to show?
faqs.answer: The tutor generates the evidence in the session. A short set of questions chosen across the components of the course, attempted under something close to examination conditions, tells a specialist more in forty minutes than a term of reports does. The student's working is as informative as their answers, because it shows whether a wrong answer came from not knowing, from misreading the command term, or from an error three lines earlier. The output should still be a named component and a named topic, not a general impression of ability.

faqs.question: What does a useful end-of-term review from an IB tutor contain?
faqs.answer: Four things. What the diagnosis was at the start of term, in the same words it was given in. What has measurably changed, with reference to marked work rather than to effort. What has not changed, which is the part that distinguishes a review from reassurance. And a recommendation for the next term, including the option of stopping or of switching the hours to a different subject. A review containing only good news is not a review, and a parent is entitled to ask which component is still costing marks.

faqs.question: What happens if a tutor becomes unavailable part-way through the Diploma?
faqs.answer: You should be told immediately and offered a replacement with a handover rather than a fresh start. The handover is the part that matters: the diagnosis, the plan, what has been covered, what was set and what the marked work showed. A new tutor who has read that is a few sessions behind; one who has not is a term behind. Ask at the outset who you contact if the tutor is ill, and keep the written session notes, because they are the handover document whether or not anyone calls them that.

faqs.question: How is the Diploma core scored, and how many points does it add?
faqs.answer: The Diploma total runs to 45 points. Six subjects contribute up to 7 points each, which is 42, and up to 3 further points come from the combination of the Theory of Knowledge grade and the Extended Essay grade read together on a published matrix. A failing grade in either core component can prevent the award of the Diploma regardless of subject points. That is why these two pieces, which feel peripheral in the first year, are worth treating as examined components from the start rather than as paperwork.

faqs.question: Why does a mark scheme reward a short answer that a well-written paragraph does not?
faqs.answer: Because most extended responses are credited against a list of specific points rather than on overall impression. An examiner reads for those points and awards a mark when one appears. A fluent paragraph that circles the topic without landing on four of the listed points scores less than a blunt list that lands on all of them. The practical consequence is that students should read the mark total as an instruction about how many creditable points to make, and write to hit them rather than to sound thorough.

faqs.question: How should a timed mock paper change what the tutor works on next?
faqs.answer: A mock is only worth the analysis that follows it. Marks lost should be sorted into three piles: content not known, command term misread, and time run out. Each has a different remedy, and lumping them together produces a revision plan that addresses the wrong one. Content gaps get taught. Misread command terms get drilled as vocabulary. Timing problems get fixed by practising question allocation, not by learning more. A tutor who reads a mock and recommends revising everything has not read it closely enough.

ib-tutors.closingHeading: Send us the subject and the shape of your week
ib-tutors.closingBody: Two things get this started: the subject and level your child is entered for, and an honest description of a normal Sunday-to-Thursday week with the latest realistic arrival home. We will come back with a named tutor, their subject background, their own rest days, and a proposed slot written as an Arabia Standard Time appointment so it cannot drift. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, the trial lesson is free and is taught rather than sold, and if nobody with the right specialism has an hour that fits your week we will tell you that rather than fill the slot with a generalist.

intro.heading: A demo class against the other ways to try before you commit
paragraphs: Every family weighing private tuition in the Kingdom is choosing between five or six options at once: a one-to-one tutor found online, a group revision course at a local centre, a recorded video course, an in-home tutor from an agency, the school's own after-school club, and whoever a neighbour recommends. All six promise improvement. The useful question is not which sounds best but which one you can test cheaply, before a term's fees are committed. That is the whole argument for a demo class.

A free one-to-one demo is the cheapest honest test available, because it costs one evening and it exposes the single thing the brochures cannot: whether this particular tutor knows this particular syllabus. A group course trial shows you pace and content coverage. A recorded course shows whether the material is complete. Neither tells you how a tutor responds when your child gets a question wrong, which is the behaviour you are actually buying.

An in-home agency trial is the closest comparison, and worth being straight about. Agencies in Riyadh and Jeddah do send tutors to houses, and the trial visit shows rapport in the room. What it cannot show is access, because the pool is limited to tutors who will drive to your district, and the scarcer the subject the thinner that pool gets. IB Gram does not sell in-home visits anywhere in the Kingdom; home visits are a service offered only in India, and lessons for Saudi families run online, one to one, over live video.

A recommendation deserves its own note, because it is the most trusted and least transferable form of evidence. That a tutor worked for a friend's child tells you they are competent and reliable. It does not tell you whether they know your child's board, tier, level and component list, which is where most mismatches actually sit. A demo class is how you convert a recommendation into something checkable in under an hour. The school's own after-school club belongs in the same category: free, convenient, run by a teacher who knows the scheme of work, and limited by the fact that the group is the whole class again. It is worth taking and it is not a substitute for a diagnosis of one student's errors.

What follows sets out what happens inside the session, how to read it, how to check an examiner claim, how the screen mechanics work, and how to pick a slot that will still be there in eight weeks. There is no obligation attached and no sales call afterwards. If the match is wrong, you will be told so and offered a different specialist, or told honestly that nobody suitable is free at the hour you need.

sections.heading: Five ways to try a tutor, and what each one proves
paragraphs: Comparison is easier when the options are laid out by what they cost you to test rather than by what they claim. The table below does that for the five routes Saudi families most often weigh. Read the final column first: every option proves something, and the differences between them are almost entirely in what they leave unproven. A group course can show you excellent teaching and still tell you nothing about one-to-one diagnosis, because those are different skills.

Two of the five deserve particular care. A recorded video course is cheap to sample and genuinely useful for content gaps, but completion is the whole problem: a library that is never finished teaches nothing, and a demo of the first module cannot tell you whether a fourteen-year-old will reach the last one. A neighbour's recommendation is the opposite failure mode. It is strong evidence about the tutor and weak evidence about the match, because your child may sit a different board, a different tier and a different component list.

The in-home option is the one most often presented as the premium choice, and the honest comparison depends on where you live. In central Riyadh or Jeddah the in-home pool is real, and the market charges accordingly; tutor-marketplace guides put general senior-school private tuition in Riyadh at above SAR 200 an hour, and tutoring companies list IB subject tutoring from around SAR 180, with Higher Level tracks advertised at roughly SAR 200 to 220. Those are other providers' advertised rates, not ours. Outside those cities the pool thins until the choice is no longer between formats.
