sections.heading: What actually happens in the forty-five minutes
paragraphs: A demo class is not an introduction to the platform. There is no slide deck, no tour and no discussion of packages. The tutor asks three questions at the start, confirms the board, the tier and the component list, and then puts a question on screen. Most of the session is the student working while the tutor watches how they work, which is the part that cannot be faked in either direction.

The question is chosen deliberately. It is a past-paper item at the level the student is entered for, hard enough to produce a mistake and short enough to finish. When the mistake arrives, the useful behaviour starts: a good tutor does not supply the answer, they narrow it. They ask what the question is asking for, point at the line where the method stopped, and let the student recover it. A tutor who talks for ten minutes at the first wrong step has shown you how every lesson will go.

The last ten minutes are spent on the script rather than on the subject. The tutor marks what the student wrote against the published scheme, says where the marks went and names the first two things that would change. That becomes the written summary a parent receives afterwards: the question, what happened, what it suggests, and what a first month would attack. If you continue, that summary is the plan. If you do not, you keep it anyway.

sections.heading: Telling a specialist from a confident generalist
paragraphs: Almost every tutor in this market sounds competent for twenty minutes, so the demo has to be read for specifics rather than for fluency. Three signals separate someone who teaches the syllabus from someone who knows the subject. The first is vocabulary: a specialist uses the board's own words for things, names the paper by number and refers to components rather than to chapters. The second is prediction: they can say where in the paper a topic usually appears and what the common distractor is.

The third and most reliable signal is the mark scheme. Ask the tutor what this answer would score and why. A specialist will point at individual scheme points, including the one the student missed by a single word, and will tell you which alternative wordings are accepted. A generalist will give you a grade and a reason that sounds sensible. The difference is not politeness; it is whether their feedback can be checked against a document.

There is also a fair question to put directly. Ask which topic in this course students most often fail to recover and what they do about it. The answer should be specific and slightly unflattering about the subject, because every course has one. A tutor who says the whole syllabus is manageable with hard work has not been in enough rooms. A tutor who names the topic, and the reason it defeats students, has been in plenty. The same test works in reverse: ask what they would refuse to teach, and a specialist will name a neighbouring course they do not cover rather than claiming all of them.

sections.heading: Examiner experience: what the claim means, and checking it
paragraphs: Marking experience is the most commonly advertised credential in this market and the least commonly explained. It can mean several different things: marking scripts for a board in a particular series, moderating other markers, writing questions, or having been trained once and not marked since. None of those is dishonest, but they are not equivalent, and the first is worth considerably more to a student than the last. Ask which board, which paper and which components, and ask when.

The verification you can actually do is indirect but effective. Someone who has marked at volume talks about scripts in a distinctive way. They describe the scheme's hierarchy, the points that are most often awarded in error, and the wording candidates use that markers are instructed not to credit. They are usually careful about what they will not claim, because marking is covered by confidentiality. Vagueness dressed as discretion is different from precision bounded by it, and ten minutes of questions separates them.

Hold the credential in proportion. A marker's instinct is valuable for technique, boundary-adjacent answers and extended responses. It is worth less for repairing a two-year content gap, where a patient classroom teacher may be the better match. Nobody should promise a grade on the strength of a marking credential, and the gap between what examiner experience improves and what it cannot touch is worth asking about in the demo itself. A fair way to put it is simply this: what would you expect to fix in six weeks, and what would you not? The answer separates a credential being used as a tool from one being used as a badge.

sections.heading: The mechanics on screen, and what a parent sees
paragraphs: The technical requirements are modest and worth settling before the demo rather than during it. A laptop is better than a tablet because two windows are often open at once, headphones cut the room out, and a cabled connection beats the household wireless at eight in the evening. The student needs the paper copy of whatever they are working on, a pen and squared paper for mathematics or physics, because writing on paper and holding it to the camera is often faster than drawing with a mouse.

Inside the session there is a shared whiteboard both sides can write on, screen sharing for a past paper or a marked script, and a chat panel for links. A scanned or photographed script can be dropped in and annotated live, which is how a marked paper gets discussed. If a connection drops, the session is paused and resumed rather than written off; a demo cut short by the network is rebooked at no cost, because the point of it is unfinished.

Parents ask two questions more than any others. Can I watch, and is it recorded? You are welcome to sit in on a demo, and most tutors would rather you did, though a teenager usually works better if you watch without joining in. Recording is available on request and is shared with the family; it is not published anywhere and is not used for anything else. If you would prefer no recording at all, say so when the slot is booked.

sections.heading: Booking a slot that will still work in eight weeks
paragraphs: The most common mistake in booking a demo is choosing a convenient hour rather than a realistic one. A Saturday afternoon demo proves that a tutor can teach; it proves nothing about Tuesday at seven when school has run late and homework is waiting. The school week in the Kingdom runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend, so the slot worth testing is a school-night slot early in that week.

The clock is the second half of it. The Kingdom keeps Arabia Standard Time, UTC+3, all year with no daylight saving, while much of the world adjusts twice. A slot agreed in the tutor's local time will therefore move by an hour twice a year without anyone deciding to move it. Booking the demo in Kingdom time, and asking the tutor what their own week and their own clock changes look like, catches that before it costs a term of rescheduling.

Ask one further question while booking: is this tutor the person who will teach the weekly lessons? A demo given by a senior tutor and lessons delivered by someone else is a bait that exists in this market. The answer should be yes by default, and where it cannot be, you should be told who will teach and offered a demo with them instead. The slot, the clock and the person are three separate commitments, and all three are worth confirming in writing before the first paid lesson rather than after it.

sections.heading: The trouble spots a good demo exposes
paragraphs: Every course has a small number of places where marks reliably disappear, and an hour spent on one of them is worth more than a survey of the whole syllabus. In Mathematics at Higher Level it is usually the junction between topics: a calculus question whose first step is algebraic, where the calculus is known and the manipulation fails. A demo that probes that junction finds in twenty minutes what a term of chapter-by-chapter revision can miss entirely.

In the sciences the pattern differs by subject. Chemistry trouble concentrates in organic mechanisms and in equilibrium, both of which reward reasoning and punish recall, so a demo asks the student to justify an arrow or a shift rather than to state a rule. Physics trouble is usually bookkeeping: units dropped, method marks never written, uncertainty treated as decoration. Biology trouble is almost always writing, because the content is known and the six-mark answers are unstructured.

The social sciences split cleanly, which makes them easy to diagnose. In Economics a student is either weak on diagrams or weak on evaluation, and one stimulus with two prompts settles which. In Business Management the tools are usually recited rather than applied to the case. In Geography the content is present and the named case-study detail is missing. A demo should end with the family knowing which of these it is, because the answer changes what the first month does and how quickly any change will show up in a marked paper.

faqs.question: What should a parent ask in the first five minutes of a demo class?
faqs.answer: Three questions, in this order. Which paper and which components make up my child's grade on this course? Where in that paper does the topic we are worried about usually appear? And what would this answer score against the published scheme, and why? The first tests whether the tutor checked the entry rather than assumed it. The third cannot be answered convincingly without the scheme in front of them.

faqs.question: How can I check a tutor's claim of examiner experience without taking their word for it?
faqs.answer: Ask which board, which paper, which components and when, then listen to how they talk about scripts. Someone who has marked at volume describes the scheme's hierarchy, the points awarded in error most often, and the candidate wordings markers are instructed not to credit. They are also careful about what they will not disclose, because marking carries confidentiality. Precision bounded by discretion sounds quite different from vagueness dressed as it.

faqs.question: Does it matter whether the demo tutor is the one who teaches the weekly lessons?
faqs.answer: It matters a great deal, and it is worth confirming in writing before the session. A demo given by a senior tutor followed by lessons from someone else tests a match that will never exist. The default should be that the person who runs the demo is the person who teaches. Where a specialist is unavailable for the slot you need, you should be told who would teach instead and offered a demo with them.

faqs.question: How do I tell a subject specialist from a confident generalist inside one session?
faqs.answer: Watch the vocabulary and the predictions. A specialist names the paper by number, uses the board's own terms for components, and can say where a topic usually appears and what the common distractor is. They answer mark questions by pointing at individual scheme points. A generalist gives a grade and a plausible reason. Then ask which topic in this course students most often fail to recover; a specialist names one and explains why, because every syllabus has one.

faqs.question: What happens if we want a different tutor after the demo class?
faqs.answer: You ask, and a second demo with another specialist is arranged at no cost. There is no penalty, no explanation required and no awkward conversation with the first tutor, who is not told your reasons. The most useful version is to have both tutors work the same past-paper question, because comparing two sessions on identical material beats comparing impressions formed on different questions.

faqs.question: What does the student need on their desk for a demo class to work?
faqs.answer: A laptop rather than a tablet, because two windows are often open at once. Headphones, to cut the room out. A cabled connection if one exists, since household wireless is at its worst in the early evening. Then paper: a pen and squared paper for mathematics or physics, plus printed copies of any marked work. Writing on paper and holding it to the camera is usually faster than drawing with a mouse.

faqs.question: Is a demo class recorded, and who can see the recording afterwards?
faqs.answer: Recording is available on request rather than by default. When it is switched on, the file is shared with the family and is not published, sold or used for anything else. Many parents ask for the first session to be recorded so they can watch it later rather than sitting in. If you would prefer no recording, say so when the slot is booked and none is made. The written summary arrives either way.

faqs.question: How does a tutor share a marked script or a diagram during an online session?
faqs.answer: Through a shared whiteboard both sides can write on, plus screen sharing for a past paper. A photographed or scanned script can be dropped into the session and annotated live, so a marked paper is discussed with both people looking at the same page. For diagrams in Economics or Physics the usual pattern is the student drawing on paper, holding it up, then redrawing it on the whiteboard once the error has been named.

faqs.question: What happens if the connection drops in the middle of a demo class?
faqs.answer: The session is paused and picked up where it stopped, usually within a minute or two. If the network makes that impossible, the demo is rebooked at no cost rather than counted as used, because an unfinished diagnosis is worth nothing to either side. Test audio and video a few minutes early, and keep a mobile hotspot available if the household connection is unreliable in the evening.

faqs.question: Can a parent sit in on the demo class without changing how it runs?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you are welcome to. Most tutors prefer it for a first session, because it means the written summary arrives to someone who has seen the evidence. The one practical caution is that teenagers tend to work differently when a parent is visible, so the usual arrangement is to watch without joining in and save questions for the last five minutes. A recording is the alternative if sitting in would make it harder for your child.

faqs.question: Which Mathematics topic should a demo probe for a student struggling at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: The junction between topics rather than any single topic. The most revealing question is one whose first step is algebraic and whose substance is calculus, because that is where Higher Level marks actually go: the calculus is understood and the manipulation collapses. Twenty minutes on one such question usually locates the real weakness, which chapter-by-chapter revision can miss for a whole term because each topic looks acceptable when tested on its own.

faqs.question: What should a Chemistry demo look at first if the problem is organic mechanisms?
faqs.answer: Whether the student is reasoning or recalling. The test is to ask them to justify a single arrow: why this attacks there, and what the intermediate must look like. A student reciting a learnt mechanism will produce the right diagram and no justification, which collapses the moment the examiner changes the substrate. Working through one unfamiliar mechanism from first principles tells you more in fifteen minutes than reviewing three familiar ones, and it sets the first month's plan.

faqs.question: How should a demo test whether an Economics problem is diagrams or evaluation?
faqs.answer: With one stimulus and two prompts. Ask for the relevant diagram drawn and fully labelled, then ask whether the policy in the extract would work and for whom. A student weak on diagrams stalls at the first prompt. A student weak on evaluation draws a clean diagram, explains it accurately, and then writes a second paragraph that describes rather than judges. The two failures need different teaching, and separating them in the demo avoids a term aimed at the wrong one.

faqs.question: What does a demo reveal about a student who writes long Biology answers and still scores badly?
faqs.answer: Almost always a structure problem rather than a content problem. The demo marks one six-mark answer against the published scheme in front of the student, and the usual finding is a long descriptive opening, one correct example, and no comparative or evaluative clause, which caps the answer around half marks. Once the missing marks are shown to have names in the scheme, the fix is a writing habit, not another pass through the content.

ibgram-book-demo-class.closingHeading: Book the demo, and judge it on the marking
ibgram-book-demo-class.closingBody: Pick the evening you would genuinely keep for the rest of the term, send the board, level and tier with your request, and ask for a past-paper question rather than an introduction. Then judge the session on one thing: what the tutor says when your child gets something wrong, and whether their mark can be checked against the published scheme. The demo costs nothing and ends with a written summary either way. If the match is wrong, take a second one with a different specialist.

ibgram-home-tuition.tutorsIntro: These are the tutors families reach for when the calendar is tight: Diploma and IGCSE specialists who ask which series the student is entered for before anything else.

intro.heading: Where the student sits in the year decides everything else
paragraphs: A search for home tuition in the Kingdom is usually a search for somebody who understands a specific syllabus, not for somebody who can reach a specific address. The in-home market here is real enough: agencies and independent tutors travel to villas and compounds in Riyadh, Jeddah and the Eastern Province, charge for the journey inside the hourly rate, and draw their tutors from whoever lives in reasonable range. That works well when the subject is common. It works badly when the subject is a Higher Level science, because the pool shrinks to the people who both live nearby and teach it. IB Gram answers the same need differently: one-to-one teaching delivered live online, which is what makes a subject specialist in another city or another country reachable at all.

The thing that decides whether any of it helps, though, is the calendar. A family in the first weeks of the first Diploma year is buying something completely different from a family eight weeks out from the May session, even when the subject and the tutor are identical. Early in the course, the useful work is foundations and habits: command terms, how working is set out, how to read a mark allocation. Late in the course, the useful work is triage: the components carrying the most marks, the topics most likely to appear, timed papers and very little else. Buying the second thing early wastes it. Buying the first thing late is worse, because the hours simply are not there any more.

Counted backwards, a Diploma year has fixed points that do not move. The written papers of the May session. The school's internal deadlines for the internally assessed components, which usually sit well before that. Predicted grades, set by the school from its own evidence. For Cambridge and Pearson candidates, entries closing several months ahead of the June series, with the school's examinations officer holding the exact date, and a November series for resits and November-entry candidates. Nothing on that list is negotiable by a tutor, and all of it is knowable in advance. A plan built against those points looks nothing like a plan built against a parent's worry in the week a report came home.

The calendar is also the part most tutoring copy about the Kingdom gets wrong, because it has been copied from somewhere else. The school week runs Sunday to Thursday. Public schools run by the Ministry of Education follow a two-semester year beginning in late August and ending in late June, with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break. International and British-curriculum schools set their own calendars and most run three terms, so two schools in the same Riyadh district can finish a month apart. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not change its clocks. Every slot described below is written against those facts rather than against a Monday-to-Friday assumption.

ibgram-home-tuition.programmesIntro: What a programme needs from outside help depends on the point in its own cycle. These are the three IB programmes and where the pressure falls in each.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led primary learning with no external papers and no entry deadlines. Support here is judged on reading and number fluency rather than on a date.
programmes.countryNote: The useful moment is a move. A child arriving mid-year into a Riyadh school is adjusting to the language of instruction as much as to content.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups marked against published criteria, with the Personal Project in the final year. The fixed points are the school's interim deadlines rather than a board series.
programmes.countryNote: Pressure lands in the final MYP year, when the Personal Project competes with everything else. Ask the school for its deadline calendar early.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher or Standard Level, Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and an internally assessed component in every subject. Written papers are sat in the May session.
programmes.countryNote: Two years with hard deadlines in both. The first ends with internal assessment work started; the second begins with it falling due, which is why spring arrivals struggle.

ibgram-home-tuition.subjectsIntro: Subject by subject, the calendar lands differently. These are the Diploma subjects Saudi families most often arrange weekly teaching in.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics and modelling dominate, and the exploration is set early. Late arrivals need the modelling language rather than the content.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The investigation is set in the first year. Explanation chains and uncertainty work are what the written papers pay for.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Energetics and organic chemistry sit late in the course, so a second-year arrival meets them cold. The data booklet must be fluent.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content volume builds across both years and command terms decide the mark. The investigation is the first hard deadline.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Commentaries fall due at the school's own dates. Diagram accuracy and earned evaluation carry the papers.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The oral and the written tasks sit at school-set points. Unseen analysis under time is what a weekly slot rehearses.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: The source paper and the essay reward different skills. Research work is set in the first year and routinely deferred.

sections.heading: What a home tuition search in the Kingdom actually buys
paragraphs: Searches for home tuition in Saudi Arabia are overwhelmingly about fit rather than about geography. The parent typing it wants somebody who knows the syllabus their child is entered for, and the word home is simply the familiar term for one-to-one teaching rather than a demand that a stranger drives to the villa. The in-home market is nonetheless real. Independent tutors and agencies in Riyadh, Jeddah and the Dammam cluster do travel to homes and compounds, and tutor-marketplace guides put general senior-school private tuition in Riyadh above SAR 200 an hour, with primary tuition advertised at around SAR 50.

Travel is where the economics of that model bend. A tutor crossing Riyadh at six in the evening spends an hour in traffic for a one-hour lesson, and somebody pays for that hour whether or not it appears as a line on the invoice. It also narrows the choice severely. A family in Al Ahsa or AlUla looking for a Higher Level chemistry specialist within driving distance is often choosing between nobody and a generalist, and in the Diploma that difference costs marks in a way a convenient arrival time does not repay.

IB Gram answers it with one-to-one teaching delivered live online, over video, with the whole specialist pool reachable regardless of where the family lives. Home visits are a service offered only in India; no tutor travels to a Saudi address, and this page would be dishonest if it implied otherwise. What a family gets instead is choice: a tutor matched on the syllabus, the level and the component rather than on a district. The table below sets the two models against each other on the things that genuinely differ between them.

sections.heading: The Diploma year counted backwards from the series
paragraphs: Plan from the series and not from today. For an IB candidate in the Kingdom, the written papers of the May session are the fixed end point, and almost every Saudi IB school sits that session. Work backwards and the next fixed point is the school's own deadline for each internally assessed component, which typically falls months earlier and is set by the school rather than by anybody else. Before that sit the drafts the school will formally review, and before those the point at which a topic or a research question has to be settled.

For Cambridge and Pearson candidates the structure is similar with different labels. Entries for the June series close several months ahead of it, and the school's examinations officer holds the exact date; a tier decision for a tiered Cambridge subject is reversible only until then. A November series exists for resits and for November-entry candidates, which is the realistic route for a student whose June attempt went badly or who joined too late to be entered at all. The Cambridge February and March series is sat in India rather than in the Kingdom.

The practical use of counting backwards is that it says what to buy now instead of what to buy eventually. Eighteen months out, the answer is one weekly session on foundations. Nine months out, it is one weekly session plus internal assessment method, because the components are about to fall due. Eight weeks out, it is timed papers, mark schemes and triage, and nothing else fits in the time. A mismatch between the point in the year and the thing being bought is the commonest reason paid teaching produces nothing visible.

sections.heading: Three calendars running inside one city
paragraphs: Two children can live in the same Riyadh compound, attend schools five minutes apart, and be on different academic years. Public schools run by the Ministry of Education follow a two-semester year that begins in late August and ends in late June, with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break. International and British-curriculum schools set their own calendars and most run three terms, with their own half-terms and their own end dates. Neither is a variation of the other; they are separate structures that happen to share a city.

That matters to a tutoring plan in three ways. The obvious one is scheduling: a slot that works inside one family's term sits inside another family's holiday. The second is pacing, because a two-semester year puts its major internal assessments in different places from a three-term year, and the weeks before each need different work. The third is siblings. A household with one child in each system has two calendars to plan against, and the only reliable source for either of them is that school's own published calendar.

The practical rule is to take the dates from the school and from nowhere else. Regional summaries of term dates are routinely wrong for individual schools, and a tutoring provider quoting one is quoting something it cannot know. Ask the school office for the published calendar at the start of the year, mark the internal assessment deadlines on it, and agree the weekly slot around the term that actually applies. A slot agreed against the wrong calendar gets cancelled in the first holiday and is rarely rebuilt afterwards.

sections.heading: Where the student is in the year decides what to buy
paragraphs: Early in a course, the best purchase is narrow and cheap: one weekly session in the subject the last report flagged, aimed at the habits that transfer everywhere. How a command term changes the required answer. How a mark allocation tells a student how much to write. How working is set out so a marker can award method even when the final answer is wrong. None of that is glamorous and all of it compounds, which is exactly why it is worth buying while there is still time for compounding to happen.

Mid-course, the purchase shifts towards the internally assessed components, because that is when they fall due and they carry real weight in the final grade. The useful work is method and criteria: what the criterion descriptors are actually asking for, whether a research question can be answered inside the word limit, where a method has a flaw that will cost marks under the analysis criterion. The student writes every word of it, and a tutor who offers to do more than review is a liability rather than a shortcut.

In the final stretch the purchase becomes triage. Count the marks available by component, rank topics by how likely they are to appear and by how far the student is from those marks, and ignore anything that cannot be reached in the weeks remaining. Two subjects at this point is usually one too many. A family arriving eight weeks before the papers asking for four subjects is asking for four thin interventions, and the honest answer is to choose the two where marks sit closest to the surface.

sections.heading: What a school cannot always staff, and when it shows up
paragraphs: The reason a family in the Kingdom needs an outside specialist is usually structural rather than a judgement on the school. An international school runs a Diploma for a cohort that is small by the standards of a national system, and a Higher Level subject needs enough candidates to justify a specialist teacher and a timetable slot. When the numbers fall short, a school either does not offer the subject at that level or asks an able teacher from a neighbouring discipline to carry it. Both are reasonable decisions and both have consequences a family should plan for.

Where it shows up is in the second year rather than the first, and usually in a mock script. A class taught by a non-specialist tends to be solid on content and weak on what the mark scheme rewards, because reading mark schemes for a subject you did not train in is genuinely difficult. The symptoms are consistent: correct material that does not answer the question set, missing precision in definitions the board examines strictly, and extended-response questions left blank because nobody rehearsed the shape of the answer.

Private and international schools in the Kingdom are licensed by the Ministry of Education, and school evaluation and accreditation run through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, which also operates e-services for national school accreditation and for the approval of international accreditation bodies. That system speaks to the quality of a school as a school. It says nothing about whether one subject at Higher Level has a specialist teaching it this year, which is a staffing question a family has to put to the school directly and in writing.

sections.heading: Arriving mid-year from another curriculum
paragraphs: Families move into the Kingdom throughout the year, and a mid-course arrival is the hardest version of this problem because the calendar does not pause for it. A student joining a Diploma cohort in the spring of the first year has missed teaching the class will not revisit, and has internally assessed work to start that their classmates began months earlier. A student joining the second year has that plus the papers in sight. Neither situation is hopeless, and both need a plan built on what is missing rather than on the whole syllabus.

What transfers between systems is content. What rarely transfers is assessment style, and in the Diploma that gap is wide. A student from a British school arrives used to modular assessment and discrete topics. A student from an American high school arrives with broader coverage and less depth, and the Higher Level sciences are where that lands first. A student from a national curriculum or a CBSE school arrives with strong content and a habit of writing down everything they know, which an IB mark scheme does not reward at all.

The sequence that works is unglamorous. Get the new school's scheme of work and the list of components already completed. Sit one past paper per subject under time and have it marked against the published scheme. Rank the subjects by marks lost rather than by the student's anxiety about them. Then take the top one or two and run three sessions a week for a month before dropping back to weekly. Spreading the same hours across four subjects moves none of them far enough to change a report.

sections.heading: The components that fall due at fixed points, and what a tutor may do
paragraphs: Every IB subject carries an internally assessed component, and each one has a school-set deadline sitting inside the calendar rather than at the end of it. A scientific investigation, a mathematical exploration, economics commentaries, the Extended Essay with its reflection sessions, the Theory of Knowledge essay and exhibition: all of them fall due at points the school publishes, and most of them overlap with the heaviest teaching weeks of the course. Knowing those dates during the autumn term is worth more than any amount of extra teaching bought later.

The line a tutor works inside is narrow and it should be stated before any money changes hands. A tutor may teach the skills a task assesses, explain each criterion and what its descriptors require, discuss whether a research question is answerable inside the word limit, identify a flaw in a method, and give written feedback on a draft the student produced. No tutor should supply text, data, analysis or conclusions that then appear in assessed work. The student writes it, and the school asks them to confirm that they did.

That is not only a rules question. An internally assessed component is marked on the student's own reasoning, and a supervisor who has watched a student work can see the difference between a submission and a purchase. A malpractice finding follows the candidate rather than the provider who sold the document, and it can cost the Diploma outright. The useful version is slower: an honest first draft, written feedback against the criteria, and a second draft the student can defend in a conversation with their supervisor.

faqs.question: We arrive in the Kingdom part-way through the first Diploma year: what does the calendar force us to settle first?
faqs.answer: The internally assessed components, before the content. Classmates began theirs months earlier and school deadlines will not move for a new arrival, so the first conversation is with the coordinator about which components are running and what has been submitted. Content gaps can be repaired across the rest of the course; a missed internal deadline cannot. Get the list in writing, then rank subjects by marks lost on a timed paper.

faqs.question: How late in the year can a student change board without losing the June series?
faqs.answer: Entries close several months ahead of the June series and the examinations officer holds the exact date, so the answer is: before that deadline and no later. A change after it means waiting for the November series. The deeper issue is teaching rather than paperwork, because the component structures differ, so a change agreed just inside the deadline still leaves a student sitting unfamiliar papers.

faqs.question: Does coursework completed before a move still count towards the same series?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and only the receiving school can say. Where the same board and the same specification are involved, work already marked and recorded may carry across; where the board or the specification differs, it usually does not. Ask the new school to confirm in writing which components it holds for the candidate and which must be done again. Plan the first month of teaching around that answer rather than around what the previous school said.

faqs.question: What is realistic to recover in the eight weeks between a mid-year arrival and the mock papers?
faqs.answer: Enough to make the mocks informative, which is the right goal rather than a grade. In eight weeks a student can learn the new school's assessment style, close one substantial topic gap, and rehearse timing in the two weakest subjects. Spreading the same hours across five subjects produces mocks nobody can read. Treat them as the diagnostic and plan the repair from the marked scripts.

faqs.question: Which Higher Level subjects does a Saudi school most often drop when numbers are too small?
faqs.answer: The pattern is consistent across small cohorts: the sciences beyond one or two, the second mathematics route, and minority languages. A school with a single Diploma cohort cannot timetable every Higher Level option, so it offers the combinations most students want. Put the question to the school before accepting a place, and ask whether the subject is taught by a specialist or carried by a neighbouring department.

faqs.question: Why do two schools on the same Riyadh street end their year a month apart?
faqs.answer: Because they follow different calendars by design. Public schools run by the Ministry of Education keep a two-semester year beginning in late August and ending in late June. International and British-curriculum schools set their own dates and most run three terms, with their own half-terms. Neither is a variation of the other. For planning, only one calendar matters: the one the family's own school publishes.

faqs.question: What does the Education and Training Evaluation Commission actually do about a school's quality?
faqs.answer: It handles school evaluation and accreditation, and operates e-services for national school accreditation and for the approval of international accreditation bodies, while the Ministry of Education licenses private and international schools. Between them they speak to the school as an institution. Neither tells a parent whether one Higher Level subject has a specialist teacher, which only the school can answer, and it is worth asking in writing.

faqs.question: When in the year should a family ask the school which components their child is entered for?
faqs.answer: In the autumn term, and again before the entry deadline. The autumn conversation establishes which papers, which options and which internally assessed components are planned, so the year can be worked backwards from them. The second conversation confirms what has actually been entered, including the tier where a Cambridge subject is tiered. Families who leave this until the spring discover the decisions have already been made and the window for changing them has closed.

faqs.question: How does a weekly slot work when our weekend is Friday and Saturday and the tutor's is Saturday and Sunday?
faqs.answer: The overlap is Sunday to Thursday for the student and Monday to Friday for the tutor, which leaves four usable evenings in common. Most families settle on a Sunday, Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday evening, a normal working day for a tutor in India, Europe or the United Kingdom. Friday suits some tutors and not others. Agree the day when the slot is fixed rather than assuming either weekend.

faqs.question: How many weeks before the June series should a weekly slot be fixed?
faqs.answer: If the aim is foundations, book in the autumn term and keep the same hour all year. If the aim is examination technique, the last eight to ten weeks are the dense period and the slot should be held well before the spring term, because that is when every other family in the Kingdom asks for the same evening. Late bookings are possible and tend to mean a generalist rather than the subject specialist a family wanted.

faqs.question: Does a slot need rebooking when a family moves between Saudi cities mid-year?
faqs.answer: The tutor and the hour stay as they are, because teaching is delivered online and the Kingdom has one time zone throughout. What usually changes is the start time, since a new city means a new school run and a different arrival home. Tell the tutor the week before the move, and expect the first fortnight to be disrupted by the move itself rather than by the teaching.

faqs.question: What happens to a weekly slot across the autumn break, and who decides?
faqs.answer: The family decides, and the useful question is whether anything falls due soon afterwards. A break with an internal assessment deadline on the other side of it is a reason to keep teaching, often at a lighter pattern. A break with nothing after it is a reason to pause and reserve the slot. Either way, say which in advance; a slot left silently empty for a fortnight gets reassigned.

faqs.question: Why does an in-home tutor's travel time end up inside the hourly rate?
faqs.answer: Because the tutor cannot teach anybody else during it. Crossing Riyadh at the end of the school day can take as long as the lesson, and a tutor doing two in-home sessions an evening is paid for two hours while spending four. Whether it shows as a travel charge or is folded into a higher rate, the family pays. Teaching online removes that cost from both sides.

faqs.question: Is there a point in the final year when starting weekly support stops being worthwhile?
faqs.answer: It stops being worthwhile for content and stays worthwhile for technique almost until the papers. With a term left, a weekly session can still fix timing, command terms and the way working is set out, and those are real marks. With a fortnight left, honest advice is usually to rehearse past papers rather than start anything new. What never works is buying four subjects late and expecting each to move.

A subject specialist takes a free trial lesson, reads whatever marked work exists, and says what the weeks before that date can carry. Teaching is delivered live online, one to one, in a slot written in Arabia Standard Time. Home visits remain a service offered only in India.

ibgram-ib-igcse-tutors.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE syllabuses alongside the IB Diploma and Middle Years Programme. Each works from marked scripts rather than from a textbook order, which is why the first session produces a number and not a reassurance.

intro.heading: Start with the evidence, then build the plan backwards
paragraphs: Most tutoring arrangements in this market start at the wrong end. A family agrees a subject, a price and an evening, lessons begin, and three months later nobody can say whether anything improved. The school report says satisfactory, the tutor says the student is engaging well, and the next marked paper is the one that counts for real. IB Gram IB IGCSE tutors are asked to work the other way round: establish a measurable starting point in the first session, then design the teaching to move that specific number.

A measurable starting point is narrower than a grade. It is a mark on a named paper, broken down by question and by syllabus topic, produced under something close to examination conditions and marked against the board's own published scheme. From that you learn which three topics are costing the most marks, whether the loss is content or technique, and whether the pacing collapses in the final twenty minutes. A grade tells you none of that, and a predicted grade tells you less.

This matters more at IGCSE than families expect, because the entry decisions are made early and are hard to reverse. Cambridge IGCSE is tiered on many subjects: Core is graded C to G and Extended runs A* to E, so a student entered for Core cannot be awarded above a C however well they perform. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE grades nine to one. A baseline mark taken before the entry deadline is the difference between an informed tier decision and a hopeful one. The same logic applies to component lists: families regularly discover a practical or coursework element nobody had planned for, months after the teaching plan was written, because nobody asked the school which components make up the grade.

The rest follows from the numbers. Weekly teaching targets the topics the baseline exposed. A timed paper every fortnight tests whether the teaching stuck. A short written note tells you the mark, the question-level breakdown and what changes next. When the marks move, the plan continues; when they do not move after a fair run, the honest conversation is about the plan or the tutor, not about effort. That conversation is easier when both sides have been looking at the same evidence.

All of this is delivered online, one to one, over live video with a shared whiteboard and the student's own script on screen. That format is what makes a national pool of subject specialists reachable from Al Khobar, Abha or Buraidah, where a school may have one teacher covering a subject across several year groups. Home visits are a service IB Gram offers only in India; nobody is sent to a Saudi address, and the case for teaching this way rests on who is available, not on convenience.

sections.heading: What measurable progress in an IGCSE subject looks like
paragraphs: Ask a tutor how a student is doing and you usually get an adjective. Ask for the evidence and you should get four things: the paper, the date it was sat, the mark by question, and the topics those lost marks belong to. That is what measurable means here. It is not a percentage improvement claim and it is not a predicted grade; it is a record of the same kind of task attempted twice, under the same conditions, marked the same way.

The reason to insist on it is that IGCSE marks are lost in patterns, and patterns are invisible in a total. A student scoring fifty-eight on an Extended-tier Mathematics paper may have lost twelve marks to one topic, eight to method marks never written down, and four to running out of time. Those are three different problems with three different fixes, and a tutor who only sees the total will teach the whole syllabus again at a slower pace. The question-level breakdown turns a vague weakness into a short list.

Conditions matter as much as marking. A paper done over two evenings with the textbook open measures something, but not the thing being examined. A baseline is worth having only if it was sat in one sitting, to time, with whatever calculator and formula sheet the real paper allows. Students dislike this and it is the single most useful forty-five minutes in the whole arrangement, because everything afterwards is measured against it.

sections.heading: The baseline: what a first diagnostic establishes
paragraphs: The first session is a diagnostic, and it is free. The student sits a past paper or a section of one to time, the tutor marks it against the published scheme in front of them, and the two of them go through where the marks went. By the end of the hour a parent has a mark, a topic list and a short written statement of what the teaching will attack first. Nothing is sold in that session, because there is nothing to sell until there is a number.

A diagnostic also tests the tutor, which is half its value. A tutor who knows the syllabus will tell you which question was off-specification for the tier entered, which mark scheme point the student missed by a single word, and which topic normally appears in the other paper. A tutor who does not will mark generously and talk about confidence. Families should treat the diagnostic as a two-way interview and ask the tutor to justify a mark they disagree with.

What a baseline cannot do is predict a grade. Grade boundaries are set after each series, so a mark that is a strong B on one paper may sit lower on another. The table below sets out what each kind of evidence a family will see actually shows, how often it arrives, and the question it cannot answer. Reading it saves the common argument where a school report and a tutor's marks appear to disagree while measuring two different things.

sections.heading: Marking to the published scheme instead of to a feeling
paragraphs: Both boards publish mark schemes, and they are the most under-used free resource in this market. A scheme does not describe a good answer; it lists the points that earn credit and the wording that is accepted. Reading one changes how a student writes within about three sessions, because it makes visible the gap between an answer a teacher would nod at and an answer a marker is allowed to pay for. That gap is where most of the recoverable marks in an IGCSE paper sit.

In practice the tutor marks the student's script to the scheme, then makes the student re-mark it themselves. The second step does the work. A student who has applied the scheme to their own answer stops writing long and starts writing in the units the scheme counts. In extended-response questions this is the whole game: the difference between four marks and six is usually a named example and a comparative clause, not more knowledge.

One line is worth stating plainly, because the search results for this query contain providers who cross it. A tutor marks, teaches and gives feedback on work the student has produced. A tutor never produces any part of a coursework component, an Internal Assessment or an Extended Essay. Those carry the student's declaration of authorship, and the consequences of a breach fall on the student. Feedback on a draft is legitimate and useful; supplying sentences for the submission is not, and no amount of time pressure changes that.

sections.heading: Cambridge and Edexcel: tiers, grades and a ceiling
paragraphs: Saudi schools run both boards, sometimes in the same building and occasionally in the same student's timetable. The content lists overlap heavily, so families assume the two are interchangeable and buy the wrong past papers. They are not interchangeable in the way that matters: the question styles differ, the component structures differ, and on Cambridge the tier entry puts a hard ceiling on the grade before anything is marked.

Cambridge IGCSE tiers many subjects. A Core entry is graded C to G; an Extended entry is graded A* to E. A student entered for Core who performs brilliantly is awarded a C, because that is the top of the tier. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE grades nine to one and is untiered on most subjects, which removes that particular trap but not the need to check the component list. Tier entry is a school decision, and it can be changed only before the entry deadline, which is why a baseline mark taken early in Year 10 is worth more than one taken late in Year 11.

The practical instruction for a parent is short. Ask the school, in writing, which board each subject sits, which tier the student is entered for, and which components make up the grade. Then buy past papers for that exact combination. A term spent practising the wrong board's question style is a term that produces marks nobody will ever award, and the mistake is common enough in mixed-entry schools to be worth checking twice.

sections.heading: The first eight weeks, and what should have changed
paragraphs: Eight weeks is roughly the shortest honest review period, because it allows a baseline, six weeks of teaching and a second timed paper with a fortnight of homework behind each session. Inside that window the thing that should move first is not the total mark. It is the pattern. Method marks start getting written down, the final questions stop being left blank, and the topics on the original list stop reappearing in the error log.

A reasonable pattern looks like this. By week two the student can explain what the baseline showed without being prompted. By week four one of the three baseline topics is closed, verified by a short timed section rather than by a conversation. By week six the pacing on a full paper has improved even if the mark has not. By week eight a second full paper, sat to time, gives the first genuine comparison. Totals can move quite slowly while the underlying error pattern changes fast, and the error log is the better early signal.

What should also have changed is the student's own account of the subject. A student who can name the two questions they lose marks on, and say why, has taken over the diagnostic work. That is the point at which weekly tutoring becomes efficient rather than merely useful, and it is a better eight-week outcome than a two-mark gain with no insight attached. It also tells a parent that the evidence is reaching the person who has to act on it, rather than stopping at the tutor's marking sheet.

sections.heading: Fitting the evidence loop into a Sunday-to-Thursday week
paragraphs: The loop needs two slots a fortnight that are not the lesson: one for the student to sit a paper alone, and one for the tutor to mark it before the next session. In a Saudi week that is less obvious than it sounds, because the school week runs Sunday to Thursday and the free days are Friday and Saturday. A timed paper sat on a Friday morning, marked over the weekend and reviewed on Sunday evening is the cleanest arrangement available, and it uses the two days that are otherwise lost.

The teaching slot itself works best early in the school week, while the student still has energy and the week's deadlines have not arrived. Thursday evening is the weakest slot on offer; it sits on the edge of the weekend and the paper that was supposed to be sat that night rarely is. Lessons are pinned to Arabia Standard Time, UTC+3, which the Kingdom keeps all year, so a tutor working from a country that moves its clocks absorbs the change rather than the student.

There is one more constraint worth planning for rather than discovering. Ramadan drifts about eleven days earlier each year against the Gregorian calendar, so it lands in a different term every few years, school days shorten and the evening study pattern shifts. Where it falls close to a series, the sensible move is to finish the content work before it and keep the lighter consolidation and paper review running through, instead of trying to hold a full timetable.

sections.heading: When the numbers do not move, and what to do
paragraphs: Sometimes a term of honest work produces no measurable change, and the useful response is diagnosis rather than more hours. There are four common causes, and they are distinguishable. The first is that the plan is treating a technique problem as a content problem, which shows up as good topic tests and flat paper marks. The second is that the homework is not being done alone, which shows up as fluent sessions and weak timed papers. Both are fixable without changing tutor.

The third cause is a mismatch between tutor and student. It is not a moral failure on either side and it is better named early than endured for a term. If two or three sessions have gone by and the student cannot say what they are working on, ask for a different tutor rather than more sessions. The fourth is that the subject or the tier is wrong: a student entered for the wrong tier, or carrying a Higher Level subject that should be Standard Level, cannot be rescued by weekly lessons, and the conversation belongs with the school.

In every one of those cases the evidence is what makes the decision cheap. A family holding four marked papers and an error log can tell within a fortnight whether to change the plan, the tutor, the entry or the subject. A family holding three months of reassuring verbal updates finds out in a live series, which is the most expensive place to learn it.

faqs.question: What does a baseline IGCSE diagnostic measure that a school report does not?
faqs.answer: A school report gives a grade and a comment, both relative to the class. A baseline gives an absolute mark on a named past paper, broken down by question and by syllabus topic, produced under timing and marked against the board's published scheme. That tells you which topics are costing marks, whether the loss is content or technique, and where pacing fails. A report cannot show any of that, which is why the two often appear to disagree while measuring different things.

faqs.question: After a month of weekly IGCSE lessons, what should a marked paper show?
faqs.answer: Usually a changed error pattern before a changed total. Method marks should be written down rather than skipped, the last questions should no longer be blank, and at least one of the baseline topics should have stopped appearing in the error log. Totals move more slowly, because a mark is the sum of several habits. If nothing in the pattern has shifted after four weeks of work done alone between sessions, the plan is addressing the wrong problem and should be changed.

faqs.question: Who marks an IGCSE practice paper between lessons, and against which scheme?
faqs.answer: The tutor marks it, using the examiner's published mark scheme for that exact paper, board and tier, not a generic answer key. The distinction matters: a scheme lists the points that earn credit and the wording accepted for each, so marking to it produces a question-level breakdown instead of a tick count. The student is then asked to re-mark their own script against the same scheme, which is the step that changes how they write in the next paper.

faqs.question: What should a fortnightly report on an IGCSE subject contain?
faqs.answer: Four things: the paper sat and the date, the mark with a question-level breakdown, what the student completed alone between sessions, and what the next fortnight will attack. It should not contain a predicted grade, a percentage improvement claim or an adjective doing the work of a number. If you cannot check the report against your own child's script, it is a summary rather than evidence, and you should ask for the marked paper.

faqs.question: What happens if the marks have not moved after a term of IGCSE lessons?
faqs.answer: You diagnose rather than add hours. Flat paper marks with good topic tests point at technique; fluent lessons with weak timed papers point at homework not being done alone; a student who cannot say what they are working on points at the match. A wrong tier entry or a subject carried at the wrong level cannot be fixed by lessons at all and belongs with the school. Four marked papers make that decision quickly; verbal updates do not.

faqs.question: How do Cambridge Core and Extended tiers change a student's realistic ceiling?
faqs.answer: On a tiered Cambridge IGCSE subject, a Core entry is graded C to G and an Extended entry A* to E. A Core candidate who performs brilliantly is awarded a C, because that is the top of the tier, so the entry decision caps the outcome before a paper is marked. Tier entry is made by the school and can be changed only before the entry deadline. That is the argument for taking a baseline mark early in Year 10 rather than late in Year 11.

faqs.question: Why does Pearson Edexcel grade nine to one when Cambridge grades A* to E?
faqs.answer: They are separate awarding bodies running separate qualifications, so their grading scales were designed independently. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE uses a nine-to-one scale and is untiered on most subjects; Cambridge IGCSE uses A* to E on Extended and C to G on Core. Neither scale converts cleanly into the other, and a university or sixth form will read whichever appears on the certificate. What matters practically is knowing which board each of your child's subjects actually sits.

faqs.question: How are IGCSE coursework components moderated, and can a tutor see the marks?
faqs.answer: The teacher marks coursework against published criteria and the board then moderates the sample, which can move the whole cohort's marks up or down. Internal marks are therefore provisional until moderation is complete. A tutor has no access to them and no standing in the process. What a tutor can legitimately do is teach the criteria, read a draft and point out where a criterion is not yet addressed, leaving the student to make every change themselves.

faqs.question: How is a weak extended-response answer diagnosed from a marked script?
faqs.answer: By comparing what the student wrote with what the scheme pays for, point by point. Most weak extended answers are not short of knowledge; they are short of structure. The usual pattern is a long descriptive opening, one correct example, and no comparative or evaluative clause, which caps the answer around half marks. Once a student sees that the missing marks have names in the scheme, the fix is a writing habit rather than a revision programme, and it transfers to every similar question.

faqs.question: What evidence should a parent ask for before agreeing a second term of lessons?
faqs.answer: The baseline script and the most recent timed paper, both marked, so you can see the two totals and the two error patterns side by side. Then the error log showing which baseline topics have closed. Then the fortnightly notes, to check that what was promised each time was actually attempted. If those three exist and show movement in the pattern, continuing is a reasonable decision. If they do not exist, that is itself the answer.

faqs.question: When in Year 10 is it worth starting an evidence-based IGCSE plan?
faqs.answer: Early in the year, because that is when the findings can still change the entry. A baseline in the first term shows whether the student is working at Core or Extended standard while the tier decision is still open with the school, and it leaves four terms to act on what it finds. Starting in the final months of Year 11 still helps with technique and pacing, but the entry is fixed by then and the ceiling it sets cannot be lifted.

faqs.question: What should a Year 11 student have measured before the June series entry closes?
faqs.answer: At least one full timed paper per subject, marked to the scheme, plus the component list confirmed in writing with the school. The paper tells you whether the current tier entry matches the current standard. The component list tells you what is actually being examined, which is where families discover a practical or coursework element nobody had planned for. Entries close several months ahead of the series, and your school's examinations officer holds the exact deadline.

faqs.question: How does an MYP student moving into IGCSE get a baseline that means anything?
faqs.answer: By sitting an IGCSE paper rather than being assessed on MYP criteria. The two measure different things: MYP marks each criterion out of eight against descriptors, while an IGCSE paper awards scheme points for specific content and wording. A strong criterion-A profile tells you little about performance on a structured written paper. One past paper under timing, marked to the scheme, exposes the gap honestly and usually takes a single session.

faqs.question: How does a DP1 student's evidence loop differ from an IGCSE one?
faqs.answer: The cycle is longer and carries more internal work. A Diploma student has internal assessment components running alongside the papers, so the loop has to track criterion coverage as well as paper marks, and a fortnightly timed section often replaces a full paper because the papers are long. The principle is unchanged: a baseline, marked evidence against the published scheme, and a written note. Only the units being measured change between the two qualifications.

ibgram-ib-igcse-tutors.closingHeading: Ask for the baseline before you ask the price
ibgram-ib-igcse-tutors.closingBody: The first conversation worth having is not about rates. Book the free diagnostic, let your child sit a timed paper for the board and tier they are actually entered for, and read the marked script with the tutor. If the breakdown tells you something your school report did not, the arrangement is worth continuing. If the marking is generous and the feedback is about confidence, you have learnt that cheaply and in one hour. Either way you finish with a number, a topic list and a decision you can defend.

intro.heading: Logistics first: the week, the clock and the school run
paragraphs: A parent searching for IB Gram online tuition in Saudi Arabia has usually already decided that online teaching is acceptable. The real question is narrower: can a weekly lesson actually survive a Sunday-to-Thursday school week, a four o'clock pick-up in Riyadh traffic, and a tutor who lives in a country that works Monday to Friday? That is a scheduling problem before it is a teaching problem, and it is the reason most private arrangements quietly collapse by the middle of the autumn term. This page answers the scheduling question first, then the quality question.

The school week in the Kingdom runs Sunday to Thursday. Friday and Saturday are the weekend. Thursday evening therefore behaves the way a Friday evening behaves elsewhere, and nobody wants a demanding Mathematics session then. Sunday evening is a working school night, which makes it one of the two strongest slots in the week. A tutor whose own country treats Sunday as a rest day will resist that slot, reschedule it twice and then lose it. Matching on the week matters as much as matching on the subject.

Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not change its clocks. A tutor in India is two and a half hours ahead; a tutor in the United Kingdom is three hours behind in their winter and two in their summer. Because their clocks move and yours do not, any slot agreed in the tutor's local time drifts twice a year. The fix is simple, and it is the first thing written down: the slot is recorded in Arabia Standard Time, and the tutor's diary absorbs the change rather than the student's evening.

Then there is the school run. Riyadh is roughly an hour across north to south at the wrong time of day, so a family in Al Olaya and a family in Al Narjis reach the same school gate at different hours and get home at different ones. Jeddah runs as a long coastal spine from the historic centre north to Obhur. The Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran conurbation behaves as one school market, and families routinely live in one city and study in another. A workable lesson slot has to clear all of that.

Once the week, the clock and the commute are settled, the argument moves to teaching. Lessons are delivered online, one to one, over live video with a shared whiteboard; home visits are a service IB Gram offers only in India. What that buys a Saudi family is reach: a Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL specialist, or a teacher with marking experience in Chemistry, rather than whichever tutor happens to live within a twenty-minute drive. The rest of this page covers the calendars, the papers, academic honesty and the university endgame.

sections.heading: What a Sunday-to-Thursday week does to a timetable
paragraphs: Start with the fact everything else hangs off: the school week in the Kingdom runs Sunday to Thursday, and Friday and Saturday are the weekend. Copy written for a British or Indian audience assumes the opposite, which is why so much tutoring advice aimed at Saudi families is quietly wrong about when to teach. A Monday-to-Friday assumption puts the heaviest sessions in the wrong half of the week and leaves the best night unused.

In practice the week has a shape. Sunday evening is the strongest slot, because the student has just come off two days of rest and the week's homework has not yet piled up. Monday evening is close behind. Tuesday and Wednesday work, but they compete with school deadlines and after-school activities. Thursday evening is the weakest night of all: the eve of the weekend, with poor attendance and worse attention. Friday and Saturday are free, which suits an intensive block but not a term-time habit, because weekend slots are the first thing a family cancels.

That shape is also a filter on tutors. A tutor who teaches in a school running Monday to Friday has Sunday as a rest day and will treat a Sunday slot as an imposition. The slot gets moved once, then again, and by the autumn term it has drifted to a Thursday nobody attends. Asking a prospective tutor what their own working week looks like is a more useful question than asking how many years they have taught.

sections.heading: Arabia Standard Time against the clocks a tutor lives by
paragraphs: Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3, and the Kingdom does not observe daylight saving. That single fact causes more cancelled lessons than connectivity ever does. A family agrees a six o'clock Sunday slot with a tutor in Europe or the United Kingdom, and then the tutor's country moves its clocks and the slot silently becomes five o'clock or seven o'clock, depending on the direction. Nothing was cancelled and nobody was told; the lesson simply stopped lining up with the school run.

The remedy is to record the slot in the student's own time and treat the tutor's clock as the variable. The table below shows what a six o'clock Kingdom evening looks like from the places tutors most often work, and what tends to go wrong with each. India is the easiest case: two and a half hours ahead, with one clock all year, so an evening lesson in the Kingdom lands in the tutor's late evening and stays there. The United Kingdom is the most common source of drift, and Central Europe behaves the same way with a one-hour difference.

Distance east or west matters less than stability. A tutor five hours ahead can teach a Kingdom morning slot comfortably; a tutor eight hours behind can teach a Kingdom evening before their own working day starts. What matters is whether the arrangement is anchored to one clock, written down, and reviewed at the two points in the year when half the world changes its time.

sections.heading: Why the tutor's own working week decides if the slot holds
paragraphs: There are three kinds of tutor in this market and their working weeks are not alike. The first is a serving teacher in a school somewhere else, tutoring in their own evenings. Their subject knowledge is usually current and their mark-scheme instinct is good, but their availability is narrow, their term dates are not yours, and their own marking load peaks exactly when your child needs the most help. The second is a full-time tutor whose diary is built around students in several time zones; far more flexible, but you have to check the syllabus knowledge properly rather than assuming it.

The third is a retired or part-time examiner. Marking experience is genuinely valuable, because someone who has applied a published mark scheme to hundreds of scripts can tell a student why an answer that looks right scores four instead of six. Tutoring-company listings in Riyadh advertise IB subject tutoring from around SAR 180 an hour, with Higher Level and premium tracks listed at roughly SAR 200 to 220; those are other providers' advertised rates from their own marketing pages, not what IB Gram charges. Scarcity moves the number more than anything else.

The practical question is narrow. Does this tutor's week contain a Sunday evening they will still want in two months? Ask it directly in the trial lesson, and ask what happens when their own term ends or their clocks change. One who has thought about it answers in a sentence.

sections.heading: The school run, and how late a lesson can start
paragraphs: A lesson time is really a commute time. Riyadh is roughly an hour across north to south when the roads are bad, and the city has grown north faster than the schools have followed, so a family in Al Narjis or Al Malqa may be driving across town twice a day. For them a five o'clock start is a coin toss and a seven o'clock start is reliable. In Al Olaya or Al Sulaimaniyah, closer in, five o'clock usually works. Two families at the same school need different slots.

Jeddah behaves differently. The city runs as a spine along the coast, so journeys are long but consistent, and a slot that works in the autumn term usually still works in the spring. The Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran conurbation is the most complicated of the three: it functions as one school market, families cross between the cities daily, and compound life adds its own rhythm of activities that pushes study later into the evening.

Outside those markets the argument changes shape. In Al Ahsa, Tabuk, AlUla, Abha or Jazan the issue is not traffic but availability: a Higher Level specialist in a particular subject may not live within driving distance at any price. The in-home market there is thin, and the families who used to drive an hour each way for a weekly lesson are the ones for whom online teaching is not a compromise but the only version of the thing that exists.

sections.heading: Calendars that disagree, and Ramadan's drift
paragraphs: Two school calendars run side by side in the same Saudi city. Ministry of Education schools follow a two-semester year beginning in late August and ending in late June, with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break. International and British-curriculum schools set their own dates and most run three terms. Two children in the same compound can be on holiday in different weeks, which matters when booking a tutor for both. Work from your own school's published calendar rather than a general one.

The examination series are steadier than the terms. Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel both run a June series, the main one for Saudi schools, and a November series used for resits and November-entry candidates. In India, Cambridge also runs a February and March series; candidates in the Kingdom sit the June series or the November one, and advice copied from Indian pages gets this wrong often enough to be worth saying plainly. Diploma students sit the May session. Entries close several months ahead, and your examinations officer holds the exact dates.

Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier each year against the Gregorian calendar, so it drifts steadily across the academic year and lands in a different term every few years. School days shorten and the family's study pattern shifts later. The sensible planning rule is to treat it as a known reduction in teaching time whenever it falls, build the heavy content work before it and keep lighter consolidation during it, rather than discovering the clash a fortnight out.

sections.heading: Once the logistics hold: what a specialist adds
paragraphs: With the week and the clock settled, the question becomes what a tutor can do that the school cannot. The honest answer is usually time and specificity. A class teacher with twenty students covering a Higher Level option has to teach to the middle of the room. A one-to-one session can spend forty minutes on the one topic costing four marks a paper, which is not a judgement on the school but a difference in what the format allows.

The specificity shows up in three places. The first is command terms: the difference between state, describe, explain, analyse and evaluate is worth more marks in Biology and Economics than any amount of extra content. The second is the published mark scheme, which rewards a particular shape of answer; students who have never read one write essays that would please a reader and disappoint an examiner. The third is paper structure, because Higher Level and Standard Level are not the same examination with more questions. In Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL, Paper 3 is a long investigative paper worth a fifth of the grade and has no Standard Level equivalent.

For IGCSE the equivalent conversation is tiering. Cambridge IGCSE is tiered on many subjects: Core is graded C to G and Extended A* to E, so a student entered for Core cannot be awarded above a C however well they perform. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE grades nine to one. Confirm the tier with the school in writing; tier entry is a school decision, reversible only before the entry deadline.

sections.heading: Academic honesty, and what a tutor does with a draft
paragraphs: This is the line separating a tutor from the essay mills advertising in the same search results, and it is worth stating plainly. A tutor teaches the skill, reads what the student has produced and gives feedback the student then acts on alone. A tutor never produces any part of an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay or a Personal Project. Those pieces carry the student's name and a declaration of authorship, and the consequences of breaching it fall on the student, not on whoever was paid.

What that looks like in a session is concrete. A tutor can teach the criterion descriptors so the student knows what a top band actually asks for. A tutor can read a draft and say that the methodology section does not justify the sample size, or that the research question is too broad to answer in four thousand words. A tutor can teach referencing properly, and can model the difference between a paraphrase and a lift. A tutor can ask the questions a supervisor would ask, so the student arrives at the school meeting prepared rather than defensive.

What a tutor cannot do is supply sentences that end up in the submission, choose a question the student does not understand, or hand back a rewritten version. If a provider offers any of that, the offer itself is the warning sign. Ask any prospective tutor how they handle a draft; a good one describes feedback, not production.
