faqs.question: At what point in the Middle Years Programme does a weekly online slot start paying off?
faqs.answer: Usually in MYP 4 and MYP 5, the two years that feed either IGCSE or the Diploma. Before that the criteria are broad and the school's own feedback is normally enough. From MYP 4 the Sciences and Mathematics criteria start demanding the investigation and modelling skills the Diploma assumes, and gaps there are expensive later. One weekly session on criterion C and criterion D work covers most requests at this stage.

faqs.question: What should a student entering DP1 have settled before the autumn term starts?
faqs.answer: Three things. The subject and level combination, because dropping a Higher Level subject later costs more than choosing carefully now. The Mathematics route, since Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation lead to different university options. And the algebra from the previous two years, which is the commonest cause of trouble in DP1 Mathematics and Physics. A short diagnostic before the term begins tells you which of the three is actually weak.

faqs.question: In DP2, how many subjects can realistically be supported in one Sunday-to-Thursday week?
faqs.answer: Two is comfortable, three is the practical ceiling and four does not work. A DP2 student already carries Internal Assessment deadlines, the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS inside a five-day school week. Two weekly sessions, ideally paired into one evening, leave time for the independent work that makes lessons worth anything. If four subjects genuinely need support, the honest conversation is about moving a Higher Level subject to Standard Level.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting IGCSE support in the final year if the school already runs revision clubs?
faqs.answer: Often yes, because the two do different jobs. A school revision club covers the syllabus for a group at one pace. A weekly one-to-one slot works only on the two or three topics where that student loses marks, and on technique for the specific papers they are entered for. Check the tier first: a student entered for Cambridge Core cannot be awarded above a C, so the entry conversation with the school matters more than any amount of tutoring.

faqs.question: How does a November-series resit candidate plan the year differently from a June candidate?
faqs.answer: The whole timetable shifts forward. A November candidate's intensive phase falls in the autumn term rather than the spring, colliding with the start of a school year and with university applications. The practical pattern is a diagnostic immediately after results, several weeks of content repair, then timed papers from early in the autumn. Entry must be confirmed with the school's examinations officer well ahead, because a resit entry is not automatic and the deadline is earlier than families expect.

faqs.question: How do Higher Level and Standard Level paper weightings change what a weekly session covers?
faqs.answer: They change it completely. At Standard Level the two written papers carry most of the grade, so sessions concentrate on core content and standard question types. At Higher Level there is usually a third paper, and in Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL that paper is a long investigative problem worth a fifth of the grade with no Standard Level counterpart. A student who only ever studies content is preparing for two-thirds of their own examination.

faqs.question: What are command terms, and why do they decide the mark more than the content does?
faqs.answer: Command terms are the instruction words the question uses: state, describe, explain, compare, analyse, evaluate. Each maps to a different answer structure and a different mark allocation in the published scheme. A student who explains when asked to evaluate has written good science and scored half the marks, because the examiner credits a shape of answer the student did not produce. Teaching the terms explicitly is often the fastest single improvement available in Biology and Economics.

faqs.question: Why do grade boundaries move between series, and what does that mean for a target?
faqs.answer: Boundaries are set after each series so a grade means the same thing even when one paper turns out harder than another. A difficult paper produces lower boundaries; an easy one raises them. That is why a raw mark from an old paper cannot be converted into a grade with any confidence. The useful target is a mark band on a specific paper, measured against the published scheme. No tutor can convert practice marks into a promised grade.

faqs.question: How is a predicted grade decided, and why is it not a promise?
faqs.answer: The school predicts it, using class work, internal examinations, Internal Assessment progress and the teacher's professional judgement. It is a forecast used by universities, not a result, and it carries no weight with the examination board. A tutor can give the school better evidence to work from, by producing marked timed papers against the published scheme, but cannot change a prediction. If one looks wrong, the route is a conversation with the subject teacher and the Diploma Programme coordinator.

faqs.question: How much of a Diploma subject is marked inside the school rather than by the board?
faqs.answer: It varies by subject, and the exact figure is worth checking in the current subject guide with the teacher. In the sciences the internal assessment is a single scientific investigation worth a fifth of the grade, and in Mathematics it is the exploration. Internal work is marked by the teacher against published criteria and then moderated by the board, which can move a whole class's marks. That is why criterion wording matters more than polish.

faqs.question: Why does an IB Diploma need a Ministry of Education equivalency decision in the Kingdom?
faqs.answer: Because a Saudi university compares applicants against the Saudi secondary certificate, and an international certificate has to be recognised as equivalent before it can be read that way. The equivalency, or mu'adalah, decision is issued by the Ministry of Education and applies to the IB Diploma, A Levels and an American high school diploma alike. It is an administrative step with its own document requirements, not an examination, and it is best started well before application season.

faqs.question: Why does Tahsili trip up a student who has only studied the Diploma syllabus?
faqs.answer: Tahsili is the achievement test, covering mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English, and its content follows the Saudi national curriculum. An IB or IGCSE student has met most of the material, but framed differently, sequenced differently and examined in a style they have never practised. Preparation therefore looks less like learning new science and more like mapping what the student already knows onto an unfamiliar syllabus and question format. Start it as separate work, not as school revision.

faqs.question: Does Qudurat test anything a subject tutor can usefully prepare a student for?
faqs.answer: Partly. Qudurat, the general aptitude test, is run by ETEC through its National Center for Assessment and measures verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content; it can be sat in Arabic or English. No tutor can teach reasoning ability in a term, but the question formats, the timing and the arithmetic fluency the quantitative section assumes are all practisable. Treat it as a technique and pacing exercise, and check registration windows on the official Qiyas channels.

faqs.question: Can a student apply to Saudi and overseas universities in the same final year?
faqs.answer: Yes, and many do, but the two tracks run on different clocks. Overseas applications turn on predicted grades, a personal statement and subject prerequisites at Higher Level, with deadlines in the autumn term. The Saudi track turns on equivalency, the Qiyas tests and each university's own published admission criteria, which differ by university and by programme. No tutor or platform can promise an outcome on either track. Check the criteria on each university's own site, because third-party summaries disagree.

ibgram-online-tuition.closingBody: The next step is small. Book a free trial lesson in the evening you would genuinely keep for the rest of the term, in Arabia Standard Time, and treat it as a test of two things: whether the tutor knows the syllabus your school teaches, and whether that evening still works for both sides in eight weeks. The session runs on a real past paper, so you see diagnosis rather than a pitch. If no specialist is free at that hour, you will be told so plainly.

intro.heading: Start with the entry, not with the subject
paragraphs: Families search for IGCSE classes and usually mean one of two things: a group that covers the syllabus week by week, or one-to-one teaching that fixes what school has not. What IB Gram provides is the second, delivered online over live video, one tutor and one student, with the student's own papers on a shared screen. We do not send a tutor to an address in the Kingdom; home visits are a service we offer only in India. That is worth saying at the top so nobody reads further under the wrong impression.

The more important point is that neither format can be planned sensibly until one question is answered: what is the student actually entered for. IGCSE is not a single qualification but a family of syllabuses from more than one board, many of them tiered, each with its own component list. Cambridge IGCSE is tiered in many subjects, with Core graded from C to G and Extended from A* to E. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE grades on the nine-to-one scale. A class planned for the wrong board teaches the right topics for the wrong paper.

The second structural fact is who decides what. Tier entry is a school decision, made by the department and submitted by the examinations officer, and it is reversible only before the entry deadline. The board sets the syllabus and the papers. Private and international schools in the Kingdom are licensed by the Ministry of Education, while school evaluation and accreditation run through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, which also operates approval processes for international accreditation bodies. None of those bodies has any view on a tutor, and no tutor can claim their approval.

So this page is built in the order the qualification is built. The components and the tiers first, then the tier decision and when it locks, then what the school's licensing and evaluation actually tell a parent and what they do not. After that the series a Saudi candidate sits, the coursework and practical components and the honesty line around them, what the certificate is for once the Kingdom's equivalency process gets involved, and finally the week the classes have to live in and what the first month should produce.

No calendar year appears anywhere here, and no examination date. Entry windows and term dates belong to your school's examinations officer and published calendar, and both differ between schools in the same city. Where this page names a series it means the series by month, which is true every year. One more thing before anything else: no tutor, ours included, can promise a grade or a tier outcome, because the entry belongs to the school and the marks belong to the candidate. What a class does is make more marks available from the same understanding.

sections.heading: The component list is the course: papers, tiers and grading scales
paragraphs: Every useful decision about IGCSE teaching follows from one document: the list of components a candidate is entered for. It names the board, the syllabus, the tier where the subject is tiered, and whether the practical element is a laboratory test or a written alternative. A family who has that list can plan a year of teaching precisely. A family who has only the word chemistry is guessing, and so is any provider quoting them a package.

The grading scales differ by board and the difference is not cosmetic. Cambridge IGCSE is tiered in many subjects: Core is graded from C to G, and Extended from A* to E. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE grades on a nine-to-one scale across a single route. A candidate entered for Cambridge Core cannot be awarded above a C however well they perform on the day, which makes the entry itself a ceiling rather than a formality. Schools do explain this, but usually once, early, in a meeting about something else.

What follows is that teaching should be built backwards from the components. If the entry includes an alternative-to-practical paper, experimental skill has to be taught on paper, not in a laboratory the family does not have. If a subject carries coursework, the calendar matters more than the content. And if the tier is still open, the first job is not teaching at all but establishing honestly which tier the evidence supports, while the decision can still be changed.

sections.heading: The tier decision, who makes it and when it stops being changeable
paragraphs: Tier entry is a school decision. The subject department recommends, the examinations officer submits, and the board processes what it receives. A parent has influence up to the entry deadline and almost none afterwards, which is why the conversation belongs in the term before entries rather than in the term of the papers. Ask for the tier and the component codes in writing, and ask when the internal deadline for changing them falls, because the school's own cut-off usually sits earlier than the board's.

The honest case for Core is real and should not be dismissed. A candidate who would be overwhelmed by the Extended papers can secure a solid C-to-G grade rather than an E or an unclassified result on a harder route, and that grade still counts on the certificate. The honest case against it is the ceiling: a C closes some sixth-form doors, particularly for mathematics and the sciences, and a student who improves across Year 11 cannot be rescued upwards after the entry has gone.

What settles the argument is evidence rather than optimism. Two or three marked papers at each tier, sat under timed conditions and marked against the real mark scheme, tell a department more than a year of classroom impressions. That is something an outside tutor can genuinely contribute: the papers, the timing, the marking and a written summary the family can take to the school. The decision stays the school's, but it is made on better information.

sections.heading: What licensing and evaluation tell a parent, and what they do not
paragraphs: Private and international schools in the Kingdom are licensed by the Ministry of Education. School evaluation and accreditation run through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission (ETEC), which operates services for national school accreditation and for the approval of international accreditation bodies. Those are real processes with real consequences for a school, and parents are right to ask about them before enrolling. The two bodies answer different questions: one decides whether a school may operate at all, the other judges how well it does the job.

What they do not tell you is whether a particular subject is well taught this year. A school's licence does not report on who is teaching Extended mathematics, how many candidates sit each tier, or whether the science department has a technician. An evaluation looks at a school as an institution, not at a component list. Neither body has any relationship with a tutor or a tutoring company, and any provider claiming approval, accreditation or partnership from a regulator or a board is making a claim nobody has granted them.

The questions that do produce useful answers are narrower and belong to the school. Who teaches this subject and how long have they taught this syllabus. How many candidates were entered for each tier last time, and how were those decisions made. Is the practical component a test or a written alternative. Does the subject carry coursework, and what is the internal deadline. Four questions, asked in an email, tell a family more about next year than any inspection summary.

sections.heading: The series a Saudi candidate actually sits
paragraphs: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel both run a June series and a November series. June is the main one for schools in the Kingdom, and November carries resits and candidates whose course finishes then. Cambridge also runs a February and March series, but that series is available only in India, so a Saudi family reading an entry deadline copied from an Indian page is reading a date that does not apply to them. This is a wrong fact families act on, and it circulates widely in this market.

Entries close months before the papers, and the dates are held by the school's examinations officer rather than published usefully anywhere else. The practical consequence for teaching is that the tier decision, the coursework deadlines and the entry submission all sit in the middle of the course rather than at its end. A plan built around the papers alone will miss all three. A plan built around the entry window arrives early enough to influence them.

For a resit the arithmetic is different again. A November attempt gives roughly a term of teaching after results, which is enough to move a grade in a subject where the problem was technique and rarely enough where the foundation is missing. Ask the school whether it enters November candidates at all, because some schools in the Kingdom do not and the family then has to find a centre that will, which takes longer than anyone expects.

sections.heading: Coursework, practical components and the line a class does not cross
paragraphs: Where a syllabus offers coursework, the work is produced by the student, marked by the school and moderated by the board. That sequence is what makes it assessed work rather than homework, and it is why the rules around help are strict. A tutor may teach the skills the task needs, discuss an approach, read a draft the student has written and explain against the criteria why it sits where it does. No part of it may be drafted, written or produced for the student by anyone else.

This matters commercially as well as academically, because several providers in this market advertise exactly what the rules prohibit. A page offering to produce coursework or to prepare an assignment on a student's behalf is offering a malpractice risk with a tutoring label on it, and schools do investigate. A family can protect itself easily: keep the drafts, keep the dates, and let the student's own progression through versions be the record that the work is theirs.

The practical components need a different kind of honesty. Where the entry is an alternative-to-practical paper, the examination tests experimental understanding on paper: identifying variables, reading apparatus, spotting what a method cannot control, interpreting results somebody else collected. That is teachable without a laboratory and it is routinely under-prepared, because it looks like a theory paper and is revised like one. Where the entry is a practical test, the school's own laboratory time is the only place to prepare, and an outside class can only support the thinking around it.

sections.heading: What the certificate is for once the Kingdom's equivalency process gets involved
paragraphs: An IGCSE certificate is a set of subject grades at sixteen, not a school-leaving certificate. Inside the Kingdom its main job is to get a student into the right sixth-form route: an IB Diploma, A Levels, or another post-sixteen programme, each with its own entry grades. That is worth stating because families sometimes treat Year 11 as the finish line and are surprised to find the document the universities want is issued two years later. Sixth-form entry grades are the first place IGCSE results are actually spent.

The step most pages in this market never mention is equivalency. A foreign or international school certificate needs an equivalency decision from the Ministry of Education before a Saudi university treats it as equivalent to the national secondary certificate, and that applies to the final certificate at eighteen rather than to the IGCSE grades themselves. The IGCSE results matter indirectly: they decide the subjects a student can take at the next level, and those subjects decide which university routes stay open.

Two Qiyas tests sit alongside that process. Qudurat, the general aptitude test run through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission's assessment centre, examines verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content. Tahsili, the achievement test, covers science-stream subjects and follows the Saudi national curriculum, which is exactly why international-curriculum students find its framing unfamiliar even where the content overlaps. No thresholds are quoted here on purpose: each university publishes its own criteria and weightings, and they differ by programme.

sections.heading: The Saudi week, and what the first month of classes should produce
paragraphs: The school week runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend, and the Kingdom holds Arabia Standard Time at UTC+3 without changing its clocks. A tutor working from a country that does change them will drift by an hour twice a year unless the booking is pinned to Saudi local time. Public schools here run two semesters from late August to late June, while international and British-curriculum schools set their own three-term calendars, so two Year 11 candidates in one city can be at different points in the same syllabus.

School days shorten during Ramadan and household evenings change shape with them, which usually means moving a class rather than suspending it. The weeks around mock examinations are the other predictable disruption: a class is worth more in the fortnight after mocks than in the fortnight before, because the marked scripts are the best diagnostic material anybody will produce all year, and they arrive free.

The first month should produce three documents, not a feeling. A baseline: one timed paper at the entered tier, marked against the real mark scheme. A written diagnosis naming the components and topics where marks were lost. And a plan for the term with the coursework and entry deadlines marked on it. If a family has those three things after four sessions, they can judge the arrangement on evidence. If they have only a report that the student is engaging well, they have bought reassurance rather than teaching.

whyPoints.description: Teaching follows the component list and the tier, because the same subject is a different course across two boards.

faqs.question: Can IGCSE classes run through the autumn term for a November-series candidate while the rest of the cohort is mid-course?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the plan has to be separate from the school's. A November candidate needs the papers finished and the technique sharp while classmates are still covering content, so the weekly hour becomes paper practice earlier than it otherwise would. Confirm first that the school enters November candidates, because some in the Kingdom do not, and a family that discovers this late has to find a centre that will accept a private entry.

faqs.question: What happens to a weekly IGCSE class in the fortnight when mock examinations are running?
faqs.answer: Keep the slot but change its purpose. During mocks the useful hour is short and targeted: one topic the next paper needs, rather than new material. Afterwards the marked scripts become the best diagnostic material of the year, so the fortnight after mocks is where a class earns most. Families who cancel through mocks and resume afterwards usually lose the slot and the momentum together.

faqs.question: What does an IGCSE class schedule look like in the last eight weeks before the June papers?
faqs.answer: Papers, not topics. A workable pattern is one full timed paper a week in the weakest subject, marked and returned with the mark scheme, plus one session reading the errors rather than re-teaching the content. Two subjects at this intensity is the realistic ceiling for most candidates alongside school. New syllabus content stops being worth teaching roughly a month out, except where a whole topic is missing.

faqs.question: Do IGCSE classes pause during the school's midyear break, or is that the best week to run an intensive?
faqs.answer: For a Year 11 candidate the break is usually the single most valuable week of the year, because there is no homework competing for the hours. Two or three longer sessions on the weakest component, with papers under time, do more than six weeks of term-time hours. For Year 10 a pause is reasonable, provided the slot is held rather than released, since a popular hour disappears quickly once it is given up.

faqs.question: Does a Saudi IGCSE class slot move when a tutor abroad changes their clocks twice a year?
faqs.answer: Not if the booking is pinned to Arabia Standard Time, which is UTC+3 and never changes. If the hour is agreed in the tutor's own local time instead, it will drift by an hour in each direction every year and the family will discover it by missing a lesson. Settle this in writing before the first session, and ask which days the tutor genuinely works, since a Sunday slot is a weekend day in much of the world.

faqs.question: What does a student moving from a Saudi national-curriculum school into IGCSE Year 10 have to cover first?
faqs.answer: Written English for examination purposes and the habit of answering a command word precisely. The mathematics content usually transfers well, but the questions are structured differently and method marks have to be earned on paper. In the sciences the gap is the practical component, whether that is a laboratory test or the written alternative. A term of weekly teaching on those three, started early in Year 10, prevents most of what otherwise surfaces in Year 11.

faqs.question: Can a student join IGCSE classes a term into Year 11 and still sit the June series?
faqs.answer: Often yes, with two conditions. The entry has to be in place, which is the school's decision and has a deadline, and any coursework component has to be realistically completable in the time left. Where both hold, a term and a half of focused teaching can move a grade, particularly if the loss is technique rather than content. Where coursework is already overdue, the honest answer may be the November series instead.

faqs.question: What happens to an American-curriculum student's credits when they move into a two-year IGCSE course?
faqs.answer: Credits do not transfer, because IGCSE is assessed by terminal papers rather than accumulated course credit. What transfers is knowledge, and the gap is usually in depth per subject rather than breadth: an IGCSE science goes further into fewer topics than a general science course does. The practical arrangement is a conversation with the school about which year group to join and which subjects to enter, before anybody buys teaching.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE subjects are hardest to pick up after a mid-year transfer into the Kingdom?
faqs.answer: Anything with a coursework or practical component, because the calendar cannot be recovered, and languages assessed by speaking components arranged inside the school. Mathematics and the sciences are the easiest to catch up on content, since the syllabus is public and the past papers are plentiful. First Language English is middling: the reading skills transfer but the directed-writing conventions need teaching explicitly.

faqs.question: We are arriving in the Kingdom in the middle of Year 10 - should the student restart IGCSE or carry on?
faqs.answer: Carry on wherever the boards and syllabuses line up, and compare component lists rather than subject names before deciding. Where the new school uses a different board for the same subject, the content overlap is usually large and the paper structure is not, so a few weeks of targeted teaching closes it. Restarting a year costs more than it recovers unless several subjects do not match at all.

faqs.question: What should the first month of IGCSE classes produce before we commit to a term?
faqs.answer: Three documents. A baseline, which is one timed paper at the entered tier marked against the real mark scheme. A written diagnosis naming the components and topics where the marks were lost. And a term plan with the coursework and entry deadlines marked on it. If after four sessions you have those, the arrangement can be judged on evidence rather than on whether everyone seems happy.

faqs.question: How is a starting point measured when a transfer student has no marked IGCSE work yet?
faqs.answer: With a past paper, sat under time, at the tier the school is proposing. It takes one session and produces more than any conversation: which topics are missing, whether the method is being shown, and how the candidate handles timing. Sitting a paper at each tier is worth the extra hour where the entry is still open, because it turns the tier conversation with the school into an evidence-based one.

faqs.question: What should an IGCSE class report tell us at the end of each half-term?
faqs.answer: Which components were taught, what the timed attempts scored and against which mark scheme, where the errors clustered, and what the next half-term will do about it. A report that names topics covered without naming marks is a record of attendance. Over a year these reports are also what a family needs if they want to question a tier decision or a predicted grade with the school.

faqs.question: What do we do if IGCSE classes are not working after two reporting cycles?
faqs.answer: Change something specific rather than everything. Check first whether the problem is the match, the hour or the diagnosis: a slot too late in the evening and a misdiagnosed weakness look identical from the outside. Ask for the marked attempts side by side; if the same component is still costing the same marks, the teaching has not reached it and a different tutor is reasonable. Handovers cost one session when the written record exists.

igcse-classes.closingHeading: Send the component list and one marked paper
igcse-classes.closingBody: Everything useful follows from those two things: the board, the syllabus, the tier and the components your child is entered for, plus one recent script to read. From there we can say what a term of teaching should cover, where the coursework and entry deadlines fall, and whether the tier still deserves a conversation with the school. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, pinned to Arabia Standard Time, and the first one is a free trial on work the school has already marked.

igcse-coaching.tutorsIntro: The coaches families ask for are specification specialists rather than subject generalists: one board, one syllabus, enough cohorts to have watched grade boundaries move. Mathematics at the Extended tier, the separate sciences and First Language English are the ones in shortest supply, and each coach starts by marking a paper the student has already sat.

intro.heading: Decide what you will measure before you buy a single hour
paragraphs: Most tuition is bought on a feeling and reviewed on a feeling, which is why families so often cannot say at the end of a term whether it worked. IGCSE is unusually well suited to a harder standard, because the whole qualification is externally examined against published mark schemes, and the papers are available. That means progress can be measured properly: a mark on a specific paper, broken into question types, compared against the same student's mark on a comparable paper eight weeks earlier. Everything on this page is organised around that measurement, and the plan is written backwards from it.

Start with a baseline that is worth having. A full paper, sat under real timing, with no notes and no help, marked by somebody against the published scheme rather than by a parent against an answer key. Then the breakdown, which is the part families never get from school: how many marks came from recall, how many from multi-step problems, how many were lost to units, significant figures or a misread command term. Two candidates on the same total can have completely different problems, and only the breakdown separates them.

That baseline then tells you what to buy, how much of it, and when to stop. A candidate losing marks to unit errors and sloppy significant figures needs a marking habit and three sessions, not a year of content revision. A candidate who cannot start a multi-step algebra question needs sustained teaching across a term, because the cause sits two years further back. A candidate whose content is secure and whose timing collapses needs papers under the clock and nothing else. Selling all three the same package is how coaching gets a bad name.

Delivery is one-to-one and online, over live video, anywhere in the Kingdom, with slots recorded in Arabia Standard Time. IB Gram does not place coaches at Saudi addresses; home visits are something we run only in India. For an IGCSE candidate that is rarely a loss, because what matters is whether the coach knows the specific specification and tier, and matching online means choosing from a national pool rather than from whoever lives nearby. Advertised rates in this market, which are published by the companies selling the lessons, run from roughly SAR 35 an hour on budget IGCSE platforms up to SAR 200 and above for senior-school examination subjects. Those are bands to judge a quote against, not a market average and not our price.

The rest of the page follows the evidence. What to measure and how often. Why a mark is not a grade, and what makes boundaries move. The tier decision, which caps the grade and has to be argued from paper evidence. How Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel differ for the same subject. The year read backwards from the June series as a sequence of checks. Where marks actually go missing, subject by subject. What a resit in the November series is really worth. Coursework and honesty. And what to ask a coach, as opposed to what to ask the school.

igcse-coaching.programmesIntro: Four things get called IGCSE in the same conversation, and they are not the same qualification. Knowing which one a student is actually entered for decides the board, the tier, the papers and the kind of coach who is useful. Confirm all of it with the school's examinations officer before buying anything.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: A two-year course examined almost entirely by external written papers, with Core and Extended routes in several subjects and the lower route capping the grade that can be awarded. Grades are reported on a letter scale. Some subjects carry a practical or coursework component and some offer an alternative-to-coursework paper instead, and which of those a student faces depends on what the school has chosen to enter them for rather than on the subject itself.
programmes.countryNote: Candidates in the Kingdom are entered for the June series as the main sitting, with the November series used for resits and November-entry candidates. Cambridge also runs a February and March series, but that series is sat only in India, so a Saudi family should disregard it entirely when planning. Entry deadlines come from your own school's examinations officer.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: The same qualification level and a different specification, reported on a numeric scale, with tiering in some subjects under Foundation and Higher labels. Paper structures differ from the Cambridge equivalents, as does the balance between calculator and non-calculator work in mathematics and the treatment of practical skills in the sciences. A coach who has taught one board well will still need the other specification in front of them.
programmes.countryNote: Schools in the Kingdom choose between the boards subject by subject, so a single student can sit Cambridge sciences and an Edexcel mathematics paper in the same series. Families regularly assume one board across the timetable and buy the wrong preparation. Check the entry, subject by subject, on the school's own confirmation rather than from a prospectus.

programmes.name: Years 7 to 9, the run-up to IGCSE
programmes.description: The years where the causes of most IGCSE problems are created, and where they are cheapest to fix. Algebraic manipulation, fraction and index fluency, writing at length under time, and the habit of reading a question for what it asks rather than for what it is about. None of it is examined externally, so nothing shows up until a Year 10 test, by which point the fix competes with new content.
programmes.countryNote: Lower secondary coaching in the Kingdom is usually bought late and in the wrong subject. A Year 9 student who is weak in algebra will present as weak in physics a year later, and the family will ask for physics lessons. Fixing the algebra first is faster, cheaper, and improves three subjects at once.

programmes.name: What IGCSE feeds: A Level, the IB Diploma or a national route
programmes.description: IGCSE grades function as entry conditions for the next stage, and the conditions are usually subject-specific. A school may require a particular grade in mathematics before allowing a science at the higher level of whatever follows, and a lower-tier entry can close that door before the student has had a chance to argue. Subject combinations two years ahead therefore depend on decisions taken in Year 10.
programmes.countryNote: In the Kingdom the next step may be A Levels at the same school, a move into the IB Diploma elsewhere, or a national route, and each reads the IGCSE transcript differently. Ask the receiving school in writing which grades in which subjects it requires, before the tier entry is confirmed rather than after results.

igcse-coaching.subjectsIntro: Each note below says what the paper actually rewards and what evidence shows the problem has been fixed, because a subject description that stops at content is no use for planning. The measurement differs by subject: in mathematics it is marks per question type, in the sciences it is marks lost to presentation, in the essay subjects it is marks against a band descriptor.

subjects.name: IGCSE Mathematics
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The tier decision caps the grade, so it has to rest on timed-paper evidence. Most lost marks in the higher routes sit in multi-step problems where a single early slip carries through, which is why method marks matter so much. Measure progress by the proportion of multi-step questions started correctly, not by the total: a candidate who attempts and half-completes them is improving before the mark shows it.

subjects.name: IGCSE Physics
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Unit conversion, significant figures and prefix errors remove more marks than missing physics does. Where the school enters for a practical paper, credit goes to candidates who have drawn, labelled and criticised real graphs rather than read about them. The evidence of progress is marks lost to presentation falling towards zero, which is measurable within three or four marked papers.

subjects.name: IGCSE Chemistry
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and organic families absorb most coaching time. Equations are marked strictly: a correct product with a missing state symbol or an unbalanced equation still drops the mark, and candidates who learn reactions as lists rather than patterns stall on unfamiliar examples. Track the error type across papers, because the same candidate usually repeats one of three specific mistakes.

subjects.name: IGCSE Biology
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Memory-heavy and examined through precise language, which makes it the subject where a rote learner can plateau while knowing everything. Definitions of diffusion, osmosis and active transport are marked tightly, and diagrams must use the scheme's own terms. Extended-response questions reward a plan: a thirty-second structure beats a longer unplanned answer, and that is trainable in a handful of sessions.

subjects.name: IGCSE Coordinated and Combined Science
subjects.description: The route many schools use when specialist staffing is thin, and the one that most often surprises families later. Each science is covered less deeply than in the separate papers, which matters if the student intends a science at the next level. Confirm what the school has entered, then check the receiving school's entry requirements against it before assuming the pathway is open.

subjects.name: IGCSE First Language English
subjects.description: Assesses reading response and directed writing against a tightly defined register, which is why confident writers often score in the middle. Marks come from controlling tone and purpose for a specified audience, not from vocabulary. Progress is visible in band descriptors rather than totals, so marked work should always come back with the descriptor the piece sits in and the one above it.

subjects.name: IGCSE English as a Second Language
subjects.description: A different qualification from First Language English, and families discover the difference too late with depressing regularity. This specification assesses comprehension, summary and controlled writing, with the summary task carrying its own strict conventions. Confirm which one the school has entered the student for before any preparation is bought, because the two reward almost opposite instincts in writing.

subjects.name: IGCSE Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy and the chain of reasoning between cause and effect carry the paper. Unlabelled axes and curves without direction account for a steady drip of lost marks, and data-response questions catch candidates who have revised definitions and not application. Measure progress by whether the student can produce a correct, labelled diagram unprompted within ninety seconds.

subjects.name: IGCSE Business Studies
subjects.description: Application rather than recall. Marks come from choosing the right tool for the question and justifying a recommendation against the case material, and candidates lose them by defining terms accurately and answering nothing. Data-response is where it shows. The useful evidence of improvement is the ratio of marks earned on justify and recommend questions to marks earned on define questions.

subjects.name: IGCSE Computer Science and ICT
subjects.description: Two distinct subjects families frequently conflate. Computer Science assesses algorithmic thinking, data representation and programming logic; ICT assesses practical application skills against defined tasks. In both, marks go missing in documentation and in following the task specification exactly rather than in capability. Check which the student is entered for, then measure against the published task criteria rather than against whether the work functions.

igcse-coaching.regionsTitle: Where IGCSE candidates in the Kingdom are coached from
igcse-coaching.regionsIntro: British-curriculum and Cambridge schools are spread unevenly across the Kingdom, and the practical constraint on a weekly session differs by place: traffic in the big cities, shift patterns in the industrial ones, and real distance everywhere else. The notes say what each setting does to a coaching slot.

regions.name: Riyadh
regions.note: Roughly an hour across in traffic north to south, so two candidates at the same school can have very different evenings. Most families settle on a slot after half past five and build it around the slowest realistic journey, because a slot chosen for a good day gets cancelled on a bad one.

regions.name: Jeddah
regions.note: A long coastal spine running north from the historic centre towards Obhur, which means the commute varies enormously within one city. Candidates living towards the northern end generally need a later start, and that gap widens during term time rather than narrowing.

regions.name: Dhahran
regions.note: Compound and camp schooling shapes the week here more than traffic does, with activities built into the school day and a strong local culture of structured evenings. Sessions tend to work best earlier than in Riyadh, and consistency matters more than length.

regions.name: Al Khobar
regions.note: Part of a three-city school market with Dammam and Dhahran, and linked to Bahrain by the King Fahd Causeway, so some families have cross-border weekends. A slot pinned to Arabia Standard Time keeps the session stable through those weeks.

regions.name: Dammam
regions.note: Households here frequently attend school in one of the neighbouring cities, which turns the school run into a cross-city commute. The workable slot usually sits later than parents first assume, and a longer session once a week beats two short ones squeezed around travel.

regions.name: Jubail
regions.note: An industrial city where shift rotas rather than school timetables decide who is at home in the evening. The written note after each session carries more weight for these families, because the parent reading it is often not the one who was in the house during the lesson.

regions.name: Yanbu
regions.note: Similar rhythm to Jubail on the Red Sea side, with a smaller international-curriculum market. Candidates here are often looking for one specific subject the school covers with a generalist, rather than broad support, so a short targeted arrangement usually fits better than a year of weekly lessons.

regions.name: Al Ahsa
regions.note: About an hour and a half inland from the Eastern Province cluster, which rules out a daily commute to a city school for most households. This is the plainest case in the Kingdom for coaching delivered over video: the alternative is not a local specialist, it is nobody.

regions.name: Thuwal and the KAUST campus
regions.note: A campus community north of Jeddah on the coast, with a school serving the university population. The academic culture is strong and the staffing is narrow in the same way any single-campus school is narrow, so demand here is usually for one scarce subject at the top of the grade range.

schoolClusters.city: British and Cambridge schools in the Eastern Province
schoolClusters.note: The Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran cluster behaves as one school market, with families living in one city and attending school in another, and the International Schools Group running several campuses across it. British and Cambridge routes are well represented here, which is why a high share of IGCSE enquiries in the Kingdom come from this cluster.

schoolClusters.city: Jeddah and the Red Sea coast
schoolClusters.note: A mixed market where Cambridge provision sits alongside IB and other international routes, spread along the coastal spine, with The KAUST School serving the campus community at Thuwal to the north. Students we support sit IGCSE papers at schools of these kinds across the city.

The widest international provision in the Kingdom, covering both Cambridge and IB routes, though breadth at city level never guarantees a particular subject at a particular school. Ask which boards a school enters for subject by subject, because mixed entries across two boards in one timetable are common and change what preparation is needed.

igcse-coaching.schoolDisclaimer: Schools are named here only to describe where Cambridge and international provision sits in the Kingdom; IB Gram has no affiliation with any of them and claims none.
igcse-coaching.modesIntro: Three arrangements cover almost every IGCSE enquiry, and the baseline paper decides which one is appropriate. Buying a long weekly arrangement for a short presentation problem, or a short block for a two-year foundation gap, is the most common way money is wasted in this market.

modes.title: Diagnostic block: three or four sessions, then a decision
modes.description: Starts with a full timed paper marked against the published scheme and broken down by question type. The sessions that follow test whether the identified problem responds, and then the arrangement either continues or ends. For a candidate whose losses are presentation errors, units or command terms, this block is frequently the whole purchase and nothing further is needed.
bullets: A full paper under real timing before any teaching
A written breakdown by question type, not a single total
Three or four sessions aimed at one identified cause
A plain recommendation at the end, including stopping

modes.title: Weekly teaching across a term or a year
modes.description: For candidates whose problem sits further back than the current specification: algebra that was never automatic, reading stamina, or a topic sequence missed in a school transfer. Sixty or ninety minutes a week with written work marked between sessions, re-baselined with a fresh timed paper every six to eight weeks so the plan is corrected against evidence rather than optimism.
bullets: A fresh timed paper every six to eight weeks
Marked written work returned before the next session
A short factual note to the parent each week
The plan revised when the evidence says it should be

modes.title: Paper clinic before a series
modes.description: Short and dense in the final weeks, organised by paper rather than by topic, with every session built on a paper sat under examination timing and then marked line by line. This converts marks the candidate already has content for and does little else, so it works only where the teaching happened earlier. Specialist availability thins sharply before the June series.
bullets: Papers sat under timing, then marked against the real scheme
Targets named by question type rather than by topic
Timing strategy for each paper, practised rather than described
Booked a term ahead, because scarce specialists fill first

sections.heading: What measurable progress in IGCSE actually looks like
paragraphs: Progress is not a feeling and it is not a weekly report saying the student is engaging well. For an externally examined qualification it is a number on a specific paper, under specific conditions, compared with the same student's number on a comparable paper some weeks earlier. Everything else is a proxy, and most proxies are flattering. A candidate who understands a topic in a lesson has demonstrated nothing about what they will do alone, under time, with a question phrased in a way they have not seen.

The conditions matter as much as the mark. A paper sat with notes available, or at home over two sittings, or marked generously by a parent, produces a number that cannot be compared with anything. The baseline that is worth having is a full paper, timed, closed-book, marked by somebody who is reading the published scheme and awarding marks the way it says. The most valuable output is not the total but the breakdown: marks from recall, marks from multi-step work, marks lost to units and significant figures, marks lost to misreading the command term.

Collect it on a sensible rhythm. A baseline at the start, then a fresh comparable paper every six to eight weeks, and nothing in between except marked written work. Testing more often than that tells you about test-day variance rather than about learning, and it eats teaching time. Testing less often means a plan can run for a whole term on an assumption that stopped being true in week three.

Two things this discipline rules out are worth stating. It rules out a provider claiming improvement it cannot evidence, because the comparison is in your hands rather than theirs. And it rules out buying lessons for a problem that has already been fixed, which is a real and common waste: a candidate whose unit errors disappeared after four sessions does not need the remaining twenty that were booked.

sections.heading: A mark is not a grade: boundaries, tiers and what moves between them
paragraphs: Families track raw marks and then get surprised on results day, because the thing that converts a mark into a grade is set after the papers have been sat. Grade boundaries are decided for each paper in each series, and they move. They move because papers differ slightly in demand from one series to the next, and boundaries are adjusted so that the same performance earns the same grade across sittings. That is the point of them, and it has two practical consequences for anyone buying coaching.

The first is that a target expressed as a raw mark is unreliable. A candidate aiming at a boundary from a previous series is aiming at a number that will not be the number. The useful target is a margin: enough clear marks above the boundary that a two or three mark shift does not matter. That is a different plan from squeezing out the last mark on a favourite topic, and it usually means fixing a weak component rather than polishing a strong one.

The second is that the tier a candidate is entered for sets a ceiling before any of this applies. In the Cambridge Core route and the Edexcel Foundation route the top grades are not available at all, regardless of how well the candidate performs. That is not a penalty for a weak student; it is a structural cap, and it is confirmed by an entry deadline after which it cannot be changed. The decision therefore belongs to evidence rather than to comfort, and the evidence is timed-paper performance on higher-tier material, not a teacher's impression.

There is a third thing worth knowing, which is that a remark is a narrow remedy rather than a general appeal. It checks whether the scheme was applied correctly to the script, not whether the candidate deserved more. Schools can advise on when it is worth pursuing. A family considering it should ask the examinations officer what the process involves before assuming it is a route to a better grade.

sections.heading: The tier decision, argued from evidence
paragraphs: This is the single highest-stakes administrative decision of the two years, and it is routinely made on the wrong basis. A candidate who finds the higher-tier material uncomfortable in Year 10 is not thereby a lower-tier candidate; they are a candidate fourteen months from a series. Conversely, a confident student who has never sat a full higher-tier paper under time is not thereby a higher-tier candidate. Both errors cost grades, and they cost them in opposite directions.

The evidence that should decide it is narrow and specific: two full higher-tier papers, sat under real timing, marked to the scheme, taken far enough apart to show a trend. Look at whether the candidate attempts the harder questions at all, whether partial credit is being earned on multi-step items, and whether the gap to a safe margin is closable in the months remaining at a realistic rate of improvement. A coach can produce that evidence in two sessions. A school usually has some of it already and will share it if asked directly.

Where the honest answer is the lower tier, it should be said plainly and early, because a candidate working towards a route they will not sit wastes months. Where the honest answer is the higher tier but the margin is thin, the plan has to be built around the specific question types that are failing rather than around general revision, and it has to start immediately rather than after the next report.

The entry itself belongs to the school. A coach can supply evidence and an opinion; the examinations officer confirms the entry, and after the deadline the ceiling is fixed. Families should ask three questions in writing: what tier is intended, on what evidence, and when is the entry confirmed. Those three answers, in writing, prevent the most expensive surprise available in this qualification.

sections.heading: Cambridge against Pearson Edexcel for the same subject
paragraphs: Families talk about IGCSE as one qualification, and schools enter students subject by subject across two boards. It is entirely normal for a candidate to sit Cambridge sciences and an Edexcel mathematics paper in the same series, and it is also entirely normal for a family to buy preparation for the wrong one. Confirm board by subject from the school's entry record, not from the prospectus and not from the textbook on the shelf, which is sometimes from a third publisher altogether.

The differences that matter to preparation are structural rather than philosophical. Paper structures differ, and so does the balance between calculator and non-calculator work in mathematics. Tier labels differ: Core and Extended in the Cambridge routes, Foundation and Higher in Edexcel's. Reporting scales differ, with Cambridge using a letter scale and the Edexcel International GCSE a numeric one, which matters when a receiving school's entry requirement is expressed in one and the student holds the other. Practical and coursework arrangements differ by subject and by what the school has chosen, including whether an alternative-to-coursework paper is being sat instead.

The series available are the same in the Kingdom: June as the main sitting and November for resits and November-entry candidates. Cambridge also runs a February and March series, but that series is sat only in India, which is worth saying because copy adapted from Indian tutoring sites regularly tells Saudi families otherwise, and a family that plans around a sitting they cannot take loses a term.

For a coach, the practical upshot is that past-paper range must be board-specific. A specialist who has taught one board for years and the other never will teach the shared content well and the paper technique approximately, and paper technique is most of what the final term is for. Ask which board's released papers they use, and in what quantity.

sections.heading: The year read backwards from the June series, as a sequence of checks
paragraphs: Working backwards turns a vague sense of being behind into a list of things that should already be true. Each stage below has a check attached, and each check either passes or does not, which is more useful than a target. No dates appear here beyond the series name, because school calendars differ even between two British-curriculum schools in the same city, and entry deadlines belong to your own examinations officer rather than to any tutoring company.

Eight weeks out, the check is simple: can the candidate sit a full paper under time and finish it? If not, the problem is pace and selection rather than content, and every remaining hour should go into timed papers with the breakdown reviewed each time. A term out, the check is whether a timed higher-tier paper is landing clear of a safe margin. If it is not, the plan should narrow to the two weakest question types and abandon everything else, including topics the candidate enjoys.

Two terms out, the check is coverage: has the specification actually been taught, or are there topics the class has not reached? That is a question for the school rather than the coach, and it is the moment to ask it, because a topic missing two terms out is recoverable and the same topic missing six weeks out is not. A full year out, the check is the tier, settled on evidence as described above. Further back than that, in Years 7 to 9, the check is whether algebra, fractions and sustained writing are automatic, because almost every expensive IGCSE problem is one of those three arriving late.

After results there is one more check that families skip. If a resit is on the table, the entry for the November series runs through the examinations officer on a short timetable, and the decision is better made with the paper breakdown in hand than on the basis of disappointment. A candidate who missed a grade by two marks across a whole paper and one who missed it by twenty are not in the same situation.

sections.heading: Where IGCSE marks actually go missing, subject by subject
paragraphs: A parent describes the problem as a subject. A coach worth paying restates it as a question type, because that is the unit the fix applies to. Across thousands of IGCSE scripts the same handful of failures recur, and they recur independently of ability: strong candidates lose marks to them just as reliably as weak ones, which is why extra content revision so often fails to move a grade that is stuck.

In mathematics the recurring loss is multi-step problems, where an early slip propagates and no further marks are available, combined with working that jumps steps and forfeits method credit. In physics and chemistry it is presentation: units, prefixes, significant figures, state symbols, unbalanced equations. In biology it is command terms, where a candidate writes everything they know rather than answering the term precisely. In the essay and data subjects it is answering the topic instead of the question, and evaluation that restates rather than weighs.

Each of those has a different cost to fix. Presentation errors are the cheapest thing in this market to correct: a marking habit, a checklist used on every piece of written work, and three or four marked papers. Command terms take a similar time. Multi-step problem-solving takes a term, because the cause usually sits in Years 8 and 9. Writing at length under time takes longer still. Knowing which one applies before buying hours is the whole value of the baseline paper.

The last column of the table below is the one families should insist on, because it is what distinguishes coaching from reassurance. Every identified problem should have a piece of evidence attached that will show it has been fixed, agreed in advance. If nobody can say what that evidence would be, the problem has not been diagnosed precisely enough to work on.

sections.heading: Resits, the November series, and what a second attempt is really worth
paragraphs: A resit is a serious decision rather than an automatic next step, and the breakdown of the original paper should drive it. A candidate who missed a grade by a small margin spread across a whole paper is in a very different position from one who missed it by a wide margin concentrated in topics never securely learned. The first is often recoverable in a short, targeted block. The second needs the teaching that did not happen the first time, which is a longer job than the window between results and the November series comfortably allows.

The practical constraints deserve stating plainly. Entries for the November series run through the school's examinations officer on a timetable the family does not control, so the decision has to be made earlier than it feels natural to make it. The candidate is usually starting a new course at the same time, which means resit preparation competes with the first weeks of the next stage. And a resit occupies the autumn term, which is precisely when the new course is laying its own foundations.

Against that, a grade that gates the next stage is worth recovering, and sometimes the only honest path. Where a receiving school requires a specific grade in mathematics or English before allowing a particular subject at the next level, a resit is not optional and the conversation is about how to protect the new course while it happens. Where the grade is not gating anything, the arithmetic is less obvious, and a family should ask what the grade is actually for before committing a term to it.

If a resit does go ahead, treat it as a component problem rather than a repeat of the course. Re-sitting means re-sitting specific papers, and the preparation should be built on the original breakdown: the question types that failed, under timing, with marked work. Repeating the whole syllabus in an autumn term is neither possible nor necessary, and attempting it is the most common reason a second attempt lands close to the first.

sections.heading: Coursework, practical components and the honesty line in a coaching arrangement
paragraphs: IGCSE is mostly externally examined, which makes the honesty question narrower than it is in a programme built on internal assessment, but it does not remove it. Several subjects carry coursework or a practical component, and where a school has entered a candidate for one, that work is assessed and must be the candidate's own. Where the school has entered for an alternative-to-coursework paper instead, there is no coursework to help with at all, and a provider offering coursework support for that subject has not checked the entry.

What a coach may legitimately do is teach the assessment criteria, explain what the task specification is actually asking for, question a method or a plan before any work is produced, and give written feedback on a draft the candidate has written themselves. In the sciences that means interrogating a plan, a variable choice or a graph before the write-up exists. In ICT and Computer Science it means pointing at a documented requirement the work does not meet. All of that teaches; none of it replaces the candidate's work.

What no coach does is write, redraft or dictate any part of assessed work, supply results or data, or provide model answers for adaptation. We do not produce coursework, and we do not rewrite paragraphs for a student to paste in. Students arriving from a Middle Years Programme route sometimes carry a Personal Project alongside, and the same line applies there: a coach may explain the criteria and the role of the process journal, and may not build the product or write the report. Internal components are marked in school and moderated by the board, so the school's own standardisation is part of the picture and worth asking about.

The record is what protects the candidate if anything is ever questioned. Dated drafts, the candidate's own notes and plans, and feedback that points at work rather than supplying text are the evidence of authorship. Ask any prospective coach the question in plain words before booking: what will you do with a draft, and what will you refuse to do? A hesitation is itself the answer, and a school that suspects malpractice is obliged to investigate.

sections.heading: What to ask a coach, and what belongs to the school instead
paragraphs: Families waste a lot of energy asking coaches questions only the school can answer, and asking schools questions only a specialist will answer properly. Sorting them saves weeks. The school owns the entry, the tier, the board, the deadlines, the coverage of the specification and the internal standardisation. The coach owns the diagnosis, the question-type breakdown, the teaching and the marked work. Where a family is unsure who owns something, the test is whether the answer appears on an entry form.

Put four questions to the coach, and expect specifics. Which board and which version of this specification have you taught, and for how many cohorts? What does each paper in this subject consist of at this tier? Where do candidates most often lose marks in the question type my child is failing, and how do you fix it? And what evidence will show it has been fixed? A specification specialist answers the second question immediately and the fourth without being prompted. A generalist answers in terms of confidence, foundations and engagement, which is a different product.

Put four to the school, in writing. Which board is my child entered for in each subject? What tier is intended, on what evidence, and when is the entry confirmed? Has the specification been fully covered, topic by topic? And is there a coursework or practical component, or an alternative-to-coursework paper? Those four answers prevent most of the avoidable damage in this qualification, and none of them require a difficult conversation.

Finally, ignore anything that cannot be checked. A percentage, a star rating, a headcount or a promise about a final grade is self-reported and unverifiable, and none of it appears on this page for that reason. Nor does any suggestion of approval or partnership with a board or a Saudi regulator: IB Gram holds no such status. If a match turns out to be wrong, the remedy should be straightforward, which is to say so after a lesson or two and have the coach changed, with the previous coach's notes and marked work carried over so the candidate does not start again.
