jeddah.programmesIntro: Jeddah schools run four programmes that families regularly need outside support for. Each is assessed differently, and the support a student needs in the Primary Years Programme has almost nothing in common with what a Diploma candidate needs eight weeks before the June series.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The Primary Years Programme has no external examination. Progress is judged through units of inquiry, teacher assessment and the Year 6 exhibition. Support at this stage is about the mechanics underneath the inquiry: number fluency, reading stamina, written structure and the habit of explaining a method rather than producing an answer. A tutor who teaches it as a watered-down secondary course misses the point and bores the child.
programmes.countryNote: Jeddah's PYP schools draw children from families who have moved between three or four education systems before Year 4. The gaps that show up are rarely conceptual; they are procedural, such as column methods learned one way in a previous country and another way here. One-to-one online sessions of thirty to forty minutes suit this age better than an hour, and they fit the gap between the school run and dinner.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The Middle Years Programme is assessed against four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight, and reported as a one-to-seven grade from a published conversion. The Personal Project runs in the final year. Marks are lost here when a student writes a correct answer that does not address the command term, or submits a project with no evidence of the process behind it. Criterion language is teachable, and it is the fastest win available at this stage.
programmes.countryNote: A large share of Jeddah students arrive in the Middle Years Programme from a British or American school and meet criterion-based marking for the first time. The content is familiar; the way it is rewarded is not. Students who hold a strong Year 9 report and then slide in Year 10 are usually hitting that wall rather than hitting a knowledge ceiling, and it responds quickly to direct teaching of the criteria.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The Diploma is six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Subject grades run one to seven, and the core adds up to three further points through the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay matrix. Internal Assessment carries roughly twenty to thirty per cent of most subject grades, and the written papers carry the rest.
programmes.countryNote: Jeddah's Diploma cohorts are small enough that Higher Level option groups can come down to two or three students, and a school may run a Higher Level subject with a teacher whose own specialism sits elsewhere in the department. This is where an outside specialist earns their fee: not to replace the school, but to cover the one paper the timetable cannot staff properly. Ask the Diploma Programme coordinator which Higher Level groups are smallest before subject choices lock.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE and Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel both examine at this level, and the differences are real: paper structure, tiering, coursework options and syllabus codes all vary. Cambridge Mathematics 0580 runs Core and Extended tiers; the sciences at 0620, 0625 and 0610 each carry a multiple-choice paper, a theory paper and an alternative-to-practical or practical component. Knowing which board and which tier your child is entered for is the first question a tutor should ask.
programmes.countryNote: Most Jeddah British-curriculum schools enter candidates for the June series, with November available for resits and November-entry candidates. Cambridge's February/March series is an India-only sitting, so a Jeddah candidate plans around June and November and nothing else. Final entry windows close months before the papers, and the examinations officer at your child's school holds the exact dates rather than any tutoring provider.

jeddah.subjectsIntro: These are the Diploma subjects Jeddah families ask for most often, with what each one actually assesses and where the marks go missing. Scarcity drives price in this market, and the subjects near the top of this list are the scarce ones.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Paper 3 at Higher Level is the component that separates grades: two extended problem-solving questions worth twenty per cent of the grade, with no scaffolding and a reading demand students underestimate. A Mathematics AA HL tutor in Jeddah is the single most requested match we handle, and the pool is genuinely small. Most marks are lost on proof, on calculus applications and on failing to state what a variable represents.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Applications and Interpretation is calculator-permitted throughout and leans on modelling, statistics and interpretation of real data. Students who switch into it from Analysis and Approaches often assume it is easier and then lose marks for writing bare numbers with no interpretation. The Higher Level course adds matrices, graph theory and a heavier statistics load than most students expect from the course description.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Physics Higher Level carries topics with no Standard Level equivalent, and the extension questions assume fluency with the data booklet rather than recall of it. Marks disappear in the extended-response items when a student describes a phenomenon instead of deriving it. A Physics HL tutor in Jeddah is the second hardest match to fill after Mathematics AA HL, which is why advertised rates for it sit at the top of the band.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The organic mechanisms and the energetics topics carry most of the lost marks, and the Internal Assessment is where strong students most often underscore. Examiners reward a clearly stated research question with controlled variables and a genuine uncertainty treatment. A tutor reviews and questions that work; they never write it. The Higher Level extension to equilibrium and acid-base chemistry needs separate teaching, not revision.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Biology looks like a memory subject and is examined as a precision subject. Definitions are marked strictly, and a six-mark answer that lists facts without linking structure to function scores poorly. The Higher Level extension topics add depth to plant biology, genetics and physiology that cannot be absorbed in a final revision sprint. Data-based questions in Paper 2 reward graph reading, not biological knowledge.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy decides Economics marks more than content does. An inaccurately labelled diagram caps an answer regardless of the prose around it. Higher Level adds quantitative questions and a theory-of-the-firm style extension. The Internal Assessment is three commentaries on published news articles, each with a word limit, and most of the lost marks there come from analysis that never touches the diagram the student drew.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The pre-released case study for Paper 1 rewards preparation that most candidates leave too late, and Paper 2 is built on quantitative tools plus a data-response structure. Higher Level adds an extension paper with an extended-response component. Students who write confident general business commentary without applying a named tool to the stimulus lose marks they believed they had earned.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The individual oral and the Higher Level essay are where the grade is made or lost, and both are internally assessed before external moderation. Paper 1 is unseen textual analysis under time pressure, and students trained to summarise rather than analyse struggle with it. A tutor works on the analytical move itself, using texts the student is not being assessed on, so the assessed work stays entirely theirs.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: The Internal Assessment is a working solution with documented development, and students routinely over-scope it in the first month. Paper 1 and Paper 2 test algorithmic thinking and data structures rather than coding fluency in any one language, which surprises students who are confident programmers. The Higher Level extension on abstract data structures and resource management needs taught time, not practice alone.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: Jeddah families regularly have one child in Arabic A as a literature course and another in Arabic B as an acquisition course, and the two are assessed on entirely different criteria. Arabic B rewards structured productive writing against a task type; Arabic A rewards literary analysis. Choosing the wrong course at the start of the Diploma is difficult to unwind later and is worth a conversation before subject choices close.

jeddah.igcseSubjectsIntro: Jeddah's British-curriculum schools sit Cambridge IGCSE and Edexcel International GCSE in roughly equal measure, and some schools split boards across departments. These are the papers that generate the most enquiries.

igcseSubjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580)
igcseSubjects.description: The Extended tier is the one almost every Jeddah school enters for, and it is the correct choice for anyone heading into the Diploma or A Level sciences. Core caps the available grade. Most marks are lost on algebraic manipulation under time pressure and on questions that ask for a method to be shown when the answer alone has been written.

igcseSubjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625)
igcseSubjects.description: The alternative-to-practical paper is a written examination about experiments, not an experiment, and it is routinely under-prepared because it does not feel like physics. Candidates who can calculate confidently still lose marks describing how to reduce uncertainty in a measurement or reading a scale on a printed instrument.

igcseSubjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620)
igcseSubjects.description: Qualitative analysis, mole calculations and the organic chemistry unit account for most of the difference between a six and an eight here. Candidates lose marks on state symbols, on balancing, and on explaining an observation when the question asked for one rather than for a conclusion.

igcseSubjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610)
igcseSubjects.description: Biology at this level is examined on exact terminology. A student who writes about something 'going into' a cell when the mark scheme wants diffusion down a concentration gradient has the biology right and the mark wrong. Transport in plants, enzymes and inheritance are the usual trouble spots.

igcseSubjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510 and 0511)
igcseSubjects.description: The reading and writing paper rewards register control and task fulfilment, not vocabulary range. Students who read widely in English still lose marks for writing an essay when the task asked for a report. Speaking is separately assessed, and the two codes differ in how speaking is counted.

igcseSubjects.name: Economics (Cambridge 0455)
igcseSubjects.description: The structured-question paper carries most of the available marks, and the command terms do the work: analyse, discuss and evaluate are rewarded quite differently. Candidates who have learned definitions and diagrams in isolation struggle to build an evaluated judgement in the final part of a question.

igcseSubjects.name: Business Studies (Cambridge 0450)
igcseSubjects.description: Both papers are case-study based, and the marks sit in application rather than theory. A correct general point about motivation scores less than a weaker point anchored in the business described in the stimulus. This is the subject where exam technique and content knowledge diverge most sharply at IGCSE.

jeddah.regionsTitle: Districts along Jeddah's coastal spine, and what each does to an evening
jeddah.regionsIntro: Jeddah is long rather than wide, and almost all school traffic moves north and south along the same corridors. The district a family lives in decides what time a lesson can realistically start, which is why we list them with the evening in mind rather than as a service-area map.

regions.name: Al Hamra
regions.note: Central-north and close to the Corniche, with a short run to several international campuses. Families here often have the earliest workable slot in the city, which makes a 5pm start realistic for a Year 10 student and leaves the 7pm slot free for an older sibling.

regions.name: Al Rawdah
regions.note: Dense, central and well connected to both the Tahlia corridor and Al Madinah Road. Parents here commonly run two children to two different schools, so the practical constraint is not distance but the second pickup. Lessons that start after 6pm tend to hold better than earlier ones.

regions.name: Al Shati and the Corniche
regions.note: Northern coastal strip with low evening traffic in its own streets and a longer run inland to the eastern campuses. The usable window is wide once everyone is home, and it is the part of the city where a 7:30pm Diploma session causes the least friction.

regions.name: Obhur
regions.note: Furthest north, past King Road, and effectively a separate commute. A family searching for an IB tutor in Obhur is the clearest case for online lessons: the drive back from a central campus can occupy the whole of the hour an in-home tutor would have been teaching. Pinning the slot to 6pm or later is the usual answer.

regions.name: Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Northern-central, residential, and within reach of the main northbound school corridor. The constraint here is usually activities rather than traffic, so families often split a week into one weekday evening plus a Saturday morning block during a heavy assessment term.

regions.name: As Salamah
regions.note: Inland and central, with access to Al Madinah Road and Prince Majid Road. Students here frequently attend schools in two different directions, and the household's realistic shared quiet hour starts late. A single ninety-minute session often works better than two shorter ones.

regions.name: Al Andalus
regions.note: Central, close to Tahlia Street and the business districts, with many working parents whose own day ends after the school run. Progress reporting matters more here than anywhere else in the city, because the parent is often not in the room; written notes after each session do that job.

regions.name: Al Basateen and the central districts
regions.note: West-central, near the coast and the older part of the city. Commutes to the northern campuses are the long ones. These are the families for whom a specialist within a twenty-minute drive is not a realistic category at all, which is the honest argument for teaching over video.

regions.name: Al Zahra and Al Faisaliyah
regions.note: Central-south, close to the hospital and university clusters, with a high share of medical and academic households. Subject requests skew towards Higher Level Biology and Chemistry, and session times are shaped by shift patterns rather than by traffic.

schoolClusters.city: North Jeddah and the Obhur corridor
schoolClusters.note: The northern corridor holds much of the city's British and American international provision, and families routinely live in one district and drive north to a campus in another. Campus addresses change as schools expand, so check each school's own published address rather than assuming a district. Students we support attend schools including the following.

Central Jeddah carries the longest-established international schools in the city, including a German-curriculum school running to Grade 12 and several schools that appear in IB listings. Diploma cohorts in this cluster are smaller than the equivalent Riyadh ones, which is the usual reason a Higher Level option group ends up with very few students in it.

schoolClusters.city: The Makkah Road corridor and the eastern districts
schoolClusters.note: East of the centre the schools serve large resident expatriate communities, with Indian, Pakistani and Egyptian curriculum provision alongside British-curriculum schools. Students here often sit Cambridge IGCSE alongside a national curriculum, and the questions we get from this cluster are mostly about how the two timetables coexist.

jeddah.modesIntro: Three formats, each with an honest use. The default is weekly one-to-one because it is the only format in which a tutor can respond to what a specific student got wrong last week, but it is not the only sensible choice.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one, pinned to Arabia Standard Time
modes.description: A fixed slot each week with the same tutor, held in Saudi local time so that a tutor's own clock change in their country never moves your evening. Sessions are usually sixty minutes for IGCSE and Middle Years students and seventy-five to ninety for Diploma candidates working through past papers, because a Higher Level paper cannot be usefully attempted in under an hour.

modes.title: Intensive block before a series
modes.description: A compressed run of sessions in the weeks before the June or November series, built around past papers under timed conditions and the specific components a student is weakest on. This is the right format for a candidate whose content knowledge is sound and whose technique is not, and the wrong one for a student with genuine gaps in the syllabus, who needs taught time instead.

modes.title: Diagnostic and periodic review
modes.description: Some families do not need weekly teaching. They need a specialist to look at a set of marked papers, tell them honestly whether the problem is content, technique or something else, and set a plan the student runs mostly alone. That is a useful and much cheaper arrangement, and we would rather sell it than sell a weekly slot a student does not need.

sections.heading: What IB and IGCSE tuition costs in Jeddah, and what actually moves the number
paragraphs: Rates in this market are published by vendors, not by any regulator, so treat every figure below as an advertised rate rather than a market average. The pattern across those listings is consistent enough to be useful. General online tutoring with no subject specialism starts at around SAR 55 an hour. Budget international platforms advertise Cambridge IGCSE one-to-one from roughly SAR 35. Local tutor-marketplace guides put general private tuition for primary years near SAR 50 and senior-school examination subjects above SAR 200. Tutoring companies listing IB work specifically advertise from about SAR 180, rising to SAR 200 to 220 for Higher Level and Advanced Placement tracks. Some international providers quote in dollars at around sixty an hour, which converts to the upper end of the local band.

What moves a rate, in order of weight: subject scarcity first, then examiner or marking experience, then level, then whether the tutor travels, then package length. Scarcity is the dominant term and it is the one parents consistently under-weight. A Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation SL tutor is a common profile; a Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL tutor who can teach Paper 3 is not, and the price difference between them has nothing to do with how hard either person works. The same gap exists between Biology SL and Physics HL, and between a general English tutor and someone who can take apart a Higher Level essay.

Travel loading is the item that disappears entirely when lessons are taught online, and in Jeddah it is not a small item. An in-home arrangement in this city has to pay for a round trip along the coastal corridor at the worst hour of the day, and that cost appears either in the hourly rate or in the tutor's willingness to hold the slot through a difficult term. Online, the money goes into teaching time and the tutor pool is not limited to people who live within range of your district.

A last point on value rather than price. The cheapest useful lesson is the one that fixes something specific, and the most expensive one is a weekly slot nobody has diagnosed. Before you compare IB tutoring rates in Jeddah, get a specialist to look at two marked papers and say where the marks went. That conversation is free here, and it frequently results in us recommending fewer lessons than the family expected to buy.

sections.heading: Jeddah's geography decides how many hours of tuition you can actually buy
paragraphs: This is the part of the decision that gets left out of every brochure. The city is a spine, not a grid: Al Balad and the central districts at the south, Al Hamra and Al Shati in the middle, Al Khalidiyah and the northern residential districts above them, and Obhur beyond King Road. Most international campuses sit along that northbound axis, and the entire school population moves along it at the same two times each day. The result is that two families paying the same hourly rate get very different amounts of usable study time, purely because of where they live relative to the campus.

Work it through for a Diploma student. School ends in the early afternoon. Add an activity or a bus, then the drive, then the gap in which a sixteen-year-old eats and stops being a passenger. A family in Al Hamra reaches the start of that quiet hour noticeably earlier than a family in Obhur whose child attends a central campus. For the Obhur family, an in-home tutor arriving at 5pm would spend part of the booked hour waiting, and would then drive home through the same corridor. Online, the lesson simply starts at 6:30pm and ends at eight, and nobody has driven anywhere.

The table below is the version of a service-area map that is actually useful: not which districts we cover, since an online lesson covers all of them identically, but what the return run in each district does to the earliest sensible lesson start. The ranges are typical patterns rather than measured data, and roadworks on Al Madinah Road or the Haramain corridor will beat any estimate. Use it as a conversation starter with your own household rather than as a timetable.

One consequence is worth stating directly. If the honest earliest start in your district is 6:30pm, then the tutor you need is one whose own working day still has an hour in it at 6:30pm Saudi time. That is a scheduling constraint on the tutor, not on you, and it is the reason the time-zone table further down this page exists. An excellent tutor in a country where 6:30pm Jeddah time is eleven at night is not a match, however good their subject knowledge.

sections.heading: What the premium actually buys at the top of the band
paragraphs: If a Physics HL tutor in Jeddah is advertised at SAR 220 and a general science tutor at SAR 60, the difference is not a mark-up on the same service. It is a different service, and it is worth naming the components so you can judge whether you need them. The first is syllabus-level knowledge: not Physics, but this Physics, at this level, on this board, with the current assessment structure and the specific extension topics that have no Standard Level equivalent. A tutor who last taught the course under a previous syllabus will be subtly wrong in ways a student cannot detect.

The second component is mark-scheme literacy. Knowing physics and knowing what a published mark scheme pays for are different skills. Examiners award marks for named steps in a defined order; a student who reaches the right answer by a route the scheme does not recognise loses marks they feel they earned. A tutor with marking experience has internalised that ordering, and the teaching consequence is immediate: they stop a student mid-answer and ask what the examiner is looking for, rather than checking whether the final number is right.

The third is diagnostic range. A specialist who has taught the same Higher Level course to many cohorts has seen most of the ways a student can be confused about, say, capacitor discharge or the Internal Assessment uncertainty treatment. They recognise a pattern in two questions instead of discovering it over six weeks. This is the part of the premium that saves money, because it shortens the engagement rather than extending it.

What the premium does not buy is a grade. No tutor can promise a seven, and anyone who does is telling you something about their business rather than about your child. Grade boundaries move between series, predicted grades are a school's professional judgement rather than a forecast, and the only honest claim available is that a specialist can tell you where the marks are going and teach the student to stop losing them.

sections.heading: The subjects Jeddah schools find hardest to staff, and why that lands on you
paragraphs: Every school in the world staffs to its timetable, and a timetable is built from option blocks. When a Higher Level option group has two or three students in it, the school has a genuine problem: it cannot justify a dedicated specialist for that group, so the subject is taught by the nearest available person in the department, or taught in a combined class with the Standard Level cohort, or in a few cases offered only if a student self-studies with supervision. None of that is negligence. It is arithmetic, and in a city where Diploma cohorts are smaller than Riyadh's, the arithmetic bites more often.

The subjects where this shows up most in Jeddah enquiries are Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, Physics at Higher Level, Computer Science, Economics at Higher Level, and the less commonly chosen Group 1 and Group 2 combinations such as a Higher Level literature course in a language with few speakers in the cohort. At IGCSE the pattern is different: the content is usually well covered, and the gap is in the practical and alternative-to-practical components, which need equipment, time and a teacher who has marked them.

The second-order effect matters as much as the first. A student who is the only one in the year sitting a Higher Level subject has no study group, nobody to argue with about a mark scheme, and no benchmark for what a good answer looks like. Working alone is a real disadvantage separate from teaching quality. An outside specialist partly replaces that function: someone who has seen a hundred versions of this answer and can say which one the examiner pays for.

The practical move for a family is to ask the school a precise question before subject choices lock, not afterwards. Which Higher Level groups are running, how many students are in each, and who teaches it. Schools answer that question honestly when it is asked in those terms, and the answer tells you whether you will be buying outside support for two years or not at all.
bullets: Ask the Diploma Programme coordinator for the size of each Higher Level option group before choices close
Ask who teaches each Higher Level group, and what that teacher's own specialism is
At IGCSE, ask specifically how the practical or alternative-to-practical component is prepared
A subject offered only by supervised self-study is a clear signal that outside teaching will be needed

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week on Arabia Standard Time, and why a tutor's own clock matters
paragraphs: The Jeddah school week runs Sunday to Thursday. Friday and Saturday are the weekend. That sounds like a detail until you try to book a weekly slot with a tutor whose own working week runs Monday to Friday, at which point it becomes the whole problem: their Friday is your weekend, and your Sunday is their day off. Copy written for a British or Indian market and lightly edited for the Gulf gets this wrong constantly, and the result is a schedule that collapses in the third week.

The Kingdom keeps Arabia Standard Time, UTC+3, and does not observe daylight saving. Any slot agreed with a tutor in a country that does change its clocks will drift by an hour twice a year unless the slot is pinned to Saudi local time. We pin it to Saudi local time. That means the tutor's own stated hour moves and yours does not, which is the right way round: your child's school day is the fixed object in this arrangement.

The table shows what a 6pm Jeddah lesson looks like from the tutor's side in the countries our tutors most often work from. Read it as a filter. A tutor in the Gulf or South Asia can hold a 6pm or 7pm Saudi slot comfortably on a weekday. A tutor in the United Kingdom or continental Europe can hold it inside their own working afternoon. A tutor in East Asia cannot hold it at all on a school night, and a tutor in North America is doing it before lunch, which works for them and constrains how many Saudi families they can take.

Ramadan changes the picture every year, and because the Islamic calendar moves against the Gregorian one by about eleven days annually, it drifts across the academic year rather than sitting in one term. School days shorten, and the productive study hours move later into the evening. We move lesson slots later for that period rather than cancelling them, and families who prefer to pause and resume afterwards keep their slot. Neither we nor anyone else should be publishing dates for it: the start is confirmed by moon sighting and differs by a day between countries.

sections.heading: Group classes, paired lessons and one-to-one: where each is honestly worth the money
paragraphs: A group class is cheaper per hour and sometimes better, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. The question is what you are buying. A group works when the content is new to everyone in the room at roughly the same level, when the teaching is expository, and when the value is in hearing a topic explained well. A revision course on the Economics diagram set, or a session on how the Theory of Knowledge exhibition is assessed, loses nothing by having eight students in it, and it costs a fraction of the one-to-one rate.

A group fails when the value is diagnostic. If the reason your child is stuck on Mathematics Paper 3 is a specific misunderstanding about how to set up an integral, a group lesson will not find it, because the tutor is teaching to the median student in the room. Diploma candidates in the last two terms are almost always in diagnostic territory rather than expository territory, which is why we sell one-to-one for that work and would rather turn an enquiry away than put a Higher Level candidate into a group and take the fee.

Paired lessons sit in between and are underrated. Two students at genuinely similar levels, on the same board and paper, with the same tutor, can work well: they mark each other's answers against the scheme, which is one of the most effective techniques available and almost impossible alone. The conditions are strict, though. The same paper, a similar current grade, and a willingness to be wrong in front of each other. Two siblings two years apart do not meet them.

We sell one-to-one only, for Jeddah and for every other Saudi city, and we say why rather than dressing it up. A platform that matches a specialist to a single student can honestly promise that the hour is spent on that student's actual errors. The moment a second unmatched student is in the room, that promise weakens, and the fee stops being justifiable at the top of the band.

sections.heading: Academic honesty: what a tutor may do with an Internal Assessment, and what we decline
paragraphs: This needs saying plainly, because several providers visible in Saudi search results are selling something else. A tutor may teach the skills an Internal Assessment requires. They may explain the assessment criteria and what each criterion rewards. They may look at a student's own draft and ask questions about it: is this research question answerable, is this variable controlled, does this conclusion follow from this data, is this uncertainty treatment defensible. They may teach referencing. They may work through an example on a topic the student is not being assessed on.

A tutor may not write any part of it. Not a paragraph, not a research question handed over to be adopted, not a rewritten conclusion, not a tidied-up methodology. We decline requests to produce or complete an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay, a Middle Years Programme Personal Project or any other assessed work, and we decline them in writing rather than quietly. The work must be the student's own, the school supervisor certifies that it is, and a student who submits work that is not their own risks the entire Diploma rather than one subject grade.

The practical shape of honest help is narrower than families expect and more useful than they expect. The highest-value hour on an Internal Assessment is usually spent before any writing happens, on the research question itself, because a badly scoped question caps the achievable mark no matter how well the rest is executed. The second most valuable hour is spent on the criterion the student has misread, which is almost always the one about evaluation rather than the one about method.

Keep your own record as a family. Dated drafts, notes from supervision meetings at school, and a clear sense of which ideas came from where. That is not defensive paperwork; it is how a student can answer a question about their own work confidently in a viva or a supervision meeting, and it is the habit the Extended Essay reflection requirement is designed to build.
bullets: A tutor teaches criteria, technique and referencing, and reviews the student's own drafts
A tutor does not write, redraft, scope or complete any assessed component
The research question is where honest help pays off most, and it comes first

sections.heading: After the Diploma: equivalency, Qudurat and Tahsili for a Jeddah school leaver
paragraphs: A Diploma or an International GCSE route does not connect automatically to a Saudi university place, and this is the single biggest gap in the content Jeddah families can find online. An international or foreign school certificate needs an equivalency decision, mu'adalah, from the Ministry of Education before a Saudi university treats it as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. That applies to the IB Diploma, to A Levels and to an American high school diploma alike. It is an administrative process with document requirements, and it is worth starting to understand it in the first year of the Diploma rather than after results.

Alongside equivalency sit the Qiyas tests, run by the National Center for Assessment within the Education and Training Evaluation Commission. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, assesses verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, and is sat in Arabic or English. Tahsili, the Achievement Test, covers the science-stream subjects: mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English. The critical point for an international-curriculum student is that Tahsili content follows the Saudi national curriculum. The material overlaps with what a Diploma student has studied; the framing, the sequence and the expected method frequently do not.

That mismatch is why a strong Higher Level Chemistry student can find Tahsili harder than their own examinations. They are not short of chemistry. They are meeting a different syllabus organisation and a different question style, in a test that does not care which board taught them. Preparation for it is a separate piece of work from Diploma preparation, and the families who handle it well start it early and treat it as its own subject rather than as revision.

We do not publish score thresholds or any university's weighting formula, and you should be sceptical of pages that do. Weightings differ by university and by programme, competitive engineering, medicine and science programmes lean hardest on Tahsili, and some universities set a maximum age for the secondary certificate they will accept. The only reliable source is the admission page of the specific university and programme your child is applying to, read in the year they apply.

sections.heading: Getting started, and what we say when no specialist is free
paragraphs: The first step is a free trial lesson, and it is a diagnostic rather than a sales call. Bring two pieces of marked work, ideally a recent past paper and one piece of coursework or an Internal Assessment draft. The tutor spends the hour finding out where the marks are going, and at the end you get a plain view of whether the problem is content, technique, pace or something that is not academic at all. We have ended trials by telling a family that their child does not need a tutor, and that is a better outcome than selling a slot.

If it makes sense to continue, we agree a slot in Saudi local time, a subject, a level and a board, and a written plan with something checkable in it. The plan names the components being worked on, not a target grade, because a target grade set by a tutor is a guess dressed as a commitment. After each session the parent gets written notes: what was covered, what the student got wrong, and what to do before the next one. For working parents in Al Andalus or Al Rawdah who are not in the room, those notes are the whole of the visibility, so they are written to be read in two minutes.

Sometimes the honest answer is that nobody suitable is available at the hour you need. A Mathematics AA HL specialist who can teach at 6:30pm Saudi time on a Tuesday is a narrow intersection of two scarce things, and we would rather tell you that and offer a different hour, a different day, or a waiting position than hand your child to a tutor who teaches the subject but not the level. If that happens we say so at the trial stage, not after the first invoice.

Changing tutor is normal and is not a failure of the match process. If after two or three sessions the fit is wrong — pace, manner, explanation style, anything — tell us and we move the student. There is no fee for the change and no argument about it. A tutor and a fifteen-year-old either work together or they do not, and the cost of discovering that late is far higher than the cost of a reassignment.

process.title: Tell us the board, the level and the hour
process.description: Not just the subject. Cambridge or Edexcel, Higher or Standard Level, which papers, and the earliest evening hour that works once your district's school run is done. Those four facts decide whether a good match exists, and giving them up front saves a week of back and forth.

process.title: Free trial lesson, used as a diagnostic
process.description: Bring two pieces of marked work. The tutor spends the hour establishing where marks are being lost rather than teaching a sample lesson. You finish with a written view of the problem and an honest recommendation, including the recommendation to buy nothing if that is the right call.

process.title: A plan with components in it, not a target grade
process.description: The plan names what is being worked on: Paper 3 technique, the alternative-to-practical, organic mechanisms, the Internal Assessment research question. It has a review point. It does not promise a grade, because nobody can honestly promise one and grade boundaries move between series.

process.title: A fixed weekly slot in Saudi time
process.description: The slot is held in Arabia Standard Time and does not move when a tutor's own country changes its clocks. Sunday to Thursday by default. Sessions run sixty minutes for IGCSE and Middle Years work, and seventy-five to ninety for Diploma candidates working through full papers.

process.title: Written notes after every session
process.description: What was covered, what the student got wrong, and one specific thing to do before the next lesson. Short enough to read between meetings. This is how a parent who is not in the room keeps track, and it is also the record that makes a review conversation useful rather than vague.

process.title: Review, change or stop
process.description: At the review point we say whether this is working, using the marked work rather than an impression. If the tutor is the wrong fit we reassign at no cost. If the student no longer needs weekly teaching we say that too, and move to periodic review or stop altogether.

whyPoints.title: The rates are on the page
whyPoints.description: Every band in this market is published above, with the source type next to it, before you have spoken to anyone. Rivals in this search put a contact form where the number should be. A parent comparing options deserves to know what the range is and what moves it, including the possibility that the answer is fewer lessons.

whyPoints.title: Matched on the paper, not the subject
whyPoints.description: A tutor is matched to the board, the level and the specific components your child sits. Someone who teaches Chemistry generally is not the same as someone who has taught Higher Level Chemistry on the current syllabus and marked the Internal Assessment against its criteria. We ask which before we match.

whyPoints.title: Built for the Saudi week and the Saudi clock
whyPoints.description: Sunday to Thursday, Arabia Standard Time, slot pinned to Saudi local time so a tutor's clock change never moves your evening. Lesson times move later during Ramadan rather than being cancelled. This is the part most imported tutoring copy gets wrong and the part that decides whether a schedule survives a term.

whyPoints.title: Honest about assessed work
whyPoints.description: We teach criteria, technique and referencing, and we review a student's own drafts. We decline to write or complete an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay or a Personal Project. Given what else is on sale in this search, that boundary is worth stating in full rather than implying.

whyPoints.title: No claims we cannot support
whyPoints.description: No grade guarantees, no success percentages, no star ratings, no tutor headcounts, no accreditation we do not hold. IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform with no affiliation to the IB, Cambridge, Pearson, the Ministry of Education or ETEC, and no office in the Kingdom. What we can do is match a specialist and show you the working.

whyPoints.title: We will tell you when to stop
whyPoints.description: A student who has fixed the thing they came for should not be carrying a weekly slot out of habit. At each review we say plainly whether continuing is justified by the marked work. Periodic review at three or four week intervals is often the right answer, and it costs a fraction of weekly teaching.

faqs.question: What does a Jeddah student actually see on screen during an online IGCSE Chemistry lesson?
faqs.answer: A shared whiteboard on one side and the tutor on the other. The tutor writes on the board with a stylus, so the student watches a mechanism being built step by step rather than looking at a finished slide. Past-paper questions are pulled up as images and annotated live. The student writes on the same board, which is how the tutor sees the working rather than just the answer. At the end the board is saved and sent to the student, so the lesson leaves a usable set of notes behind. No software install is needed beyond a browser.

faqs.question: Is a lesson recorded, and who in the family can watch it back afterwards?
faqs.answer: Recording is optional and is set by the family, not by the tutor. When it is switched on, the recording goes to the parent and the student and to nobody else. Many Diploma students use it to revisit a derivation they half-followed the first time; some students are more self-conscious with it running, which is a legitimate reason to leave it off. The saved whiteboard is sent either way, so a family that prefers no recording still ends the session with the written record of what was taught.

faqs.question: Our villa in Obhur has patchy evening bandwidth. What happens if the connection drops mid-session?
faqs.answer: The tutor waits and reconnects, and lost minutes are added to the end or to the next session. If the connection is unstable rather than briefly dropped, the lesson switches to audio with the shared whiteboard still running, which uses far less bandwidth and keeps the teaching going. Obhur and the outer coastal districts raise this more than anywhere else in Jeddah. Families there usually find a wired connection or a position close to the router solves it, and we test the connection during the free trial rather than discovering it in week three.

faqs.question: How does a tutor work through a Mathematics AA Paper 3 question on screen without losing the student?
faqs.answer: By making the student do the writing. The question goes on the shared board, and the tutor asks what the first move is before writing anything. The student types or writes their attempt on the board, and the tutor annotates it in a second colour, so the student can see exactly where their line of reasoning diverged from the one the mark scheme pays for. It is slower than a demonstration and considerably more effective, because a Paper 3 question is lost in the setup rather than in the algebra.

faqs.question: Can a parent in Al Rawdah sit in on the first few sessions without making it awkward?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for a younger student it is often helpful. For a Diploma candidate it usually is not, because a sixteen-year-old performs rather than admits confusion when a parent is listening. Our usual suggestion is to sit in on the trial lesson, then step out and read the written notes instead. If you want visibility without being in the room, ask the tutor to record one session a month. Younger Primary and Middle Years students are different, and a parent nearby for the first two or three sessions helps them settle.

faqs.question: What equipment does a Jeddah family need at home before the free trial lesson?
faqs.answer: A laptop or desktop with a working microphone, a reasonable internet connection, and somewhere quiet. A tablet works for a Primary Years student but is awkward for Diploma maths and sciences, because the student needs to see a full past-paper page and write on it at the same time. Headphones help in a busy household. A graphics tablet or stylus is useful but not required; many students write on paper and hold it to the camera, and that is perfectly workable.

faqs.question: Why does a Physics HL tutor cost more per hour in Jeddah than a Mathematics AI SL one?
faqs.answer: Scarcity, not effort. Applications and Interpretation at Standard Level is taught by a large share of maths teachers, so supply is wide and the advertised rate stays near the middle of the band. Higher Level Physics needs someone who has taught the extension topics, knows the data booklet as a working tool, and has marked the extended-response items. Far fewer people match that, and fewer still are free at a Saudi evening hour. Vendor listings in this market reflect that gap, with Higher Level tracks advertised at roughly SAR 200 to 220 against SAR 55 to 180 for general work.

faqs.question: How do the SAR rates advertised by Jeddah tutoring centres compare with online one-to-one?
faqs.answer: Local tutor-marketplace guides put senior-school examination subjects above SAR 200 an hour for private tuition, and tutoring companies listing IB work advertise from about SAR 180, reaching SAR 200 to 220 for Higher Level tracks. Online specialist rates sit inside that band rather than below it, because the cost is the specialist, not the room. What disappears online is the travel loading and the limit on who is available, which in a city laid out like Jeddah is the larger of the two savings.

faqs.question: What happens in the free trial lesson, and what does it cost if we decide not to continue?
faqs.answer: Nothing. There is no fee for the trial and no obligation attached to it. The hour is spent diagnosing rather than demonstrating: the tutor works through marked papers with the student and establishes where marks are going. You receive a written summary afterwards, including the honest recommendation, which is sometimes that no weekly tuition is needed or that a different subject is the real problem. If you do not continue, you keep the summary and we do not chase you.

faqs.question: Is a small group class ever better value than one-to-one for an IGCSE resit candidate in Jeddah?
faqs.answer: For content that is new to everyone at a similar level, a group is good value and we would say so. For a resit it rarely is. A resit candidate has a specific, already-diagnosed failure: a component they did not prepare, a topic they never understood, or timing in the paper. A group lesson teaches to the median student in the room and cannot chase that. The honest middle option is a few one-to-one diagnostic sessions followed by independent work on past papers, which costs less than a term of weekly group classes.

faqs.question: Do we pay per lesson or per block, and what happens to a lesson missed for a school trip?
faqs.answer: Per lesson is the default, which suits families who want to start carefully, and blocks are available for intensive work before a series where the whole point is continuity. A lesson cancelled with reasonable notice is rescheduled rather than charged, and school trips, examinations and illness are exactly the cases that notice exists for. A session missed without notice is treated as taught, because the tutor held the hour. Unused lessons in a block are rescheduled, not forfeited.

faqs.question: How do I check that a tutor has genuinely taught the Cambridge syllabus my child's Jeddah school follows?
faqs.answer: Ask three specific questions and listen for specifics. Which syllabus code, since Cambridge Mathematics 0580 and Physics 0625 each have their own paper structure. How is the alternative-to-practical component prepared, which a tutor who has only taught theory cannot answer in detail. And what changed in the most recent syllabus revision for this subject. A tutor who has taught the course answers all three in concrete terms. One who knows the subject generally will answer the first and become vague on the second.

faqs.question: What does examiner experience mean on a tutor profile, and how would I verify it?
faqs.answer: It means the tutor has marked candidate scripts for an awarding body against its published mark scheme, usually as an assistant examiner, and so has internalised how marks are actually awarded rather than how answers look. Boards do not publish examiner lists, so there is no public register to check. What you can do is test it: ask the tutor to mark a piece of your child's work against the scheme and explain each decision. Someone who has done the job explains the ordering of marks instinctively, and that is harder to fake than a line on a profile.

faqs.question: Can we change tutor after two lessons if the match is wrong, and what does that cost?
faqs.answer: Nothing, and you do not need to justify it. Tell us what did not work — pace too fast, explanations pitched too high, the student not talking — and we use that to make a better second match rather than treating it as a complaint. The reassignment is free and the new tutor reads the notes from the previous sessions, so the student does not repeat the diagnostic. Discovering a mismatch at lesson two is a good outcome; discovering it at lesson twelve is an expensive one.

faqs.question: Should a Diploma student in Jeddah have different tutors for their Higher Level and Standard Level subjects?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, because the match is to the level rather than the subject. The Higher Level extension topics are genuinely separate content with their own assessment style, and the specialist who teaches them well is often not the best choice for a Standard Level course where pace and confidence matter more than depth. The exception is a single subject taken at one level, where one tutor obviously covers it. Running two subjects with two specialists on two evenings is the common pattern for Jeddah Diploma candidates.

jeddah.closingHeading: Start with two marked papers and an honest hour
jeddah.closingBody: If you are weighing up IB and IGCSE tutors in Jeddah, the useful first step is not a brochure. Send us the board, the level, the papers your child sits and the earliest evening hour that works once your district's school run is finished. We will match a specialist on the syllabus rather than the subject, run a free trial lesson as a diagnostic, and give you a written view of where the marks are going. If the answer is that no weekly tuition is needed, you will get that answer too. Everything here is one-to-one IB tuition in Jeddah or Cambridge IGCSE tuition in Jeddah, delivered online, Sunday to Thursday, pinned to Arabia Standard Time.

jubail.heroSubtitle: IB and IGCSE tutors for Jubail families work one-to-one over live video, on Arabia Standard Time, in slots that sit after the school run rather than across it. The industrial city's international-school set is small, so a student's subject combination is often decided by who the school can staff. This page explains what Jubail schools typically cover, where the gaps fall, what the market charges in SAR, and how a family chooses between an in-home tutor, a group class and online one-to-one teaching.

jubail.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach the Diploma Programme, the Middle Years Programme and Cambridge or Edexcel IGCSE to students across the Eastern Province. Each profile names the syllabus, the level and the papers that tutor prepares students for, so you can judge whether anyone genuinely knows your child's course before you book a trial lesson.

intro.heading: Deciding how to support a Jubail student, in the order the decision happens
paragraphs: The decision in front of a Jubail parent is rarely about tutoring in general. It is about one subject, one level and usually one paper. A student is coasting through Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level but cannot hold the Higher Level algebra their chosen engineering course expects. A Cambridge IGCSE candidate is comfortable with Core-tier questions and loses most of the available marks on Extended-tier Paper 4. A DP2 student has a scientific investigation due and a teacher carrying two year groups at once. Each of those is a different purchase, and the right answer differs for each.

What makes Jubail distinctive is the size of the pool. This is an industrial city, built around the petrochemical complex, with an expatriate school population serving Jubail Industrial City and the surrounding districts. The number of adults living within a short drive who have taught Mathematics AA at Higher Level, or who have marked Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 Paper 4, is small. In Riyadh a parent can usually find somebody. Here the search often ends with a generalist who is willing rather than a specialist who is qualified, and the two are not the same purchase at all.

There are four realistic options and they are worth laying out plainly. The school's own support comes first and costs nothing: a subject teacher's clinic, a revision session, a departmental past-paper evening. A private tutor who drives to the house is the familiar option, priced in the Eastern Province at the top of the general tuition band because travel time is built into the hour. A group class at a centre is cheaper per head because the hour is shared, which also means the pace is set by the middle of the room. Online one-to-one teaching removes distance from the problem entirely and widens the pool to anyone who teaches the course.

IB Gram sits in the fourth column. Lessons for families in the Kingdom are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video, and that is the whole of the offer. IB Gram does not send a tutor to an address in Jubail; home visits are a service we run only in India. The argument for online IB tutoring in the Eastern Province is not convenience. It is selection: a Jubail family gets the Physics HL teacher who knows where the HL-only topics bite, instead of whoever happens to live twenty minutes away and once taught the subject at Standard Level.

The rest of this page is built to help you make that choice rather than to sell it. There is a table of what local schools typically staff and what they typically do not, a side-by-side comparison of the four options, the SAR rates various providers advertise with the source type attached, a clock table for tutors in other countries, and a plain account of what a tutor may and may not touch on assessed coursework. If you finish reading and decide the school's own clinic is enough this term, that is a sound decision and it is free.

jubail.programmesIntro: Jubail students arrive from several curricula at once: the Diploma Programme, the Middle Years Programme, Cambridge and Edexcel IGCSE, and in some households a national-curriculum or Indian-curriculum school. The four programmes below are the ones tutoring requests cluster around, with a note on how each behaves in a city where the local cohort for any one course is small.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The PYP is organised around transdisciplinary units of inquiry rather than discrete subjects, and the final year ends in the exhibition, a long collaborative inquiry the student presents. There are no external examinations. Support at this stage is almost always about reading fluency, number sense and the habit of recording thinking in writing, because those three are what the Middle Years Programme immediately starts assessing.
programmes.countryNote: Primary provision is the least scarce part of the Jubail market, and most families are well served by the school itself. Where tuition helps is a child moving in from a different system mid-year, who has the mathematics but not the written explanation the exhibition will ask for. One lesson a week for a term is usually the right size of intervention.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The MYP runs five years across eight subject groups, with every subject assessed against four criteria marked out of eight. The programme ends with the Personal Project, assessed on planning, applying skills and reflecting. Some schools enter students for MYP eAssessment, which combines on-screen examinations with ePortfolios for the MYP Certificate. The criteria, not the content, are what decide the grade.
programmes.countryNote: The common Jubail request at this stage is a student in MYP Year 4 or 5 whose school is small enough that one teacher covers two year groups in the same subject. The gap that shows up is criterion-matching: strong knowledge, weak Criterion D, because nobody has had the time to teach the difference between describing a result and evaluating a method.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus the core: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Higher Level courses carry more recommended teaching hours and extra assessed content. The Extended Essay and TOK are graded together on a matrix that can add up to three points to the total, and the Diploma itself has pass conditions beyond the point score. An IB Diploma tutor in Jubail is usually asked for by subject, not by programme.
programmes.countryNote: The Diploma is offered in the Eastern Province at a handful of schools, including ISG Jubail, and whether a particular Higher Level course runs depends on how many students chose it. A Jubail DP student with an unusual combination often ends up studying at least one subject with very little specialist contact time, which is precisely the case where outside teaching changes the grade.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses examined by written papers, with most sciences adding either a practical test or an alternative-to-practical paper. Cambridge Mathematics 0580 is tiered: the Core papers cap the available grades, the Extended papers open the top of the range. Sciences such as Chemistry 0620, Physics 0625 and Biology 0610 split the same way, and the tier a school enters a student for decides the ceiling before the candidate writes a word.
programmes.countryNote: British-curriculum schools in and around Jubail carry most of the IGCSE cohort, and a Cambridge IGCSE tutor in Jubail is most often wanted for the Extended tier in mathematics or a science. The tiering conversation matters locally: a student entered for Core because the class was mixed can find the grade they need is simply not available on that paper.

jubail.subjectsIntro: These are the Diploma Programme subjects Eastern Province families request most, with what each one actually assesses and where the marks tend to go missing. Levels are listed because a Higher Level course is not the Standard Level course with extra homework; it carries its own content and, in several subjects, an extra paper.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: At Higher Level, Papers 1 and 2 carry thirty per cent each, Paper 3 twenty per cent and the exploration twenty. Paper 1 is sat without technology, which exposes algebraic fluency immediately. A Mathematics AA HL tutor for Jubail students usually starts with manipulation speed, then the Paper 3 extended problem, where marks come from structured reasoning rather than a remembered method.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The same paper structure as AA, with a graphic display calculator allowed throughout and a heavier statistical and modelling load. Standard Level is the common default class in a small cohort. Marks are most often lost in interpretation: a correct regression that is never explained in context, or a model whose limitations are never stated.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics, fields, waves and nuclear physics, with the Higher Level extension adding both depth and whole topics. The scientific investigation is internally assessed and worth twenty per cent at both levels. Higher Level Physics support in Jubail is requested more than any other science here, usually because one teacher is covering both levels in one room.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Structure and reactivity across quantitative chemistry, energetics, kinetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms, with twenty per cent of the grade from the internally assessed investigation. The reliable trouble spots are multi-step calculations where units are dropped, and organic mechanisms drawn without the curly arrows the mark scheme expects.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Concept-led content from molecular biology to ecology, examined in part through data-based questions on unfamiliar experiments. The internally assessed investigation carries twenty per cent. Strong students still lose marks here by writing everything they know instead of the three things a six-mark question is actually paying for.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Microeconomics, macroeconomics and the global economy, assessed by extended response, data response and, at Higher Level, a quantitative Paper 3 worth thirty per cent. The internal assessment is a set of commentaries built on published news articles. Diagram accuracy and explicit real-world application are where the marks sit.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Organisational structure, human resources, finance, marketing and operations, with a pre-released case study for one paper. Students usually know the tools and lose marks on evaluation: a SWOT that lists rather than judges, or a recommendation with no stated criteria. Finance calculations are the other recurring gap.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is a guided analysis of an unseen text and carries thirty-five per cent at both levels. Higher Level adds the HL essay on a studied work. The individual oral is internally assessed. The skill being examined is close reading under time pressure, which responds well to weekly timed practice and detailed marking.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Receptive, productive and interactive skills across five prescribed themes, with text types that must be used correctly: a blog is not a formal report. Many Jubail students are strong speakers and weaker writers, so the work is usually register, structure and the accuracy of less common tenses.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: System fundamentals, computer organisation, networks and the Higher Level extensions in abstract data structures and resource management, plus a developed solution as internal assessment. Rarely timetabled in a small school, so this is one of the subjects most often studied with almost no specialist contact time.

jubail.igcseSubjectsIntro: The IGCSE requests that reach us from Jubail cluster tightly around the Extended tier, where the top grades live and where the extended-response papers reward technique as much as recall. Syllabus codes are given because a tutor who cannot name the paper structure for a code has probably not taught it recently.

igcseSubjects.name: Mathematics 0580
igcseSubjects.description: Core candidates sit Papers 1 and 3 with a capped grade range; Extended candidates sit Papers 2 and 4 and can reach the top grades. Most tuition requests are Extended Paper 4, where multi-part questions need working set out so that method marks survive an arithmetic slip.

igcseSubjects.name: Chemistry 0620
igcseSubjects.description: Multiple-choice, theory and either a practical test or the alternative to practical. An IGCSE 0620 Chemistry tutor is usually asked for moles and stoichiometry first, then electrolysis and organic chemistry. The alternative-to-practical paper is its own skill: reading apparatus, spotting a variable, improving a method.

igcseSubjects.name: Physics 0625
igcseSubjects.description: Forces and motion, thermal physics, waves, electricity and atomic physics, with the same practical or alternative-to-practical split. The recurring loss is graph work and the wording of definitions, which the mark scheme treats strictly: a definition that is nearly right earns nothing.

igcseSubjects.name: Biology 0610
igcseSubjects.description: Characteristics of living organisms through to ecology and human influences on ecosystems. Extended candidates face longer structured questions on unfamiliar data. Command words decide the mark: a question asking students to suggest wants reasoning, not a recalled fact.

igcseSubjects.name: English as a Second Language 0510
igcseSubjects.description: Reading, writing and listening, with the speaking component assessed separately. The writing tasks are graded on content and language together, and students who read fluently often still lose marks by misreading the task's audience and purpose.

igcseSubjects.name: Economics 0455 and Business Studies 0450
igcseSubjects.description: Two courses commonly chosen together and commonly taught by one teacher. Both are examined by structured and extended questions where definitions must be precise and examples must be specific. Data-response questions reward reading the stimulus material carefully before writing anything.

jubail.regionsTitle: Where Jubail families live, and what that does to a lesson slot
jubail.regionsIntro: Jubail spreads from the old town and the port up the coast into the industrial city's residential districts, with a wider catchment that reaches Ras Tanura to the south and the Dammam cluster an hour further on. Where a family lives changes the school run, and the school run decides what time a lesson can realistically start.

regions.name: Al Fanateer
regions.note: A northern coastal district with Corniche frontage and a large share of the city's expatriate professional households. School runs head inland or south, so a five o'clock lesson is usually optimistic in term time and a seven o'clock start is the slot most families settle on.

regions.name: Al Deffi
regions.note: Established residential streets closer to the centre, mixed Saudi and expatriate. Shorter school runs than Al Fanateer, which makes an earlier evening slot workable for younger students who fade after dinner.

regions.name: Al Huwaylat
regions.note: Residential and newer in parts, with families spread across several schools rather than concentrated in one. That spread is why requests from here cover an unusually wide range of syllabuses, from Cambridge IGCSE to the Diploma Programme.

regions.name: Jubail Industrial City
regions.note: The planned industrial city with its own residential districts, services and schooling. Shift patterns at the complex shape household evenings more than traffic does: a parent who finishes at seven cannot supervise a six o'clock lesson, and the slot has to acknowledge that.

regions.name: Jubail Balad
regions.note: The old town and port area, denser and older than the industrial city's grid. Families here more often use national-curriculum or Indian-curriculum schools, and the tutoring requests that come from this area lean towards IGCSE rather than the Diploma.

regions.name: Mutrafiah
regions.note: A residential area with a mix of villas and apartments and several school options within a reasonable drive. Requests from here are often for a second subject added mid-term, once the first one has settled into a routine.

regions.name: Ras Tanura and the northern camps
regions.note: Company camp life gives an unusually structured week: facilities on site, short commutes, and a social calendar that fills the weekend. Families here often prefer two shorter weekday sessions to one long Thursday block.

regions.name: Qatif and Safwa
regions.note: South of Jubail on the coast road, with families who commute into either the Jubail or the Dammam school markets depending on where a place came up. The commute is the reason online slots are often set after seven o'clock.

regions.name: Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran
regions.note: About an hour down the coast and effectively one school and labour market, with the widest curriculum choice in the province. Jubail families who cannot get the subject combination they want locally often look here first, and then at online teaching when the commute proves unworkable.

schoolClusters.note: A small international-school set serving a largely expatriate population, alongside national-curriculum and Indian-curriculum schools. The Diploma Programme is offered at ISG Jubail. Whether a particular Higher Level course runs in any given intake depends on how many students chose it, so ask the school directly rather than assuming the prospectus list is the timetable.
schools: Royal Commission schools in Jubail Industrial City

schoolClusters.city: The Dammam, Al Khobar and Dhahran cluster
schoolClusters.note: An hour down the coast, this conurbation behaves as one school market: families routinely live in one city and attend school in another. The International Schools Group runs several campuses here, the Diploma Programme is offered at the American School of Dhahran, and the British-curriculum schools carry a large IGCSE cohort. Al Ahsa sits roughly an hour and a half further inland.

jubail.modesIntro: Three ways of working cover almost every request that reaches us from the Eastern Province. They differ in intensity and in what the student is expected to bring, and families often move between them across a year: weekly through the autumn term, intensive before a series, clinics when coursework deadlines land.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one, Sunday to Thursday
modes.description: One subject, one tutor, one fixed slot in the week, held for as long as the family wants it. Work is set between lessons and marked before the next one, so the hour is spent on what the marking found rather than on recapping the week. This is the default and the only mode that reliably changes technique, because technique changes through repetition and feedback.
bullets: A fixed weekly slot pinned to Arabia Standard Time
Written work marked between lessons, not during them
A short note to the parent after each session
Pause and resume around school holidays without losing the slot

modes.title: An intensive block before a series
modes.description: A compressed run of sessions in the weeks before examinations, built entirely around past papers under timed conditions. The content review is deliberately thin: by this point the gain is in question selection, timing and command-term discipline. Families usually buy two or three sessions a week for a fixed number of weeks rather than an open-ended arrangement.
bullets: Timed papers sat first, marked to the published scheme, then taught from
Per-paper timing plans, including what to do in the last ten minutes
A short list of topics to abandon when time runs out
Works best when the student has already covered the syllabus once

modes.title: Coursework clinics on the student's own draft
modes.description: Scheduled sessions around an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay or a Personal Project, where the tutor reads what the student has written and teaches against the published criteria. The student writes; the tutor explains which criterion a paragraph is failing and why. Nothing is drafted, rewritten or supplied for the student, and the school supervisor remains the person who signs the work off.
bullets: Feedback against criterion descriptors, not line edits
Research-question shaping before the writing starts
Method and data-handling review for science investigations
A record of what was discussed, so the school can see the trail

sections.heading: The choice a Jubail family is actually making
paragraphs: A search for IB and IGCSE tutors in Jubail is usually not a search for somebody nearby. It is a search for somebody who teaches the exact course a child is sitting. The practical question is not who lives closest; it is who knows the syllabus, who has marked the paper, and whether they are free at a time the student can still think. Distance is only a proxy for availability, and in a city this size it is a poor one.

Put the four options in order of cost and the shape of the decision becomes clearer. The school's own support is free and should be exhausted first: ask the subject teacher what the clinic covers and whether past papers are marked. A group class at a centre is the next cheapest and suits a student who needs structure rather than diagnosis. A private tutor who drives to the house costs the most per hour in this province, because travel time is priced into the rate whether anyone says so or not. Online one-to-one costs somewhere in between and buys the widest choice of teacher.

The honest recommendation depends on what is wrong. If a student has missed content, almost anything structured will help. If a student knows the content and still scores poorly, the fix is technique against a specific mark scheme, and that needs somebody who has taught or marked that paper. In Jubail the second case is where local supply runs out fastest, and it is the case where opening the search beyond the city changes the outcome rather than merely changing the invoice.
bullets: Exhaust the school's free support before buying anything
Missed content is a teaching problem; lost marks on known content is a technique problem
Travel time is priced into an in-home rate whether or not it is itemised
Ask any prospective tutor which paper they have marked, and when

sections.heading: What Jubail schools can staff, and what they usually cannot
paragraphs: Small cohorts drive almost everything about subject availability here. A school timetables a Higher Level course when enough students choose it, and drops or combines it when they do not. That produces a predictable pattern across the Eastern Province: the common courses run properly, the scarce ones run in a combined class, and a handful never appear on the timetable at all. None of this reflects badly on the schools. It is arithmetic.

The consequence for a family is that the subject a child needs for a university course may be the subject the school can least afford to staff with a specialist. Mathematics AA at Higher Level is the clearest example, because it is the course competitive engineering and economics applications most often expect and the one a small cohort is least likely to fill. Higher Level Physics support in Jubail is requested for the same reason: the course runs, but frequently with one teacher covering both levels in the same room and the Higher Level extension taught last and fastest.

The table below is a generalisation of what tutoring requests from this province look like, not a statement about any named school. Use it as a checklist of questions for an admissions meeting. Ask which Higher Level courses ran in the last intake, whether any were taught as a combined class, who teaches the scientific investigation, and what happens if a student is the only candidate for a subject. The answers tell you more about the next two years than any prospectus will.

sections.heading: Four ways to buy support, side by side
paragraphs: Comparisons in this market are usually made on the hourly rate alone, which hides most of what a family is actually buying. The variables that decide whether tuition works are who is available, how the pace is set, whether the slot survives a school trip, and what happens when a tutor has to be replaced. Those differ sharply between the four options and barely appear in anyone's advertising.

Two of them deserve a word of caution. A group class is good value when the group is genuinely at one level and a liability when it is not, because the pace follows the middle of the room and a student at either edge pays for an hour aimed at somebody else. An in-home tutor solves the supervision problem elegantly, which matters for younger students, but narrows the choice of teacher to the people who both know the syllabus and live near enough to drive. In Jubail that intersection can be empty for a scarce Higher Level subject.

Online one-to-one is the option this site sells, so read the comparison critically. Its real advantage is selection rather than price: the pool is everyone who teaches the course, so the match can be made on syllabus and paper experience instead of postcode. Its real cost is that a student has to be able to work on screen for an hour with a parent somewhere in the house, and a student who cannot do that yet is better served by something else this term.
