sections.heading: What the market charges in SAR, and what moves the number
paragraphs: Rates in the Kingdom are published inconsistently, and most of what a parent finds online is a provider's own advertised figure rather than a market average. That is worth saying plainly before any number appears. The table below collects the bands various provider types advertise, with the source type attached to each, so you can see which end of the range you are being quoted and why. None of these figures is an IB Gram price; ours is quoted for the specific subject, level and schedule after a trial lesson.

The variables that move a quote are stable across the market. Subject scarcity does the most work: a Mathematics AA HL or Physics HL specialist costs more than a Standard Level generalist everywhere, because fewer people can do it. Examiner or marking experience comes next, and is worth paying for when the problem is technique rather than content. Then level, with Higher Level above Standard Level, and both above Middle Years Programme and IGCSE work. Whether the tutor travels is a cost most in-home quotes absorb silently. Package length is the only one that usually moves the number downwards.

Two patterns are worth watching. A provider quoting in dollars is not charging more because the teaching is better; currency is not quality, and the exchange rate is not a credential. And a rate at the very bottom of the band is usually buying availability rather than expertise, which is fine for a student who needs supervised practice and poor value for one who needs a specific paper diagnosed. Ask what the figure includes: marking between lessons, past papers, a written report.

sections.heading: The Sunday to Thursday week against a tutor in another country
paragraphs: The school week in the Kingdom runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. Most tutoring copy on the internet is written for a Monday to Friday week and quietly assumes a Saturday morning session is available. For a Jubail family that assumption is wrong twice over: Thursday evening is the start of the weekend, and Sunday morning is a school day. Sunday to Thursday lesson slots are therefore the default here, with the weekend used for longer intensive work when a series is close.

The second fact is Arabia Standard Time, UTC+3, with no daylight saving anywhere in the Kingdom. A tutor in India is two and a half hours ahead; one in Pakistan is two hours ahead; one in the United Kingdom is three hours behind in their winter and two in their summer. That last difference is the one that catches families out. A slot agreed in a tutor's winter moves by an hour when their clocks change unless it has been pinned to Saudi local time from the start. Arabia Standard Time lesson times should be written into the arrangement, not inferred.

Household rhythm then decides the rest. In the industrial city, a parent's shift pattern matters more than traffic: if the working day ends at seven, a six o'clock lesson has nobody in the house to notice it is not happening. Ramadan shortens school days and shifts study into the evening, so lessons usually move later for that period and then move back. The long summer break is the one window where a student can work in the morning, which makes it the natural time for catch-up on a subject that went badly.

sections.heading: The first month: diagnosis, a plan, and the evidence you should see
paragraphs: A good first month produces evidence, not reassurance. It starts with a free trial lesson in which the tutor opens the syllabus and the student's most recent marked work and finds out what is actually wrong. That is a different activity from teaching, and a tutor who spends the trial lecturing has not done it. By the end of the hour you should have heard a specific diagnosis: not that your child needs to work harder, but that they are losing marks on Paper 2 structured questions because they answer the command term they expected rather than the one printed.

The diagnostic session that follows uses past-paper evidence rather than conversation. One timed section, marked to the published scheme, tells you more than a term of general impressions. The output is a written plan: the topics to teach, the papers to practise, the order, and what the parent is responsible for. The plan should name the thing that will be different in four weeks and how it will be visible. A plan nobody can check is a plan nobody can be held to.

From there the shape is weekly: teach, set work, mark the work, teach from the marking. Reports should be short and specific, naming the paper, the topic and the error pattern rather than offering an adjective. At the end of the first month, ask one question: has the error pattern named in week one changed? If it has not, something in the plan is wrong, and a tutor who cannot say what should be replaced. Changing tutor after three lessons is a normal event, not a failure, and is far cheaper than a term spent hoping.
bullets: Trial lesson: a diagnosis you can repeat back in one sentence
A timed past-paper section marked to the published scheme in week one
A written plan naming what changes in four weeks and how you will see it
A week-four review against the error pattern identified at the start

sections.heading: Where marks go missing once the content is known
paragraphs: The most common profile in a tutoring request from this province is a student who knows the material and is not being paid for it. The gap is almost always in the mark scheme rather than the textbook. Command terms are the clearest case: describe, explain, analyse, evaluate and justify ask for structurally different answers, and an examiner marking against a scheme pays only for the one that was asked. A student who writes a beautiful description for an evaluate question has not misunderstood the topic. They have answered a different question.

The second pattern is answer length and shape. A six-mark question usually wants a small number of distinct, developed points, not everything the student can recall. In the sciences, data-based questions on unfamiliar experiments reward reading the axes and the uncertainty before writing. In mathematics, method marks survive an arithmetic slip only if the method is visible on the page, which is why working set out in full is worth real marks to a student who makes careless errors under time pressure.

Grade boundaries and predicted grades are the third place families lose confidence unnecessarily. Boundaries are set after each session against the demand of that paper, so the raw mark needed for a grade moves a little from one session to the next. A predicted grade is a school's professional judgement of what a student is on course to achieve, made for university applications; it is not a result and no tutor can change it. The useful work around a predicted grade for a Jubail DP2 student is making the next piece of evidence better than the last one.
bullets: Command terms decide the mark more often than content does
A six-mark answer wants distinct developed points, not volume
Visible working protects method marks when arithmetic goes wrong
Grade boundaries move by session; a predicted grade is a judgement, not a promise

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do with an IA, an Extended Essay or a Personal Project
paragraphs: This is the part of the market that needs saying out loud, because several providers in these search results are quietly selling something else. A tutor may teach the criteria, explain what a descriptor means, read a draft the student wrote and say which criterion it is failing, suggest reading, challenge a research question that cannot be answered in the word count, and teach the statistics or the referencing conventions a student has not met. That is teaching, and it is useful.

A tutor may not write, redraft or supply any part of assessed work. They do not produce the Internal Assessment, the Extended Essay, the Theory of Knowledge essay or the Personal Project, and they do not provide text for a student to paste. Line-editing a draft into shape is the same offence wearing a tidier jacket. The school supervisor signs the work as the student's own, the student signs an authenticity declaration, and a school that suspects malpractice is obliged to investigate it. The consequences land on the candidate, not on the tutor.

The practical form this takes is a record. Internal Assessment feedback for a Jubail student is given against the published criteria, in writing, in a form the school can see: this paragraph addresses the criterion weakly, here is why, go and fix it. Word and page limits are worth knowing in advance, because they are enforced: the Extended Essay runs to four thousand words, the Theory of Knowledge essay to sixteen hundred, a science investigation to three thousand, a mathematics exploration to around twelve to twenty pages. Work beyond a limit is simply not read.
bullets: A tutor teaches the criteria and reviews the student's own draft
No part of assessed work is ever written or redrafted by a tutor
Feedback is written against criterion descriptors, so the trail is visible

sections.heading: After school: equivalency, Qudurat and Tahsili for a Jubail leaver
paragraphs: Families planning for a Saudi university need to know about a step that almost nothing in this search result set mentions. An international school certificate, whether an IB Diploma, A Levels or an American high school diploma, needs an equivalency decision from the Ministry of Education before a Saudi university treats it as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. That process is administrative and it takes time, so it belongs in the final-year plan rather than in the panic after results. Some universities also set a limit on how old a secondary certificate can be when it is submitted.

Two national tests then sit alongside school grades. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, is run by the Education and Training Evaluation Commission through its National Center for Assessment, Qiyas, and tests verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content. It can be sat in Arabic or English. Tahsili, the Achievement Test, covers the science-stream subjects: mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English. Its content follows the Saudi national curriculum.

That last sentence is the one international-curriculum families need. An IB or IGCSE student has usually met most of the Tahsili material, but framed differently, sequenced differently and examined in a style they have never practised. The overlap is real and the framing is not, which is why strong Diploma candidates sometimes find Tahsili harder than their own examinations. Preparation is therefore a separate piece of work from Diploma teaching, and it starts with past papers in the test's own format. Universities publish their own admission criteria combining school grades with these tests, and weightings differ by university and by programme, so check the institution's own published requirements rather than a third-party summary.
bullets: Equivalency from the Ministry of Education is a separate step with its own timeline
Qudurat tests reasoning; Tahsili tests national-curriculum subject content
Tahsili preparation is distinct from Diploma teaching and needs its own practice

process.title: A free trial lesson, with the syllabus open
process.description: You tell us the subject, the level, the syllabus code and what the last report said. The tutor spends the trial lesson on the student's most recent marked work rather than on introductions, and ends with a specific statement of what is going wrong. Nothing is paid before that conversation has happened.

process.title: A diagnostic built on past-paper evidence
process.description: The first full session usually includes a timed section of a past paper, marked against the published scheme. That produces an error pattern instead of an impression: the topics that are missing, the command terms that are misread, the questions abandoned for want of time.

process.title: A written plan, with the parent's part named
process.description: The plan names the topics to teach, the papers to practise, the order and the date of the first review. It also says what the family is responsible for: the slot being protected, the work being attempted before the lesson, the school being told that outside support is in place.

process.title: Weekly teaching, with marking between lessons
process.description: The fixed slot runs Sunday to Thursday on Arabia Standard Time. Work set after a lesson is marked before the next one, so the hour is spent on what the marking found. A short note goes to the parent after each session, naming the paper and the error pattern rather than offering adjectives.

process.title: A review at the end of the term, and an honest answer
process.description: At the review we compare the current evidence with the error pattern identified in week one. If it has moved, we say what to do next. If it has not, we say what should change, including stopping or changing tutor. A term of hoping is more expensive than a difficult conversation.

whyPoints.title: Matched by syllabus, not by distance
whyPoints.description: The tutor is chosen because they teach that course and know that paper, not because they can reach a Jubail address by seven o'clock. In a city where the specialist pool is small, that is the difference between a willing generalist and somebody who can name where the marks go missing in Paper 3.

whyPoints.title: Pinned to Saudi local time
whyPoints.description: Slots are written in Arabia Standard Time and held there. When a tutor's own country changes its clocks, the lesson does not move. The week is built around Sunday to Thursday, with the weekend kept for longer work in the run-up to a series.

whyPoints.title: Straight about coursework
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach the criteria and give written feedback on work the student has written. No Internal Assessment, Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge essay or Personal Project is drafted or redrafted for a candidate. That line is not negotiable, and knowing exactly where it sits protects the student's result.

whyPoints.title: Rates explained before anything is booked
whyPoints.description: You are told what a subject and level costs, what moves the figure, and what is included: marking between lessons, past papers, the written note after each session. Advertised market bands are quoted on this page with their source type so you can see where any quote sits.

whyPoints.title: Continuity when the family moves
whyPoints.description: Eastern Province households relocate: along the coast, to Riyadh, or out of the Kingdom. An online arrangement survives that. The same tutor keeps the same student through a move, which matters most in the Diploma years, when losing a term to a handover is expensive.

faqs.question: What should a first diagnostic session cover for a Jubail student whose school cannot staff their Higher Level subject?
faqs.answer: It should establish how much of the course has actually been taught, which is the real question when a subject runs as a combined class. The tutor works through a recent topic test and a section of a past paper under timed conditions, then maps what is missing against the syllabus. The output is a teaching order, not a confidence rating: which topics have to be built from the beginning, which need only consolidation, and which can wait. Where a Higher Level extension has been taught quickly at the end of a unit, expect that to appear as the first priority.

faqs.question: How is a Jubail student's starting point measured when the school reports percentages instead of IB grades?
faqs.answer: Percentages from school assessments are not comparable to IB grades, because they reflect one teacher's paper rather than a moderated boundary. The starting point is therefore measured directly: a past-paper section sat under timed conditions and marked against the published mark scheme. That gives a raw mark, a profile of where marks were lost by question type, and something repeatable to measure against later. A school percentage is still useful context about effort and classwork, but it is not a baseline, and treating it as one tends to produce surprises at the first real examination.

faqs.question: What should a Jubail family expect in a tutor's written note after the first four weeks?
faqs.answer: Specifics, briefly. The note should name the papers covered, the topics taught, the error pattern identified at the start and whether it has moved. A sentence of the form: structured questions on energetics are now scoring the method marks, extended-response answers are still describing where they should be evaluating. It should also say what work was set, whether it arrived, and what the next four weeks will target. If the note could have been written about any student in the Kingdom, ask for a better one.

faqs.question: Our Jubail school runs two semesters while our tutor assumes three terms. How is the plan aligned?
faqs.answer: The plan follows your school's calendar, not a generic one. Ministry of Education schools run a two-semester year while most international and British-curriculum schools set their own three-term calendars, and in the same city two schools can have different holiday weeks. We work from the calendar your school publishes: internal examination dates, report dates, coursework deadlines and holidays all go into the plan at the start. The series date is then the fixed point everything counts backwards from, since that does not move with the school's choice of structure.

faqs.question: How late can an evening lesson start for a Jubail family when a parent's shift at the industrial complex finishes at seven?
faqs.answer: Later than most published timetables assume, and that is normal here. Sessions commonly start between seven and half past eight for secondary students, because somebody has to be in the house and awake while a teenager works. For younger students a late start rarely works, so the better answer is a weekend morning, since Friday and Saturday are the weekend in the Kingdom. The slot is agreed around the household's actual week, and a slot that fights the shift pattern gets quietly abandoned within a month.

faqs.question: Does a slot agreed with a tutor in the United Kingdom shift twice a year for a family in Jubail?
faqs.answer: It does unless the arrangement is written in Arabia Standard Time from the beginning. The Kingdom stays on UTC+3 all year with no daylight saving, while the United Kingdom moves its clocks twice. A lesson agreed in their winter will arrive an hour earlier or later in their summer if the booking lives in their time zone. Fix the slot in Saudi local time and the tutor absorbs the change at their end. This is the single most common scheduling problem with a tutor in a clock-changing country.

faqs.question: What happens to a weekly Jubail slot during the long summer break when the family travels?
faqs.answer: Most families either pause or move to mornings. The summer is long and the household is often out of the Kingdom for part of it, so the practical options are a clean pause with the slot reserved, or a lighter schedule in the student's local morning wherever they are, which suits catch-up work on a subject that went badly. Mornings are the only time of year a student is genuinely fresh, so a family rebuilding a weak foundation should use them rather than wait for the autumn term.

faqs.question: How do shortened school days during Ramadan change a Jubail student's weekly lesson pattern?
faqs.answer: School days shorten and the evening becomes the active part of the household's day, so lessons usually move later and sometimes shorten. A ninety-minute session often works better as two shorter ones in that period. Study patterns shift rather than stop, and the practical approach is to agree the revised timing before the month starts and to put heavier work either side of it. The period moves earlier against the Gregorian calendar each year, so it lands in a different part of the school year over time.

faqs.question: How much of a Diploma Programme science grade is decided by the internally assessed investigation?
faqs.answer: Twenty per cent, at both Higher and Standard Level, in biology, chemistry and physics. That is a fifth of the grade decided by work done over weeks rather than in an examination hall, which makes it the most controllable component of the course and the one most often left too late. It is marked against published criteria covering the research design, the data analysis and the conclusion and evaluation. A tutor can teach those criteria and comment on a draft the student has written; the investigation itself has to be the candidate's own work.

faqs.question: How do command terms such as analyse and evaluate change the mark a Jubail student earns for the same content?
faqs.answer: They change it completely, because the mark scheme is written against the command term rather than the topic. Describe asks for an account, explain asks for reasons, analyse asks the student to break something into parts and show how they relate, and evaluate asks for a judgement supported by both sides. A student who explains when asked to evaluate can write a page of accurate material and score very little. The fix is mechanical and quick: identify the term, plan the shape of the answer it demands, then write.

faqs.question: Why do IB grade boundaries move from one session to the next, and what does that mean for a target grade?
faqs.answer: Boundaries are set after the papers are marked, so that a grade means the same standard of performance even when one session's paper proves harder or easier than the last. The raw mark needed for a grade therefore moves a little each session. For a family this means two things: a target expressed as a raw mark is unstable, so set the target as a grade, and the comparison that matters is your child's performance against the standard rather than against last session's arithmetic. Past-paper marks are still the best available evidence, read as a trend.

faqs.question: Who decides a predicted grade at a school in Jubail, and can a tutor change it?
faqs.answer: The school decides it. Subject teachers make a professional judgement about the grade a student is on course to achieve, usually from internal assessments, coursework and mock examinations, and that judgement goes to universities. A tutor has no role in setting it and should never offer to influence it. What outside teaching can do is improve the evidence the judgement rests on, which means the next mock, the next piece of coursework and the next timed paper. If you believe a prediction is wrong, the conversation belongs with the school and should be about evidence.

faqs.question: How does Paper 3 at Higher Level differ from the earlier papers for a Jubail DP2 student?
faqs.answer: Where a subject has one, Paper 3 generally rewards sustained reasoning on a single demanding problem or data set rather than coverage of the syllabus. In Mathematics at Higher Level it is worth twenty per cent and presents extended problem-solving, where marks accumulate through a structured chain of argument. In Economics at Higher Level it is quantitative. The practical consequence is that Paper 3 practice has to be done whole and timed, because the skill being examined is holding a long argument together under pressure, and short exercises never rehearse it.

faqs.question: What happens if the match between a Jubail student and the first tutor is not working after three lessons?
faqs.answer: Say so and change it. Three lessons is enough to know whether a student is talking, attempting the work set and following the explanation, and those three things predict almost everything that follows. A change of tutor is a normal event, not a complaint, and the new tutor starts from the diagnostic and plan already written rather than from nothing. What should not happen is waiting a term in the hope that it settles, which costs money and, in the Diploma years, costs time that cannot be recovered.

faqs.question: How is progress tracked across an autumn term for a Jubail student taking two subjects at once?
faqs.answer: Separately, with one shared calendar. Each subject keeps its own error pattern, its own teaching order and its own past-paper record, because progress in chemistry says nothing about progress in mathematics. What is shared is the week: two subjects in one evening rarely works for a secondary student, so the slots sit on different days, with coursework deadlines from both subjects on one calendar so that two drafts never land in the same week. The term review then reports both, side by side, against where each started.

jubail.closingHeading: Start with the free trial lesson, then decide
jubail.closingBody: The useful next step is small. Tell us the subject, the level, the syllabus code and what the most recent marked work showed, and we will put the student in front of a tutor who teaches that course for a free trial lesson. You will leave that hour with a specific statement of what is going wrong and what it would take to change it, which is worth having even if you then decide the school's own clinic is enough this term. Lessons for families in Jubail are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video, in a slot pinned to Arabia Standard Time and fitted around the Sunday to Thursday week.

intro.heading: Why an 'Asir family ends up looking outside the city
paragraphs: Khamis Mushait is the larger of the two 'Asir cities by population and sits roughly 25km from Abha, which means the two share one catchment and one small pool of international-curriculum teaching. A family here is rarely short of schools. What they are short of is a teacher who has taught the exact course their child is sitting and has read the mark scheme for the paper that is coming. That is a different problem from school choice, and driving further does not solve it. Between them the two cities hold a substantial school-age population and very few international-curriculum places, which is the whole reason remote specialist teaching matters more here than it does in Riyadh.

The geography is the second half of the problem. Khamis Mushait sits at around two thousand metres on the 'Asir plateau, with Abha a little higher again, and the escarpment drops away west towards the Tihama plain. Families are spread across that terrain: some in the city centre, some out towards Ahad Rafidah or Sarat Abidah, some an hour or more down the mountain road at Muhayil, some north along the ridge at Tanomah or Al Namas. The 'Asir school run is therefore not one journey but a dozen different ones, and the length of that journey is what decides the hour at which a lesson can realistically start.

So the choice in front of you is narrower than it looks. You can hire a local tutor who travels to the house, and pay for the drive in both money and dead time. You can put the child back in the car and drive to a tuition centre in Abha on a school night. You can take a small group class and accept a fixed hour and a shared teacher. Or you can teach the gap one-to-one over live video and stop paying for distance altogether. Each option has a real cost; this page lays all four out in a table rather than asserting one of them.

IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform. We match a student to a subject specialist and deliver the teaching online, one-to-one, over live video, on a slot fixed to Arabia Standard Time. We do not arrange a tutor at a Khamis Mushait address, and in-home visiting is a service we offer only in India. That is stated plainly because the alternative is to let a parent assume otherwise, and because the honest argument for online teaching in 'Asir is strong enough without it: your child gets a Physics HL specialist rather than whoever already lives within a half-hour drive.

What follows is the detail a parent actually needs: what the school run does to a workable lesson window, what the market charges and why, how the Sunday-to-Thursday week and a tutor's own working week have to be reconciled, how the examination series is counted backwards, what a small school genuinely cannot staff, and what Ministry of Education equivalency, Qudurat and Tahsili will ask of your child at the end of all this. None of it is a pitch. All of it is checkable, and where a figure cannot be checked, this page says so.

khamis-mushait.programmesIntro: Four International Baccalaureate programmes run in the Kingdom, and a family in 'Asir may meet them in any order: a child entering the Primary Years Programme after a relocation, a sibling finishing the Middle Years Programme, a Diploma student arriving mid-course. Each programme is assessed differently, and the kind of help that works in one is the wrong help in another.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The Primary Years Programme is transdisciplinary and inquiry-led. There are no external examinations; the final year ends in the PYP exhibition, a collaborative piece of work the student presents. Assessment is continuous and teacher-led against learning outcomes rather than against papers. For a parent, that makes progress harder to read than a mark out of a hundred, and it makes the mechanical skills underneath the inquiry easy to miss: number bonds, written methods, reading fluency, handwriting stamina and the habit of explaining a method in a sentence.
programmes.countryNote: In 'Asir the practical issue is continuity. A family posted into the region part-way through a primary year often finds the child has met a topic in a different sequence and is being assessed on an inquiry that assumes earlier work. Short, specific online sessions on arithmetic fluency and written explanation close that gap faster than general homework help, and they can run from Khamis Mushait on a weekday evening without a drive at either end.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The Middle Years Programme assesses every subject against four criteria, each marked out of eight, and those criterion marks are converted to a one-to-seven grade using published boundaries. The final year carries the Personal Project, assessed on investigating, planning, taking action and reflecting. Some schools enter students for MYP eAssessment, which combines on-screen examinations with ePortfolios. The common failure is a student who knows the content but has never been taught to write to a criterion descriptor, and who therefore keeps landing in the middle band.
programmes.countryNote: An MYP tutor in Khamis Mushait is usually asked for one of two reasons: a Personal Project that has stalled at the planning stage, or a criterion-based report that a parent cannot interpret. Both are tractable online. The project work is coaching on process and reflection, never on content a student has to generate themselves, and the criterion work is simply teaching a student to read the descriptor they are being marked against before they start writing.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The Diploma is six subjects, normally three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus the core: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Subject grades run from one to seven, and Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay together contribute up to three further points through the published matrix, for a maximum of forty-five. Twenty-four points is the minimum for the award, subject to the failing conditions. Most Saudi IB schools sit the May session.
programmes.countryNote: A Diploma Programme tutor in Abha or Khamis Mushait is most often needed for a Higher Level science or Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches, because those are the courses a small school finds hardest to staff with a specialist. The second common request is Internal Assessment supervision support, where the school supervisor is stretched across several subjects. Both run well over live video, with the student sharing their own working on screen.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme pairs at least two Diploma Programme subjects with a career-related study, plus a core of personal and professional skills, service learning, language development and a reflective project. It is far less common in the Kingdom than the full Diploma, and families meet it mainly where a school offers it alongside the Diploma for students who want a vocational strand. The Diploma subjects inside it are assessed exactly as they are in the full Diploma, with the same papers and the same Internal Assessment.
programmes.countryNote: If a student in 'Asir is on a Career-related Programme, the subject teaching they need is identical to a Diploma student's, which matters because it widens the pool of tutors who can genuinely help. The part that needs different handling is the reflective project, which is assessed on the student's own reasoning. Support there is questioning and feedback on their drafts, and that is where it stops.

khamis-mushait.subjectsIntro: These are the Diploma subjects families in 'Asir ask about most, with what each actually assesses and where marks tend to go missing. A tutor who can recite the syllabus is not the same as one who knows which command term is costing your child two marks a question, and the difference shows up in the first diagnostic session.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: At Higher Level this is Paper 1 and Paper 2 at thirty per cent each, Paper 3 at twenty, and the Exploration at twenty. Paper 3 is two long problem-solving questions with scaffolding, and it is where students who have only ever practised short routine questions come apart. A Mathematics AA HL tutor spends most of the early sessions on proof, on calculus technique and on reading a multi-part stem properly.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The Standard Level course is Paper 1 and Paper 2 at forty per cent each plus a twenty per cent Exploration. It is calculator-heavy and modelling-led, and the marks lost are usually about interpretation rather than algebra: a correct regression with no sentence saying what it means in context scores less than the student expects. Statistics and the graphical display calculator are the two things worth drilling.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Under the current guide Physics is Paper 1 at thirty-six per cent, Paper 2 at forty-four, and the Scientific Investigation at twenty. Paper 1B is data-based and catches students who have never been taught to handle uncertainties properly. The HL-only extensions are the second pinch point, because a school that teaches HL and SL in the same room often leaves them to the end of the course.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Same assessment pattern as Physics: Paper 1 at thirty-six per cent, Paper 2 at forty-four, Scientific Investigation at twenty. Marks go missing in energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms, and in the data booklet skills nobody formally teaches. A Chemistry HL tutor usually starts by having the student work a past Paper 2 question aloud, because the gap is almost always in how the answer is set out rather than in what is known.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Biology rewards precision of language more than any other science. The same paper weightings apply, and the extended-response questions are marked against specific terminology, so a student who writes a good general account of a process can still score two out of six. Command terms matter here more than content volume, and the Scientific Investigation needs a question narrow enough to be answered with the apparatus a school actually has.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is unseen textual analysis and Paper 2 is a comparative essay on studied works, with an Individual Oral and, at Higher Level, an HL essay. The usual problem is not reading ability but the absence of a repeatable method for the unseen paper. Students who are strong in a tutorial and weak under timed conditions almost always need a structure they trust rather than more texts.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: English B assesses receptive, productive and interactive skills, with a listening component, a reading component, a written assignment and an individual oral. Students in international schools in the Kingdom often sit it alongside strong classroom English and still lose marks on register and text type, because the paper asks for a blog, a letter or a speech and marks the conventions of that form as well as the language.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: Arabic A is studied as a literature or language-and-literature course with the same structure as English A, while Arabic B is a language acquisition course. For a bilingual student in 'Asir the decision between them has real consequences for the Diploma total and for how an application reads later, and it is worth taking advice on before the choice is locked in during the first Diploma year.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Economics is examined through short-response and extended-response papers plus a data-response paper at Higher Level, with a portfolio of commentaries assessed internally. The marks lost are almost entirely in diagram work and in evaluation: a diagram drawn without axes labelled correctly loses marks it did not need to, and an essay that explains without weighing caps itself in the middle band.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The papers are case-study based, with a pre-released case for one of them, and the Internal Assessment differs between Higher and Standard Level. Students treat it as a content subject and then meet a paper that rewards applying tools to the specific firm in front of them. A tutor's first job is usually to stop the student writing textbook definitions into an applied answer.

khamis-mushait.igcseSubjectsIntro: Most families in 'Asir meet IGCSE before they meet the Diploma, through either Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel. The syllabus codes matter: a tutor who knows Cambridge 0620 inside out is not automatically the right tutor for Edexcel 4CH1, and the tiering decision made in Year 10 sets the ceiling on the grade available in Year 11.

igcseSubjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580)
igcseSubjects.description: The Core tier caps the available grade, and the Extended tier assumes algebraic fluency that a student who has drifted through Year 9 does not have. An IGCSE maths tutor should be asked, in the trial lesson, which tier they would enter the student for and why. The answer tells you whether they know the paper or only the subject.

igcseSubjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE International Mathematics (0607)
igcseSubjects.description: Often chosen by schools heading towards the Diploma, because its graphical-calculator work and investigation component sit closer to what Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches expects. The Extended papers include a graphics-calculator paper, so calculator technique is examined rather than assumed, and that is a teachable skill rather than a talent.

igcseSubjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Physics (0625) and Chemistry (0620)
igcseSubjects.description: Both run a multiple-choice paper, a theory paper and a practical component that is either a laboratory examination or the alternative-to-practical paper. The alternative-to-practical is where a Cambridge IGCSE tutor earns their fee, because it tests experimental reasoning on paper and almost nobody practises it until the term before the series.

igcseSubjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610)
igcseSubjects.description: Content-heavy and marked on exact terminology. The Extended theory paper asks for processes in sequence, and a student who understands the biology but writes it loosely loses marks steadily across the paper. Past-paper work with the mark scheme open is the fastest correction, and it works perfectly well on a shared screen.

igcseSubjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE English (0500 and 0510)
igcseSubjects.description: First Language English is reading and directed writing with a composition paper; Second Language is a different qualification with its own structure, and some schools in the Kingdom enter students for the wrong one. The directed-writing task rewards reading the audience and purpose in the question before writing a word, which is the single most coachable thing on the paper.

igcseSubjects.name: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE Mathematics A (4MA1) and the sciences
igcseSubjects.description: Edexcel tiers Mathematics A as Foundation and Higher, and runs the separate sciences as 4PH1, 4CH1 and 4BI1 with no practical examination, assessing experimental skills inside the written papers instead. A family moving between a Cambridge and an Edexcel school mid-course needs this difference explained before the entry is made, not after.

khamis-mushait.regionsTitle: The 'Asir catchment, and what the drive does to a lesson slot
khamis-mushait.regionsIntro: Khamis Mushait and Abha share a school catchment, and families commute into it from across the province and from down the escarpment. The notes below are about travel and timing rather than about property, because the length of your school run is the single fact that decides which lesson slots are actually available to you.

regions.name: Khamis Mushait city centre
regions.note: The shortest run in the catchment. Families here can usually hold a mid-afternoon slot, which is the most sought-after hour because a tutor in India or the United Kingdom is still inside their own working day. It also means a second subject can run later the same evening without the child losing a meal.

regions.name: Abha
regions.note: About 25km away and a little higher on the plateau, Abha is the provincial capital and holds part of the international-curriculum provision the two cities share. The drive is short in theory and unpredictable in practice at school-closing time, which is why Abha families often find early evening more reliable than mid-afternoon.

regions.name: Ahad Rafidah
regions.note: South-east of Khamis Mushait and close enough that the school run is routine rather than a journey. The practical consequence is a late-afternoon slot that holds all term, and enough margin to reschedule a single lesson into the same week rather than losing it.

regions.name: Sarat Abidah
regions.note: Further south along the plateau, with a run of around three quarters of an hour each way in normal conditions. Families here tend to settle on one fixed early-evening slot per subject and resist moving it, because a reschedule has to survive two journeys as well as a tutor's calendar.

regions.name: Muhayil
regions.note: Down the escarpment towards the Tihama plain, which makes the journey a mountain descent rather than a commute. Over an hour each way is normal, and that pushes lessons into the evening or into a Friday or Saturday block. It is the clearest case in the province for teaching over video rather than over a road.

regions.name: Tanomah
regions.note: North along the 'Asir escarpment, well outside the daily reach of the Khamis Mushait and Abha schools. Families here either board, relocate for term time or accept a long drive, and in all three situations the subject teaching a student is missing has to come from outside the province.

regions.name: Al Namas
regions.note: Further north again on the high ground, with the same arithmetic as Tanomah and a longer road. An online slot on a fixed evening is often the only form of specialist teaching a family here can sustain across a full Diploma year without rearranging the household around it.

regions.name: Bisha
regions.note: North-east of the escarpment on the drier side of the province, in a different driving world from the mountain towns. Distance here is the constraint rather than terrain, and the honest position is that no in-home specialist pool exists at this range; the teaching has to arrive over a connection.

schoolClusters.note: Where 'Asir families most often transfer in from or out to, and where several of the Kingdom's Diploma Programme schools are concentrated. A student moving between a Riyadh school and an 'Asir one mid-course usually arrives with a different subject sequence and a half-finished Internal Assessment, which is a specific catch-up job rather than general support.

The nearest large concentration of international-curriculum places to 'Asir, and the usual destination for a family that decides relocation is cheaper than commuting. Schools here run Cambridge, IB and other national curricula side by side, so a transferring student's board can change at the same time as their city.

The Eastern Province cluster behaves as one school and labour market, and families posted there from 'Asir meet a very different picture: several campuses within a short drive and a Diploma available at more than one. It is the clearest contrast to the 'Asir position, where the same subject may exist at a single school.

khamis-mushait.modesIntro: Four ways of working cover almost every request from 'Asir. The right one depends on how many subjects are weak, how far away the examination series is and how much of the week the school run has already taken. All four are delivered one-to-one over live video on a slot fixed to Arabia Standard Time.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one on a fixed slot
modes.description: The default and the one that works for most families: one subject, one tutor, the same hour every week, held across the term. Progress is cumulative and the tutor sees the same student often enough to know what has actually stuck. For a family in Muhayil or Sarat Abidah this is also the only arrangement that survives a long school run without being cancelled every third week.
bullets: One named tutor for the subject, not a rota
The slot is pinned to Saudi local time, so a tutor's own clock change does not move it
Work set between lessons and marked before the next one
A short written note to the parent after each session

modes.title: Two subjects on the same evening
modes.description: A Diploma student carrying two weak Higher Level subjects often cannot find two separate evenings once the school run is counted. Two shorter back-to-back sessions with different specialists solves that, at the cost of concentration in the second hour. It is worth doing for a term, not for a year, and it works better earlier in the course than in the final weeks.
bullets: Different specialist for each subject, back to back
Shorter sessions than a single-subject evening, by design
Suited to the autumn term rather than the run-up to a series

modes.title: An intensive block before a series
modes.description: A concentrated run of sessions in the weeks before the June or November series, built around past papers under timed conditions rather than around content. It is the right tool for exam technique and the wrong tool for a syllabus gap, because content learned under that kind of pressure rarely holds. Two subjects at most, and only when the content is broadly in place.

modes.title: Internal Assessment and coursework feedback cycles
modes.description: Short, spaced sessions around a draft the student has already written, where the tutor asks questions, points at the criterion the work is being marked against, and hands the writing back. This is deliberately not a drafting service. A tutor who offers to produce the piece is offering academic malpractice, and a school that detects it has to report it.

A record of what was discussed, so authorship stays provable
No writing, redrafting or supplying of text by the tutor

sections.heading: The choice an 'Asir family is actually making
paragraphs: Before any of the detail, name the decision. A parent in Khamis Mushait looking for an IB tutor or an IGCSE tutor is choosing between four things, not browsing a market. The first is a local tutor who travels to the house. The second is driving the child to a tuition centre, almost always in Abha. The third is a small group class, which is the cheapest per head and the least adaptable. The fourth is one-to-one teaching over live video, which removes the journey from both sides of the arrangement.

Each of those has a genuine case. The local tutor who comes to the house is the easiest to supervise and the easiest to trust, because you can see them. The centre in Abha has structure, other students and a teacher who is accountable to someone. The group class is affordable and gives a student peers to measure against. Online one-to-one gives you a specialist you could not otherwise reach, and gives back the hour the car would have taken. Nothing on this page argues that three of those four are worthless.

What this page does argue is that in 'Asir specifically the constraint is supply, not preference. The number of people within reach of Khamis Mushait who have taught Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, or marked Cambridge 0620 Extended papers, is small. That is not a criticism of the province; it is what a small international-curriculum population produces anywhere in the world. Once supply is the binding constraint, the question stops being how a lesson is delivered and becomes who is delivering it.

So the recommendation at the end of this page is already visible at the start of it: match on subject and level first, then work out the logistics. The next three sections put numbers against that, starting with the one most families underestimate, which is what the school run has already taken out of the evening before any tutor is involved.

sections.heading: What the school run does to the hours a lesson can occupy
paragraphs: The school week in the Kingdom runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. That alone rules out the pattern most imported tutoring copy assumes. On top of it sits the specific geography of the 'Asir catchment: the schools are concentrated in a band between Khamis Mushait and Abha, and families commute into that band from across the plateau and from down the escarpment.

The arithmetic is simple and unforgiving. A child who leaves school at the usual hour and has a ten-minute run home can be sitting at a desk by mid-afternoon, which is the most valuable slot on the board because a tutor in India or the United Kingdom is still inside their own working day. A child with an hour-long descent from Muhayil cannot. That family's realistic window starts in the evening, and the evening is also when a tutor in Europe is finishing and a tutor in East Asia has gone to bed.

The table below is deliberately approximate. Driving times in 'Asir move with weather on the escarpment, with roadworks and with the hour, and your own run is the only one that matters. Use it to work out which column you are in, then ask for a slot that fits that column rather than asking for the one everyone wants. A slot you can keep every week beats a better slot you cancel twice a month, and the cancelled lesson is the real cost of over-reaching on timing.

One more practical point. Because Saudi Arabia does not change its clocks, a slot agreed in Saudi local time stays where it is all year. A slot agreed in the tutor's local time will move twice a year, in opposite directions, and will land on top of your school run at some point. Always agree the hour in Arabia Standard Time and let the tutor's calendar absorb the shift.

sections.heading: Four ways to buy tutoring in 'Asir, side by side
paragraphs: Comparing these four honestly means comparing them on the things that actually differ, which are cost, dead time and the size of the pool you are choosing from. Quality is not a column, because a good tutor and a poor one exist in all four formats and no table can tell you which you are being offered.

The in-home option carries a cost most families only notice in the second month. A tutor who drives to a house in Khamis Mushait from Abha is spending an hour on the road for an hour of teaching, and that hour is priced into the rate whether or not it is itemised. The same drive makes a cancellation expensive for both sides, which is why in-home arrangements tend to be the first to collapse when a school trip or a family journey lands on the slot. Published rates for senior-subject private tuition in the Kingdom start at around SAR 200 an hour before any travel loading is added, according to tutor-marketplace guides.

The centre option trades the tutor's drive for yours. Rates per hour are usually lower, because a centre fills a room, and the structure suits a student who works better out of the house. Against that, you are driving the 25km to Abha on a school night, twice, and the staff a centre can retain in a city of this size is the pool you are choosing from. The group class is cheaper again and the least adaptable: one start time, one pace, and one teacher holding several syllabuses at once.

Online one-to-one removes travel from both sides and removes geography from the selection. That is the real argument, and it is worth stating without decoration: a family in Bisha and a family in Khamis Mushait city centre are choosing from the same set of Physics HL specialists. What online does not give you is the thing you can see in your own living room, which is why the trial lesson exists and why a parent should sit in on the first one.

sections.heading: What tutoring costs in this market, and what moves the number
paragraphs: Every figure in the table below is an advertised rate published by a tutoring platform, a tutor marketplace or a tutoring company. None of them is a market average, none is verified against what families actually pay, and none is what IB Gram charges. They are published here because the Saudi tutoring market usually hides rates behind a contact form, and a parent comparing options deserves a band to argue from.

What moves the number, in rough order of weight, is subject scarcity, marking experience, level, whether the tutor travels and how long the commitment is. Subject scarcity does most of the work. A Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches Higher Level specialist or a Physics Higher Level specialist costs more than a Mathematics Standard Level tutor in every market in the world, because the supply of people who can teach the Paper 3 extension material is genuinely smaller. A parent who asks why one subject is quoted higher than another is usually being told the truth.

Marking experience is the second lever and the one most worth paying for, with a caveat. A tutor who has marked the paper your child is sitting knows how the mark scheme is applied rather than how it reads, and that is a different kind of knowledge. The caveat is that the claim is easy to make and hard to check, so ask which board, which paper and which component, and ask what the most common avoidable error on it is. A vague answer to that question is the answer.

The levers that are not worth paying for are also worth naming. A longer package does not improve teaching; it improves cash flow for the provider. A rate that rises as the June series approaches is pricing scarcity, not quality. And a cheaper non-specialist is sometimes exactly right, for a Middle Years Programme student who needs study habits rather than Higher Level content, or for arithmetic fluency in a primary year. Paying specialist rates for general help is the commonest way families waste money here.

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week at two thousand metres
paragraphs: Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not observe daylight saving. Those two facts together are the most useful scheduling information on this page, because they mean a Saudi slot is stable and everyone else's is not. A tutor in the United Kingdom or in continental Europe moves twice a year; a tutor in India and a tutor in South Africa do not. Pin the hour to Saudi local time at the start and the problem disappears for good.

The week itself is the other half. Sunday is a school day and Thursday evening is the start of the weekend, which makes Thursday the worst evening of the week for a lesson and Sunday through Wednesday the best. Friday and Saturday sessions are perfectly workable and are often the right answer for families out at Muhayil or Bisha, where a weekday evening slot competes with a long drive. They are harder to staff, because a tutor in a Monday-to-Friday country is working then, so ask early.

The altitude matters less than families expect and the seasons matter more. 'Asir is cooler and wetter than most of the Kingdom, and the escarpment roads are genuinely affected by weather in a way that the Riyadh ring road is not. A lesson plan that assumes the child will always be home by a fixed hour will break a few times a term. Online lessons absorb that better than a tutor who has already set out, which is a small practical argument rather than a large one.

Ramadan shifts earlier against the Gregorian calendar each year, so it drifts across the academic year rather than sitting in one term. School days shorten and household routines change, and the sensible response is to agree a different slot for that period in advance rather than cancelling and losing the tutor. Many families move to a later evening session and keep the frequency; some drop to one subject. Both work. Deciding in the week it starts does not.

sections.heading: The examination series, counted backwards
paragraphs: Almost every rival page in this market describes the academic year forwards, from the start of term, which is the least useful direction. A family making a decision about tutoring is working backwards from a series, and the questions that matter are how long is left, what is already locked in, and what can still be changed.

Two calendars run in parallel in the same city, which confuses relocating families constantly. Ministry of Education schools run a two-semester year that begins in late August and ends in late June, with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid break. International and British-curriculum schools set their own calendars and most run three terms, and term dates differ school by school inside Khamis Mushait and Abha. Never plan from a published calendar you found online; plan from your own school's.

For Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel candidates in the Kingdom there are two series, June and November. June is the main one. November carries resits and November-entry candidates. Cambridge also runs a February and March series, and that series is available in India only, which matters because a great deal of tutoring copy aimed at Gulf families is adapted from Indian pages and quotes those dates. A Saudi family acting on that information would miss their actual entry window.

The table below is written without a single year in it, deliberately. Entry deadlines, study-leave dates and results days move, and your school's examinations officer holds the real ones. Ask for them in writing at the start of the final year, because the two decisions that depend on them, whether to enter for a tier and whether to resit, both have hard cut-offs that nobody will chase you about. For IB candidates, the May session is the one almost every Saudi IB school sits, and the Diploma Programme coordinator is the person who confirms what that means for your child.
