sections.heading: What a small school cannot staff, and why that is the real problem
paragraphs: Private and international schools in the Kingdom are licensed by the Ministry of Education, and school evaluation and accreditation runs through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, which operates e-services for national school accreditation and for the approval of international accreditation bodies. Those are real and useful facts, and they tell you nothing about whether a particular school can staff Physics at Higher Level this term. Licensing is about the institution. Staffing is about one person leaving.

That gap is the honest reason most 'Asir families end up looking outside the province. In a city with a small international-curriculum population, a subject at Higher Level may be taught by one person. If that person leaves, the school covers the class with a non-specialist, teaches it in combination with the Standard Level group, or in the hardest cases cannot offer it at all. None of that appears in an inspection report, and all of it lands on a Diploma student in the same term.

The subjects it happens to are predictable. Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, Physics at Higher Level, Chemistry at Higher Level, Computer Science and the less common language A options are the ones that go first, because the pool of teachers who can deliver them is smallest everywhere. The ones that are usually fine are the large-entry Standard Level courses and the humanities, where a strong generalist teacher genuinely can carry the class.

This is also what to ask a school before enrolling, and the question is more specific than most parents make it. Not whether the school offers the Diploma, but which Higher Level subjects ran last term, how many students were in each, and whether Higher and Standard Level are taught in the same room. The answers predict where your child will need outside teaching far better than any ranking does, and a school that answers them straight is telling you something good about itself.

sections.heading: Equivalency, Qudurat and Tahsili: the part nobody writes about
paragraphs: If your child may apply to a Saudi university, there is a process ahead of them that almost no tutoring page in this market describes. A foreign or international school certificate needs an equivalency decision, mu'adalah, from the Ministry of Education before a Saudi university treats it as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. That applies to the IB Diploma, to A Levels and to an American high school diploma alike. It is administrative rather than academic, and it is the step families discover late.

Alongside it sit the Qiyas tests, run by the National Center for Assessment under the Education and Training Evaluation Commission. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, assesses verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, and can be sat in Arabic or in English. Tahsili, the Achievement Test, covers the science-stream subjects: mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English. The important thing about Tahsili is where its content comes from, which is the Saudi national curriculum.

That single fact explains why international-curriculum students often find Tahsili harder than their own examinations. The material overlaps substantially with what a Diploma or IGCSE student has studied, but the framing does not. Topic order differs, terminology differs, the expected method for a question differs, and the test does not reward the extended reasoning an IB paper is built around. A strong Chemistry Higher Level student can sit Tahsili and be surprised, and the surprise is about format rather than ability.

Universities publish their own admission criteria combining school results with the Qiyas tests, and the weightings differ by university and by programme, with competitive engineering, medicine and science programmes leaning hardest on Tahsili. Some universities also state a maximum age for the certificate they will accept. No number on any of that appears on this page, because third-party sites disagree with each other and a parent acting on a wrong figure loses a year. Read the criteria on the university's own site, and start the equivalency paperwork earlier than feels necessary.

sections.heading: Academic honesty on the Internal Assessment, the Extended Essay and the Personal Project
paragraphs: This section exists because several providers visible in this market will do the opposite of what it describes. The rule is simple and it is not negotiable: assessed work must be the student's own. A tutor may teach the skills the task needs, explain the criteria it is marked against, ask questions about a draft the student has written, and hand it back for the student to change. No tutor on this platform will write the Extended Essay, redraft an Internal Assessment or produce a Personal Project for a student.

In practice the line is clearer than parents fear. Choosing a research question is a conversation, and a good tutor will push a student towards a question that is actually answerable with the apparatus and the word count available, which is legitimate supervision. Explaining what an uncertainty analysis is, or what the difference between describing and evaluating looks like in a mark scheme, is teaching. Supplying a paragraph, correcting the prose of an assessed piece line by line, or handing back a restructured draft is not, and a school that detects it must report it.

The mechanics matter too. Keep the student's own drafts, dated, in their own files. If a tutor gives feedback, let it be feedback the student then acts on themselves, in their own words, in their own sitting. That record is what protects a student if authorship is ever questioned, and it is worth maintaining even when nobody expects a problem. Plagiarism detection software catches copied text; it does not catch work written by someone else, which is exactly why schools interview students about their own work.

For Middle Years Programme families the same logic covers the Personal Project, which is assessed on investigating, planning, taking action and reflecting, all of which are things only the student can do. A tutor who helps with a Personal Project should be visibly making the student work harder rather than making the product look better, and if what comes back is suddenly polished and the student cannot explain it, that is the warning sign to act on.

sections.heading: Starting, and what happens when no specialist is free
paragraphs: The honest version of getting started is shorter than most providers make it. You tell us the board, the subject, the level and the series the student is working towards, and roughly what the problem looks like. We propose a specialist. There is a free trial lesson, which is a real diagnostic session rather than a sales call, and a parent is welcome to sit in on it. If the match is wrong, you say so and we change it; nobody should be arguing about a tutor in the fourth week.

The part worth being straight about is scarcity. Sometimes the specialist a student needs is not free at the hour an 'Asir family can actually use. A Physics Higher Level tutor with marking experience, available at a late-afternoon Saudi slot, is a narrow intersection, and in the term before a series it narrows further. When that happens there are three honest answers: wait for the slot, take a different hour including a Friday or Saturday, or start with a strong generalist on technique while the specialist slot opens. What we will not do is put a student with someone who does not know the paper and call it a match.

What happens in the first month is also worth setting out, because it is where most of the value sits. The first session diagnoses: a past-paper question worked aloud, with the tutor watching how the student sets an answer out rather than whether they get it right. The second and third build a short plan with two or three specific targets, not a syllabus sweep. By the end of the first month a parent should be able to name what their child is now doing differently, and if they cannot, something is wrong with the arrangement rather than with the child.

Reporting is deliberately plain. A short note after each session saying what was covered and what was set, and a fuller view at the end of a term with a view on whether to continue. A tutor who reports only good news is not reporting. If the right recommendation after a term is to stop, or to drop to one subject, or to move a Higher Level subject to Standard Level before the entry is made, a parent should hear it from the tutor rather than work it out from a results sheet.

process.title: Tell us the board, subject, level and series
process.description: Cambridge or Edexcel, Diploma or Middle Years Programme, Higher or Standard Level, and which series the student is working towards. A syllabus code helps more than a year group does. This is also the point to say what your school run looks like, because that decides which slots are genuinely available to you.

process.title: We propose a specialist, not a department
process.description: You are matched to one named tutor for one subject and level, with their relevant teaching and marking experience described specifically enough to check. If two subjects are weak, that is two tutors. A single person offered for Chemistry Higher Level and English A is a staffing convenience rather than a match.

process.title: A free trial lesson, with the parent welcome to sit in
process.description: A working diagnostic session rather than an introduction. The tutor sets a past-paper question and watches how the student approaches it. You should come out of it knowing what the tutor thinks the problem is and roughly how long they think it takes to fix. If you do not, say so.

process.title: Fix the slot in Arabia Standard Time
process.description: The hour is agreed in Saudi local time, which means a tutor's own clock change does not move it twice a year. Families beyond daily commuting range often take a Friday or Saturday block instead of a weekday evening, and that is worth asking for early because it is harder to staff.

process.title: Two or three targets, then weekly work
process.description: A short plan with specific, checkable targets rather than a sweep of the syllabus. Work is set between sessions and marked before the next one, and a short note goes to the parent after each lesson saying what was covered and what was set.

process.title: Review at the end of the term, honestly
process.description: A fuller view on what has moved, what has not, and whether to continue. If the right answer is to stop, to drop to a single subject or to move a subject to Standard Level before entries close, you should hear it here rather than infer it later from a results sheet.

whyPoints.title: Matched on syllabus, not on driving distance
whyPoints.description: The binding constraint in 'Asir is how few people within reach have taught the specific course and read the specific mark scheme. Removing the drive from the arrangement removes that constraint, which is the whole argument. A family in Bisha chooses from the same specialists as a family in Khamis Mushait city centre.

whyPoints.title: Rates quoted with their source, never as a market average
whyPoints.description: Every SAR figure on this page is an advertised rate published by a platform, a marketplace or a tutoring company, and is labelled as such. None is a verified market average and none is our price. The Saudi tutoring market usually hides rates behind a contact form, and that is not helpful to a parent comparing options.

whyPoints.title: A slot that survives the year
whyPoints.description: Arabia Standard Time does not shift, so an hour agreed in Saudi local time stays where it is. Tutors in countries that change their clocks absorb the difference instead of the family rearranging a school night twice a year. Ramadan arrangements are agreed in advance rather than in the week it begins.

whyPoints.title: Assessed work stays the student's own
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches the skill, explains the criteria and gives feedback on a draft the student has written. No writing, no redrafting, no supplying of text. That is a genuine difference from several providers in this market, and it is the difference between help and a malpractice report.

whyPoints.title: No claim we cannot evidence
whyPoints.description: No success rates, no star ratings, no tutor headcounts, no regulator approval. IB Gram holds no accreditation from the Ministry of Education, the Education and Training Evaluation Commission, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and says so rather than implying otherwise. There is no office in the Kingdom either.

whyPoints.title: The whole of the 'Asir picture, including the parts that do not suit us
whyPoints.description: A local tutor you can see in your own home has real advantages, a centre in Abha has structure, and a group class is cheaper. Those are stated on this page because a parent weighing four options deserves the case for all four, and because the online argument in this province does not need help.

faqs.question: Does a family in Khamis Mushait pay more for a tutor than a family in Riyadh does?
faqs.answer: For online one-to-one teaching, no, because the rate reflects the tutor's subject and experience rather than the student's address. For in-home teaching the picture reverses: a smaller local pool means less competition on price, and a tutor covering the Abha to Khamis Mushait run prices that time in. Published rates for senior-subject private tuition in the Kingdom start around SAR 200 an hour according to tutor-marketplace guides, before travel. The practical consequence is that geography costs an 'Asir family money in the in-home market and costs nothing in the online one.

faqs.question: What does the free trial lesson cover for a Khamis Mushait student, and who sits in on it?
faqs.answer: It is a diagnostic session, not an introduction. The tutor sets a past-paper question from the student's own board and level, then watches how they set an answer out, where they stop, and which command term they misread. A parent is welcome to sit in, and on a first lesson it is usually a good idea. By the end you should be able to repeat back what the tutor thinks the problem is and roughly how long fixing it takes. No payment is taken before that session, and no commitment follows from it.

faqs.question: Why does a Physics HL slot cost more than a Mathematics AI SL one on the same evening?
faqs.answer: Scarcity. The number of people who can teach the Higher Level Physics extension material and explain how its Paper 2 mark scheme is actually applied is far smaller than the number who can teach Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation at Standard Level, in the Kingdom and everywhere else. Level and marking experience add to it, but supply does most of the work. A provider who quotes one flat rate across all subjects and levels is either averaging or is not matching on specialism, and both are worth asking about directly.

faqs.question: Is a small group class with other Khamis Mushait students ever better value than one-to-one?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth being honest about when. A group works for shared content revision at Standard Level or IGCSE, where several students are weak on the same topics and benefit from seeing each other's working. It works badly for a Higher Level student with a specific diagnosable gap, and badly for Internal Assessment work, because the feedback has to be about one piece of writing. The other consideration in 'Asir is timing: a group has one fixed hour, and a family with a long school run cannot move it.

faqs.question: How does an advertised SAR rate change once a tutor has to drive from Abha to Khamis Mushait?
faqs.answer: The drive is paid for either way, so look for it. Some tutors add an explicit travel charge, some quote a higher hourly rate for out-of-city work, and some quote the same figure and then limit themselves to two-hour minimum sessions to make the journey worth it. All three are reasonable; none is free. Ask the question plainly before the first lesson, and ask what happens to the fee if a lesson is cancelled on the day, because a drive already made is a cost someone absorbs.

faqs.question: Can we pause a weekly slot during the long summer break without losing the tutor to someone else?
faqs.answer: Ask before the break, not during it. A regular slot is the tutor's income, and a slot left empty for two months is a slot they will fill. Families who want to hold an hour across the summer usually either keep a reduced frequency, one session a fortnight, or agree the return date in writing before the break starts. Families who stop entirely should expect to be rematched, which is not a disaster but does mean losing the continuity that made the arrangement work in the first place.

faqs.question: What is Ministry of Education equivalency, and when should a Khamis Mushait family start it?
faqs.answer: Equivalency, mu'adalah, is the Ministry of Education decision that treats a foreign or international school certificate as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. A Saudi university needs it before it will consider an IB Diploma, A Levels or an American high school diploma. It is paperwork rather than an examination, and the sensible time to find out exactly what your child's school and certificate require is early in the final school year, not after results. Your school office will usually have done it before for a student with the same certificate.

faqs.question: Why do 'Asir students sitting the Diploma often find Tahsili harder than their own papers?
faqs.answer: Because Tahsili's content follows the Saudi national curriculum, while a Diploma student has spent two years inside a different framing of the same material. The mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English overlap substantially, but topic order, terminology and the expected method differ, and Tahsili does not reward the extended reasoning an IB paper is built around. A strong Chemistry Higher Level student can be caught out by format rather than by difficulty. Preparation is therefore mostly translation work, and it should start well before the final term.

faqs.question: Does Qudurat test anything my child has actually been taught in the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Not directly. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, is run by the National Center for Assessment and tests verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, and it can be sat in Arabic or in English. A Diploma student will recognise the quantitative reasoning as familiar in kind but not in presentation, and the verbal section is a different exercise from anything in an English A paper. The useful preparation is familiarity with the question types and the pacing, which is practice rather than teaching.

faqs.question: Can a student in Khamis Mushait apply to a Saudi university and an overseas one in the same cycle?
faqs.answer: Yes, and many do, but the two processes ask for different things on different timetables. An overseas application usually wants predicted grades, a reference and a personal statement during the final year. A Saudi application wants the equivalency decision, the Qiyas test results and the certificate itself. The practical risk is that the Saudi paperwork is treated as the fallback and started late. Run both from the beginning of the final year and read each university's own published criteria rather than a summary of them.

faqs.question: What does my child need at home in Khamis Mushait to make an online lesson work?
faqs.answer: A laptop rather than a phone, a connection that holds a video call, headphones, and a flat surface where they can write with the camera seeing both their face and their page if the tutor asks. A tablet with a stylus is useful for mathematics and the sciences because the student can write naturally on a shared whiteboard, but it is not required. The one thing that matters more than the hardware is a door that closes, because a Diploma session with a television audible behind it loses a third of its value.

faqs.question: How does a tutor show working on a graph or a titration calculation over video?
faqs.answer: On a shared whiteboard, with both people able to write on it. In practice the tutor writes less than parents expect: the better pattern is the student working on the shared board while the tutor questions each line, because a tutor's neat solution teaches far less than a student's corrected one. Diagrams, graphs and past-paper extracts are pasted onto the board and annotated live. For a titration or a mechanism, the student is usually asked to set it out from scratch and then explain each step aloud.

faqs.question: Are lessons recorded, and can a parent in another room see what was covered?
faqs.answer: Recording is arranged with the family rather than assumed, and where a recording exists it is for the student's revision. The whiteboard from a session can be saved and sent, which is often more useful than a video because it is the working rather than the conversation. A short written note after each session says what was covered, what was set and what the tutor wants done before the next one, and that note is the thing a parent should actually read.

faqs.question: What happens to a lesson if the connection drops in the middle of a past paper?
faqs.answer: Tutors are expected to rejoin and continue, and a short outage costs a few minutes rather than a session. Where a connection fails properly, the lesson is rescheduled and not charged, and the whiteboard up to that point is saved so nothing is repeated from the start. Two practical habits help in 'Asir: have a phone hotspot available as a fallback, and agree in advance what counts as a lost lesson rather than discussing it for the first time while it is happening.

faqs.question: How does a tutor in another country hand back marked written work between lessons?
faqs.answer: The student photographs or scans the work and uploads it, and the tutor annotates it and returns it before the next session, usually with the relevant mark scheme attached so the student can see where the marks sat. For Internal Assessment drafts the annotation is questions and references to criteria rather than corrections to the prose, because the writing has to stay the student's own. The turnaround should be agreed up front; work handed back an hour before the next lesson is not feedback.

khamis-mushait.closingHeading: Start with the subject, then solve the drive
khamis-mushait.closingBody: If you are looking for IB and IGCSE tutors in Khamis Mushait, the decision that matters is which specialist your child needs, not how far away they live. Tell us the board, the subject, the level and the series, and say what your school run does to your evenings. We will propose one named tutor, run a free trial lesson you are welcome to sit in on, and fix the slot in Arabia Standard Time so it holds all year. Lessons are one-to-one and online. If the specialist you need is not free at an hour you can use, we will say so rather than offer you someone who does not know the paper.
